Will all-out war in Yemen reignite as the Houthis escalate attacks?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:27:52 UTC
00:27:52 KST

Will all-out war in Yemen reignite as the Houthis escalate attacks?
Analysts say Saudi Arabia is strengthening its position with regional allies as the Houthis escalate their attacks.
A series of Houthi attacks in recent weeks, which are among the deadliest in years, is raising fears that Yemen could be sliding back towards all-out war as conflict spreads across the Middle East.
A 2022 truce led to the end of heavy fighting between the pro-Iranian Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, which had been ongoing since September 2014.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Japan protests as Russia’s Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands
- list 2 of 4What postcolonialism looks like in Southeast Asia
- list 3 of 4Life and loss as a first responder in southern Lebanon
- list 4 of 4Triple-double king Russell Westbrook announces NBA retirement
But a series of clashes over the last month between the two sides – intensifying in the last two weeks – has led to civilian and military casualties and threatened to reignite the war.
Here is what we know.
What are the latest attacks?
The Houthis have killed a number of civilians in a series of attacks on the government-controlled west coast port of al-Makha, also known as Mocha.
There was also an attack on a commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, which Yemen’s coastguard said killed six people and injured 10 others. The Houthis said the vessel was carrying weapons.
It followed the Houthis targeting Yemeni government military sites in eastern Yemen with drones and rockets, killing at least 30 government soldiers and causing further clashes. The Houthis have also attacked Saudi Aramco’s Jazan oil refinery.
In response, Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), said the internationally -recognised government would not accept “a new truce that reproduces previous experiences”.
“No action by the Houthi militias will go unanswered or unchecked,” al-Alimi said, according to Yemen’s Saba news agency.
But he also appeared to leave space for a political way back, saying the Houthis could still “lay down their arms, engage in political life and compete through the ballot box on an equal footing with all other Yemenis”.
What is behind the latest tensions?
The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and have since fought a war with the government for control of the country.
Although the intensity of the war declined significantly after the 2022 truce, no comprehensive peace settlement followed.
The fragile status quo came under increasing pressure after the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran on February 28 .
On July 13 , Yemeni government forces – which are backed by Saudi Arabia – attacked Sanaa airport, reportedly to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The government accuses Iran of arming the Houthis.
The rebel movement responded by launching missiles towards Saudi Arabia. Then, on July 20 , the Houthis announced a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia, threatening oil shipments diverted towards the Red Sea and attacking Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu.
Is Saudi Arabia changing its approach?
As the attacks have intensified, Saudi Arabia has begun to take a more proactive approach to its security – both in Yemen and across the region, according to experts.
Some analysts believe the prospect of the Houthis ultimately blocking Bab al-Mandeb – the narrow strait connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean – may have helped push the Saudis to change their strategy.
Saudi Arabia was somewhat insulated from Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz because it could use its East-West Pipeline to transport oil from fields in the east to the Red Sea, bypassing the strait.
If the Houthis were to severely restrict shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, that would threaten the Red Sea route for one of the world’s largest oil exporters.
Last month, Riyadh announced a new international alliance intended to protect shipping in the Red Sea from Houthi attacks. Dozens of countries were invited, with the kingdom saying 13 had agreed to participate.
It is also deepening its security relationships with Pakistan and Turkiye through a new joint defence agreement, while Saudi coordination with Washington also appears to be strengthening.
The Saudi Defence Minister, Khalid bin Salman, recently met US Vice President JD Vance amid reports that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had secured US support for potential military action against the Houthis.
But in Yemen, the shift in the Saudi position may have been more visible when the Saudis intervened against the United Arab Emirates-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) at the end of last year. That allowed Yemen’s fractious anti-Houthi coalition to coalesce around the Yemeni government and present a more united front against the rebels.
Simon Mabon, professor of international relations at Lancaster University in the UK, said Saudi policy on the issue has changed significantly.
“After years of attempting to de-escalate and work towards an accommodation with the Houthis, Riyadh appears to have concluded that approach is no longer viable,” Mabon told Al Jazeera.
“Saudi Arabia’s concern has become particularly acute because conflict around the Strait of Hormuz has increased the importance of alternative oil and shipping routes through the Red Sea.”
But rather than trying to totally defeat the Houthis and retake the capital Sanaa, Mabon said Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government now appear to be focused on pushing Houthi forces away from the coast.
“That’s a marked shift from what we had been seeing previously,” he said.
Could Pakistan and Turkiye be drawn into the war?
The Saudi-Pakistan-Turkiye agreement potentially raises the stakes of any further Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said the latest attacks were being interpreted by some experts as a direct defiance of the new defence pact.
Pakistan has been directly affected by the recent escalation. Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said three Pakistanis were killed and another person injured in a Houthi attack on a vessel in the Red Sea.
“Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel,” Dar said, adding that the government was in contact with Saudi and Yemeni authorities.
But experts say the defence pact does not mean that Pakistani or Turkish troops will join the war in Yemen on behalf of their ally.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the agreement so -far is “just ink on paper”.
What role is Iran playing?
Iran has long cultivated a so-called “axis of resistance” of governments and groups opposed to Israel and the United States, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, armed groups in Iraq and Syria and the Houthis in Yemen.
The Houthis supported Iran towards the end of March by launching attacks towards northern Israel and have since threatened to expand their operations in the Red Sea.
Last month, Iran reportedly asked the Houthis to prepare to close the Red Sea oil route if the US attacked Iranian power infrastructure.
A source close to the Houthis told Reuters that missiles and drones had been positioned near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in Yemen’s highlands overlooking Hodeidah and the Gulf of Aden.
Mohammed Albasha, a Yemeni American analyst and former spokesperson for Yemen’s embassy in Washington, said the Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia should therefore also be understood within the broader US-Iran confrontation.
“By threatening Saudi shipping there, the Houthis can increase pressure on both Riyadh and Washington, while supporting Iran in its wider confrontation with the United States,” Albasha said.
Is another all-out war imminent?
Analysts say the crucial question is whether the latest attacks are intended to pressure the Saudi and Yemeni governments, or whether the Houthis believe they are simply taking the initiative in a new potential ground war.
The Houthis also say Saudi Arabia is using the port of al-Makah to reinforce and resupply government forces and believe Riyadh and its Yemeni allies are preparing an offensive against Houthi-held territory.
Nadwa Al-Dawsari, Associate Fellow at the Middle East Institute, said those fears may be fuelling the current escalation.
“Since January, there has been significant progress towards bringing Yemen’s different government forces under a more unified command,” Al-Dawsari told Al Jazeera.
“Government forces have also demonstrated growing air capabilities, carrying out air and drone strikes against Houthi missile and drone launchers and other military sites.”
“The Houthis’ objective in this recent escalation is to disrupt these preparations before government forces are ready, degrade their capabilities and force them onto the defensive.”
Ultimately, she said, the Houthis are trying to shape the rules of any coming confrontation so that “if escalation takes place, it happens on their own terms”.
While a Saudi-led ground offensive is not inevitable, the Houthis have also shown over the past decade that they cannot be defeated by air power alone, Mabon said.
“Yemen’s mountainous terrain makes a ground campaign exceptionally difficult, while Riyadh has little appetite to become trapped again in a prolonged war,” he said.
A Saudi-backed offensive led by Yemeni government forces is still more plausible than a large Saudi ground deployment, he added.
The consequences of major fighting on the ground between the two sides will inevitably mean that civilians will suffer most.
“Amidst all of this, the tragedy is that people in Yemen are paying the price,” Mabon said.
“It wasn’t long ago that Yemen was facing one of the worst humanitarian crises since the Second World War. People are struggling, and continued fighting will make it far worse.”

Iran can fight on for years to defeat US – senior IRGC commander
Iran can stay in the fight in a prolonged armed conflict with the US, even if it lasts the rest of Donald Trump’s term in office, a senior Iranian general has said.
Brig. Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) voiced confidence in Tehran’s ability to sustain a long-term confrontation during an interview with PBS on Tuesday. His remarks came amid media reports of pressure on US munitions stockpiles and declining morale among American forces deployed in the Middle East.
Tehran’s objective is “to attain deterrence so that the enemy never dares to attack us, so we can live with security,” Naqdi told the US broadcaster when asked whether Iranian commanders intended to “drag out” the conflict until Trump was no longer in office.
“One way is to prolong this war until we get to the next term of the presidency and cause attrition, so that if anyone else wants to attack Iran, they will know there is a cost,” he said.
Trump launched a 40-day bombing campaign against Iran in late February. Despite the loss of senior officials, the government in Tehran retained control of the country and responded with attacks on US military facilities in the region, while also exerting economic pressure on Washington’s allies and global markets.
The conflict has become increasingly unpopular among US voters, raising concerns among Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump has alternated between threats of further military escalation and claims that Iran has been weakened to the point of almost accepting a peace agreement favorable to Washington. On Wednesday, he claimed that the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, imposed in April, had been widely described as a “wall of steel” and that Tehran “has no money.”
“The longer this war lasts, the more experience we gain,” Naqdi told PBS. “We had never seen a real war to gain real experience to learn how to fight with America. In these five months, we have learned how. We have also seen how the American military is weaker than what we perceived.”
Naqdi also claimed that Iran is producing drones and missiles at a faster rate than it is expending them and could continue fighting for years.
Should those stockpiles eventually be exhausted, he added, Tehran could instead target what he described as “thousands of [American] economic interests throughout the world.”

Hong Kong public rental housing wait edges up to 4.8 years, urban allocations rise
Despite increase in ‘composite’ figure, Housing Bureau says average wait for standard public rental home fell by 0.1 years to 5.5 years
The composite waiting time for general applicants for long- and short-term subsidised public rental housing in Hong Kong has edged up slightly to 4.8 years at the end of June, authorities have said, adding that a higher proportion of coveted homes in urban areas was allocated in the second quarter.
Despite an increase in the “composite” figure, which includes temporary flats under the light public housing initiative, the Housing Bureau said on Thursday that the average waiting time for general applicants – families or single elderly people – to be housed in a standard public rental home in the past 12 months dropped by 0.1 years to 5.5 years, compared with the first quarter.
The average waiting time for single elderly applicants remained at 3.9 years.
The bureau said the short-term fluctuations in the average waiting time reflected a “positive sign” because applicants who had waited longer for a home in urban areas were allocated one.
“[It proves] that we are effectively tackling the long-standing backlog of waiting cases and laying the foundation for significant improvements in the future. In the long run, the average waiting time for public rental housing will clearly trend in a positive direction,” the bureau said.
The data showed that about 3,200 general applicants, including 330 single senior residents, were housed in standard public rental homes between April and June.
As of the end of June, 100,500 general applications from families and single elderly people were waiting for a standard public rental home.

‘Since it’s written, it has to be done’: Law minister's delimitation push comes with Constitution jibe at Opp
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 13, 2026, 20:55 IST
Comments

Meghwal on delimitation and opposition
NEW DELHI: Union law minister Arjun Ram Meghwal on Thursday said delimitation is a “constitutional mandate” and asserted that the exercise must be carried out after 2026, as provided under the Constitution.Speaking in ANI , Meghwal criticised the Opposition over its objections to delimitation, saying that while opposition leaders “carry the Constitution around with them”, they do not read its provisions.“Delimitation is a constitutional mandate. They certainly carry the Constitution around with them, but they don't actually read what is written in it,” Meghwal said.
He said the Constitution provides for the freezing of Lok Sabha seats until 2026, after which delimitation must take place.“Seats are to remain frozen until 2026, after which delimitation must take place. Since it is written there, it has to be done,” the Union minister said.The concerns are particularly among southern states, that a population-based redistribution could reduce their relative representation.
What is delimitation?
Delimitation is the process of redrawing the boundaries of Lok Sabha and state assembly constituencies based on population.
Under Article 82 of the Constitution, the exercise is to be carried out after every census.The aim is to ensure that constituencies have broadly similar population sizes, although their geographical areas can vary significantly. Each state is allocated a certain number of seats in Parliament and its assembly based on the population figures used for delimitation.
India carried out delimitation exercises in 1952, 1962 and 1972. However, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976 froze the number of Lok Sabha seats based on the 1971 Census, in part to ensure that states that had successfully implemented population-control measures were not penalised with fewer parliamentary seats.The 84th Constitutional Amendment in 2001 extended the freeze on the allocation of seats among states until after 2026.A delimitation exercise was undertaken in 2008, but it used the 1971 Census to retain the existing distribution of Lok Sabha seats among states. It primarily involved redrawing constituency boundaries.

A British firm starts containment of oil spill from stricken tanker off Oman

A British firm starts containment of oil spill from stricken tanker off Oman
BEIRUT (AP) — A British company said Thursday it has been hired to salvage a grounded Russian shadow fleet tanker off Oman’s coast and stop an oil spill that is threatening wildlife as it reaches the country’s shoreline following its dramatic spread in recent weeks.
Satellite images have shown that oil from the tanker Caroline Bezengi has exponentially spread over hundreds of square kilometers during stormy weather, endangering a marine protected area. The region’s “Khareef” monsoon season peaks in July and August.
Ambrey, a UK-based maritime risk and response company, said its personnel boarded the vessel with help from the Omani air force to assess its condition before stabilizing it.
The vessel has been grounded off Qabiliyah Island in southwestern Oman following an explosion of unclear cause in early June. Its cargo previously has been estimated at more than 800,000 barrels.
Satellite images also have shown that the tanker is increasingly submerged, and experts have warned of an unprecedented environmental disaster if the vessel sinks or breaks open and leaks its entire cargo.
“This is an extremely challenging situation, compounded by adverse weather conditions associated with the Khareef monsoon,” Ambrey’s global response director Ed Wollaston said in a statement. The company did not immediately have any estimates of how long the salvage operation would take or cost.
Oman’s Environment Authority said Wednesday the oil spill has reached the shores of Ras Madrakah, more than 200 kilometers (more than 120 miles) north of Qabiliyah Island. Authorities said they estimated the spill could reach more than 100 kilometers further north, to Masirah Island.
Hanen Keskes, a campaigner for the environmental group Greenpeace, said it is “extremely concerning” that the oil has spread from an offshore spill to the shoreline where it can contaminate coastal sediments.
“It can make the cleanup significantly more complex than containment at sea,” she said. “Even after the slick has been contained and removed, the environmental impact can last for years.”
The marine protected area of Qabiliyah Island includes coral reefs, seagrass meadows and endangered turtles, and offers breeding sites for migratory birds. The area is also home to the rare Arabian Sea humpback whale.
The remote area lacks infrastructure, making the salvage and containment more challenging and requiring more safety measures, Keskes said.
The 247-meter (899-foot) Caroline Bezengi is believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” and has been sanctioned by the British government and the European Union for carrying cargoes of Russian oil.
It had left the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, in Russia, in May, according to geospatial data tracking company SynMax Maritime. The vessel’s owners are believed to be Shanghai-based. The vessel is unflagged, and it is not clear if it is insured.
It is only one of the environmental crises affecting the region. Off the coast of Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian authorities are cleaning up an oil spill off of Qeshm Island that has been attributed to the conflict between Iran and the United States.
Images distributed by Iran’s semi-official news agency ISNA show oil damage to the sandy beaches of Qeshm. It is not immediately clear what caused the spill.
Iran has said it should receive compensation for its efforts to contain the damage. But maritime tracking firm TankerTrackers.com posted satellite images on X saying it appears the spill was caused by an Iranian attack on a bulk container ship off of Oman. The spill drifted across the strait to Iran.

We sat out by the green outside our house with a bunch of our neighbours, colanders and pizza boxes in hand! We felt the heat shift and our shadows lengthen in the reflection of the sun, reflected through our colander on to a pizza box! We saw crescent circles of light shifting on the cardboard as the moon moved across the sun – it looked like scales. My partner and I were really young in 1999, so this is the first eclipse we’ve seen IRL. I’m so glad we could share the colander silliness with each other and our community. Annayah, 31, lecturer, Bradford-on-Avon, Wiltshire
‘It was lovely to listen to children playing whilst taking in the atmosphere’
I’m a 41-year-old physics graduate who loves amateur astrophotography. I use my telescope in my back yard, but last night I took it to Brightlingsea, along with my dog. It’s one of the few west-facing beaches in the south-east. Lots of people made their way there. It was lovely to listen to children playing whilst taking in the atmosphere. All the kids were absolutely enjoying it. There was a very community feel on the beach. There was one child who didn’t have any glasses so I passed them mine and they said: “It just looks like the moon.”
Laura Ngo, 41, Essex
‘My sister called to say she had 10 pairs of glasses’
We went with my siblings, parents and my husband to watch the eclipse. It was my sister who got the glasses because I thought we weren’t going to get to see it, and then she messaged everyone like, “Let’s gather, let’s go.” And I was telling her, “But we don’t have glasses.” but she had 10 pairs of glasses. We even gave some to the people there who didn’t have any so it was really very cosy. I loved capturing our little social gathering. 
Pauline Vandewiele, 30, interior architect, northern Belgium

Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes
August 13, 2026
Israel has sent soldiers to try to protect three homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra that have been surrounded by a small group of Israeli settlers for several days.
One of the three homes is owned by a Palestinian American, and the incident prompted an unusually critical reponse from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically considered an ally of Israel's settler movement.
The case comes amid continued Israeli settlement building, which is considered illegal under international law, in parts of the occupied West Bank, and allegations from critics of the Israeli government that it sometimes turns a blind eye to, or does too little to prevent, settler violence against Palestinians.
What is happening and where?
Starting on Sunday, a group of settlers started gathering around three houses in the village of Qusra.
One of the buildings belongs to Palestinian-American homeowner Loui Ridi. Local officials said the settlers sometimes numbered several dozen. They supposedly threw strones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving their homes as their supplies dwindled.
Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida — who had holed up in the house with his son — said on Thursday morning that they had been moved to another home by the Israeli military but still could not leave the area some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Palestinian city of Nablus. Loui Ridi resides in Ohio but owns the property.
Israel's IDF military said its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" near the homes, and detained one Israeli. It wasn't immediately clear if the individual was subject to arrest or investigation, or just detention.
The local mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, said that Israeli forces evacuated seven Palestinian households from their homes to make space for soldiers to take up positions in the village. He said that the settlers remained in other parts of the village, despite being removed from their outposts.
Locals said the village was on effective lockdown.
"No one is allowed to enter. Even food and water are prohibited from reaching those besieged," the Associated Press cited Yasser Ahmad, a resident of a neighboring village, as saying as he watched the operation unfold from one hilltop over.
Qusra is in one of the most violent pockets of the northern West Bank, surrounded by settlements. Its mosque was damaged in attacks last month.
What did US Ambassador Huckabee say about the incident?
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically a supporter of the Israeli settler movement — but also critical of settler violence — spoke out in unusually sharp terms against an incident impacting a US citizen in the West Bank.
"The actions of those doing this to this family's home is criminal," he said. "Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."
However, Huckabee also repeatedly defended both US and Israeli authorities response to the incident, saying the US Embassy in Jerusalem had been "very involved," and that "the IDF and Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this."
He later repeated this message, posting video footage seeming to show Israeli security vehicles driving into the area.
The UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory on Thursday called on the Israeli authorities to "immediately" act against the settlers .
"These criminal actions by the settlers, supported or acquiesced to by Israel, the occupying power, are making life unbearable for these Palestinian families, and are clearly aimed at forcing them to leave their homes and land," it said in a statement.
EU foreign policy spokesperson Anitta Hipper called on Israel to take "concrete action to prevent settler violence."
What's the wider issue with West Bank settlement building and settler violence?
Palestinians and some in the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, as such cases have increased in recent years since the October 7 attacks and amid the war in Gaza.
Israeli government officials tend to describe the violence as the actions of a few fringe youth acting outside the law. The UN's human rights office (OHCHR) said 18 Palestinians have died in the first seven months of this year in attacks involving settlers.
Most of the international community condemns Israeli settlement building in the West Bank as an impediment to a lasting peace and the so-called two-state solution.
More than 500,000 Israelis live — most with but also some without Israeli government authorization and support — in the West Bank, which is home to roughly 3 million Palestinians.
The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, as part of a future state. Many settlers and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government claim the area should belong to Israel, often citing a mixture historical, religious and security reasons.

DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:17:13 UTC
00:17:13 KST

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.
The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.
Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.
There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.
The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.
Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.
Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.
The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.
Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.
The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.
Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.
Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”
Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.
Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.
This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.
Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.
Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

Europe boosts aid to Ukraine, allocating about 11 billion euro in May, June — institute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:17:07 UTC
00:17:07 KST

BERLIN, August 13. /TASS/. Europe expanded its assistance to Ukraine in May and June to almost 11 billion euros, according to the Kiel Institute for World Economy, which tracks data on Kiev's support.
The sum is split into 4.3 billion euros that was allocated to military aid and 6.7 billion euros to financial and humanitarian aid. The European Union allocated most of the funds under the new 90 billion euro Ukraine Support Loan designed to finance the Ukrainian budget and military spending in 2026 and 2027.
Besides the funds from the EU institutions, individual European countries have also provided new aid packages. Germany disbursed 700 million euros in military aid, Denmark - 600 million euros, and the Netherlands - 500 million euros.
The United Kingdom with about 1.5 billion euros led by of financial and humanitarian assistance among bilateral donors.
While the volume of military aid in the first half of 2026 almost equals the previous year’s sums, financial and humanitarian support for Ukraine has decreased by 41%.
The report says that while Europe continues to lead in military assistance, weapons from the United States play a key role in this European support. The share of the United States in European military aid, according to IfW, continued to grow both through the purchases from defense companies and through supplies from the US arsenals. Between January and June 2026, European donors purchased weapons worth at least 3 billion euro from US defense companies, or a third of European military aid supplied through the industrial sector.
Supplies from the US stocks have also played a critical role, providing over 90% of the military assistance under the NATO PURL initiative.
"Europe continues to depend on the access to US weapons systems to sustain its military support for Ukraine," says Federico Mellace, Lead Analyst of the Ukraine Support Tracker.
According to him, the United States remains a key supplier of systems such as Patriot, to which Europe currently has almost no alternatives. In the long term, the main question will be whether Europe can develop and produce its own reliable analogues to gradually reduce this dependence.
Russia has repeatedly said that arms supplies to the Kiev regime only prolong the conflict in Ukraine.

US flags dozens of trade partners as risks for aiding tariff evasion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

US flags dozens of trade partners as risks for aiding tariff evasion
Washington – The Trump administration flagged dozens of US trading partners on Aug 13 as potential risks in aiding Chinese tariff evasion, vowing to tap artificial intelligence to help detect illegal practices in the future.
Among those named are the European Union and Taiwan, alongside US neighbours Mexico and Canada. Others include India, Japan, South Korea and Vietnam.
The White House report takes aim at its longstanding concern surrounding “illegal transshipment,” where goods could be sent through a third country that faces lower US tariffs to avoid paying higher levies imposed by President Donald Trump.
“For years, the great transshipment scam has let Communist China launder its exports through more than 40 countries,” White House trade adviser Peter Navarro told reporters.
The US report released on Aug 13 pointed to “more than 40 countries associated with elevated illegal transshipment risk.”
For some economies, transshipment risk is “embedded within broad legitimate trade flows,” the report said.
Others were found to be more integrated with China-linked supply chains, while a third group had advantages such as preferential US access that make them “attractive opportunistic targets” for rerouting.
Navarro added that the White House is working closely with US Customs and Border Protection on an AI-enabled “detective border” to help assess whether a shipment involves transshipped goods.
This system would tap information like shipment data, routing histories and other tools, the report said.
Experts have long noted supply chain diversions from China since Trump’s first presidency, when Washington and Beijing engaged in a tariffs war around 2018.
Among those who benefited as businesses diversified their supply chains were countries like Vietnam, economists added.
Since returning to the White House in 2025, Trump has imposed sweeping tariffs on US trading partners, adding to existing duties that Chinese imports face. AFP

Lebanon passes long-disputed General Amnesty Law aimed at relieving prison overcrowding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:14:17 UTC
00:14:17 KST

Lebanon’s parliament passed the long-disputed General Amnesty Law on Wednesday, legislation aimed at easing severe overcrowding in the country’s prisons by reducing or commuting the sentences of thousands of prisoners and detainees.
The controversial law has inflamed Lebanon’s longstanding sectarian divisions in recent months, with Islamist protesters taking to the streets and burning tires in protest over provisions that would exclude some prisoners from the amnesty.
The Free Patriotic Movement and Hezbollah deputies notably did not take part in the vote as a form of protest, according to Lebanese media reports.
Those convicted of terrorism offenses, collaborating with Israel, repeat drug offenses, premeditated murder, and rape were excluded from the amnesty, which has been a particular point of contention for the families of those detained in the Abra clash. The altercation in 2013, which left 29 dead, saw members of the Lebanese Armed Forces attacked by heavily armed terrorists loyal to radical Sunni cleric Sheikh Ahmad al-Assir in a two-day battle in Sidon.
Those convicted of crimes not covered by the general amnesty may still see their sentences reduced. Those sentenced to life imprisonment will serve 12 years, the death sentence to 21 years, and any other prison terms will be served for a third of the duration.
Pretrial detentions have lasted longer than the sentences the alleged crimes would carry
The COVID-19 pandemic, Lebanon’s economic struggles, and war have severely disrupted the judicial process, leaving many in a state of detained limbo in which their pretrial detention has extended beyond what the sentence for their crime would be.
As of 2023, 80% of those detained in Lebanese prisons were awaiting trial, according to the Lebanese Interior Ministry. At the time, detention centers across Lebanon had a capacity of 4,760, but they held 8,502 prisoners, including 1,094 who had actually been sentenced, Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces reported.
Defense Minister Michel Menassa complained on Thursday that the military had been prevented from speaking at the Parliament, which spoke firmly against releasing those involved in the killing of military officials.
Inmates at Raoumieh prison celebrate legislative announcement
Sunni Lebanese Member of Parliament said that 79 Islamists would be released now that the legislation has passed, according to L’Orient Today, and footage circulating online showed inmates at Roumieh prison celebrating the legislation.
Those sympathetic to the prisoners have argued that they were tried by a court too heavily influenced by Hezbollah.
The legislation notably followed only a day after Lebanon abolished the death penalty in a regional first.
Assir, who was already sentenced to death, is currently being retried, and his daughter-in-law told The National that he is unlikely to be released immediately.
Sunni MP Walid Baarini described the law as a “national achievement” that he hoped “restores the meaning of justice”.

Disabled IDF veteran says he was forced to leave McDonald's with service dog

2026-08-13
15:13:35 UTC

Aviv Levy, a disabled IDF veteran, was asked to leave a McDonald's at Gan Shmuel Junction in northern Israel on Monday because of his service dog, he told Israel's Channel 12 News on Thursday.
In the interview, Levy explained that he does not often go out, especially to crowded places, because of his post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
Explaining why he relies on his service dog in such environments, Levy said: "I need the dog; he helps me in crowded places where there are children screaming and [lots of] noise. I absolutely would not have come to...McDonald's with my family without the dog."
He said that he and his family had already placed their order and sat down with the dog when he was asked to leave.
"The dog sat, didn't bark, didn't bother [anyone], nothing," Levy told Channel 12. "People even came and asked if they could pet him."
Soon afterward, an employee approached Levy and insisted that he could not have the dog inside the McDonald's, telling him that the manager required him to leave.
This was despite the fact that Levy explained the situation and presented the employee with the relevant documents proving the dog's status as a service animal.
Incident at McDonald's leaves disabled IDF vet with heightened stress, anxiety
When it became clear that the situation would not be resolved quickly or easily, Levy and his family left the restaurant. The incident left him in a state of heightened stress that lasted for several days, according to Channel 12.
The incident continued to affect Levy after he left the restaurant. "I didn't sleep all night," he said. "It's very frustrating. It's not about money. I take one step forward and five steps back."
PTSD service dogs were granted the same legal status as guide dogs in 2022, along with medical alert dogs and dogs that assist people with physical and developmental disabilities.
The law states that people with such service dogs, including those training and fostering them, are entitled to equal access to public spaces, workplaces, and services. This includes businesses, restaurants, and public institutions.

1. Where, when and what was exactly going on in these exercises and why were Ukrainians there?
The exercise was a two-week field wargame called Combined Resolve that took place in the second half of April 2026 and into the first days of May. The main unit doing the training was a US-based “heavy” unit – primarily armed with tanks, infantry fighting vehicles, artillery and helicopters – called the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team of 1st Cavalry Division, based in Fort Hood, Texas. The brigade was deployed in Europe as part of a US deterrence plan, now probably cancelled by the Trump administration, to field US ground combat brigades in East Europe. About 3,500 US soldiers participated in the exercise. Hohenfels is NATO’s largest training area for maneuver training. Force-on-force training at Hohenfels has been a standard NATO training evolution since the 1950s.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine, Hohenfels has become NATO’s premier training site for practicing maneuver warfare against a peer adversary in conventional combat conditions. Weapons effects are simulated by using weapons loaded with blanks and lasers attached to the weapons that shoot when a blank is fired, and by fitting laser-sensitive sensors to soldiers and combat vehicles. Observation officers/judges use artillery simulators and lasers of their own to simulate artillery and some long-range systems. Although the training, amounting to a giant wargame using laser tag, can’t replicate the fear of war, most soldiers say force-on-force exercises at Hohenfels fairly accurately replicate how weapons work in simulated battles: intelligent tactics mostly work, and bad tactics almost always fail.
Ukraine Receives Bodies of 261 Fallen Soldiers From Russia
Units deployed to Hohenfels for the training included, according to open sources, the 3rd ArmoredBrigade headquarters, 6th Squadron, 9th Cavalry Regiment, a heavy reconnaissance formation, alongwith attachments of combat engineers, artillery, and support units. The brigade HQ at the exercises,with call sign Greywolf, was beefed up by helicopters and M1A1 tanks from 2-37 Armor. These are all Regular Army ground combat formations mostly based in Ft. Hood, Texas, with the permanent mission of immediate readiness to deploy to and fightin a conventional war.
The Hohenfels training area has a permanently based US Army unit called 1st Battalion, 4th Infantry Regiment, whose full-time job is simulating the “enemy” for units coming to fight simulated battles there. The unit, usually called OPFOR, tries to use Russian/Iranian/Chinese tactics and operates vehicles that simulate tanks and other fighting vehicles from those countries. In December 2025, the unit stood up a brand-new company that only uses drones, primarily a short-range quadcopter aircraft called Archer Nero. The OPFOR drone unit at Hohenfels is nicknamed Eerie Company.
A small number of Ukrainian operators and aircraft, reportedly two or four actual flight teams or fewer than 20 pilots and technicians, participated in the Hohenfels training. They were from a well-known Ukrainian drone unit called the 412th Brigade of the Unmanned Systems Forces, “Nemesis.” Ukrainian drone units participating in NATO maneuver training dates back at least to 2025. During the exercise, the Ukrainians first flew on the side of the OPFOR against the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 1st Cavalry Division units, and then later on switched to work as support units and trainers for the 3rd ABCT units as they continued their battles against the OPFOR. The simulated war was fought on mostly dry ground in fair weather, so flying conditions were good.
2. Is it true the Ukrainians in simulated combat demolished a major US force operated by 3rd Brigade?
The answer to that is clearly “yes,” but there are some qualifications. According to the WSJ and US military news reports, in at least one of the battle scenarios, a movement to attack or an actual attempted assault by US forces against an OPFOR position, operators from 412th Brigade “Nemesis” easily located the approaching Americans thanks in part to dust plumes. Ukrainian pilots scored simulated hits on the attacking tanks and infantry fighting vehicles with first-person-view (FPV) drones with relative ease, and that US armored vehicles evaluated damaged and stopped were hunted down and destroyed by follow-up bomber drones, as were US infantrymen and light vehicles that took to cover once their protecting armored vehicles were lost. The tactics used by the Ukrainians at Hohenfels were, per reports, identical to tactics used by Ukrainian drone units in combat against Russia for more than two years.According to the reports, the American units had standard electronic warfare and counter-drone systems, and the supporting intelligence networks had full access, at least theoretically, to tactical intelligence generated by major US reconnaissance assets like satellite overflights, electronic intercepts, and deep spy networks. Nevertheless, at least in the large attack/heavy reconnaissance evolution of the training, the Ukrainian drone operators inflicted heavy enough “losses” on the US forces to render them combat ineffective and force judges to “bring back to life” destroyed equipment and soldiers, because had the 3rd Armored HQ been obliged to make up the losses using standard replacement and supply, the training would have ground to a halt for lack of US combat units available to go fight.
Available sources don’t specify the actual numbers of US “casualties”; however, a 3,500-man US brigade battle group would normally field at least 200 armored vehicles of various types. The main training unit, 6th Squadron 9th Cavalry, if performing a movement to contact with reinforcements, would probably field about 30-40 infantry fighting vehicles or other light armored vehicles, and about a dozen tanks.In the Russo-Ukrainian War, probably the most massive Russian armored assault to be stopped by drones took place on March 30, 2024, near the city of Tonenke, just west of Avdiivka, during which Kremlin forces pushed 48 armored vehicles towards prepared Ukrainian defenses and lost half that force in a few hours to drone strikes backed by artillery. A similar defeat was suffered by Russian forces this year, attacking near the village of Shakhove, on July 22, with some 70-80 vehicles sent out into the open and at least 65, among them seven tanks, destroyed by Ukrainian drones.
It’s important to keep in mind that the Ukrainians’ use of drone tactics widely practiced throughout the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) to “demolish” six of nine US Cavalry took place in only one of several battle scenarios during the Hohenfels training.
3. What else happened in the exercise and what was the Ukrainians’ role?
Open-source information covering the exercise points to a standard set of training scenarios intended to put the training units through their paces and to force them to work under pressure. One description of the training event script, unconfirmed, suggested that in the early phases of the exercise the Greywolf/3rd Armored force conducted a reconnaissance and advance to contact into territory held by OPFOR, and then set up a hasty defense to hold ground gained and recover from casualties.
In subsequent days, elements of the Greywolf force probed the OPFOR position to find strongpoints and other targets, while dispersing and concealing friendly forces. Later on in the exercise, the Ukrainians switched sides and worked side by side with 3rd Armored headquarters officers and NCOs to practice cooperative reconnaissance and fire support.
According to an official report on Eerie Company’s activities, a main focus of the exercise was determining best practices and tactics in a drone-dense battle environment. As OPFOR, Eerie’s job was to “replicate modern battlefield threat” using drones to detect and attack training units and electronic warfare systems (jammers) to make communications for the training units more difficult. A May 4 article published on the US Army website army.mil identified the main drone used by the Americans to simulate “enemy” drones as a Neros Archer, a small quadcopter aircraft similar in performance to Ukrainian FPV drones used in actual combat, but costing about three times more.
The 412th Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) Brigade “Nemesis,” like most Ukrainian drone units, is armed with a packed golf bag of combat aircraft ranging from throwaway FPV drones costing less than $400 to Vampire hexacopter bomber/minelayer drones, Hornet interceptor drones, Morrigan fixed-wing drones, and R18/R34 heavy octocopter drones. Reports did not say which pieces of that inventory deployed to Hohenfels to augment the Americas’ Archer drones.
A little surprisingly, given the Ukrainians’ skill and actual performance in the training, the US Army write-up on Eerie did not mention the Ukrainians’ presence. US Army video and still images from the training, likewise, showed plenty of drone activity, but gave no hint of Ukrainian soldiers or aircraft ever participating in training with 3rd Armored Brigade at Hohenfels.
4. What’s there to know about this Ukrainian drone unit Nemesis?
Ukraine’s USF Brigade Nemesis is usually considered one of the most experienced and combat-effective drone units in all the AFU, and therefore, likely in any military anywhere. Yaroslav Honchar, a former IT marketing consultant and co-founder of the unit in 2014, during Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine, is the commander.
According to the commander of Ukraine’s unmanned forces, a former grain trader named Robert Brovdi, a typical Ukrainian Unmanned Aircraft Brigade usually numbers between 1,000-1,500 men and women and fields around 300 individual drone teams collectively able, under normal circumstances, to control and absolutely deny Russian advance across 100 kilometers (62 miles) of fighting front. Based on open sources, aside from support elements like headquarters, medical, personnel, and logistics, in a typical day of combat, a brigade like Nemesis flies somewhere between 150-400 air missions daily, along with another 10-20 field movements by ground drones.
As the NATO training exercise was happening, with a probable 15-20 operators absent, the majority of the men and women of the 412th Unmanned Systems Brigade “Nemesis” were in combat or supporting tactical combat operations in the southern Hulyaipole sector in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
Per the unit news feed, back in Ukraine, in wartime operations, both the brigade’s FPV and bomber drone units reported successful strikes against Russian armored vehicle parks 10-30 kilometers behind enemy lines, including an April 14 night of sorties destroying most of the vehicles and earth-moving equipment of a Russian combat engineer battalion.
A count of vehicle kills for March and April published by the brigade identified 260 Russian vehicles, some motorcycles, and dune buggies, destroyed by drone strikes. All kills reportedly were documented by drone video, but Kyiv Post was only able to review about 10% of the strike imagery. Five days later, the brigade anti-aircraft division scored a rare kill using an interceptor drone of a Russian Shahed kamikaze drone.
An elite long-range strike element of the brigade, during April, flew more than 30 attacks against Russian shadow fleet tankers operating in the Black Sea, and against Russian shore facilities servicing shipping and oil transfers. Reportedly, seven ships were hit. The brigade’s air defense suppression unit claimed 17 Russian anti-aircraft missile systems and 12 Russian air defense radars destroyed in 2026 strikes through April.
5. Is NATO learning the lesson that Ukrainian drones and drone tactics (which don’t differ significantly from Russia) are devastating to conventionally configured and commanded NATO ground units?
That doesn’t seem to be the case. The Combined Resolve exercise was not the first but the third in two years, in which NATO training units were pitted against Ukrainian drone units and found themselves cut to pieces in simulated combat.
The very first time such a training defeat took place was during NATO’s Hedgehog 2025 exercise in Estonia, from May 5-23. More than 16,000 troops from 12 countries participated in the exercise, among them, ironically, bomber and reconnaissance drones from 412th Brigade Nemesis.During the maneuvers, 412th operators, along with FPV crews from another highly competent Ukrainian drone unit, 427th USF Brigade “Rarog,” helped play the role of OPFOR against a crack British infantry unit (1st Mercian Battlegroup) and the 1st Infantry Brigade, the Estonian Division. During a simulated counterattack by those NATO units, a group of about 10 Ukrainian drone operators found and, in simulated combat, destroyed at least 17 British/Estonian combat vehicles, inflicted dozens of notional casualties, and bottled up survivors on woodland roads overflown by Ukrainian FPVs.
Trapped vehicles included Challenger 2 tanks, Warrior IFVs and artillery. Exercise commanders following the Ukrainian successes “brought the killed and wounded back to life” so that the training could continue.The second time NATO forces encountered Ukrainian drones in training was during the Aurora 26 exercises held in Gotland, Sweden, taking place from April 27-May 13, almost simultaneously with 3rd Armored’s rotation to Hohenfels. The main training formation was the professional Swedish Gotland Regiment under the command of the Gotland Brigade Combat Group, with Danish Home Guard, US air defense, and British infantry attachments.
The Ukrainian contingent was drawn not from the elite USF forces but from frontline drone units supporting the veteran 1st Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine “Azov,” among them pilots and technicians from a former public duties brigade called “Presidential,” and a newly raised infantry brigade called “Lubart.” News reports put the total number of Ukrainian soldiers participating in the training at 15-17. Drones used were only FPV replica drones carrying sandbags.
According to one report, the Ukrainians also brought along jamming-proof fiber-optic drones but found them unnecessary because the training NATO units seemed either unwilling or incapable of jamming the drones attacking them. According to Swedish news reports, the Ukrainians repeatedly located and notionally destroyed Swedish/NATO vehicles, and in one scenario “destroyed” 28 of 32 vehicles attempting an advance.
According to Ukrainian military news reports, the casualty-producing NATO tactics inappropriate to drones used in the Hedgehog exercise in 2025 had not changed in the Combined Resolve and Aurora exercises taking place a full 11 months later. A news report in Ukraine on the Gotland training from that time, unconfirmed but widely reported, said that Ukrainian pilots quit counting once the kill count passed 30.

Wildberries and sellers’ combined losses from Ukrainian drone attacks estimated at hundreds of billions of rubles
Rebuilding Wildberries’ warehouses and other infrastructure destroyed in Ukrainian drone attacks could cost the online retailer between 147 billion and 223 billion rubles, Sergei Semko, lead analyst at the Data Insight research agency, told Forbes Russia. If the retailer has to fully demolish the damaged buildings, clear the debris, and reclaim the land, the cost could climb to between 169 billion and 278.9 billion rubles, he said.
Semko put sellers’ potential losses on Wildberries at 445-507.8 billion rubles.
Combined, the damage to Wildberries and its sellers could currently total 600-800 billion rubles, by his estimate.
Margarita Evstigneeva, head of the Association of Suppliers of Goods for Trading on Electronic Platforms, said the attacks on Wildberries’ warehouses have affected more than 400,000 sellers, whose total losses — including lost profit — amount to 600-700 billion rubles, against production costs of 200 billion to 300 billion rubles for the goods themselves. Many sellers, she said, lost up to 95% of their entire inventory in the fires.
Ukraine has regularly struck logistics centers belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s largest online marketplace, since mid-July. According to The Bell’s estimate as of August 5, Wildberries’ direct losses from Ukrainian attacks could exceed 100 billion rubles. Sellers’ own losses were estimated at 215-280 billion rubles in early August.
The Bank of Russia has recommended that banks support small and medium-sized businesses affected by the drone attacks. In late July, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak instructed the Economic Development Ministry, the Finance Ministry, and the Federal Tax Service, together with the Central Bank and the business community, to develop support measures for entrepreneurs affected by the attacks on Wildberries.

Kyiv • UNN
Law enforcement officers found the fighter jet’s flight recorder, which sustained thermal damage. Specialists are working to recover data about the last minutes of the flight.
Law enforcement officers found the flight recorder of the fighter jet that crashed on August 10, 2026, while carrying out a combat mission in Odesa region’s Berezivskyi district, UNN reports, citing the State Bureau of Investigation.
"The black box" sustained thermal damage as a result of the fire. Specialists are currently working to restore it and retrieve data about the final minutes of the flight
The investigation is considering several versions of the causes of the aviation incident. None of them has been definitively confirmed so far.
The investigation is under the personal control of the Director of the State Bureau of Investigation.
"We will make every necessary effort to establish objectively and as fully as possible the causes of this aviation incident. The investigation must provide a clear answer as to exactly what happened during the combat mission and what factors led to it. None of the versions will be dismissed without thorough verification," Oleksii Sukhachov emphasized.
In particular, investigators are examining the technical condition of the missile that the pilot launched at an enemy drone, as well as whether it was fit for use at the time of launch.
Investigators are also checking compliance with the rules for preparing for the flight, conducting it, and operating the aircraft. The fighter jet’s wreckage, materials from the scene, and servicemen’s testimony are being examined.
To recap
On the evening of August 10, a MiG-29 of the Armed Forces of Ukraine was carrying out a combat mission to destroy enemy drones. An emergency situation occurred, the aircraft caught fire, and the pilot lost control.
The pilot managed to eject. His life is not in danger.
In connection with the air crash, criminal proceedings were initiated under Part 2 of Article 416 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — violation of flight rules or rules for preparing for them, as well as rules for operating aircraft, which caused a crash.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing.

Brussels unveils giant flower carpet inspired by Hokusai masterpiece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:09:07 UTC
00:09:07 KST

Volunteers worked through the morning of Thursday, 13 August, placing the flowers by hand on a numbered carpet to gradually reveal the design inspired by the famous woodblock print by Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai. Visitors gathered around the square to watch the work take shape and photograph the finished sections. Japanese Ambassador to Belgium Takeshi Osuga also joined the volunteers, placing flowers on the carpet as Japanese sponsors supported the event.
The design is part of the 24th edition of the biennial Flower Carpet, a once‑in‑a‑decade celebration in Brussels that marks the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Belgium and Japan. It brings together Belgian and Japanese cultural traditions, with the pattern created by Japanese artist Hiro Sugiyama and his collective Enlightenment, who describe the work as “Neo‑Hokusai”, a modern reinterpretation of Hokusai’s masterpiece.
Volunteers worked from a small reference image, with each colour assigned a number to ensure the pattern was reproduced accurately. The finished carpet, measuring 70 metres long by 24 metres wide, will give visitors a new way to see one of Japan’s best‑known artworks, framed by the historic buildings of Brussels’ Grand Place. The installation will remain on display until Sunday, 16 August, with a nightly sound and light show from 9 p.m. to 11 p.m.

The Kremlin has pushed to reduce university enrollment in favor of vocational training, with public high schools redirecting teenagers into trade colleges to address industrial labor shortages.

Turkiye’s AK Party turns 25: A journey of change and renewal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:07:42 UTC
00:07:42 KST

Turkiye’s AK Party turns 25: A journey of change and renewal
The party’s record of stability, development and democratic change has laid the foundations for a stronger, more independent Turkiye.
The initial step taken on August 14, 2001 cannot be viewed merely as the submission of a political party’s founding petition within the annals of international political history; rather, it is the reincarnation of a millennium-old, deep-rooted civilisational vision on the modern world stage. Today, having left a quarter of a century behind, the AK Party is not merely a tale of national development within its borders, but an unparalleled 25-year epic of democracy on a global scale. Coming to power with immense public favour just 16 months after its founding, and steering the country with uninterrupted stability for a quarter of a century, this political movement has secured a highly exceptional place in world political history.
The greatest power behind this stability lies in the fact that this movement is not a rootless structure blown about by the wind. It carries on its shoulders, as a historical trust, the democratic struggle of the late Prime Minister Adnan Menderes and his companions, who sacrificed their lives for the nation’s beliefs during the arduous days of the single-party era. The mighty plane tree founded by our President and Chairman Recep Tayyip Erdogan – under whose shade our nation and oppressed geographies have drawn a breath of relief for 25 years – is the very embodiment of this tremendous historical legacy.
While the lifespans of political parties are generally measured by election results or their terms in government, the AK Party’s ability to overcome successive global and national crises with the continuous support of vastly diverse social segments over 25 years can be explained by a much more structural concept: Its “capacity for political translation”.
This capacity is the process of accurately hearing the expectations, needs, and objections within society, transforming them into viable party programmes, budgets, and public policies, and submitting the resulting outcomes back for societal evaluation. Social needs do not always arrive in politics as ready-made texts; it is here that the AK Party has established a colossal “translation” mechanism that turns seemingly disparate experiences into common problems and solutions. Indeed, for someone of a generation like mine – who grew up in a Turkiye shaped by the AK Party, took on responsibilities in its youth branches since childhood, and today serves as a member of parliament and the party’s secretary-general – this political ground is the very essence of that transformation.
To grasp the magnitude of this transformation, one must look back at the Turkiye of the 1990s. It is essential to read those years not just as an “era of a unipolar world and severe economic crises”, but as a colossal “age of political collapse and instability” that paralysed the state and deepened societal fault lines.
The 90s were a lost decade in which fragile coalitions lasting only months, political bargaining and recurring crises shook state authority. While unsolved murders and an escalating spiral of terror threatened citizens’ lives on the one hand, the heavy fist of tutelage brought down upon civilian politics via the February 28 post-modern coup explicitly usurped the nation’s will on the other. Even though voter turnout reached 87 percent in parliamentary elections during that era, this high public interest in politics could not translate into a stable and effective governing capacity, with no single party able to form a majority government.
The closure of the Refah Party in 1998 and the Fazilet Party in 2001 through judicial tutelage created a profound crisis regarding the continuity of legitimate channels of representation for the masses. Therefore, the year 2001 was a historical threshold – not merely a year of economic bankruptcy marked by cash registers being thrown in protest, but the absolute peak of political fragmentation, tutelary regimes, governance vulnerabilities, and constitutional rights remaining strictly on paper. Inheriting this multidimensional political and economic wreckage, the AK Party built the world’s most experienced cadres in every field, from security to economics, from foreign policy to social policies, establishing a “game-changing” political style.
At the core of this game-changing politics lies the dismantling of the “state commands its citizens” mentality, replacing it with the principle that “the state is the servant of the nation”. Believing that true change lies in execution rather than packaging, the AK Party tore down the cold walls built between the state and the nation, making the nation’s red lines the same as the state’s.
The silent majority, who for decades had been left disheartened like “tenants” in their own homeland, rose with self-confidence to become the true “landlords” of their country. Today, as the world’s largest and most dynamic school of politics with more than 12 million members, the AK Party conducts politics not by pontificating from television screens, but by directly sharing the burdens of the people and keeping a finger on the pulse of the streets. The secret behind these victories is hidden in these devoted organisations that hold the nation’s consent above all else, and in the vision of the leader of this great march, our President and Chairman Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The party’s quarter-century has gone down in history not through noisy destructions and polarising conflicts, but through institutional “silent revolutions” woven stitch by stitch. The Health Transformation Program and national fighter jets and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) produced in the defence industry are the building blocks of this revolution.
Moreover, Turkiye does not view technological transformation merely as instrumental progress; it presents a brand new vision. By openly opposing the algorithmic exploitation of global digital giants, it advocates for a value-oriented and ethical technological order that places human dignity, privacy, and the family at its centre. TEKNOFEST is not just a technology fair; it is a ceremony of institutional self-confidence where a generation – once intended to be manipulated in the streets during past coup eras – becomes the builder of this very moral and fully independent technological future.
The greatest outcome of this will for full independence is the historic struggle waged against the scourge of terrorism – which has made the nation weep blood – under the ideal of a “Terror-Free Turkiye”. Recipes dictated from the outside have been crumpled up and thrown away; terrorism has been dried up at its source, and the dirty corridors intended to be established at our borders have been shattered by the “Turkiye Model”. A Turkiye completely cleansed of terrorism has thwarted Israel’s expansionist ambitions built on dividing, weakening, and destabilising the region; it has become the greatest hope for the Palestinian cause, for Jerusalem, and for the oppressed in Gaza.
Viewing democracy not as a tool but as an unshakable value, this political mindset forever closed the dark parenthesis of tutelage opened on May 27, 1960, on the night of July 15, when the nation lay down in front of tanks and braved gun barrels. This democratic resilience achieved at home has today made Turkiye the vanguard of a global conscience movement abroad.
The objection raised by our President and Chairman Recep Tayyip Erdogan that “The World is Bigger Than Five!” has transformed into an “Erdogan Doctrine” that maps the conscience of humanity against those who fancy themselves masters of the globe. This quest for justice – embodied in the human tragedy in Gaza, in baby Aylan whose washed-up body shook the world, and in a little boy who recited the Quran with his last breath under the rubble – is the clearest indicator of Turkiye’s determination to defend the rights of the innocent in international diplomacy.
Today, moving far beyond being a passive ally in global politics, Turkiye has risen to the position of a subject that rewrites the rules of the international system, produces solutions to geopolitical crises, and personally steers diplomatic change.
Having long transcended artificial agendas and polemics in domestic politics, the AK Party’s true power in this multipolar world lies not only in the country’s economic and strategic capacity. It lies in the unshakeable democratic legitimacy behind our President and Chairman Recep Tayyip Erdogan – one of the most senior and experienced heads of state in world politics – and in the profound trust that all oppressed peoples across the earth place in Turkiye.
Our tremendous state experience over the past quarter-century is our most solid reference; yet, this political movement, with its face always turned towards the future, is determined to build the “Century of Turkiye” vision on the axis of justice, compassion, and sustainable global peace by blending it with the nation’s internal dynamics. In this new age marked by great trials that deeply affect humanity, under the leadership of our President and Chairman Recep Tayyip Erdogan – who shapes global politics with his unparalleled state experience and vision in the international arena – Turkiye marches forward with strong steps, shoulder to shoulder with our nation, as a playmaker towards new targets and a bright new quarter-century.

Ukraine Not Invited to the Largest Military Parade in Polish History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:07:19 UTC
00:07:19 KST

Representatives of Ukraine were not invited to the military parade in Poland, which will take place on August 15 in Warsaw to mark Polish Armed Forces Day.
The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine informed Suspilne of this.
Polish Armed Forces Day is celebrated in honor of the victory of Polish troops over the Bolshevik army in the Battle of Warsaw in 1920. This victory was one of the key episodes of the Polish-Soviet War and halted the Bolsheviks’ advance into Western Europe.
Units of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic also fought on Poland’s side. In particular, in August 1920, the 6th Sich Division, under the command of Mark Bezruchko, defended Zamość against Semyon Budyonny’s 1st Cavalry Army.
For several days, Ukrainian units, together with Polish troops, held back the Soviet offensive. After unsuccessful assaults, Budyonny’s forces were forced to retreat from Zamość.
This year’s parade will be the largest in Polish history. In Warsaw, it will feature approximately 1,800 service members, over 300 pieces of ground equipment, and more than 60 aircraft.
In total, approximately 9,000 Polish military personnel will be mobilized to support the land and naval parades.
In addition to Polish military personnel, representatives from allied nations will participate in this year’s parade. Among them are service members from the United States, Canada, Australia, Lithuania, Estonia, Sweden, Romania, and other countries.
A significant amount of modern military equipment will be on display during the parade in Warsaw. In particular, American Abrams tanks, South Korean K2 tanks, and German Leopard tanks will be showcased, as well as Gladius unmanned aerial systems.
The air component of the parade will include F-35 and F-16 fighter jets, as well as Black Hawk, AW149, and Apache helicopters. In addition, spectators will be shown the Patriot and Poprad air defense systems.
A separate part of the celebrations will be a naval parade in Gdynia. More than 20 ships will take part, including frigates, corvettes, minesweepers, and hydrographic vessels.
Previously, for example, in 2020, Poland proposed that Ukraine jointly celebrate the victory over Russia.
And for the 2024 parade marking the same occasion, servicemen from the joint Lithuanian-Polish-Ukrainian brigade, whose headquarters were located in Lublin, Poland, were involved.
As a reminder, Ukrainian pilots and ground forces recently participated in the Bastille Day parade in Paris.

Poland thwarts unprecedented plot by Russia to kill Ukrainian-US citizen in a NATO country, PM Tusk says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:05:38 UTC
00:05:38 KST

Poland, a NATO and EU member state along the alliance's Eastern flank, has accused Russia of "sabotage" on several occasions since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Poland detained a Russian citizen accused by Warsaw of planning to kill a Ukrainian-American dual citizen in the Polish capital on Moscow's orders, Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced on Thursday.
Tusk told journalists the suspect had been arrested last Friday.
"He was inconvenient from the point of view of the Putin regime and at the last moment...we managed to prevent this execution," he added.
"This is the first situation of its kind in which someone, acting on Russian orders, decided to carry out an attack against an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country," he added.
Tusk said agents of the Polish Internal Security Agency (ABW) and police had arrested the suspect, with cooperation from American services.
"We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons," Tusk said.
Warsaw, he added, "will likely come under similar pressure again."
Poland, a NATO and EU member state along the alliance's Eastern flank, has accused Russia of "sabotage" on several occasions since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In June, Russian caricaturist and Putin critic Semyon Skrepetsky, whose real name was Robert Kuzovkov, was shot dead in eastern Poland. Tusk later called the killing a "political murder."
While last November, a railway line linking Warsaw to southeastern Poland was damaged by an explosion that Tusk called an "unprecedented act of sabotage."
Tusk said the line is "crucially important for delivering aid to Ukraine."
Several opponents of the Russian authorities have been victims of attacks abroad, including in the United Kingdom, Germany and Lithuania.
Moscow has always denied any involvement in these attacks.

Ukraine repatriates remains of 20th-century military leader Yevhen Konovalets with state honors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:04:08 UTC
00:04:08 KST

Ukraine repatriates remains of 20th-century military leader Yevhen Konovalets with state honors
The remains of 20th-century military leader Yevhen Konovalets were given full state and military honors upon being brought back to Ukraine for reburial, Iryna Vereshchuk, deputy head of the President's Office, reported on Aug. 13.
As the founder of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), Konovalets devoted his life to the cause of Ukraine's independence.
The OUN was established in 1929, amid the turmoil following Ukraine's defeat in the 1917–1921 War of Independence, which led to the country's territory being divided between the Soviet Union and Poland.
From exile, Konovalets worked to unite Ukrainians into an organized independence movement and also sought foreign support for Ukraine's cause, warning that Moscow's expansionism posed a broader threat to international security.
In 1938, an undercover Soviet agent who had been tasked with infiltrating the OUN assassinated Konovalets in Rotterdam by gifting him a box of chocolates rigged with a bomb.
According to the President's Office, the exhumation ceremony for Konovalets at Crooswijk Cemetery in Rotterdam was attended on Aug. 11 by government officials, members of the local Ukrainian diaspora, and clergy from the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church.
Konovalets will be reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery just outside Kyiv.
Konovalets' repatriation was preceded by that of Andriy Melnyk, another prominent 20th-century military leader who headed the OUN-M, an offshoot of the organization that formed after Konovalets's assassination.
The return of historical leaders like Konovalets and Melnyk comes as Ukraine seeks to establish a National Pantheon to honor its heroes, past and present.
However, government officials involved with the project told the Kyiv Independent that there is no official list yet of which figures will be included — only an established protocol that will be used to decide once the bill becomes a law.
