These are Europe’s best-value cities for a weekend break - and Poland dominates the top five
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:40:46 UTC
23:40:46 KST

A new study has revealed the best-value European cities for a weekend away, with Polish destinations sweeping the top five and some of the continent’s biggest tourist hotspots proving much pricier.
Planning a last-minute European escape doesn’t have to mean paying a premium.
A new study by virtual card provider Getsby has revealed the best-value cities for a weekend break, analysing data from travel cost site Budget Your Trip across 100 destinations.
It compared the typical daily costs of accommodation, meals and local transport for two people travelling on a mid-range budget, revealing where your money will go furthest.
Flights aren’t included in the final figure, as they can vary hugely but, if in doubt, head to Poland. The Slavic nation takes six out of the top 10 spots, and the entire top five.
Poland reigns supreme
According to the data, Wroclaw in Poland is Europe’s most affordable city for a weekend trip for two people.
If you head to the City of Bridges, you can expect an average daily cost of €41 per person, and a total weekend trip which costs just €163 for two people.
Here, travellers tend to spend around €18.75 on food and €5.85 on local transport costs. There’s plenty to do, too, including a visit to the Rynek, one of Europe’s largest medieval market squares, and the Centennial Hall, a striking UNESCO-listed architectural landmark.
In second place is Poznań, where a weekend trip for two people costs an average of €168.50, or around €42 per person per day.
Travellers can expect to spend roughly €18.75 a day on food and €34 on accommodation, making it another particularly affordable option for a city break.
There’s lots to see without spending a fortune, including the colourful Old Market Square and Poznań Town Hall, where the famous mechanical goats appear each day. Cathedral Island is also worth a visit and is considered the birthplace of the Polish state.
Katowice takes third place, with a weekend for two costing around €239, or €60 per person per day.
Food accounts for about €32.75 a day, while hotels cost an average of €37.50, keeping the overall price relatively low.
The Silesian Museum is one of the city’s standout attractions. Built on the site of a former coal mine, it combines art and history with panoramic views from its observation tower.
Gdańsk comes fourth, with a two-day trip for two costing around €275.25, or €69 per person per day.
Visitors spend an average of €35 a day on food and €54 on hotels, with plenty of sights to fill a weekend.
The picturesque Long Market is a good place to start, while the historic waterfront around the Gdańsk Crane offers a glimpse into the city’s long maritime history.
Kraków rounds out the top five, costing around €295 for two people for a weekend, or €73.75 per person per day.
Hotels account for around €83 of the total, while local transport is particularly cheap at just €7 on average.
Once there, travellers can explore the atmospheric Jewish Quarter of Kazimierz, browse the historic Sukiennice Cloth Hall and visit St Mary’s Basilica, where the famous trumpet call rings out every hour.
Affordability varies across the continent
If you’ve been everywhere in Poland already, fear not – there are other, very affordable options across Europe.
Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria, takes sixth place, with a weekend trip costing around €77.25 per person per day.
Zagreb in Croatia follows in seventh, with the average traveller spending around €95 a day.
Sweden’s Malmö comes next at €105 per day, followed by Budapest in Hungary at €111.
Rounding out the top 10 and it’s back to Poland, namely the capital, Warsaw, a spot where visitors can expect to spend around €112 per person each day.
The least affordable options
At the other end of the scale is Zurich, Switzerland, where a weekend away costs an eye-watering €1,325 for two people, or around €331 per person per day.
Food is a major expense, with travellers spending around €112 a day on meals, while a hotel costs an average of €359.
Switzerland dominates the more expensive end of the ranking too, with Bern and Basel taking second and third place. A weekend for two costs around €1,240 and €1,189 respectively.
Venice and Paris complete the top five most expensive cities, with a two-person weekend costing around €1,180 and €1,133 respectively once food, accommodation and local transport are factored in.

+ Nicolas Wadimoff wins Solothurn Film Festival prize

Sybiha condemns Putin's visit to Etorofu, expresses Ukraine's solidarity with Japan
Sybiha stated this on X, according to Ukrinform.
"Ukraine's position is unwavering: Japan's sovereignty over the Northern Territories is grounded in historical facts and international law… Russia uses the same imperial playbook everywhere. It occupies foreign land, militarizes it, threatens its neighbours, and then tries to make the world accept the illegal as irreversible," the Foreign Minister said.

Etorofu is part of a group of islands off the eastern coast of Hokkaido Prefecture that were occupied by the former Soviet Union after World War II.
Japan claims the southern Kuril Islands, which it refers to as its Northern Territories, based on the 1855 Treaty of Commerce, Navigation and Delimitation.
Russia, meanwhile, insists that the Kuril Islands became part of the Soviet Union as a result of World War II.
In spring 2022, the Japanese government restored the wording "illegally occupied" in its annual Diplomatic Bluebook in reference to the Northern Territories — the islands of Etorofu, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai Islands.

Settler leaders denounce Kusra violence: ‘This is not our way’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:37:21 UTC
23:37:21 KST

Settler leaders, including the heads of the Yesha Council and Beit El Council, on Thursday publicly denounced the violence surrounding the Palestinian village of Kusra, warning that it was seriously damaging to Israel and the settlement movement.
Yisrael Ganz, chairman of the Yesha Council and head of the Binyamin Regional Council, said there was no justification for violence against uninvolved Palestinians or Israeli security forces.
“The events in Kusra are serious and are not our way,” Ganz said.
“There is no place for privately deciding to establish a hilltop outpost in the yard of a house, even when it is an illegal house or there is an attempt to take control of the area,” he said. “There is absolutely no justification for violence against uninvolved people or against the security forces.”
Ganz’s condemnation was joined by Beit El Council head Shai Alon, who gave an unusually blunt assessment of the events in an interview with Ynet on Thursday.
Alon said the violence was causing “irreversible damage” to Israel and to the settlement movement, and described those responsible for attacks on innocent Palestinians as criminals.
“These are criminal offenders who take out their rage on an innocent population,” Alon said, adding that the phenomenon had to be eradicated.
Alon said he had warned for years about what he described as a group of “lost youth” in the West Bank and accused the state of failing to deal adequately with the problem before it developed into violence.
“The State of Israel is not doing enough to deal with this phenomenon,” he told Ynet. “It begins with education and welfare, and when it is not dealt with, it reaches the places we are seeing today.”
Alon criticizes Ben-Gvir, Son Har-Melech
Alon also directed criticism at National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit MK Limor Son Har-Melech, saying that the young extremists involved in these incidents were politically closer to them.
He argued that greater pressure should have been applied to prevent what he described as the “terrible and horrific scenes” being seen in the West Bank.
Alon also criticized the Israel Police’s Judea and Samaria District, saying that, while he respected its officers, law enforcement had not done enough to address the phenomenon. He backed the IDF’s handling of the latest events.
He said that West Bank municipal leaders were united in opposing the violence, describing those involved as a relatively small group that did not represent the broader settlement movement.
Alon added that reservists who participate in such incidents while wearing IDF uniforms should immediately remove their uniforms and be released from reserve duty.
The condemnations came after several days of tensions in the Kusra and nearby Jalud areas of the northern West Bank.
The IDF said Israeli civilians had entered Palestinian homes and land in the area earlier this week, describing the activity as “illegal, reprehensible, and unacceptable.” The area was subsequently declared a closed military zone.
Dozens of settler extremists clashed with IDF forces on Wednesday after security forces evacuated an outpost established near Kusra. Footage seen by The Jerusalem Post showed extremists dismantling fences, blocking roads, and surrounding the area.
According to the IDF, security forces demolished two unauthorized outposts near Kusra and Jalud during Wednesday night, and one Israeli was detained. Golani Brigade Battalion 51 was also deployed to the area to carry out patrols and security missions.
Central Command chief Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth visited the area and met with a Palestinian family living there, the IDF said.
Commanders expressed concern over the conduct of Israeli civilians toward the family and ordered measures to restore order.
Ganz: Critics exploiting events against settlements
Ganz said the violence should be condemned regardless of attempts by opponents of the settlement movement to exploit it.
“There is no doubt that there are those who are exploiting these events for a campaign against the settlement movement, but that must not obscure the simple fact: What happened in Kusra is improper and unacceptable to us,” he said.
Ganz said that the Yesha leadership would continue working to expand Jewish settlement through organized and authorized channels.
“We are leading and will continue to lead settlement in Binyamin, Judea and Samaria with determination and responsibility, in an organized and proper manner,” he said.
At the same time, he called on the government to repeal the Oslo Accords and permit regulated Jewish settlement throughout open areas of the West Bank.
“I call on the Israeli government to cancel the Oslo Accords and allow legitimate and regulated Jewish settlement throughout all the open areas,” Ganz said.
The statements from Ganz and Alon placed two veteran settlement officials publicly against those responsible for the violence. The two have, thus, rejected attempts to portray the perpetrators as representative of the hundreds of thousands of Israelis living in West Bank settlements.

“A permanent Israeli military presence in southern Lebanon is inconsistent with the commitments given in the framework agreement and does not align with the long-term peace and security of both countries,” the official added.

Then we have Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav announcing 14 extra seats for the Dalits to cement his PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) politics. Congress too is trying to win back voters it lost decades ago. Then there is Chandrashekhar Azad, who is trying to consolidate his own space in the state.As Uttar Pradesh heads towards 2027, the question is: if the BSP continues to lose ground, where does Mayawati’s old support base go and which of her rivals stands to gain the most?
From 206 seats to one: How BSP lost ground
The BSP’s rise in UP politics was as dramatic as its fall. The party was founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984 with the idea of giving Dalits and other marginalized communities an independent voice.
Mayawati, who emerged as his political successor, took the BSP to great heights in Uttar Pradesh. Under her leadership, the BSP won a majority on its own in the 2007 assembly elections, winning 206 seats with a vote share of 30.43%.Dalits, who constitute around 21% of UP’s population as per the 2021 census, have for years been the core base of Mayawati’s Bahujan Samaj Party. But that dynamic has now changed.BSP is a much weaker force today. Mayawati has failed to mobilise Dalit support for her BSP in the last two elections in the state, thereby opening up the space for other political contenders. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BSP could win just 1 seat with a vote share of 12.88%. This was a sharp decline from the 19 seats and a 22.23% vote share that Mayawati had got in 2017.The 2024 Lok Sabha elections went on to showcase that Mayawati’s dismal 2022 performance was not an aberration. The BSP supremo failed to win even one Lok Sabha seat, while her party’s vote share dipped to 9.4% from 19.43% in 2019. Clearly, the results reinforced the gradual decline in BSP’s influence among Dalits.As Mayawati gears up for the 2027 assembly challenge, she faces an uphill road. The BSP chief has not just lost support of voters, but also control over her party. So, when Mayawati issued a stern message that all the candidates for the upcoming poll will be finalised by her and not by her nephew Akash Anand, it was an indication of the internal tussle in her party.Akash Anand, who has been in and out of Mayawati’s favour in the past, launched the party’s 2027 assembly poll campaign from Sadabad in Hathras this week.Mayawati, who has often been accused of helping the BJP, has ruled out any pre-poll alliance. She has claimed that some candidates have already been finalised for the upcoming assembly elections. Mayawati has asked party cadres to start rebuilding the party and drum up OBC support ahead of the polls. The cadres have apparently been asked to remind people of the party's past governance and convince them that the real benefit and welfare of the OBC community lie with the BSP and its "iron lady government".Mayawati, however, must consider that it will be difficult for the BSP to come back to power only by holding on to its core Dalit vote alone. It will have to recreate the Dalit-OBC combination that originally carried Mayawati to power in Lucknow with a majority of her own.
BJP's Dalit outreach gets sharper ahead of 2027
One interesting fallout of BSP’s decline has been the BJP’s aggressive outreach to woo the Dalits. When Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath announced the renaming of Bhadohi district as Sant Ravidas Nagar last month, he put the BJP right at the middle of the Dalit outreach battle ahead of 2027 polls.The move also revived an old political contest over name-change politics. Mayawati was the one who had renamed Bhadohi as Sant Ravidas Nagar in December 1997. Akhilesh Yadav restored the old name in 2014. Now, by bringing Sant Ravidas Nagar back, Yogi sought to make a bigger political point, accusing the SP of erasing a Dalit symbol while positioning the BJP as a party willing to restore it.Mayawati publicly welcomed the decision, a rare moment of agreement with the ruling party. She was quick, however, to remind voters that it was her government that had changed the district's name in the first place and that the decision was later reversed under Akhilesh.The party realises that Dalit votes are up for grabs and hence is going all out to woo them. The party’s 'Samrasta Sankalp Abhiyan’ appears planned to coincide with assembly elections in two key states, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab, early next year.Both these states have a sizeable population of Dalits who play an important role in many constituencies. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP and its ally Apna Dal (Soneylal) together bagged 63 Scheduled Caste (SC) seats compared to 20 won by the then Samajwadi Party-led opposition alliance. But the 2024 Lok Sabha polls changed the dynamics, with the SP and the Congress winning 43 of the 80 seats in the state and pushing the BJP to make an aggressive outreach. The loss of Faizabad seat to SP's Awadhesh Prasad, a Pasi leader, was particularly significant and gave Akhilesh Yadav fresh ammunition for his PDA pitch.Earlier this year, the Yogi Adityanath government approved the “Dr B R Ambedkar Murti Vikas Yojna" under which Rs 1 crore is to be allocated to each of the state's 403 assembly constituencies for the beautification and development of statues of social reformers.The BJP's efforts to woo Dalits has also been visible in its recent Cabinet expansion. Of the six new ministers inducted into the Yogi government, two were Dalits, Krishna Paswan from the Pasi community and Surendra Singh Daler from the Valmiki community. Three others were from OBC groups. Two non-Yadav OBC ministers were also given independent charge.The BJP's primary task ahead of 2027 would be to hold on to the non-Jatav Dalit support it built over the past decade and prevent a repeat of 2024.
SP’s Dalit outreach
The 2024 Lok Sabha elections also showed that the Dalits in UP were ready to back other political parties who wooed them. Dalit support played a key role in the spectacular success of Akhilesh Yadav’s Samajwadi Party, which won 37 seats in 2024.Together with its alliance partner Congress, the INDIA bloc won 43 of the 80 seats in the state, pushing the BJP on the back foot. Akhilesh Yadav, who has centred his politics around PDA (Pichhde, Dalits and Aplasankhyaks), gained from his Dalit outreach in the 2024 elections. His Samajwadi Party fielded two Dalit candidates from general seats. While one of them went on to win the all-important Faizabad seat, the other lost by just 10,585 votes to the BJP in Meerut.
How Samajwadi Party performed when they contested independently
Little wonder, in the run-up to the 2027 assembly elections, Akhilesh has already announced plans to field 14 Dalit candidates from general seats. Uttar Pradesh has 84 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and two for Scheduled Tribes. With 14 more candidates on general seats, the total tally of reserved candidates for SP will increase to 100. This will help reinforce his message to the Dalits in line with his PDA politics. The move will also help the SP shed the narrative of being a Muslim-Yadav party.
Congress tries to reclaim lost ground
Rahul Gandhi has made it clear that Dalits would now play a 'central role' in Congress. Before Mayawati and the BSP built their massive Dalit vote bank in the 1990s, Congress was the primary choice for Uttar Pradesh's Dalits. For nearly three decades after that, Congress was almost pushed out of UP politics.Rahul Gandhi has started his road to the UP election by acknowledging that the party had failed to take the right steps for the community in the 1980s and 1990s. He even praised Kanshi Ram for bringing Dalits together and giving the community a sense of confidence.Rahul has also made the Constitution a regular part of his social justice pitch. He is often seen carrying the red book of the Constitution while warning that constitutional rights and reservation are under threat. He has repeatedly invoked BR Ambedkar in the same pitch, asserting that Congress wants to position itself as a guardian of the Constitution.The party has also put a Dalit leader in charge of Uttar Pradesh. Rajendra Pal Gautam, who heads the Congress’s Scheduled Castes Department, has been appointed UP in-charge ahead of the 2027 polls. Interestingly, Gautam had also made an unsuccessful attempt to meet Mayawati at her Lucknow residence earlier this year.Whether the party will be able to translate this outreach into votes remains to be seen.
Chandrashekhar Azad adds another claimant
Then there is Chandrashekhar Azad, whose 2024 victory from Nagina made him a prominent figure in UP’s Dalit politics. Unlike BJP, SP or Congress, Azad is trying to build an independent space outside the BSP. His challenge now is to take that appeal beyond one constituency and build an organisation strong enough to matter across the state in 2027.
That is what makes the coming assembly election in Uttar Pradesh interesting. For decades, politics in Uttar Pradesh has revolved around caste. Political parties build their electoral strategies around social coalitions, loyalty of communities and traditional vote base.Mayawati may no longer command the Dalit vote the way she once did, but that vote bank has not disappeared. It simply has more claimants. And in 2027, where those voters eventually move could make a significant difference.

Syria turns to Interpol to pursue former Assad regime figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:35:04 UTC
23:35:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria turns to Interpol to pursue former Assad regime figures
Syria’s Justice Ministry has formed a committee to work with Interpol to pursue former regime officials abroad, an effort experts say could widen Damascus’s search for figures accused of crimes under Bashar al-Assad but faces significant legal and political obstacles.
Roger Lu Phillips, legal director at the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre, told The New Arab that the formation of the committee was a "meaningful first step in seeking to obtain custody of perpetrators of atrocities in Syria."
Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem announced the committee on Wednesday, telling Al-Ikhbariyah TV that it would coordinate international efforts to extradite suspects, pursue crimes linked to transitional justice and recover Syrian funds allegedly taken abroad.
He said greater cooperation with foreign governments could help Syria bring back suspects who fled the country and face prosecution at home.
The announcement came a day after a Damascus criminal court sentenced several former officials to death in absentia, including Assad and his brother Maher. The former president fled to Russia after his government was overthrown in December 2024.
But Damascus’s ability to bring former officials back to Syria will depend far less on Interpol itself than on the governments now hosting them.
Phillips said that Syrian authorities will need to compile thorough documentation on the accused, and that there will likely be follow-up questions from states responding to such requests, noting that responses to such requests will be essential.
Syrian human rights lawyer Anwar al-Bunni told The New Arab that extradition could not take place simply because Damascus requested it.
“Extradition does not simply happen because a country asks for a suspect to be handed over. There must be a proper legal process, and in some cases agreements between the countries concerned,” al-Bunni said.
“You need a complete case file containing the charges, evidence and other relevant material so that the authorities can establish that this is a genuine criminal case and not a politically motivated prosecution or a case related to someone’s opinions.”
"From a legal perspective, extradition is only available for cases of sufficient gravity and not for political or military crimes," Phillips explained.
"The request must also establish “dual criminality” i.e. that the alleged acts of the accused were a crime both in Syria and the state from which extradition is sought. There must be some evidence to show that the alleged crimes were committed by the accused, but the court examining the request will not assess the guilt or innocence of the accused which would require a higher evidentiary threshold," he continued.
He also said that some states may refuse extradition based on a number of reasons, including if they believe the accused could face torture or will not receive a fair trial.
What Interpol can do
Interpol can help locate suspects and circulate requests for their detention, but it cannot order an arrest or force a country to extradite someone.
As an Interpol member, Syria can seek a Red Notice, an international request asking police forces to locate and provisionally arrest a wanted person while extradition proceedings are considered.
Such requests generally require a domestic arrest warrant or judicial decision, along with information identifying the suspect and detailing the alleged crimes.
But a Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant. Governments remain free to decide whether to act on one according to their own laws and international obligations.
Al-Bunni said Syrian authorities would first have to assemble the relevant case material before seeking international action.
“The file has to go through the relevant authorities and then to Interpol,” he told The New Arab. “Interpol will examine the case and, if it meets its requirements, it can issue a Red Notice requesting that the person be located and provisionally arrested.”
“It is not a case of saying, ‘I want this person returned because he is a criminal,’ and Interpol simply acting on that request,” he added. “It is a much more complicated process, with a number of conditions that have to be met.”
Even an arrest would be only the beginning.
Extradition proceedings can involve courts, government ministries and lengthy appeals. Authorities in the country receiving Syria’s request could scrutinise the evidence against the suspect, the fairness of the Syrian proceedings and whether extradition would expose the person to treatment prohibited under domestic or international law.
That could make the pursuit of some of the most prominent former officials particularly difficult.
Assad, for example, has been granted asylum in Russia, which is unlikely to surrender him to Damascus regardless of whether Syria seeks Interpol assistance.
In practice, the committee may initially prove more useful in assembling case files, locating suspects and testing the willingness of individual governments to cooperate than in securing the immediate extradition of senior figures from the former regime.
Death sentences complicate extradition efforts
Syria’s pursuit also faces another obstacle of its own making: the death sentences handed down against Assad and other former officials.
Many countries will refuse extradition when a suspect could face execution, torture or other ill-treatment, or when there are concerns that a trial would not meet international standards. Governments that permit extradition in death-penalty cases can demand binding assurances that the punishment will not be imposed or carried out.
Al-Bunni said both the prospect of capital punishment and questions over due process could prove decisive when foreign governments consider Syrian extradition requests.
“The country where the suspect is located will also need to be satisfied that the person will receive a fair trial,” he told The New Arab. “The death penalty is another major issue, particularly for countries that do not recognise or apply capital punishment.”
“A complete file, evidence, witnesses and guarantees of a fair trial will all be important,” he added. “The possibility of a death sentence could also create serious difficulties for an Interpol request and for any eventual extradition.”
According to Phillips, any extradition request from a state party to the European Convention cannot agree to extradite for capital crimes, but in such cases Syria could make assurances that it would not apply the death penalty in order to facilitate extradition requests.
The fact that the latest sentences were issued in absentia could bring additional scrutiny from foreign courts.
Damascus may have to demonstrate that suspects extradited to Syria would receive a full opportunity for a new trial, with access to lawyers, sufficient time to prepare a defence and proceedings before an independent court.
Al-Qassem said the ministry was seeking the “highest degree of compatibility” between Syria’s judiciary and international standards while maintaining Syrian sovereignty over the transitional-justice process.
That balance is likely to become increasingly important as Damascus seeks cooperation abroad.
Human-rights organisations and legal experts have already raised concerns over the use of the death penalty and the safeguards surrounding trials of former regime figures. Foreign governments asked to extradite suspects will have to make their own assessment of those proceedings before agreeing to send anyone back.

The real story behind Israel's Gaza plan 'Rejection' — and where it goes from here – analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:34:01 UTC
23:34:01 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel-Hamas war
- The real story behind Israel's Gaza plan 'Rejection' — and where it goes from here - analysis
The real story behind Israel's Gaza plan 'Rejection' — and where it goes from here - analysis
Netanyahu explicitly said the "IDF will not make any withdrawal until Hamas disarms" - something that seemingly contradicts what is written in Articles 8 and 13 of the Gaza Roadmap. But does it?
Since US President Trump took office, we've rarely seen Prime Minister Netanyahu publicly rejecting any of his plans or ideas - but that happened last Sunday, when Netanyahu declared that Israel "rejects the Gaza roadmap." Or did it?
Netanyahu explicitly said the "IDF will not make any withdrawal until Hamas disarms" - something that seemingly contradicts what is written in Articles 8 and 13 of the Gaza Roadmap, published by the Board of Peace on July 30. Yet since last weekend, Israel has refrained from conducting targeted strikes in Gaza, and various reports in Israeli media describe much stricter rules of engagement for anything perceived as a “threat.” So why did Netanyahu say Israel rejects the plan?
Israel has major problems with certain clauses of the Roadmap, especially regarding how the verification mechanism works. The International Verification Committee (IVC) leans on Turkey and Qatar - two mediators Israel has long distrusted over their ties to Hamas - to help oversee compliance. And under Article 8, the weapons handed over aren't destroyed - they're "decommissioned and stored" until rendered unusable, meaning heavy weapons, production sites, and even personal weapons stay inside Gaza rather than being removed. These issues make it nearly impossible for the Israeli government to accept and therefore fully commit to the plan.
Furthermore, there is no doubt that the Israeli government - and the Israeli public - do not believe Hamas will actually hand over its weapons, or that if it does, it won't find a way to regain control of them, or rebuild its arsenal, down the line. In fact, according to a newly released poll, this skepticism isn't just widespread - it's close to a national consensus.
The Jewish People Policy Institute's (JPPI) August Israeli Society Index found that 58% of all Israelis believe the disarmament agreement will not be fulfilled, and that the situation in Gaza will essentially remain as it is today. Among Jewish Israelis specifically, the pessimism is even sharper - 63% don't believe the agreement will hold. Only 3% of all Israelis believe in the full scenario the roadmap envisions - Hamas disarming completely and Israel withdrawing from the entire Strip - and among Jewish respondents, that figure is effectively zero.
Suggested articles
- IDF to allow residents in West Bank's Qusra to remain in homes as soldiers confront violent settlers | LIVE BLOG | i24NEWS, Ariel Oseran, Yana Suryadnaya
- US allies question Trump's leverage in Middle East after Netanyahu’s rejection of Gaza plan - report | i24NEWS
- In response to Iran, Trump demands compensation for victims and families killed by Islamic Regime | LIVE BLOG | i24NEWS, Ariel Oseran, Yana Suryadnaya
Seen through that lens, Netanyahu's rejection is simple electoral math. With elections approaching, and nearly two-thirds of Jewish Israelis not believing the disarmament deal will ever happen, there is no electoral benefit in being the prime minister who publicly endorsed a plan most of the country already expects to fail. Rejecting the roadmap costs him nothing with a skeptical electorate - regardless of what Israel actually does on the ground.
President Trump, for his part, seems, for now, to be indulging Netanyahu's position. His reaction to the rejection was notably thin. Asked in the Oval Office whether he had any response to Netanyahu's statement, he said: "I have a response. I put it out today on Truth - a good response." No such post ever appeared. He added, as he often does, that his relationship with Netanyahu is "very good."
That muted, almost evasive response is itself becoming the story. According to Politico, diplomats and officials familiar with US Middle East policy say Netanyahu's rejection has exposed a deeper problem: Washington either lacks the leverage to move the Gaza plan forward, or isn't willing to use it. An Arab diplomat quoted in the report warned the rejection carries "significant implications for long-term regional stability and Israel's security," and said Trump is the only one capable of pressuring Netanyahu to reconsider.
Certain Arab and regional countries likely want to see Trump apply harsher pressure on Netanyahu to advance their own interests in Gaza - but so far, the two leaders appear aligned, which is slowing the process down - but doesn’t stop it.
This Israeli military restraint in Gaza is an earlier commitment made by Israel back in October when the ceasefire started. Article 2 of the 15-point plan states: "Israel shall fully complete, without delay, all remaining commitments under the Sharm el-Sheikh Protocol, particularly the cessation of military operations as detailed in the annex". Israel simply never implemented it, on the pretext that Hamas had not met its own disarmament obligations under the Gaza Peace Plan and UNSCR 2803.
By doing this, Israel has effectively given the Board of Peace a "green light" to move forward with the step-by-step process in Gaza. From the Israeli government’s perspective, they are now fulfilling a commitment they made last year after Hamas agreed to the process of disarmament - yet Israel doesn’t formally commit to the new 15-point plan.
The next phase is meant to include the entry of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) and the International Stabilization Force (ISF), which the Israeli cabinet approved last month.
Meanwhile, the Board of Peace's director-general for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, announced that the International Verification Committee (IVC) has been established and has started working in Gaza. This is the same body that will verify the "decommissioning and storing" of Hamas's heavy weapons, military production sites, weapons depots, and tunnels, according to Article 8.
So is Netanyahu really rejecting "Trump's peace plan"? The longer answer is that Israel is, in practice, already behaving as if bound by the roadmap - very limited targeted strikes, restraint at the Yellow Line, a cabinet that approved NCAG and ISF entry weeks ago - while rejecting its public statement in order not to commit to it. The rejection shields Israel from having to endorse a plan it doesn't believe will work, and also shields Netanyahu politically, less than three months before the elections.

Russia, Ukraine conduct another civilian exchange in Belarus — media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:32:47 UTC
23:32:47 KST

MINSK, August 13. /TASS/. Another civilian exchange between Russia and Ukraine took place in Belarus, the BelTA news agency reported.
Eight people went to Russia, while seven returned to Ukraine. The humanitarian exchange took place at the Novaya Guta checkpoint on the Belarusian-Ukrainian border. According to BelTA, the civilians received hot meals including soup and a main course, as well as drinking water and fruit.
The humanitarian mission was accompanied by the Regional Delegation of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Russia and Belarus. Assem Elessawy, the ICRC Regional Delegation's deputy head of operations, stressed the importance of such humanitarian operations in reuniting families and returning people to their countries of citizenship. In some cases, he said, people experience difficulties with transportation.
"For example, they cannot return home on their own. We can provide this kind of support by arranging transport, regular or specialized, depending on the request. We handle every case individually, from the route to ensuring the necessary conditions," BelTA quoted him as saying.
Belarusian ambulance crews are on duty at the checkpoint. Paramedics are ready to provide necessary assistance and advice to civilians.
More than 70 exchanges between Russia and Ukraine have taken place in Belarus in recent years, BelTA reported.

"Russia uses the same imperial playbook everywhere": Kyiv condemns Putin's visit to Kuril Islands

"Russia uses the same imperial playbook everywhere": Kyiv condemns Putin's visit to Kuril Islands
Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has commented on Vladimir Putin's visit to Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, describing Russia's control of the island as an occupation of Japanese territory and calling on international partners to further isolate and increase pressure on Russia.
Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter)
Quote: "Putin's provocative visit to Japan's Etorofu island demonstrates utter disrespect to Japan and represents a deliberate attempt to intimidate, escalate tensions and normalise illegal occupation.
However, no provocative visits can change the reality: Etorofu is part of Japan's Northern Territories, occupied by Russia.
We believe that Putin's visit to Etorofu also proves that Moscow only understands the language of strength. The aggressive Russian regime does not appreciate, respect, or reciprocate constructive steps."
Details: Sybiha said Ukraine's stance on the issue remains unwavering, as Japan's sovereignty over the Northern Territories – as Japan refers to the four southernmost Kuril Islands – is based on historical facts and international law.
"Russia uses the same imperial playbook everywhere. It occupies foreign land, militarises it, threatens its neighbours, and then tries to make the world accept the illegal as irreversible. Ukraine knows this pattern all too well. It must not succeed, whether in Europe or in the Pacific," he noted.
The foreign minister also expressed solidarity with Japan and called on international partners to condemn Putin's visit to Iturup, reject any attempt to normalise Russia's occupation, further isolate Russia and step up sanctions pressure.
The Kuril Islands belonged to Japan until 1945 but are now controlled by Russia. Japan claims the four southernmost islands and has long demanded their return. The Soviet Union annexed the chain of islands at the end of World War II and deported around 17,000 Japanese residents.
In 2022, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree recognising the Kuril Islands as Japanese territory temporarily occupied by Russia.
Background:
- On Thursday 13 August, Putin travelled to Sakhalin Oblast, where the Kuril Islands are located, to observe the final stage of exercises conducted by Russia's Pacific Fleet. He also visited Iturup during the trip.
- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has criticised Putin's visit to Iturup, the largest of the disputed Kuril Islands. In response, Dmitry Medvedev, former Russian president and deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, called the islands "Russian land" and threatened anyone who disagreed with "monstrous consequences".

Scientists report very low radioactivity value on Arctic archipelagos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:31:39 UTC
23:31:39 KST

ARKHANGELSK, August 13. /TASS/. Participants in the Arctic Floating University expedition recorded very low values of radioactivity during missions ashore Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land, Senior Researcher at the Laverov Federal Research Center for Integrated Arctic Studies' Environmental Radiology Laboratory (the Russian Academy of Sciences' Urals Branch) Andrey Puchkov told TASS. Results of studies conducted in the 2025 season have shown an increase in the radon flux in the coastal area of the Russian Harbor Bay on Novaya Zemlya compared to results of observations conducted in 2024. The expedition in 2026 has found no anomalies.
"We measured radon at all missions ashore. The values ranged from the minimum - less than one millibecquerel (mBq) per square meter per second - to 200 millibecquerels per square meter per second. All the recorded indicators are background values. Permafrost, which performs a barrier, shielding function, does not allow radioactive gases to the surface. The radon flux density's highest values most likely are related to geological features of the territories, to fault and fractured zones," the expert said.
Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that is formed by the decay of uranium. The gas is volatile, and its ecological role is very high. Warming in the Arctic leads to the permafrost melting and increases radon's release to the surface.
While measuring the alpha particle flux, scientists have found almost zero values. This indicates extremely low activities of alpha-emitting radionuclides in the near-surface soil layer. The laboratory has measured also gamma radiation. Results showed only background values. Alpha radiation points to the presence of radioactive decay of heavy elements such as uranium, radium, thorium; Gamma radiation is the number and energy of photons (gamma quanta) that pass through a certain site per unit of time. The gamma particles flow indicates the radiation intensity and the activity of radioactive sources.
The expedition's researchers carried out measurements in the area of the Tikhaya Bay polar station on the Hooker Island, on the Franz Josef Land Archipelago's Heiss, Wilczek and Prince Georg Land Islands and in the area of the Russian Harbor polar station on the Novaya Zemlya Archipelago's Severny Island. At all the locations, the scientists sampled soil, mosses, lichens and vascular plants.
Bottom sediments' radioactivity
In the Barents Sea's northeastern part, during the sections and in areas of missions ashore, the expedition's radiologists sampled bottom sediments. Similar work was carried out in 2019 and in 2024. Results of 2026 tests will be used to structure the temporal dynamics of the distribution of natural and man-made radionuclide activities and to determine how much the man-made load on the Arctic ecosystems has changed. Right now, it is decreasing and there are no powerful man-made sources of radiation: there are no tests, nor dumping from burial sites.
However, monitoring needs to be continued, as the situation may change due to the redistribution of radionuclides from terrestrial ecosystems. In particular, climate warming may cause the release of man-made radionuclides, deposited in glaciers during past nuclear tests.
About the expedition
The 20th voyage of the Arctic Floating University scientific and educational expedition continued from July 1 to July 22, 2026 on board the Professor Molchanov scientific research vessel. The expedition organizers are: the Lomonosov Northern Arctic Federal University and the Northern Department for Hydrometeorology and Environmental Monitoring (Sevhydromet). The project's official sponsors and partners are: the Russian Federation's Ministry of Science and Higher Education, the Russian Geographical Society, general sponsor - VTB, the Norilsk Nickel Company, and the Floating University Coordination Center based at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology (MIPT).

Oman says massive oil spill reaches coastline: What damage could it do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:29:58 UTC
23:29:58 KST

Oman says massive oil spill reaches coastline: What damage could it do?
Oil has been spilling from the Caroline Bezengi, a tanker that has been leaking crude since running aground off Oman.
A vast oil spill from a leaking tanker reached Oman’s coastline on Wednesday, its environment agency said.
This oil spill threatens to become one of the world’s worst in years after spreading largely unchecked for several weeks, experts say.
On Monday, Oman said it was working to contain the spill, which had by then affected roughly 390 square kilometres (150sq miles), according to analysis by the country’s environment agency.
The slick now covers an area of more than 2,000sq km (770sq miles), said John Amos, an oil spill specialist who reviewed satellite imagery obtained by Reuters. It could affect about 40km (25 miles) of coast near Ras Madraka, as well as Masirah Island, Oman’s Environment Authority said.
Here’s what we know.
What happened?
Oil has been leaking from the tanker Caroline Bezengi since it ran aground about 22 nautical miles (41km) from the Omani coastal town of Sharbithat some time after the crew reported a suspected explosion on June 8. It had been en route from Russia to India.
Reuters reported that the tanker was carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of sanctioned oil and that it ran aground on June 30.
An investigation by the news agency AFP found that the ship had been stranded for several weeks near Oman’s al-Qibliyyah Island.
In the meantime, the oil has been spreading towards Oman’s coastline.
The Oman News Agency (ONA) quoted the country’s environment authority saying that “today’s monitoring results showed that some beaches in the Ras Madrakah area were affected by oil pollution”.
The Indian Ocean town sits about 200km (125 miles) from al-Qibliyyah.
The slick is now concentrated around the Hallaniyat Archipelago off the southern coast, where a marine reserve was established last year to protect sensitive ecosystems home to diverse marine life, including rare sea turtles.
On Wednesday, the ONA reported that “a coastal stretch of up to 40 km in the [Ras Madrakah] area is expected to be affected”.
The southern beaches of Masirah Island, which lies 15km (nine miles) off the coast of Oman, could be contaminated “in the coming hours”, affecting a 10-20km (six-to-12-mile) stretch of coastline, it said.
An unnamed spokesperson for the United Nations International Maritime Organization said it was “closely monitoring” the leakage.
How did this happen?
British maritime security company Vanguard told AFP that the tanker had suffered “explosions” in early June as it sailed off the coast of Yemen, causing water to enter several sections of the vessel. It ran aground off the coast of Oman some time after this.
There has been no official explanation for the explosions and no party has claimed an attack. However, the vessel was navigating two separate wars on its journey from Russia to India. Tankers have been frequently targeted in the Gulf region in recent months as the US war on Iran has continued.
In April, the Caroline Bezengi sailed from the Russian port of Novorossiysk on the Black Sea, a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war.
It is believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” used to circumvent Western sanctions on its oil exports. It last sailed under a Cameroonian flag.
Rentoor Shipmanagement and Villar Shipmanagement, both based in China, are registered as the ship’s owner and operator, respectively, according to the open-source database OpenSanctions.
Russia’s shadow fleet includes ageing vessels that have often been criticised for poor maintenance, lack of insurance and lacklustre safety standards.
Ukraine has previously carried out assaults on shadow fleet vessels believed to be carrying Russian oil.
The Caroline Bezengi then passed through the Suez Canal at the end of May, ship-tracking data shows, before sailing through the Red Sea and past Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthi fighters have entered a wider regional war between the United States, Israel and Iran and are targeting Saudi Arabia-flagged ships.
What damage could the oil spill cause?
Last week, advocacy group Greenpeace warned that the spill was on the verge of causing an “environmental disaster”.
Christopher D’Elia, a specialist in oil spills and a professor emeritus at Louisiana State University in the United States, told Al Jazeera the estimated 800,000 barrels of crude on board the Caroline Bezengi would amount to a “fairly large spill”.
“This spill raises a lot of issues,” D’Elia told Al Jazeera.
“These illegal tankers don’t comply with the ‘polluter pays’ principle that is the basis for how the US and other developed nations regulate spills,” D’Elia said.
“The ‘responsible party’ must finance the cleanup in the US. In this case, there is no responsible party.”
Meanwhile, Iranian media reported on Wednesday that a separate oil spill in the Strait of Hormuz had reached the island of Qeshm, affecting beaches and an environmentally sensitive mangrove forest.
State-run news agency IRNA said the slick had affected areas on Qeshm’s southern coast, as well as parts of the smaller neighbouring island of Hengam.
Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said pollution had been observed at three locations and on the sea surface, adding that its source seemed to be a “foreign bulk carrier”, without specifying the name of the ship.
The risk of oil spills in the Gulf has risen sharply because of strikes on tankers during the five-month US-Iran war. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has reported 65 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and across the Middle East since the beginning of March.
“Any party that benefits from commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is legally and morally obligated to take action to compensate for and remedy the environmental damage caused to the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman,” he said.

Can US rights groups stop Washington's unlawful ICC sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:29:25 UTC
23:29:25 KST

Last month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was stepping up efforts to “dismantle” the ICC, including by expanding the use of sanctions and pressing the court’s member countries to withdraw.
The White House action falls into a pattern: ever since the start of Israel’s genocidal war in Palestine, people involved in documenting the war crimes and prosecuting the accused have been targetted by the US.
To date, the US administration has used Executive Order 1420 to sanction ICC prosecutors, eight ICC judges, the UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, and three leading Palestinian human rights groups in an effort to shield Israel from scrutiny.
Those targeted have had bank accounts frozen or closed, financial transactions rejected, digital services cut off, and travel restricted.
That pressure campaign now faces its most direct legal challenge yet. On Tuesday, four major US human rights groups sued the US administration over the sanctions on the ICC.
The plaintiffs, Human Rights Watch, the Centre for Constitutional Rights, the American Friends Service Committee and the Open Society Institute, argue that the current sanctions violate their First and Fifth Amendment rights and the Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
“Our lawsuit is seeking to put an end to the sanctions regime as a whole,” according to Elizabeth Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
“We are asking the court to stop the US administration from enforcing the sanctions already in place and to prevent it from issuing any additional sanctions,” Evenson tells TRT World.
“We aim to make sure that the ICC and all those working with it can do so without fear of reprisal,” she adds.
Intimidation as a tool of US policy
Washington has long argued that the ICC's investigation of American citizens violates US sovereignty because it does not recognise the court's jurisdiction over its nationals.
But US citizens accused of crimes committed abroad can already face prosecution in the countries where those crimes occurred, in line with a principle of international law.
In 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese was sanctioned by Washington just days after publishing a report detailing how dozens of corporations, including Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Palantir, were enabling and profiting from Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territory and its genocide in Gaza.
Albanese lost her US bank account and, briefly, her only apartment after Washington accused her of "biased and malicious activities" for doing exactly what her mandate requires: documenting violations in the occupied Palestinian territories and reporting them to the UN system.
Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan, on the other hand, who opened the Gaza investigation and sought Netanyahu's arrest warrant, was forced to step aside in May 2025 amid a misconduct allegation.
Khan was cleared of any wrongdoing by an ICC judicial panel in March 2026, but a bureau of member states voted to disregard that finding and removed him anyway.
Khan later in July revealed that US senators threatened him directly.
“Twelve senators wrote, and they said, ‘If you target Israel, we will target you and your family. You have been warned.’ That’s almost a verbatim quotation,” Khan said.
In September 2025, three of Palestine's most prominent human rights groups; Al-Haq, the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights, and Al-Mezan, were also sanctioned for supplying the ICC with the testimonies, forensic data, and casualty records their teams have compiled for decades, material that helped underpin the arrest warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant.
But Washington's intimidation failed to silence anyone documenting or prosecuting Israel's war crimes in Gaza, where the Palestinian death toll has passed 75,000 since October 2023.
The US administration’s campaign to dismantle the ICC and punish those seeking accountability for grave human rights violations would have consequences far beyond the individuals and organisations directly targeted, according to Joyce Ajlouny, General Secretary of the American Friends Service Committee.
“It is an affront to all victims and survivors of war crimes and genocide.”
The US “seeks to intimidate human rights defenders and deter people of conscience from advocating for the rights and dignity of others,” Ajlouny adds.
Built on what's already succeeded
The groups are not challenging the sanctions on untested legal ground.
These sanctions are an assault on the rule of law, independent judges and prosecutors, and civil society in the US and around the world, according to James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative.
“They betray historic US leadership in the cause of international justice and are a slap in the face to victims and survivors of grave crimes everywhere who depend on the ICC as a court of last resort,” Goldston adds.
In 2020, the US administration sanctioned senior ICC officials, including then Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda, after the court announced it would investigate war crimes by US forces in Afghanistan and Israeli forces in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Bensouda had reportedly received direct threats from Israeli intelligence officials warning her against pursuing cases that could put her or her family at risk. The US then froze her assets and barred her from entering the country. A federal judge later struck down the sanctions, ruling that they violated the First Amendment.
Similarly, in May 2026, a federal judge in Washington blocked Albanese's sanctions outright, finding that her ICC recommendations were nothing more than protected speech with "no binding effect" on the court.
The rights groups argue that the same reasoning that led courts to find sanctions against lawyers and rights defenders unconstitutional under the First Amendment should apply again.
“The fact that so many leading human rights and humanitarian organisations have come together to challenge Trump’s unlawful executive order demonstrates the widespread harm it is causing across civil society groups dedicated to bringing those responsible for grave crimes to justice,” says lead counsel Andrew Loewenstein of Foley Hoag LLP.
“... They are seeking an end to this sanctions regime, which transgresses the president’s authority and violates international and US law, including the rights to freedom of expression and religion,” Loewenstein adds.
Their complaint also argues the order exceeds presidential authority altogether, built on what they call a manufactured "national emergency" that doesn't survive scrutiny under US sanctions law itself.
If they win, it would be the first ruling to challenge the sanctions structure as a whole, rather than carving out exceptions one name at a time.
Governments should not allow sanctions to become a tool for shielding alleged war criminals from accountability, according to Evenson.
“We are asking the court to protect justice. In the meantime, there is a clear role here for all ICC member countries around the globe.”
“They can stand together and make clear that they support the ICC’s work, and that they will work together to protect the court’s independence,” she tells TRT World.

‘I’ve reached the limit of how much I can worry’: brother joins search for missing Israelis in Vienna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:29:09 UTC
23:29:09 KST

“I’ve reached the limit of how much I can worry,” Ronen Yahalomi said from Vienna, where he has joined efforts to find his sister Mali and her daughter Liel, who have been missing since Friday.
Ronen, Mali’s older brother, arrived in the Austrian capital on behalf of the family and has spent recent days in contact with Austrian authorities, Israeli officials and members of Vienna’s Jewish community as the search for the two women continues.
The disappearance has already prompted an extensive investigation, with Austrian media reporting that the Mossad is also involved in efforts to locate them.
“You have to understand,” Ronen told ynet. “Last Monday we celebrated her 50th birthday in Modi’in.”
According to Ronen, Mali had virtually no advance notice of the trip. Liel had organized it as a surprise gift for her mother, booking the flights as well as accommodations in Prague and Vienna.
“The whole trip came as a surprise to her. She had no time to prepare for it,” he said.
“The trip to Prague was planned by Liel as a surprise gift. Mali had no idea about it. That’s the impression everyone had. Liel organized everything, bought the plane tickets and booked a room in Prague and a room in Vienna.
“How much time did Mali really have to prepare?” Ronen said. “The party was Monday, and they left the next day, Tuesday.”
That detail has taken on added significance amid speculation surrounding the circumstances of their disappearance, including claims linking it to Mali’s senior position at Bank of Jerusalem. The rumors have already affected the bank’s share price.
Ronen said he had no information supporting such theories.
“I have no idea about that,” he said. “I really have no idea. I don’t get into rumors. My sister earned well and was completely financially independent.”
A police source has said the investigation is being handled by Lahav 433’s national financial crime unit because of its capabilities, its contacts with police and law enforcement agencies abroad and its experience managing complex international investigations. All possible directions are being examined.
Mali grew up in Tel Aviv’s Yad Eliyahu neighborhood in a secular family and became religious after completing her military service. She later married another ba’al teshuva, and the couple divorced when their two children were young.
She raised the children while studying and building a career, eventually earning a master’s degree in economics and reaching a senior position at Bank of Jerusalem, where she works in the bank’s control division overseeing money transfers.
Relatives describe her as responsible and stable, a devoted mother and, for the past six months, grandmother to a baby boy born to her eldest son.
“She and her children are religious, but they’re not fanatics,” relatives said. They are familiar with the secular world and live comfortably alongside it, they added.
Travel was something Mali and Liel shared. This was not their first trip together. Ronen could not recall every destination, but said the two traveled once or twice a year, usually for several days, and regularly sent videos and remained in contact with the family.
This trip initially appeared no different.
Shortly before Shabbat began, the women sent a video from the studio apartment they had rented in Vienna. Liel filmed the room, her mother and herself reflected in mirrors. Both sounded happy and pleased with the apartment.
Nothing in the video appeared to suggest what would follow.
The women observe Shabbat, making several details of their final known movements particularly puzzling.
They rented the Vienna apartment for only one day and apparently left on Saturday. Their phones’ final location signal was also recorded that day.
“When religious Israelis come here, they usually make contact,” a secretary at the city’s Chabad House told ynet. “They reserve a place for a Shabbat meal. We didn’t hear anything from them. Nothing.”
The central mystery remains how two adult women, traveling together, could disappear without leaving an apparent digital trail.
Their phones were last located near a public park by Vienna’s main railway station. After that, there was nothing.
In an era when phones, credit cards and smartwatches routinely leave electronic traces, disappearing without a detectable trail is extraordinarily difficult, particularly for travelers who need navigation, public transportation schedules and other digital services to move around an unfamiliar city.
The apartment where Mali and Liel stayed Friday is in Vienna’s fourth district, at 13 Hauptmannstrasse, about two kilometers from the city center. The address contains a courtyard with several buildings and roughly 60 apartments.
Reaching major tourist attractions or Jewish institutions generally requires public transportation, an unusual choice for two women who observe Shabbat.
Also unexplained is why they apparently carried their belongings on Saturday and traveled roughly 2.2 kilometers from the apartment toward the central railway station.
For now, those questions remain unanswered, leaving Ronen and the rest of the family waiting for any sign of Mali and Liel.

Transport costs soar amid low water levels in Rhine

23:26:51 KST

Transport costs soar amid low water levels in Rhine
The exceptionally low water level of the Rhine is causing difficulties for fuel logistics to Switzerland, with transport costs soaring from CHF22–28 ($27-34) to as much as CHF240 per tonne from Rotterdam to Basel.
According to the Swiss Touring Club (TCS), this increase translates into a rise in prices at the pump of between 12 and 16 centimes per litre of petrol.
The cause is the river running dry, forcing barges to travel with loads reduced to a minimum, with the stretch at Kaub (Rhineland-Palatinate) effectively cut off for vessels coming from northern European ports. The result is a crisis that compounds the already delicate summer situation, with Switzerland relying on the Rhine for around a fifth of its oil imports.
Despite the surge in costs, supplies remain guaranteed. This has been confirmed by the Federal Office for Economic Supply (FOES), which refers to “severely limited” transport capacity but states that this can be offset by rail, road, oil pipelines and company stocks.
+ Rhine almost no longer navigable owing to low water levels
Government minister Albert Rösti has, however, admitted that it may soon be necessary to draw on strategic reserves of petroleum products. “We are experiencing record-breaking heat and the heatwave is extraordinary: there is still no end in sight,” said the Minister for Transport and the Environment yesterday. Distribution companies such as Volenergy, which supplies the BP, Shell and Ruedi Rüssel brands, are already tackling the crisis by drawing on their warehouses and the refinery in Cressier in canton Neuchatel.
Like so many other sectors, the oil industry is also waiting for rain: but even an isolated thunderstorm would not be enough to raise the river level, which would require heavy and prolonged rainfall. Motorists must therefore remain on guard: for the time being, price rises at the pump have been partly masked by a slight fall in crude oil prices due to an easing of international tensions, but the logistical costs remain unchanged.
Meanwhile, economists at Swiss bank Raiffeisen are playing down the impact that the low water levels of the Rhine will have on the national economy, estimating an effect on gross domestic product (GDP) of no more than 0.1%.

Hundreds still missing in Colombia as desperation grips earthquake rescue effort
CALI/PEREIRA, Colombia, Aug 13 - Hopes of finding more survivors from the powerful earthquake that rocked Colombia early this week were fading on Thursday as rescue workers narrowed their searches, while families in the worst-hit areas waited for news of missing relatives.
In Cali, the country's third-largest city, crews have turned their attention from a search-and-rescue effort to debris removal at most sites, a sign the disaster response was entering a grimmer phase after the crucial first 72 hours.
The 7.4-magnitude quake struck shortly after 7:30 a.m. local time on Monday, toppling apartment blocks, damaging homes, schools and hospitals and sending residents into the streets across western Colombia, home to the country's coffee farms.
At least 273 people were killed — many in Cali and Pereira, a city in the coffee region — and more than 3,800 injured, according to government data on Thursday morning. It also said 377 people were still reported to be missing.
In Pereira, Enrique Marin said he drove more than 10 hours from Bogota after getting a call from a friend who told him Marin's mother was trapped underneath the rubble of her home.
"My mother was rescued six hours after the earthquake. They pulled her out with vital signs, but she died on the way to the hospital," Marin told Reuters as he stood in front of the debris clutching a bicycle from his childhood, the only item he said he was able to recover from the house.
He said his mother was found in her pajamas with the house keys still in her hand.
At the Torres del Limonar residential complex in southern Cali, rescue brigades with buckets and cranes continued to search for 15 people still missing. Rescuers have found seven survivors and 13 corpses at the site.
Monica Mina, a 38-year-old restaurant owner, told Reuters she and other chefs in the city were working almost around the clock to distribute about 1,000 meals a day — including scrambled eggs and bits of pork — for rescuers, medics and volunteers.
FIRST MAJOR TEST FOR NEW COLOMBIAN GOVERNMENT
Outside major cities, rescue groups said smaller towns and communities were still struggling with little or no response from the Colombian government.
Nazly Lozano, the International Rescue Committee's program assistant at the port city of Buenaventura northwest of Cali, said rescue workers had not reached some stricken areas until Wednesday night, leaving locals to dig through the rubble with their bare hands in a desperate search for survivors.
IRC workers said some neighborhoods in Buenaventura remained inaccessible due to armed groups, some of which seized food donations, vowing to distribute these items themselves. Residents still lack basic services such as water and electricity and were using logs to cook their meals, the IRC workers said.
More than 150 aftershocks have been recorded since Monday, adding to the risks for rescue workers combing through the debris as well as people made homeless by the initial quake, which was one of the strongest felt in Colombia in several decades.
The government has estimated the quake destroyed more than 12,500 homes.
President Abelardo De La Espriella, who took office just days before the disaster, said on Wednesday he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund to channel domestic and international aid toward rebuilding hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure.
The disaster is shaping up as the first major test for the conservative president, who campaigned on cutting public spending and now faces the task of financing relief and reconstruction while showing his government can manage a national crisis.
Colombian officials have also pushed back against criticism over the handling of foreign assistance, saying the government has not rejected any country's offer but will only accept international search-and-rescue teams that meet recognized certification standards. REUTERS

Ice cream manufacturers are changing their recipes due to consumer demand for healthier treats
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
17:23:48 EEST

Ice cream manufacturers are changing their recipes due to consumer demand for healthier treats
Kyiv • UNN
Because of the popularity of GLP-1 medications and demand for healthy food, ice cream manufacturers are reducing portion sizes, increasing protein content, and simplifying ingredients. Ice cream sales in the United States fell by 1.5%, but manufacturers are betting on low-calorie products.
Ice cream manufacturers may receive an additional boost to summer sales due to the rapid rise in temperatures, but behind the scenes they are preparing for a future in which consumers will look for fewer reasons to feel guilty about indulging in sweets. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The growing popularity of appetite-suppressing GLP-1 drugs, demand for healthier food, and increased attention to product ingredients are forcing manufacturers to reduce portion sizes, increase protein content in recipes, and simplify product formulations.
According to NielsenIQ, ice cream sales volumes in the United States fell by 1.5% year over year as of June 13, while a Boston Consulting Group study showed that people taking GLP-1 drugs had reduced their consumption of frozen treats by at least 10%.
At the same time, manufacturers see little evidence that consumers are giving up ice cream altogether. Instead, they are betting that shoppers will continue to indulge if treats contain fewer calories, more protein, and simpler ingredients.
For example, Ferrero-owned Blue Bunny reports high demand for its 150-calorie Mini Swirls and is reformulating products to remove ingredients such as high-fructose corn syrup, as well as artificial colors and flavors.
This trend reflects a broader challenge for the industry, as changing eating habits reshape consumers’ expectations of products they consider treats.
Rethinking treats
The Magnum Ice Cream Company, which owns the Magnum and Ben & Jerry's brands, has accelerated the development of products focused on healthy lifestyles, citing significant growth for the frozen Greek yogurt brand Yasso.
According to the manufacturer, Yasso has recorded average annual growth of about 20% over the past five years, while other brands in the group, including Breyers CarbSmart and Popsicle Sugar-Free, are especially popular among consumers taking GLP-1 drugs.
Consumers are increasingly seeking products that combine the enjoyment of a treat with such attributes as higher protein content, fewer calories, and controlled portion sizes. Magnum brands account for 26% of the $2.2 billion American healthy-lifestyle and functional ice cream segment.
According to Boston Consulting Group, about 16 million Americans are taking GLP-1 drugs, and this number is expected to grow substantially by the end of the decade. Food companies from Nestle to Conagra are reformulating their products as consumers seek more protein, fiber, and nutritional value.
For ice cream manufacturers, the challenge is to preserve its appeal as a treat while adapting to consumers who are increasingly considering nutritional value alongside taste.
Ferrero’s Halo Top brand, which aims to offer the same ice cream-eating experience with half the calories of leading competitors, has recorded double-digit percentage sales growth over the past two years. For the market as a whole, the figure was about 2.5%, according to Chicago-based market research company Circana.
Rather than reducing portion sizes, Halo Top said in response to an email inquiry that it prefers to combine "flavors you want to eat again and again with a good source of protein and fewer calories than traditional ice cream."
According to Circana, U.S. ice cream sales in monetary terms rose by approximately 2.8% over the past year. At the same time, NielsenIQ data showed that only the premium ice cream segment recorded growth in sales volume.
The trend toward healthier eating is not limited to the United States, prompting ice cream manufacturers to consider how to remain relevant amid global changes in eating habits.
Glacier, one of Europe’s largest manufacturers of private-label products, reports growing demand for smaller portions, premium products, and low-calorie fruit ice cream, which align with consumers’ broader health and well-being goals.

Doc Rivers reflects on getting into the Basketball Hall of Fame, and those who made it possible
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:23:02 UTC
23:23:02 KST

Doc Rivers reflects on getting into the Basketball Hall of Fame, and those who made it possible
Doc Rivers needed some time to write the speech that he’ll give when formally inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.
The storytelling, that part was easy. He’s a natural at that.
But what Rivers wound up learning during the trial-and-error process of speechwriting was that the words he’ll say from a stage in Springfield, Massachusetts aren’t going to be about him. They’re going to be about everyone else who played a role in him getting to that moment.
“You go through this journey of writing it and you realize it has nothing to do with you in a very good way,” Rivers said. “People are happy for you, and I am happy for them because they got me there. You hear all your life, ‘You don’t do anything alone.’ When you get in the Hall of Fame, you really understand that you don’t do anything alone. It’s all the coaches in your life, your parents, the players. It’s a thankful journey and that’s what the Hall of Fame should be about.”
The numbers prove he’s among the best
A winner of 1,194 regular season games as an NBA coach — and that’ll be all, he insists, saying his retirement is a real one — Rivers ranks sixth in league history. The only others ahead of him: Gregg Popovich, Don Nelson, Lenny Wilkens, Jerry Sloan and Pat Riley, all of whom are Hall of Famers, so it was obviously a lock that Rivers would be joining them.
He won a championship with Boston in 2008, won 114 playoff games as a coach, played 13 seasons, was an All-Star once, has been a broadcaster and — if he goes back to work, and his family currently has a pool that he will — he’ll be a broadcaster again.
But there’s more to life now. The Illinois native and Marquette legend has seven grandchildren, a house on the water and can’t play enough golf. He’ll still be involved in the game, somehow. It just won’t be as a coach. It’ll be as a Hall of Famer.
“Doc is a proven, extraordinary leader and communicator during his renowned NBA coaching career,” Milwaukee general manager Jon Horst said when the Bucks hired Rivers in 2024. “As a championship coach, he’s widely respected as an established innovator, and the right coach to lead our experienced and talented team.”
He was, until he wasn’t.
Injuries derailed every chance the Bucks had at being a winner this past season, and when the season came to its dismal close Rivers was fairly certain it was the end for him as well — after 27 seasons on the sideline, and whole lot of missed moments along the way.
“The one thing that people have no idea about is the toll it takes on you and the family component,” Rivers said. “It is rough. You’re never home. You make sacrifices and your family has to make them as well.”
That won’t be an issue now.
A hit from the beginning
Rivers won coach of the year in his very first season, taking a team he called “the 301s” in Orlando and leading it to a 41-41 record. On the surface, there’s nothing special about going .500. But the Magic were supposed to be bottom dwellers that season and Rivers used a preseason ranking of the league’s top 300 players as inspiration — since none of those top 300 were playing for the Magic.
“That season gave me great confidence,” Rivers said.
He has some regrets, of course. Critics have long pointed to the 10 losses that Rivers-coached teams had in Game 7s, by far the most of any coach in NBA history. And his fans will retort by pointing to his 114 playoff wins, fourth-most in NBA history. But the biggest do-over, if Rivers had such an option, would be changing his mind about leaving the Celtics for the Los Angeles Clippers in 2013.
Rivers got to the Clippers not long before the end of Donald Sterling’s ownership of the team; Sterling made racist comments and wound up getting banned by NBA Commissioner Adam Silver.
“I underestimated what a great situation I was in, and I took that for granted, like you can just go anywhere and create that,” Rivers said. “I messed that one up. But then when I go to the Clippers, the team is pretty damn good. The organization, it was the worst organization in sports with the ownership problem. Within a week there, I remember telling my assistant, ‘We’ve got a lot to do here.’”
The championship with the Celtics in 2008 — Ray Allen, Paul Pierce and Kevin Garnett, the stars of that team, will be together again to present their former coach for his Hall enshrinement — was an obvious high point for Rivers’ career. There were other moments he’s particularly proud of as well, such as delivering on a promise that he made to someone who barely played for him.
Tyronn Lue succeeded Rivers as coach of the Clippers. Lue played 11 games for Rivers in Orlando during the 2003-04 season; that was all the time it took for Rivers to be convinced that Lue would one day be a coach. He told Lue to call him if he ever wanted a job and Lue took him up on it. Rivers wound up going to the Hall of Fame, and few within the game would be surprised if Lue joins him there one day.
“It’s the stories like that that you think about,” Rivers said. “Rajon Rondo played for me in Boston. We had a very tumultuous relationship when I coached him and now, I probably talk to Rondo more than probably than any player that I coached.”
It’s what the game does, Rivers said. The lucky ones get guided along the way. He played that role with players like Rondo — who coached with Rivers — and Lue, and in Rivers’ own case, it was Riley who gave him the push he needed.
Riley and Rivers clashed at times in their player-coach relationship, and their biggest fights came when Riley was telling Rivers that he belonged in coaching.
Riley was right.
“When I was doing TV, he kept writing and sending me these freaking messages about getting into the fray,” Rivers said. “He knew it. And here I am, going into the Hall of Fame.”
___
AP NBA: https://apnews.com/nba
