New waterway charges aim to make shipping more environmentally friendly  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:02:35 UTC
23:02:35 KST

TALLINN - The government on Thursday approved and sent to the Riigikogu for deliberation new waterway charge rates aimed at encouraging the use of ships with a lower environmental impact.
A waterway charge is a fee for ensuring navigation, icebreaking, and maritime safety. It must be paid when a ship enters an Estonian port or anchorage area.
"The new waterway charge regulation means lower costs for more environmentally friendly ships and provides them with an additional reason to prefer Estonian ports. This way, we support both cleaner shipping and the competitiveness of Estonian ports, while also mitigating the impact for shipowners that comes with the inclusion of the maritime sector in the European Union's Emissions Trading System," said Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis.
The new waterway charges will take into account the ship's environmental impact - the fee for a vessel with better environmental performance can be up to 25 percent lower than the standard rate.
As one of the changes, waterway charges will now be payable for bunkering-the refueling of a ship with motor fuel or oils-at anchorage areas. Bunkering at sea poses a risk of marine pollution, making the continuation of the current exemption from the charge unjustifiable. In 2027, half the standard rate will be charged for bunkering, with the full rate applying from 2028. An exception will be maintained for the bunkering of alternative and renewable fuels.
The waterway charge for cruise ships, which currently has a unit price about 2.5 to 3 times lower than that of other vessels, will also be gradually increased. The current rate will remain in effect in 2027, with higher rates being implemented in 2028 and 2029.
The implementation of the new waterway charge rates is scheduled to begin on January 1, 2027.

Lebanese Americans sue US over Israel’s rights abuses in Lebanon war
Dozens of Lebanese Americans have filed a class action civil lawsuit against the US government and several defence contractors, saying their role in Israel’s war in Lebanon is a violation of a US law that bars assistance to foreign governments known to be committing human rights abuses.
The lawsuit, filed on Tuesday in the US District Court in Michigan, names Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as well as Lockheed Martin, Boeing, and Caterpillar as defendants.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2Iran rejects Trump’s claim to ‘control’ Hormuz: What’s the latest in talks?
- list 2 of 2Lebanon passes long-sought amnesty law, a day after death penalty repeal
The plaintiffs are the Michigan-based Arab American Civil Rights League group and 16 individuals, all US citizens with property in Lebanon that has been impacted by what they claim is indiscriminate use of force by Israel during the war.
Plaintiffs include Nasser Beydoun, a prominent Michigan businessman and politician who alleges in the lawsuit that Israeli forces destroyed his family home in Bint Jbeil, southern Lebanon, “without any military necessity or justification”.
The lawsuit argues that by supplying Israel with funds and weapons used in this manner, the US government is in violation of the Leahy Law, which bars military assistance, training, or equipment to foreign militaries that are credibly linked to gross human rights violations.
Defence contractors selling equipment to Israel, the plaintiffs claim, similarly should be halted as the companies are knowingly helping the country commit illegal actions in the conflict.
“The law is very clear and has been enforced around the world, but when it comes to Israel, there is zero enforcement,” Nabih Ayad, a lawyer and the head of the Arab American Civil Rights League, said on Wednesday.
In the Lebanon conflict, Ayad said, “You have credible information about gross human rights violations that have happened…yet you are doing nothing about it.”
This June, US President Donald Trump acknowledged Israel’s indiscriminate use of force in Lebanon, saying, “You don’t have to knock down an apartment house every time you’re looking for somebody”.
The lawsuit is seeking to become a class action, representing what the plaintiffs say are tens of thousands of Lebanese Americans with property in Lebanon that has been damaged, or could later be damaged, by Israeli air strikes and other military activity.
The Arab American Civil Rights League has been involved in several major civil rights lawsuits in recent years, including a challenge against the previous Trump administration’s so-called “Muslim ban”, a lawsuit that sued major banks for discriminating against Muslim and Arab Americans, and a 2023 suit seeking to compel the US to help evacuate US citizens trapped in Gaza.

MOSCOW, Aug 13 - The leader of Russia's only registered anti-war party said he will stay in the country and keep pushing for change, despite increased pressure from the authorities that has led to the party's exclusion from upcoming parliamentary elections.
On Monday, the Supreme Court ruled to bar the post-Soviet liberal party, Yabloko, from September's vote, a decision that leader Nikolai Rybakov told Reuters reflected the authorities' concern that its call to end the more than four-year-old war in Ukraine was striking a chord with voters.
"For us, the support of the people that exists now, which is completely obvious and impossible to hide, is far more important than the court's decision," he said in an interview at his Moscow headquarters, relating how, after the verdict, hundreds of supporters on the street had chanted "Shame!" loudly enough to be heard clearly inside the court.
Yabloko only has a handful of regional seats and no representation in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, which is dominated by the Putin-backed United Russia party.
The September vote will elect members to the 450-seat lower house. United Russia is all but certain to retain its dominance, although Rybakov said Yabloko would be a stronger-than-expected contender if allowed to run.
Yabloko is appealing the Supreme Court ruling, which followed a lawsuit alleging that the party received undeclared campaign support from Western sources, among other charges that it denies.
'PEOPLE DON'T KILL EACH OTHER'
"I tell everyone that this is only the beginning, because many people have only now begun to pay attention," he said in his office, where a handwritten placard said: "People, don't kill each other".

"I am in Russia and will remain in Russia," said Rybakov, who wore a peace dove pin on his lapel. "It is only possible to change what is happening in Russia, to change the political situation in Russia, by being inside the country."
Public opposition to the war is difficult to assess due to strict state controls on dissent, but the share of Russians who say they support the actions of their armed forces in Ukraine fell to 66% in July, the lowest level since February 2022, according to the Levada Center, a non-governmental pollster that is on Moscow's foreign agent list.

Chinese missile AI tracks F-22, F-35-like heat signatures with over 90% accuracy
Lightweight, low-cost, heat-seeking missiles could be used to identify stealth fighters in future air combat with strong accuracy
2-MIN READ2-MIN
18
 Listen
Chao Kongin Beijing
The F-35 and F-22 may be among the world’s most advanced stealth fighters, but they cannot hide one thing: heat.
When heat-seeking missiles lock onto aircraft, fighters release flares to confuse infrared sensors and break missile tracking.
But the infrared signals produced by fighters, including heat from engine exhaust and air friction over the fuselage, are different from those generated by flares.
These heat signatures could provide valuable infrared information for target detection and recognition in future air combat, while making flares useless.
Chinese researchers have created a lightweight artificial intelligence (AI) system that could help heat-seeking air-to-air missiles identify advanced fighter jets, and they demonstrated its high accuracy in laboratory tests against mock-up F-22 and F-35 targets.
“Lightweight recognition models could become widely used in future air-to-air missiles because they can provide high-speed recognition while maintaining strong identification capabilities,” An Jiangshan, first author of the study, said on August 10.

In the summer of 1987, I saw two men in a subway station force a third to crouch down to wipe his spit off the platform, while other commuters cheered them on. The incident was remarkable, and has remained in my memory, for two reasons. First, it was in Calcutta, a city synonymous with squalor. Second, the two men were not officials responsible for enforcing cleanliness in public places but simply commuters, like the man they had taken to task.
Had he committed his offense on the street above the station, it would almost certainly have gone unnoticed: in much of urban India, expectorating in public places was, and remains, commonplace. But the platforms and cars of Calcutta Metro, India’s first subway system, only a few years old at the time of this incident, were spanking clean—and among commuters, this aroused a sense of pride and responsibility. Those two citizens were prepared to delay their own journey in order to keep the platform spotless.
I was reminded of that incident a couple of weeks ago, during a ride on the Dubai Metro. On a blazing-hot Sunday morning, a group of six Hindi-speaking Indians was walking ahead of me toward a station, sipping sodas and eating ice cream. One of the group, judging by the fact that she was pointing out the landmarks, was obviously a resident; the others were her guests, evidently visitors from back home. When they arrived at the station, she stopped the group and asked them to drop their bottles and cups into the garbage bin.
Why, one of her visitors asked, sardonically, “Is there a fine? As it happens, there is a fine for littering in stations, and it would have been easy enough for her to say so. But she said this: “Yeh fine ka sawal nahin, safai ka sawal hai.” (It is not a question of a fine but of cleanliness.)
As a social scientist would tell you, both these incidents demonstrate the corollary of the Broken Window Theory. The idea is usually cited in the context of criminology, but it applies more generally in urban studies. The concept is summed up nicely by Psychology Today: “visible signs of disorder and misbehavior in an environment encourage further disorder and misbehavior.”
If broken windows in a neighborhood remain unmended, it leads some members of the community to think that it is acceptable to break windows. Likewise, studies on littering show that people are much more careless with their trash in dirty places than in clean ones. The obverse of the theory is that if a city maintains clean public places, the public will take it upon itself to keep them that way.
A bet on cleanliness and soft power
The important difference between the two incidents is that whereas the Calcutta Metro stood in contrast to its surroundings, the cleanliness of the Dubai Metro is an extension of the city as a whole. The emirate is routinely ranked the world’s cleanest city by the Global Power City Index, compiled annually by the Mori Memorial Foundation.
This is all the more remarkable since the majority of Dubai’s residents come from places where filthy public spaces are the norm—countries like India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Egypt and the Philippines. “People coming from places where civic sense is almost nonexistent land at DXB, and there’s this immediate transformation,” said Sunil Kanchan, a native of Bombay who has lived in Dubai for 30 years. “The same guys who were dropping their tissues on the floor of the plane are now looking for dustbins in the arrivals terminal.”
Do they do this out of fear of being caught and fined? Certainly, rules—and strict consequences for breaking them—are important for creating and maintaining clean spaces. Singapore, my home of two years in the early 2000s, may be the most striking example of the effectiveness of punishment.
But it is too facile to ascribe cleanliness to enforcement alone. Research shows that, over time, people stop littering even when there’s no risk of being caught and punished, because it feels wrong. That was true in Singapore, and it is true in Dubai. “Maybe for the first few weeks or months, you think about the penalties for breaking the law,” remarked Kanchan. “Then you start thinking, ‘This is my town, it’s a pretty clean town… I’d like it to stay that way.”
Dubai and a question of civility
Dubai takes its ranking in global indices very seriously, since the quality of life it offers is a major draw for investors, immigrants and tourists as well as an instrument of its soft power. So you won’t be surprised to learn that municipal authorities are testing AI cameras to supervise how people treat public space. Those found to be littering can expect stiff fines. But in addition to the stick, the emirate is also investing in carrots. Last fall, it launched the Dubai Civility Committee, with an ambitious mandate to “promote positive behaviors” among residents. “No matter how good your enforcement mechanisms are, there’s always a chance of a window breaking somewhere,” said Saeed al Nazari, secretary general of the committee. “We want the whole community to be involved in prevention—and, when necessary, in repair.”
One of the committee’s first initiatives involves honoring people who display simple acts of civility, including but not limited to keeping public spaces clean. “If a resident makes an effort to improve the quality of life for us all, that should be celebrated,” added al Nazari.
Will it work? Social experiments don’t allow for snap judgements, and it may be years before we know for certain. But it is both instructive and reassuring that Dubai isn’t content to place all its bets on technological solutions.
Back to Calcutta. Nearly four decades on, the subway system there remains cleaner than the city at large, but some of the behavior from the surface has begun to seep down into the underground. So much so that the authorities have been obliged to employ anti-littering squads to try to prevent spitting and other unclean behavior. If commuters won’t take that responsibility upon themselves, the threat and enforcement of fines will have to serve the purpose.
Dubai, which already has fines and enforcement, knows that these aren’t enough, which is why it is now supplementing those tools with some social engineering. It is an exercise that other cities ought to watch closely.

U.S. Marine veteran Robert Gilman was almost on "death's door" before Russia released him, advocate says
Robert Gilman, a U.S. Marine veteran who was imprisoned in Russia for over four years, was nearly on "death's door" before he was released this week, according to a hostage crisis expert who advocated for Gilman's release.
The 32-year-old is now in Texas, where he faces a long road to recovery, said Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer with Global Reach, an organization that worked to free him.

Gilman is being treated at the Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio where he is "getting the world's best medical care," Ramsey said.
Lebson claimed last week that Russian authorities subjected Gilman to mistreatment, including harassment, forced exercise sessions lasting up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs. Lebson also alleged Gilman was pressured to fight in Ukraine.
CBS News has not independently verified those claims. Russian officials have not publicly responded.
A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration had raised his case with the Russian government repeatedly, and requested he be released on humanitarian grounds, given Gilman's health concerns.
"The situation with Robert is far beyond anything we have seen with any other American detained in Russia," Lebson said.
The Trump administration previously secured the release of several other Americans held in Russia. Multiple others are still being held in the country.
"We have 10 others in Russia," said Ramsey. "We have two designated in Iran. We have one designated in China. Let's hope that he's able to bring all of these folks home as soon as possible."

The 10-lesson email course, which includes step-by-step videos as well as write-ups, covers everything you need to know about booking a trip by rail.

What the RSF's battlefield setbacks mean for Sudan's war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:57:52 UTC
22:57:52 KST

Breadcrumb
What the RSF's battlefield setbacks mean for Sudan's war
Cairo, Egypt - On 26 July, Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF) lost control over a major highway linking the strategic city of El-Obeid to the wider capital of Khartoum.
The national army, known as the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), captured the road to secure a vital supply line to its fighters in El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan.
The city sits at a crossroads between SAF-controlled northern and eastern Sudan and RSF-held territory to the south and west, making it a logistics hub for military operations.
For weeks, the RSF targeted El-Obeid with drones, striking vital provisions such as generators, fuel, and water tankers. Despite the attacks, the RSF has struggled to hold ground in the sprawling region.
Shortly after losing control over the 350km highway, RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo vowed to fight on until his forces reached Khartoum, which is currently under SAF control.
Analysts say that Hemedti’s statement reflects his desperation to halt the SAF's advances.
“Since losing control of villages around the highway, the RSF has called on all tribes in Darfur to mobilise and enlist,” Mohamed al-Fatih Yousif, a journalist from Darfur who recently visited the region, told The New Arab.
“Many of the new recruits are being trained in South Darfur and in Libya,” he added.
Since the SAF and the RSF plunged Sudan into a civil war in April 2023, they have fought each other to a near stalemate.
In recent weeks, SAF-aligned forces have attacked the RSF on three fronts - in southeastern, central, and western Sudan.
The attacks have inflicted a series of strategic blows against the RSF, pushing the group to launch a major recruitment drive and reactivate vital supply lines, say analysts.
On Wednesday, the RSF reportedly targeted El-Obeid and other Sudanese cities with drone attacks in response to the losses.
“The local tribal authorities have answered the RSF’s call. They are sending many young men to fight, including children,” Yousif told The New Arab.
Tribal allies
Most RSF fighters come from nomadic or pastoralist Arab tribes in the sprawling regions of Darfur and Kordofan.
Like tribes across Sudan, they are governed by native administrations – a hierarchical, British-imposed system from the 1920s. The British created these to bestow individual chiefs with significant power, making them easier to co-opt.
More than a century later, many tribal chiefs are backing the RSF in exchange for money and power. Others fear that their communities could be ethnically targeted if SAF recaptures the region.
Throughout the war, the SAF has labelled young men and women originally from Darfur as RSF “cooperators” or “spies” to justify detaining, torturing, and sometimes executing them.
“Many tribes believe that they don’t have a choice. They believe that they have to enlist their young men into the RSF in exchange for security,” Yousif explained to The New Arab.
At the same time, the RSF poses an existential threat to Arab and sedentary farming “non-Arab” communities that oppose them, say analysts. Back in February, the RSF raided the town of Misterai, the primary base of the Mahamid clan of the Rizeigat Arab tribe - the same ethnic group that the RSF’s own leaders hail from.
The RSF was trying to assassinate Musa Hilal, a rival tribal sheikh who eventually escaped to SAF-controlled areas. Weeks later, the intra-tribal rivalry prompted several RSF commanders from the Mahamid tribe to switch sides. They were lured with promises of amnesty, money, and power.
The UN and human rights groups also accuse the RSF of committing genocidal violence against non-Arab communities in West Darfur and in North Darfur’s capital of El-Fasher.
During the offensive to capture both areas, the RSF gunned down young men in their homes and as they were fleeing into Chad and through RSF checkpoints. The RSF also systematically abducted women and girls and subjected them to sexual violence.
Still, some non-Arab tribes such as the Fur have agreed to back the RSF out of fear that they could suffer a similar fate, according to Noon al-Baramaki, a journalist who survived the atrocities in el-Fasher.
The Fur have reportedly mobilised four battalions of young fighters to enlist with the RSF.
“It’s practically a forced recruitment campaign,” Al-Baramki, a journalist who survived the atrocities in North Darfur, told The New Arab. “[Non-Arab] tribes know that the communities who resisted joining the RSF were subjected to genocide and ethnic cleansing.”
UAE support
The RSF relies entirely on the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to fuel its war against SAF, according to numerous reports published by the UN, human rights groups, and media outlets.
Some of the support includes shipments of Chinese-made drones and artillery.
The UAE has also used shell companies to hire former Colombian mercenaries to train RSF fighters in Sudan.
“There is a sort of stubbornness on the side of the UAE that is very, very clear. They are not going to stop [backing the RSF],” Jalel Harchaoui, a political scientist closely observing the UAE’s role in Libya and across North and East Africa, told The New Arab.
Weapons, fuel, and mercenaries often cross into RSF-held territory from neighbouring Chad, South Sudan, and Libya. In exchange, the UAE receives billions of dollars’ worth of illicit gold and preserves its massive strategic influence across the Sahel.
Over the last several weeks, Harchaoui said that the UAE has gradually reactivated a direct supply line from the Libyan town of Kufra into North Darfur.
Libya’s eastern authorities closed that route when Egypt and Turkey began bombing convoys heading directly into Sudan from Kufra in November 2025. The bombing started shortly after the RSF committed mass atrocities during its capture of El-Fasher.
Harchaoui now says that there has been a noticeable increase in the number of cargo planes and hangars stationed in the town since July. He also suspects that the UAE is planning to build air defences to protect convoys traversing this critical route.
“Turkey and Egypt conduct airstrikes very easily, which means that route is really dangerous,” Harchaoui told The New Arab.
“But the UAE is preparing to absorb a percentage of loss - in terms of fighters and munitions - to keep the route open. For the UAE, this is just the cost of doing business.”
Mat Nashed is an award-nominated journalist who has covered the MENA region since the Arab Spring
Follow him on X: @matnashed

Maghreb sees demographic shift with fertility at historic low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:57:14 UTC
22:57:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Maghreb sees demographic shift with fertility at historic low
Economic pressures and changing social norms are driving couples in Tunisia, Morocco, and Algeria to have fewer babies, with a recent study saying Maghreb fertility was at a historic low.
Experts and couples interviewed by AFP spoke of a combination of factors, including longer educations and growing professional ambitions among women, along with rising divorce rates and financial strain on young professionals.
The trend mirrors changes seen in many parts of the world. But in the Maghreb, it challenges stereotypes of families tending to be large.
A recent study by France's Institute for Demographic Studies (INED) said the decline has been exceptionally rapid and appeared to be "lasting", while Tunisian demographer Mohamed Ali Ben Zina described it as "profound".
In Tunis, Nadia Jaouadi, 42, said she does not regret the decision she and her husband made a decade ago not to have children.
"Nothing encourages having even a single child," said Jaouadi, a civil servant, blaming Tunisia's current economic woes and social climate.
Across all three Maghreb countries, fertility rates fell by more than half since the 1970s, according to official figures.
Social changes
Tunisia now has the lowest fertility rate in the Maghreb, with 1.58 children per woman in 2023 and an estimated 1.53 in 2024, compared with 1.97 in Morocco and 2.61 in Algeria.
Tunisian demographer Hassen Kassar said Tunisia's fertility drop was primarily the result of deep social changes, including the "modernisation of families" and urbanisation, which have reduced family size.
In Algiers, Said, a 66-year-old retired former finance executive who did not provide his full name, said he came from a family of 10 children.
"My father struggled to provide for the whole family," he recalled. "So I decided not to have more than two children. What's important is that they eat their fill, dress properly and live in good conditions."
Chaimae Drioui, a researcher and professor at Morocco's National Institute of Statistics and Applied Economics (INSEA), said the decline in fertility was "a rational decision by families in response to a new economic and social context".
Having children was at times seen in popular culture as an investment in the future, particularly among poorer families who relied on their children for prospective support.
But that view "has now been reversed," Drioui said. "The child today costs more than he brings in immediate economic terms."
Economic hardship, however, is not the only factor as the mental and physical demands of parenthood also weigh on many.
"After giving birth, I realised how much motherhood was a challenge for my mental and physical health," said Zina, a 42-year-old Algerian who gave birth to a daughter at 38 and no longer plans to have another child.
In Rabat, Kaouthar, a 38-year-old public-sector manager who did not provide her full name said she will remain child-free: "I chose to live a peaceful life away from the worry and stress inherent in raising a child."
Drioui said women's education and empowerment were key to changing traditional family patterns.
Foreign workers
Yet a decline in birth rates also translates to an ageing population across the Maghreb.
In Tunisia, people aged 60 and over now account for 17 percent of the population, or nearly 2 million people.
The trend is less advanced in Algeria, where people aged 60 and over represented a 10th of the population in 2023 -- and in Morocco, where the same category accounted for 13.8 percent of the population in 2024.
The demographic shift could put pressure on pension systems and weaken the balance between working-age people and retirees.
INED said that if deaths eventually outnumbered births, only immigration could sustain population growth.
And foreign workers could help fill labour shortages as the working-age population shrinks.
But that prospect could prove difficult in the countries where migration is already a highly sensitive topic.
For Kassar, one possibility is already emerging: "We will need sub-Saharan migrants."

Hosting Eurovision 2027 as a test of Bulgaria’s new image
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:56:29 UTC
22:56:29 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
Thursday 13 August 2026 16:39
Thursday, 13 August 2026, 16:39
PHOTO BNT
Font size
When a country is given the right to host Eurovision for the first time, the logic usually seems straightforward: the contest goes to the capital. That is where the largest infrastructure, international connections, hotels, media, and institutions are located.
Bulgaria, however, has chosen a different path.
On August 13, 2026, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and the Bulgarian National Television (BNT) announced that Burgas will host Eurovision 2027. The seaside city won the domestic competition against the capital, Sofia, and will welcome artists, delegations, journalists, and thousands of fans next May.
Bulgaria's coastal city Burgas will host Eurovision 2027
The semi-finals will take place on May 11 and 13, with the grand final on May 15.
BNT director general Milena Milotinova and Burgas Mayor Dimitar Nikolov
PHOTO BTA
The decision undoubtedly has significance beyond a single music event. It places Burgas at the center of international attention and demonstrates that Bulgaria is ready to present to the world not only its capital, but also other cities.
A brief look at Eurovision’s history shows that the contest has repeatedly “left” European capitals over the years. The Netherlands chose Rotterdam to host the competition following the COVID-19 pandemic, while in 2022 Italy selected Turin rather than Rome. The United Kingdom gave hosting duties to Liverpool in 2023, Sweden chose Malmö in 2024, and Basel hosted the contest in 2025 instead of the capital, Bern.
In other words, Burgas’s selection as host of Eurovision 2027 can be seen as part of a broader European trend - or perhaps a concept - in which major international events are not necessarily concentrated in countries’ administrative centers.
Aerial view of Burgas
PHOTO BTA
Burgas’s strongest asset is undoubtedly the sea. When millions of viewers around the world hear “Burgas! Bulgaria!”, images of the sea, the Sea Garden, and the beach will inevitably come to mind, along with the cultural events and atmosphere of the Bulgarian Black Sea coast. This represents enormous tourism potential. The official Eurovision website already presents Burgas as a Black Sea city, highlighting its history, culture, and role as the host city in 2027.
For Bulgaria, this is arguably the best advertising campaign possible - not funded solely through the national tourism budget, but also driven by the interest of the huge European television market and thousands of Eurovision fans, many of whom may see the Bulgarian coast for the first time through the world’s biggest music competition.
PHOTO BTA
But after every wave of enthusiasm comes an important “but”. It is crucial how Bulgaria, and Burgas’s administration in particular, handles the challenge. Eurovision brings not only publicity but also enormous responsibility. The city will need to provide transportation, accommodation, security, logistics, and services for a huge number of people over a short period.
If all of this is managed successfully, the long-term benefits for both the city and the country could be enormous. Burgas’s success will not be measured solely by beautiful television images of the Sea Garden and beaches.
This is where the enormous potential for Burgas lies: transforming itself from a summer tourist destination into a modern and sought-after city for international events throughout the year.
PHOTO BTA
The choice of Burgas as host of Eurovision 2027 is also a logical continuation of the city’s development. In recent years, it has become increasingly difficult to describe Burgas simply as a summer tourism center. The sea and traditional summer season remain part of its identity, but behind them a new image is gradually emerging - a city that invests in infrastructure, attracts industrial companies, educational institutions, and healthcare professionals, develops sustainable transport, and seeks to make culture a year-round driver of urban life.
Burgas already has a rich calendar of festivals, concerts, cinema, art, and outdoor events. These include the International Film Festival, “Jazz in Burgas”, “With a Book on the Beach,” music festivals, and various initiatives in the Sea Garden and other cultural spaces.
In May 2026, Burgas was one of the Bulgarian cities to host the prestigious Giro d’Italia cycling race. Just days ago, on August 7 and 8, Burgas’s Sea Station once again became the stage for Bulgaria’s largest event dedicated to music from the 1990s to the present - the SPICE Music Festival 2026. Performers included Thomas Anders of Modern Talking, Jenny Berggren of Ace of Base, and Ruslana from Ukraine.
The city’s summer program also features concerts by Bulgaria’s biggest pop stars, as well as a rich calendar of theatre productions, opera performances, and classical concerts.
So the conditions and foundations are already in place.
The test for Burgas - and for Bulgaria - is about to begin.

'If you can, move!' say Rome's viral dancing seniors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:55:15 UTC
22:55:15 KST

Viral dancing seniors inspire Italy's ageing population to move
An elderly dancing duo has become a viral sensation in Italy after a tour operator shared one of their street performances online last week, striking a chord with many in Italy, whose population is the oldest in the EU. The pair said that they hope their sudden popularity will push their peers off the sofa into a more active lifestyle.
Bopping to Michael Jackson and Elvis Presley in a Roman square, an elderly dancing duo has become a viral sensation in Italy – something they hope will inspire other seniors to take up a more active lifestyle.
Retired dance teacher Pasquale Iannotta, 70, and his dancing partner Elisa Fava, 79, have won praise from Rome's mayor and twisted and twirled on national TV since one of their street performances was shared online by a social media savvy tour operator last week.
Watch moreDance Theatre of Harlem: The ballet revolution hits Paris
"No one ever thought we could go viral like this," Fava said on Wednesday, as the pair returned to Testaccio square, in the namesake historic working-class district of the Italian capital, for another spin.
Their moves have struck a chord with many in Italy – whose population is the oldest in the European Union.
The original clip posted by The Tour Guy gathered more than 370,000 likes and thousands of comments on Instagram, including from mayor Roberto Gualtieri, who complimented the "excellent dancers", writing: "There's so much beauty in this simple video".
Iannotta and Fava have since been invited to perform on the flagship morning TV show of national broadcaster Rai Uno and other television programmes.
The two met at dance class, where Fava was one of Iannotta's pupils, and started performing outdoors regularly in the summer since, as Iannotta puts it, they both "hate sitting around at home".
Now they hope their sudden popularity will push others off the sofa and onto the dance floor, they said.
"I have many friends who, unfortunately, when they retire, like many others end up sitting on the sofa watching television. I'd like to see them get a bit more active," Iannotta, who wore a floral short-sleeve shirt and sunglasses, said after the duo showed off their skills to the tune of Presley's "Jailhouse Rock".
With a median age of 49.1, Italy is the EU's oldest country, according to the bloc's data agency.
Births fell last year by nearly 4 percent, plunging the fertility rate to an 80-year low, national statistics show.
As the country ages, putting pressure on care among other challenges, doctors say physical activity is vital for older people, helping with brain and heart health among other benefits.
"Don't be idle: if you can, move," Fava, who recently became a great-grandmother, said in a message to fellow seniors. "Particularly, dancing is good for you".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Winning ticket for $1 billion Powerball jackpot was sold in Illinois
A Powerball ticket sold at a gas station in western Illinois was the sole winner of the $1 billion jackpot, ending a three-month drought without a top-prize victor.
The ticket that won the jackpot Wednesday night was purchased at a Hy-Vee station in Quincy, about 100 miles (161 kilometers) west of the state capital of Springfield along the Missouri border, Illinois Lottery officials said. The winning numbers were 4-26-66-67-69 with the Powerball number of 9.
It wasn’t immediately clear if the winner has come forward yet.
The prize comes in the form of either an annuity of $1 billion paid over 29 years or a lump-sum payment of $450.5 million. Winners almost always take the lump sum.
It was the first Powerball jackpot won since May 2, when the top prize was $20 million, and the first since ticket sales began in the United Kingdom last month. At $2 per play, the odds of winning the jackpot are one in 292 million.
The $1.04 billion grand prize was the eighth-largest in Powerball history, game organizers said. Another lottery game, Mega Millions has also had a $1 billion jackpot winner.
“Congratulations to our newest Powerball jackpot winner in Illinois,” Stephen Durrell, chair of the Powerball Product Group and executive director of the Kansas Lottery, said in a statement. “For more than three decades, Powerball has shown that a winning ticket can be sold anywhere the game is played, giving every $2 ticket the chance to change not only a winner’s life, but generations to come.”
Four tickets sold for Wednesday’s drawing — in Arizona, California, Florida and North Carolina — hit five of the numbers but missed the Powerball number. They were worth $1 million apiece. A ticket sold in Massachusetts also matched all the numbers except the Powerball number, but won $2 million because of the “Power Play” multiplier option costing an extra $1 per play.
More than 3 million tickets won lesser cash prizes.
The Powerball jackpot resets to $20 million for the next drawing on Saturday.
The record lottery jackpot still stands at just over $2 billion, won with a Powerball ticket purchased in California in 2022.

Poland says a Russian was arrested after officials thwarted plot to kill Ukrainian American citizen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:53:02 UTC
22:53:02 KST

Poland says it thwarted a Russian plot to kill an American citizen in Warsaw
WARSAW (AP) — A Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister said Thursday, adding it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” sought to attack a U.S. citizen on the territory of another NATO country.
Western officials have previously warned that Russia stepped up a campaign of targeted killings since President Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, saying they have disrupted several plots across Europe. But Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this incident was unprecedented.
The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia’s secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on Aug. 7. He will be held in custody for three months, the Warsaw police said in a statement.
The American Ukrainian citizen “was uncomfortable for the Putin regime,” Tusk said in a news conference, without elaborating.
The operation was carried out in cooperation with U.S. services, said Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing intelligence services. He said the targeted victim was a U.S. citizen “of Ukrainian origin.” Officials did not immediately provide further details.
The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports but said it had no additional information.
Western countries believe Russia seeks to undermine Ukraine’s allies
Russia has long been accused of targeting its enemies abroad, including by using rare poisons. But intelligence officials previously told The Associated Press that Russia’s security services are now more brazen in their choice of targets, going after Russian activists and foreign supporters of Ukraine as well as military defectors.
“We must assume that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons, in various places around the world,” Tusk said on Thursday. He said that Poland and others must be prepared to counter such actions.
Western officials see the campaign as connected to Russia’s broader efforts to undermine European countries that support Ukraine. The AP has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson and other disruption across Europe since the start of the war that officials have linked to Russia. President Vladimir Putin told the AP in June that Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe.
In 2006, British authorities accused Russia of being behind the killing of former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko in London with radioactive polonium. The U.K. also blames Russia for the attempted killing of former Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Salisbury in 2018 with the nerve agent Novichok.
German authorities said Russia organized the 2019 killing of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili, a former Chechen rebel commander who was shot in a Berlin park by Vadim Krasikov, a hitman who was later greeted by Putin after he was exchanged in a spy swap.
In June, a Russian artist who was critical of Putin was shot and killed at close range near his home in eastern Poland. Tusk said at the time that the killing of Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky, had the hallmarks of a political assassination. He suggested it was possible Russia was behind it but Polish officials have not yet attributed it to Moscow.
Last year French officials disrupted a plot which they believe was aimed at killing Vladimir Osechkin, a Russian exile who lives under police protection and works to help military defectors flee Putin’s war. Lithuanian officials also disrupted a plot last year to kill a Lithuanian supporter of Ukraine and another against a Russian activist. Officials in Germany have similarly broken up two plots: one to target the head of a German weapons company supplying Ukraine, the other against a Ukrainian military official.
Polish authorities arrested a man in 2024 in what they said was a plot to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. That year, a Russian helicopter pilot who defected was killed in Spain — with Russian operatives the prime suspects.
“This campaign is not by accident or chance,” a senior European intelligence official previously told the AP. “There is political authorization.”

Wildlife expert: Rising bear numbers could increase risk of human attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:53:00 UTC
22:53:00 KST

Wildlife expert: Rising bear numbers could increase risk of human attacks
Estonia's bear population has grown for two decades, and one wildlife expert warns that new, tighter hunting limits could increase the risk of conflicts with people.
Recent court decisions have significantly restricted bear hunting in Estonia, and Peep Männil, a wildlife expert at the Environment Agency, expects the country's brown bear population to grow faster as a result.
That could mean more agricultural damage, greater impacts on other wildlife and more encounters with people, including potential attacks.
Estonia was home to about 1,100 brown bears as of fall 2025, according to agency estimates. The population has grown by an average of 5 percent a year over the past decade, with growth accelerating in recent years.
Männil explained that officials estimate bear numbers using sightings, particularly of females with cubs, rather than trying to count individual animals. More than 7,000 observations were recorded across Estonia last year, most by hunters and other wildlife enthusiasts using trail cameras.
The Environment Agency then maps and analyzes the resulting data, in the same approach used to estimate wolf, lynx and other wildlife populations.
No deadly attacks
While the abundance of sightings and trail-camera images can make it seem like there are suddenly far more bears in Estonia, Männil said bear numbers have actually been growing steadily for about 20 years already.
"The growth rate of the bear population will likely increase now, which is logical," he said, commenting on recently tightened hunting restrictions.
The expert said a growing bear population could lead to more crop damage as well as affect moose numbers, as bears prey heavily on moose calves in their first weeks of life.
"Studies in Sweden have found that the impact [on moose] can be quite significant," he added.
While the risk to people remains relatively low in Estonia, Männil warned that a larger bear population still also means a greater chance of dangerous encounters.
Seven bear attacks on people have been recorded in Estonia in the past 25 years. None were fatal, but three resulted in injuries, most recently in 2022. Four occurred during hunting situations, after the bear had been shot.
"That number is too small to draw any conclusions about an upward trend, but the likelihood of more such incidents will certainly increase," he said.
Simple safety tips
Männil explained that attacks here are generally defensive rather than predatory, and can occur when a person and bear unexpectedly encounter each other at close range. The possibility of an encounter, however, should not keep people out of the woods.
"It would be so unfortunate if people stopped foraging for mushrooms or spending time in nature because they're afraid there are too many bears," he said.
With risks rising as bear numbers grow, the agency expert stressed that careful wildlife management is increasingly important.
"One of the broader goals of hunting is to prevent these kinds of large swings in wildlife populations as much as possible," Männil said. "They're no good for the species themselves or for the balance between species."
While urban sightings do happen, encounters are more likely while hiking or foraging. A few simple tips shared by the Estonian Hunters' Society (EJS) can help keep you safe if you run into a brown bear in the wild.

Taiwan Cabinet backs tougher crypto money-laundering rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:51:47 UTC
22:51:47 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet on Thursday approved draft amendments that would bring unregistered crypto services and unauthorized stablecoin issuance within the scope of Taiwan's money-laundering law.
Providing virtual-asset or third-party payment services without registration, or issuing stablecoins without authorization, would be classified as specified offenses under the law, allowing money-laundering penalties to apply to proceeds from those activities, according to CNA. The amendments will be sent to the Legislative Yuan for review before they can take effect.
The draft will also define a beneficial owner as the person who ultimately owns or controls a client, transaction, or legal entity. Regulators would be authorized to set procedures for identifying and inspecting beneficial owners.
Government agencies could access information on fines imposed on financial institutions and designated nonfinancial businesses when needed to prevent money laundering. Banks and virtual-asset service providers could also share information with other institutions to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.
CNA quoted Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) as saying Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) believes anti-money-laundering efforts are essential to fighting crime and protecting financial stability. Cho added that the law must keep pace with changing criminal methods and international standards, while agencies strengthen cooperation and information sharing.

Hong Kong holds first large-scale drill at revamped Huanggang border crossing
About 1,000 civil servants joined exercise testing passenger flows and transport, with further tests planned before the new crossing opens
Hong Kong has conducted its first large-scale drill at the revamped Huanggang border crossing, with authorities describing traffic flows at the facility as smooth.
About 1,000 civil servants from more than 20 departments mobilised for Thursday’s drill. They were instructed to travel by public transport to the Hong Kong port area of the revamped Huanggang Port, enter the port building and leave by similar means.
Authorities said the exercise aimed to assess the management of passenger and vehicular flows, passageway capacity, on-site guidance arrangements, traffic control and various supporting measures at the port building and its public transport interchange.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung and transport minister Mable Chan inspected the drill and both expressed satisfaction with the arrangements.
“The whole process was largely smooth and controllable, but we also identified some pain points. Some participants had said through on-site questionnaires that the signs were not clear enough, and the queuing flow could be improved,” Tang said.
Chan also said the management of passengers boarding, alighting and queuing, as well as passenger and vehicular flows, had operated smoothly during the drill.
The exercise involved more than 120 departures to simulate the movement of people and vehicles arriving at and leaving the port.

Russia’s GDP Rebounds 1.3% as War Spending Masks Deeper Economic Weakness

Russia’s GDP Rebounds 1.3% as War Spending Masks Deeper Economic Weakness
Russia's economy returned to growth in the second quarter of 2026, months after the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, publicly rebuked his economic team over a downturn and demanded steps to reverse it.
The state statistics service, Rosstat, released the 1.3% second-quarter figure on August 12, as reported by The Moscow Times. Both the agency and independent economists tied the rebound to factors unrelated to Putin's April intervention.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The result marked Russia's strongest showing in six quarters and exceeded official projections, with the Ministry of Economic Development having forecast 0.9% and the central bank 0.8%. Cumulative growth for the first half reached just 0.6%, roughly half last year's pace and nearly seven times slower than the 2023–2024 wartime boom.
Economist Yegor Susin tied the improvement to additional working days, better external conditions, and a fiscal boost. The war in Iran briefly lifted oil revenues, he noted, while budget spending climbed 16%, with about a third directed to the army and weapons production.
The economy had contracted 0.2% in the first quarter, its first decline since 2023. In April, Putin summoned officials and criticized the economic bloc for failing to meet forecasts, demanding "concrete measures" and later urging that any recovery be solid and sustainable.
The second-quarter reading surprised even government forecasters. Civilian industry nonetheless remained weak, contracting 3.2% year-over-year and 4.6% against 2024 levels, according to the Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting.
Analysts doubted the surge would last. Liam Peach of Capital Economics expects Russia to remain mired in stagnation, weighed down by high interest rates and the fuel crisis.
Economist Vladislav Inozemtsev, cited by the Moscow Times, warned that Ukrainian long-range strikes on oil refineries and major Wildberries warehouses are seriously eroding the economy.
He projected inflation 2 to 3 percentage points above earlier expectations, alongside stalled real incomes and a wave of business failures. Inozemtsev cast Kremlin policy—tax increases, business seizures, heavy regulation, and a possible new mobilization—as the graver danger. A renewed mobilization, he cautioned, “will be the end of the entire Russian economy.”
The refinery strikes cited as a drag on output are part of a widening Ukrainian long-range campaign against Russia's fuel sector. On August 8, Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky refinery in the Krasnodar region and the Rosneft-operated Syzran plant in the Samara region, extending an effort aimed at cutting the oil revenues that bankroll Moscow's war.

'Free Palestine' party enters New Zealand's election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:47:28 UTC
22:47:28 KST

Breadcrumb
'Free Palestine' party to contest New Zealand election after official registration
"Free Palestine" party has become an officially registered political party in New Zealand and will appear on ballot papers in the general election scheduled for 7 November.
The party's founder and leader, Paul Hopkinson, told The New Arab on Thursday, 13 August, "The party secretary sent me a message informing me that we had been officially registered after receiving an email from the Electoral Commission."
"I knew that there was enormous external pressure being exerted on them not to register the party. The commission received 207 objections from Zionists and Zionist organisations against recognising us as an official party," he added.
The New Zealand Electoral Commission announced its approval of the registration of the "Free Palestine" party as a political party after examining its registration application in accordance with the provisions of the Electoral Act 1993.
The decision followed a public consultation during which the commission received 207 submissions opposing the application.
The commission concluded that the party had met the legal requirements, including providing evidence that it had at least 500 current financial members who were eligible to enroll as voters.
It also found no legal grounds requiring it to reject the registration.
The commission said it had carefully considered objections concerning the name "Free Palestine" party and whether it was offensive or likely to cause anger or disgust in a reasonable person.
"The phrase, while highly sensitive and the subject of widespread political disagreement", it noted, was not in itself "offensive" under the legal standard set out in the legislation.
It said supporters viewed it as a call for human rights, freedom and an end to occupation, while opponents considered it offensive or antisemitic or an implicit call for hostility towards Israel and Jewish communities.
The commission stressed that it was required to assess the party's name itself, rather than its positions, slogans or campaign material.
The commission, however, rejected registration of the party's logo, which includes the Palestinian flag and the words "Free Palestine" party, because it could confuse or mislead voters.
This was particularly because they might believe the party officially represented a Palestinian political entity or international movement, or that it had the support or control of Palestinian institutions.
It said the decision was also based on similar electoral precedents.
As a result, the "Free Palestine" party will be able to contest the upcoming general election, compete for party-list votes and nominate candidates in electoral districts.
However, its logo will not appear beside the name of the party or its candidates on the ballot paper, as the legal deadline for submitting an alternative logo has expired.
The party leader said to TNA that the party's official registration had multiple benefits for the Palestine solidarity movement in New Zealand.
"It gives us government funding of $82,000 to help raise awareness of the Palestinian cause, allowing us to increase pressure on any incoming government to listen to more than 60% of the New Zealand public who, according to opinion polls, are calling for action to impose sanctions on Israel," he added. "Most importantly, this registration makes it extremely difficult for any New Zealand government to restrict freedom of expression or the activities of Palestine supporters."
In the first official reaction opposing the party's registration, the Coalition of Ministers Supporting Israel (COMS), which comprises 136 Protestant Christian clergy in New Zealand from Pentecostal, Baptist, Brethren, Presbyterian, Anglican and Methodist churches and others, who support the right of the State of Israel to protect itself, issued a statement.
"The Coalition of Ministers Supporting Israel is concerned about the Electoral Commission's decision to register the "Free Palestine" party as a political party in the general election scheduled for November," it said.
"New Zealand's electoral system has been hijacked by foreign interests and influence seeking to use the electoral process in our country to promote the twisted ideology of those who call for the elimination of Israel," the statement continued.
Next steps for "Free Palestine"
Commenting on this, Hopkinson described the statement, in remarks to TNA, as "shameful" for its support of an apartheid state and the ongoing genocide of the Palestinian people.
He stressed that "calling for the downfall of the Israeli apartheid state is something we are proud to stand in solidarity with, just as many veteran Palestine supporters and activists in New Zealand were proud to support the struggle that ended the apartheid state in South Africa".
Asked about the next steps the party intends to take after its official registration, he said the party "will hold a launch event in the city of Christchurch, and we hope it will be before mid-September, followed by the launch of the campaign at a national level".
"Planning to contest this election is still under way; however, we are of course considering putting forward candidates on the party list, as well as candidates in electoral districts for key single-member seats," he added.
"We hope to be able to bring this issue to the heart of New Zealand politics, where it should be. It is time for New Zealand and its people to be leaders in the struggle against Zionism and Israel, just as we were leaders in the anti-nuclear weapons and anti-apartheid movements," he continued.
For his part, Maher Nazzal, head of the Palestine Forum in New Zealand, told The New Arab that "registering a party to participate in the upcoming general election is a very important step, not only for Palestinians in New Zealand but also for everyone who believes in justice, human rights and accountability".
He stressed that "this registration means that the voice calling for justice for Palestine now has a clear democratic political framework capable of addressing voters directly and raising issues that traditional parties have ignored".
He added that "this step represents the beginning of the road, not its end; the challenge now is to build a strong and organised campaign, reach as many voters as possible, explain the party's programme to people, and not only talk about Palestine but also about issues that matter to all New Zealanders".
Regarding the forum's mechanisms for helping the newly formed party, Nazzal said that "there are several ways, including joining, volunteering and donating within electoral laws, helping the campaign communicate with different communities, spreading the party's messages, and organising meetings and events across the country".
"The most important thing is to show that supporting Palestine does not conflict with being New Zealanders; rather, defending human rights, justice and equality is a fundamental part of the democratic society in which we live," he added.
The New Zealand-Palestinian activist considered that "we are facing a historic opportunity. It will not be easy, but if we work together in an organised and professional manner, we will succeed in turning this registration from a mere announcement into an influential political voice inside the New Zealand Parliament".
He noted that "small parties, under New Zealand's mixed-member proportional representation system, have a real opportunity to exert influence if they manage to reach the required electoral threshold or win an electorate seat".

Ukrainian drone strike fully shuts down oil refinery Russia’s Orsk, governor says. Repairs could take 6 months.
Ukrainian drones knocked out the oil refinery in Orsk, forcing a complete shutdown, Orenburg Governor Yevgeny Solntsev said.

Inside the Specs of Ukraine’s Long-Range Drone-Missiles That Struck Novorossiysk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:46:58 UTC
22:46:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Inside the Specs of Ukraine’s Long-Range Drone-Missiles That Struck Novorossiysk
Following the historic coordinated strike on Russia’s naval base in Novorossiysk, technical details have emerged regarding the long-range drone-missiles deployed in the operation, RBC-Ukraine reported on August 13.
The overnight strike on August 12 damaged four Russian warships—including the frigates Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen—along with an S-300 air defense radar, port infrastructure, and an oil depot entrance, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The operation forced local authorities to declare a state of emergency in Novorossiysk and temporarily close two major grain terminals at the port.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strike marked the first time Ukrainian forces operated multiple hybrid missile classes in tandem, combining Palianytsia , Peklo , Bars , and Long Neptune systems alongside naval and aerial drones.
Classified as an intermediate weapon between suicide attack drones and conventional cruise missiles, these ground-launched systems allow Ukraine to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, according to RBC-Ukraine.
Palianytsia
The Palianytsia is a 320-kilogram drone-missile measuring 3.5 meters in length with a 1.7-meter wingspan, carrying a warhead payload of up to 100 kilograms. Powered by a single-spool turbojet engine and launched using a solid-fuel booster, it reaches cruising speeds of up to 900 kilometers per hour.
It operates at low altitudes between 15 and 500 meters. The weapon features a combined INS/GPS guidance system and has an operational range of 650 kilometers.
Developed in just 1.5 years, the system was designed to bypass Western weapons restrictions by independently targeting up to 20 Russian airfields. The ground-launched missile costs well below $1 million per unit and made its successful combat debut in August 2024 during a complex operation against a Russian military target in occupied Crimea.
Peklo
The Peklo represents a newer iteration of Ukraine’s hybrid arsenal. Developed from scratch within a single year and first delivered to military units in December 2024, the Peklo flies at speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour with an extended range of 700 kilometers.
The weapon quickly entered mass production, with 100 units manufactured in just three months following its introduction. Built using 70% locally sourced components, Peklo is strategically designed to force Moscow to relocate its combat aviation further from the front lines by threatening distant air bases.
In contrast, Russia’s conceptual equivalent—the S8000 Banderol cruise missile manufactured by Kronstadt—faces distinct operational limitations, aviation expert Kostiantyn Kryvolap told RBC-Ukraine.
The Russian system features a smaller warhead capacity, costs roughly three times as much as a standard Shahed drone, and requires an aircraft for launch, restricting its potential for mass deployment compared to Ukraine’s ground-launched fleet.
This strike campaign coincides with wider efforts to dismantle Russian maritime logistics in the region. Between August 1 and 8, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck 12 additional Russian vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. The strikes brought the total number of Russian vessels targeted since the launch of Operation “MoLoChKa” in early July to 218, further disrupting military supply routes and shadow fleet operations across both seas.

Russian oil tankers and port facilities are increasingly being fitted with anti-drone nets and protective cages as Moscow seeks to shield its energy and military infrastructure from continued Ukrainian attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The 28-year-old Caruzo, a tanker under EU and UK sanctions, recently left the Black Sea through the Bosphorus equipped with anti-drone netting and stackable water tanks attached along its sides, according to Financial Times on August 13, citing footage recorded by shipping analyst Yoruk Isik.
The vessel’s bridge was covered with netting, while metal structures were installed over its roof. The crew had also effectively “boxed themselves in” behind the protective measures, according to Samir Madani, co-founder of the shipping monitoring website Tankertrackers.com.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that Novorossiysk serves as Russia’s last major naval stronghold in the Black Sea and is located more than 300 kilometers from the frontline.
