LOS ANGELES, Aug. 12 (Xinhua) -- U.S. lettuce prices fell 16.4 percent in July from June on a seasonally adjusted basis, the largest one-month decline on record, as a Cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico weakened consumer demand, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday.
Lettuce is included in the bureau's fruits and vegetables category, whose overall price index fell 0.1 percent in July. Despite the monthly drop, lettuce prices remained 7.5 percent above a year earlier.
Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the Cyclospora parasite, which can spread through contaminated food or water, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Retail data also pointed to weaker demand. Forbes reported Sunday, citing NielsenIQ data, that fresh-lettuce unit sales fell 9 percent in the week ending July 18 from the previous week, while dollar sales of prepackaged salads dropped 14 percent in the four weeks ending July 25 from a year earlier.
The impact has extended to restaurants. Sweetgreen, a major U.S. salad and fresh-food chain, said last week that the outbreak had reduced demand for fresh prepared foods since mid-July. It now expects same-store sales to decline 7 to 8 percent this year, compared with its previous forecast of a 2 to 4 percent decline.
Salad and Go, a smaller salad chain, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on Aug. 4 and closed its remaining 70 restaurants the following day. The company said the outbreak had further weakened consumer confidence, adding to existing pressures including sustained weak demand, rising costs and difficulties stemming from earlier expansion.
The CDC and the Food and Drug Administration have linked the multistate outbreak to iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico and recalled by Taylor Farms de Mexico on July 17.
As of Tuesday, the CDC had received reports of 13,895 laboratory-confirmed domestically acquired cases since May 1, including 740 hospitalizations and two deaths.
The CDC said it was investigating multiple clusters and expected reported case numbers to rise further, noting that it can take several weeks for illnesses to be reported and classified. ■

China Focus: Smart manufacturing fuels construction industry upgrade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
20:20:17 CST
21:20:17 KST

TIANJIN, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Even in the blazing summer heat of Urumqi in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, workers at a residential project are kept surprisingly cool by a "residential building machine" whose giant canopy shades the entire construction area.
From a distance, the smart platform looks like a blue square cap perched atop the rising structure. Stepping inside, one finds a spacious steel platform supported by 16 columns, surrounded by safety railings and netting.
"This is essentially a movable airborne factory," said Han Junqiang with China Construction Third Engineering Bureau Co., Ltd. "It turns traditional open-air, high-rise work into an enclosed, safe indoor operation."
But the system does more than shield workers from the elements. It also drastically reduces the heavy lifting workload. Building materials and equipment are hoisted along with the platform as it climbs, delivering everything directly to the new floor.
To ensure precision on large single-floor layouts, the system uses a "digital twin" integrated with multiple sensors that collect real-time operational data from all angles, enabling instant warnings and automatic corrections. With this setup, each floor can be completed in as little as four days, while every step of the process is continuously monitored.
With new technologies, construction is now moving toward greater precision, safety, and environmental sustainability. The shift is being driven from the top down. Since 2022, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development has launched smart construction pilot programs in 24 cities.
Tianjin Municipality is among them, and a growing number of projects there are showcasing what AI-enabled construction can achieve. One example is the Tianjin Liulin urban-renewal project. Covering 82,000 square meters, it is designated as one of the city's pilot smart-construction projects.
The contractor, China Construction Sixth Engineering Bureau Co., Ltd., has deployed an AI-powered "smart-site" camera system, tower-crane sensors with visualization, virtual safety-training modules, and VR hazard simulations. These tools detect unsafe behavior in real time and issue automatic warnings or corrective instructions, significantly reducing accident risks.
To improve the occupant experience, the project has also used Building Information Modeling to simulate outdoor wind flows, improve natural daylight inside apartments, and optimize residential energy efficiency.
Smart devices are becoming more common inside the houses, including cameras with algorithms that detect falls by elderly residents or children, and gas sensors that automatically shut off valves and open windows in case of leaks. These are increasingly being built into new urban housing.
The policy backing is clear. This year's government work report called for developing smart construction and cultivating a modernized industrial chain for the sector. The housing ministry has also issued technical guidelines to accelerate the adoption of smart technologies across the entire lifecycle of building projects.
Analysts noted substantial untapped potential for AI-driven productivity gains in construction as data shows that the value added by China's construction industry has exceeded 6 percent of GDP every year since 2021. In 2025, the sector generated 8.64 trillion yuan (about 1.27 trillion U.S. dollars) in added value, accounting for 6.16 percent of the national economy.
Wang Guangbin, dean of the center of innovation and development in construction at Tongji University, described smart construction as a game-changer. "It improves quality through digital design, intelligent production, and lean construction. At the same time, it redefines resource allocation through platform-based collaboration, online supervision and smart maintenance."
Wang added that the shift is turning a traditionally labor-intensive industry into a technology and knowledge-intensive one, while also driving upgrades in related sectors that include building materials, engineering machinery, industrial software and smart terminals.
The smart approach extends to more complex infrastructure as well. In east China's Fujian Province, construction is underway on the Tian'an Expressway. The project marked progress recently when the left bore of the Guangping Tunnel was holed through, despite challenging ground conditions in a karst landscape where rock is unstable and prone to collapse.
Yu Canxin, project manager from China Railway 18th Bureau Group Co., Ltd., said the team used geological radar and horizontal directional drilling to map hidden hazards ahead of the tunnel face. The data helped fine-tune the excavation plan. Multiple smart sensors were also installed along the bore, feeding back constant readings on rock movement and settlement. This real-time data stream allowed the team to continuously monitor ground settlement and other critical indicators, ultimately ensuring the successful completion of the left bore.
From site surveys and construction execution to long-term maintenance, AI is now embedding itself across every phase of construction. Technologies, including intelligent monitoring, digital twins and automated construction, are fundamentally re-engineering the industry's value chain.
Experts say the goal is not merely faster or cheaper construction, but a fundamental shift toward modern industrial practices -- where design, production, and logistics are all integrated into a data-driven workflow. The aim is to strengthen domestic supply chains, upgrade materials and equipment, and revitalize the broader innovation ecosystem around construction. ■

HARBIN, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- A new collection of historical records about Unit 731, the notorious Japanese germ warfare division during World War II (WWII), has unveiled more evidence of Japan's war atrocities in China.
Released Wednesday by the Exhibition Hall of Evidences of Crime Committed by Unit 731 of the Japanese Imperial Army in northeast China's Harbin, Heilongjiang Province, the records confirm that the Japanese military buried large quantities of chemical shells in China on the eve of its defeat.
The 70-minute oral testimony from Hitoshi Tanizaki, a former medic at the Hailar branch of Unit 731, provides first-hand evidence useful for further research into Japan's abandoned chemical weapons in China.
The testimony was collected in 2016 when researchers from the Exhibition Hall visited Japan. Tanizaki, whose original name was Hitoshi Ozaki, said in the video that he was 21 when he joined the military. Before enlistment, he had assisted a doctor and attended a night commercial school.
Tanizaki said that after being assigned to the Hailar branch, he realized that it was a military unit that violated international law. The Hailar branch was under the direct command of Unit 731's headquarters in Harbin, the provincial capital. Its First Section was responsible for cultivating bacteria, while its Second Section conducted toxicity tests on water sources, among other duties.
Of particular significance, Tanizaki disclosed that the Japanese military had destroyed evidence of its crimes and buried chemical shells when it was defeated. He confirmed that, during the retreat, the Hailar branch set fire to all its facilities, while the Japanese military's chemical warfare unit secretly buried large quantities of chemical shells.
"It wasn't bacteria, but poison gas," said Tanizaki. He added that there was a chemical warfare unit, based in the Fulaerji district of Qiqihar, Heilongjiang.
Jin Shicheng, a researcher at the Exhibition Hall, said the testimony directly corroborates that the Japanese military had abandoned chemical weapons in China when it was defeated. It also sheds light on the historical origins of the harm caused by abandoned chemical weapons after the war, giving it contemporary significance.
Jin also introduced the personal information registration files of the Unit 731 Hailar branch, another piece of evidence disclosed on Wednesday to Xinhua.
The files were military service records that Japanese military personnel were required to complete as individuals when they were demobilized after the war at the request of Japan's then Ministry of Health and Welfare. The records released this time comprise 185 pages and contain key information on 156 members of the Hailar branch, including their names, ranks, dates of enlistment, duties, transfers and whereabouts after the war.
Jin said research into these files yields two major findings. First, it exposes how the Japanese military concealed its biological warfare crimes by recruiting personnel under the names of regular infantry units.
For example, personnel were recruited under the names of standard infantry units, before receiving three months of training at Unit 731 headquarters and being assigned to the Hailar branch.
Such recruitment was clearly deceptive and was intended to conceal Unit 731's secret criminal activities, including human experimentation, Jin said.
Second, the records confirm the continuity of postwar investigations into Japanese biological warfare crimes.
The records reveal that 145 of the 156 unit members were captured by Soviet forces after the war and detained in the Soviet Union, while four of them were tried in Khabarovsk between April and September 1950.
Jin said the findings confirm that Soviet investigations and judicial accountability for Japanese biological warfare criminals had continued after the public trials held in 1949.
Jin noted that the disclosed records will deepen research into the branches of Unit 731 and, together with previously obtained oral testimonies from former members, form a solid evidence chain of Japan's gruesome war crimes during WWII.
Unit 731 was a top-secret biological and chemical warfare research base established as the nerve center for Japanese biological warfare in China and Southeast Asia during WWII. At least 3,000 people were used in human experiments conducted by Unit 731, and more than 300,000 people in China were killed by Japan's biological weapons.
This year marks the 81st anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War.
Yang Yanjun, a researcher at the Exhibition Hall, said that during the past eight decades since the war ended, the world outside of China and Japan has remained relatively unaware of the medical atrocities committed by Unit 731.
"Today, the international community has largely reflected on the Doctors' Trial during the Nuremberg Trials and Nazi Germany's medical crimes. However, the awareness of Japan's wartime medical atrocities remains insufficient," Yang said.
Yang called on scholars worldwide to further enhance the academic rigor and objectivity of studies on the crimes committed by Unit 731, and help foster a correct historical understanding in the international community. ■

Ukraine may avoid gas imports this winter as energy system becomes more protected – expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
15:20:14 EEST
21:20:14 KST

Ukraine has done significant work to get through the 2026-27 winter heating season, but Russian occupiers will still look for weak and vulnerable spots in the country's energy system, energy expert Andrian Prokip has said.
"As for winter, there are grounds to believe the first half will be fairly warm. It's often the case for us that frosts start in the second half of winter, but last winter, remember, we had frosts that were the coldest in 20 years and snowfalls that were the heaviest in 10 years," Prokip said during a discussion titled "Winter Is Near: Are the State and Society Ready?" at the Interfax-Ukraine press center on Thursday, adding that if the whole winter is warm, the problems for the population from strikes on energy infrastructure will be largely offset.
He described the gas situation in Ukraine as "completely normal."
"Gas production is constantly under fire, but the situation with gas storage is fundamentally different from what we had, let's say, a year ago. Last year, in literally four months, we imported 1.7 billion cubic meters of gas, while over the same period this year we've had practically no imports and are ahead of plan for filling gas storage facilities — it's possible we won't import gas at all," the expert said.
On electricity, Prokip said Ukraine has used up all its margin of safety, but the energy system is becoming more resilient to wartime risks with each passing year.
"We're constantly getting new generation, distributed generation, and facilities are becoming more and more protected," he explained.
The expert noted that Russian occupiers are constantly changing their equipment, strategy and tactics for strikes.
"They're constantly looking for weak spots. Last year we saw them targeting facilities they hadn't hit before. This year they'll be looking for weak spots in exactly the same way. So we have this kind of double race to stay ahead — we're thinking about where they might strike and trying to protect those places, while they're looking for places to strike. Given that the enemy is essentially cornered, without gains on the battlefield, while our defense forces are effectively destroying Russian oil refining, they'll try to deliver the strongest possible strikes and will keep looking for these weak spots," Prokip said.
He is therefore convinced Ukraine will see outages and faces high risks of local heating problems, but that the coming winter will be no worse than last year's.
"Overall, I'm fairly optimistic about winter. But optimism doesn't mean there won't be problems — it means there won't be problems we can't get through. So, of course, it's worth preparing for a scenario roughly like the winter we had last year," Prokip said.
The discussion also featured a presentation of the "Winter. City Will Hold" project, which envisages comprehensive preparation of communities for the 2026/2027 heating season — from risk assessment to specific action algorithms in the event of shelling, prolonged blackouts, loss of heat and water supply, and other emergencies. The project's second stage will begin with the onset of cold weather and will focus directly on helping community residents.

Interview: Jordan ready to expand economic cooperation with China, says investment minister
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
20:19:45 CST
21:19:45 KST

Jordan's Minister of Investment Tareq Abu Ghazaleh speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Amman, Jordan, on July 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Xin Mengchen)
AMMAN, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Jordan regards China as a strategic partner in advancing investment, industrial cooperation and economic transformation, Jordan's Minister of Investment Tareq Abu Ghazaleh has said.
"We look forward to elevating Jordan's economic partnership with China to broader and more diversified levels in a way that serves our shared interests and supports sustainable development in both countries," Abu Ghazaleh said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
Recalling his visit to China in June, Abu Ghazaleh said the trip provided him with an opportunity to gain first-hand insight into China's development experience and the progress it has achieved in infrastructure and long-term strategic planning.
China has established itself as one of the world's leading industrial, technological, and trading economies, the minister noted, adding that its continued development creates broad opportunities for cooperation with Jordan, particularly in the fields of investment, industry, and trade.
The importance of this partnership continues to grow in light of China's leadership in a number of sectors that are national priorities for Jordan, "including advanced industries, electronics, renewable energy, energy storage technologies, electric mobility, railway systems, logistics, agricultural technology and pharmaceuticals," he added.
Investment is a key pillar of Jordan's economic development, underpinning efforts to diversify the country's productive base and foster sustainable growth. In recent years, Jordan has introduced a comprehensive package of reforms aimed at creating a more competitive and attractive investment environment.
These efforts contributed to a nearly 25 percent increase in foreign direct investment inflows in 2025, which exceeded 2 billion U.S. dollars.
According to the minister, Chinese investment in Jordan has expanded steadily, particularly in the renewable energy, manufacturing, and logistics sectors. These investments have helped create employment opportunities, support local suppliers, and introduce advanced production technologies to the Jordanian market.
Describing China as an important partner in supporting Jordan's economic growth, the minister said bilateral cooperation is evolving toward a more advanced stage.
Referring to the partnership between Chinese investors and Jordan's Arab Potash Company as a successful example of economic cooperation between the two countries, Abu Ghazaleh said the partnership has strengthened production capacity, expanded exports, and enhanced Jordan's position as a leading global supplier of fertilizers and agricultural inputs.
As regards Jordan's advantages in attracting investment, he added that the Kingdom is connected to more than 50 global markets through an extensive network of free trade agreements, supported by a highly skilled workforce and advanced infrastructure, logistics and digital capabilities.
These advantages complement China's industrial and technological capabilities, creating broader opportunities to develop investment and industrial partnerships that generate added value for both sides, Abu Ghazaleh noted.
"With its competitive investment environment, strategic location and modern legislative framework, Jordan is well positioned to serve as a trusted partner and a regional platform for Chinese companies seeking to expand into regional and international markets," he said. ■

NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government on Thursday withdrew the Banga Bibhushan award from BJP Rajya Sabha member Ananta Maharaj over his alleged derogatory comment against Netaji.Banga Bibhushan is one of West Bengal’s highest civilian honours, awarded by the state government to eminent personalities for outstanding contributions in fields such as art, culture, literature, social service and other areas. Ananta Maharaj was conferred the Banga Bibhushan on February 21 this year, by then-West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee at a state government programme in Kolkata marking International Mother Language Day; which has now been revoked.The controversy erupted after BJP Rajya Sabha MP Nagendra Roy, alias Ananta Maharaj, questioned Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's role in forming and leading the Azad Hind Fauj. Speaking at a meeting in Dinhata on July 19, Roy asked, “Did Netaji have the capacity to organise and form the Azad Hind Fauj?” He then claimed that “they were all British soldiers” and alleged that “the Indian National Army (INA) was misused.”Roy also claimed that the Azad Hind Fauj originated from British-Indian troops who had been handed over by Germany.
His remarks triggered a backlash in West Bengal, with political leaders and Rajbanshi organisations condemning the comments and demanding action against the BJP MP. Prominent Rajbanshi figures issued a joint statement condemning the remarks as false, insulting and damaging to social harmony. Forward Bloc, a party founded by Netaji, also lodged police complaints and demanded the immediate revocation of his Rajya Sabha membership.
The controversy also drew criticism from within the BJP, with veteran party leader Tathagata Roy urging the central leadership to intervene.The remarks have since escalated into a wider political row, with former CM Banerjee accusing the BJP of insulting Netaji and West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari warning that anyone making derogatory remarks about the freedom fighter would face action under the law.

Unknown Publisher

21:19:00 KST

Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) has issued an official warning about a Russian disinformation campaign ahead of several state and local elections scheduled for September. The agency directly linked the campaign to the Russian Matryoshka bot network, which The Insider has extensively covered in its reporting.
“This campaign is characterized by short English-language videos that mimic the layout of well-known German media outlets. Using sensationalist headlines and biased claims, it spreads narratives aimed at polarizing East and West Germany, stirring up anti-federal sentiment, and discrediting state and local politicians,” the agency said.
The BfV found that in August, bots on X (Twitter) spread posts with the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany, promoting the renewed division of Germany into East and West while calling such a split a “historical necessity.” The agency said that in 2026, regional and local politicians were the targets of smear campaigns.
“Those particularly affected are politicians from parties that represent political positions not in line with the strategic interests of the Russian Federation,” the BfV said.
Germany will hold elections this fall to the state parliaments (Landtags) of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, both in the former East Germany. Elections will also be held for Berlin’s parliament and for local offices in Lower Saxony.
Earlier, Gabriel Attal, a French presidential candidate and leader of the Renaissance party, filed a complaint over alleged foreign interference by Russian online networks. Attal’s lawyers said France’s General Secretariat for Defense and National Security— along with the Viginum agency, which monitors foreign digital interference — had warned of disinformation campaigns targeting the politician.
Viginum confirmed to AFP that it had linked the operation to the pro-Russian Matryoshka bot network with a high degree of confidence. On Aug. 4, the day before Attal’s first complaint, The Insider reported on eight fake videos designed to look like reports by BFM, RFI, Le Parisien, AFP, France 24, Le Figaro, Libération, and Le Monde.

Burç Eruygur
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
Russia and Ukraine traded overnight strikes Thursday, with at least two people killed when a passenger train was hit in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, while Kyiv said it struck an oil refinery deep inside Russia.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service said on Telegram that two people were killed in the Odesa region's Berezivka district after a Russian strike hit a passenger train, sparking a fire in the locomotive that was later extinguished.
"There were 340 people on the train. And whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on the US social media platform X, claiming the train was hit by a jet-powered drone.
"More air defense support and more pressure on Russia are needed if the world is serious about stopping this war in Europe," Zelenskyy added.
Separately, the Izmail District State Administration said Russian strikes hit port infrastructure in the Odesa region overnight, causing damage and a fire.
The administration later said power was cut in the southeastern part of the port city of Izmail, on the left bank of the Danube River, after local electricity networks were damaged.
Ukrainian private energy company DTEK was working to restore supplies, it added.
Ukraine's Air Force separately claimed that air defenses shot down 111 of 133 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces carried out overnight strikes against what it described as a temporary deployment point for a Ukrainian Armed Forces unit in the port of Izmail and port infrastructure “used for unloading and storing military cargo.”
It also claimed to have struck a Ukrainian Navy command post in the port of Reni, also on the left bank of the Danube.
Strikes in Russia
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses shot down 362 Ukrainian drones over 17 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.
Radiy Khabirov, head of Russia's Bashkortostan region, said two people were injured in an overnight Ukrainian drone attack targeting a logistics center in the Chishminsky district.
He earlier said debris from a downed drone fell in an industrial zone in the city of Salavat, sparking a fire.
Wildberries, Russia's largest online marketplace, separately said a fire broke out in the industrial zone where one of its facilities is located.
"Firefighters are working at the scene. A pre-emptive evacuation was carried out at the facility in accordance with safety regulations. No goods are stored at the specified facility," the company said.
Ukraine's General Staff later confirmed that it targeted the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Bashkortostan, claiming the facility was hit and a fire broke out afterward.
Ukraine has intensified drone strikes on logistics facilities operated by Wildberries in a campaign that began in mid-July and has spread across several Russian regions.
Since July 18, Ukrainian drones have targeted more than 15 Wildberries logistics centers, including facilities in the Moscow, Tambov, Leningrad, Krasnodar, Volgograd and Stavropol regions, as well as in Crimea.
Kyiv has accused the e-commerce retailer of playing a role in Moscow's military supply chain, while Moscow and Wildberries maintain that the facilities are purely civilian.
Separately, Orenburg Gov. Yevgeny Solntsev announced that key infrastructure at the Orsk oil refinery cannot be immediately restored following a Ukrainian strike earlier this week.
"The equipment is imported, and given the sanctions, repairs will take up to six months,” he said. "The plant is completely shut down. We are preparing for the worst-case scenario. We will have to rely on imported fuel. Logistics is already being reconfigured. Of the 287 gas stations (in the region), 80% are operational.”

21:17:00 KST

How Germany's drone defense fails
August 13, 2026
How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."
Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.
The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.
Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange.
"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.
The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.
The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.
Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police
Germany has so far done little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.
In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.
Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.
Unclear responsibilities
Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.
Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.
Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.
Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?
As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.
A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.
In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."
Airports, train stations still lack protection
There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.
"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."
The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.
An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.
The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.
This article was originally written in German.

Morocco threatens to suspend extradition treaty with Spain over migration crisis

Morocco threatens to suspend extradition treaty with Spain over migration crisis
Kyiv • UNN
Morocco’s justice minister said that the extradition agreement with Spain could be suspended over the legalization of migrants. Rabat is also demanding the immediate return of more than 1,300 Moroccan minors from Ceuta.
Morocco is studying the possibility of suspending its extradition treaty with Spain, the kingdom’s Justice Minister Abdellatif Wahbi said. He accused Madrid of legalizing refugees whom Rabat is trying to deter, UNN reports, citing Euronews.
The list of mutual grievances between Rabat and Madrid following the recent crisis in Ceuta is growing.
Moroccan Justice Minister Wahbi said in an interview with international media that he was prepared to suspend the extradition treaty with Spain over disruptions in the transfer of detainees, and demanded the immediate return of Moroccan minors from the Spanish enclave.
Extradition: the first threat
In an interview with the EFE agency, the minister accused Spain of creating a “pull effect,” explaining that the mass legalization of migrants in Madrid motivates new attempts to storm the border in Ceuta and Melilla. The Moroccan side pointed to a contradiction whereby Rabat spends resources curbing migration while Spain grants amnesty to people who have already entered the country. Wahbi made it clear that Morocco does not want to continue sending personnel to arrange the transfer of migrants detained in Spain when those transfers are ultimately called off.
Time for the children to go home
Answering a question from DW Arabic, the minister, speaking on behalf of the country, demanded that Spain immediately repatriate all Moroccan minors, including those who reached Ceuta during the recent crisis. Wahbi stressed that the new school year was approaching and that the children should study at home, living with their families. The minister addressed the Spanish authorities harshly: “If you want these children and believe that you can provide them with the best conditions, take them together with their families. Separating a child from their parents under the pretext of their “best interests” is a crime, and it must stop.”
Rabat is demanding the return of more than 1,300 Moroccan minors who remained in Ceuta after the mass border breach in July. Spain’s official response, despite the political disputes, comes down to a willingness to cooperate in compliance with EU laws. However, Spain’s former Minister for Youth and Children, Sira Rego, previously stated that the collective deportation of children was impossible. Spain is obliged to conduct an individual legal assessment of each case to guarantee the safety of the minor.
Ceuta and Melilla on the agenda
Answering a question from Ashraq News, a representative of Morocco’s cabinet also addressed the issue of sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla. Asked directly whether Morocco was considering reclaiming the enclaves, he avoided making any promises regarding timelines or mechanisms but did not rule out such an option. According to Wahbi, Ceuta and Melilla are Moroccan territories, and the dispute over their status remains “in limbo” today; however, the crisis can be overcome through a long-term strategy and political dialogue.
Madrid sees the situation differently. “The Spanish status of Ceuta and Melilla is beyond doubt,” diplomatic sources in Madrid told Euronews. — Ceuta and Melilla form part of the concept of Spain’s territorial integrity, recognized internationally. Spain’s territorial integrity has not been discussed and will never be discussed with anyone.”

Anthropic investors eye $2T valuation in potential Wall Street debut: Report

Anthropic investors are betting that the artificial intelligence company could seek a valuation of at least $2 trillion in a potential October stock market debut, a figure that would eclipse SpaceX and make it the largest initial public offering on record.
Six investors in the five-year-old company told the Financial Times that Anthropic's rapidly rising revenue could support more than a doubling of its current valuation, according to a report published Thursday.
Investors said they expect Anthropic's annualized revenue to reach between $100 billion and $120 billion by the end of 2026, using a measure that projects full-year sales from recent performance. That would represent more than tenfold growth during the year.
“If Anthropic is growing 800% a year, you’d think at the incredibly low end they would trade at 30 times [revenue],” one investor told the Financial Times. “That would make them a $3 trillion company.”
Anthropic has no directly comparable publicly listed US AI lab, leaving investors to look to companies such as Palantir and Nebius, which have traded at roughly 55 times revenue this year.
The company has not yet set an initial public offering (IPO) valuation target, according to several investors. Its bullish backers nevertheless argue that demand for its AI models and business tools justifies a lofty valuation.
The optimism comes as Anthropic faces growing risks. Revenue growth slowed in June, two investors familiar with the matter told the UK daily, amid a temporary US Commerce Department ban affecting its leading models.
The company has also faced disputes with the Trump administration and remains in litigation with the US Department of Defense.
High AI costs and growing competition could also put pressure on the company. Anthropic's leading model costs more than two and a half times as much to use as OpenAI's flagship model, while Chinese open-weight alternatives are available at a fraction of the price, according to the Financial Times.
Anthropic filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, placing it in a quiet period ahead of a possible listing.

Russian drone attack on passenger train in Ukraine's Odesa region kills two people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:15:37 UTC
21:15:37 KST

The latest attack comes as the United Nations recorded a record-number of civilian deaths in Ukraine in July, the highest monthly toll since May 2022.
Russian forces struck a second passenger train, which was carrying 500 people, in Ukraine's Odesa region on Thursday, injuring a child.
It comes just hours after a Russian drone struck a passenger train carrying 340 people in the same region earlier in the day, an attack that had killed two crew members.
The victims of the attack were two crew members, the train machinist and his assistant, the CEO of Ukrainian Railways Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a post on Facebook.
None of the passengers were harmed.
"Today in the Odesa region, the Russians once again destroyed an ordinary passenger train locomotive with a jet-powered drone. There were 340 people on the train," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"Whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian," he added.
It is not the first time Russia has targeted a passenger train, which Kyiv says is part of an effort to disrupt logistics while increasingly targeting civilian infrastructure.
Russia also targeted port infrastructure in the Izmail district of the Odesa region, local media reported. In total, Russia launched 133 drones at Ukraine overnight into Thursday, targeting 15 locations across the country.
Civilian deaths in Ukraine highest in July since May 2022, UN finds
A recent report by the United Nations revealed civilian deaths in Ukraine hit a record-high in July, the highest since May 2022, the first months of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 percent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 percent increase compared with July 2025," the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a statement on Thursday.
"The number of those killed is the highest recorded since May 2022," it added.
The UN said it verified 16,874 civilian deaths since the start of Russia's invasion, although notes that the toll is likely higher since it cannot confirm casualties in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Kyiv, in particular, has frequently come under fire. At least 54 civilians were killed in the Ukrainian capital during the month of July, the UN said, calling it "one of the hardest hit cities".
Both sides have significantly escalated their long-range attacks this year, causing a spike in civilian deaths, according to the UN.
Ukraine, on its end, has also also ramped up its campaign against Russia's critical and military infrastructure in recent months.
Near-daily barrages targeting Russian oil facilities with long-range drones in recent months have caused fuel shortages, reduced Russia’s refining capacity, and unsettled the Russian public.
On Thursday, a fire broke out at the Gazprom Neftohim Salavat oil refinery, one of the country's largest, in Russia's Bashkortostan Ukrainian media reported.
A fire was also reported at a Wildberries hub nearby. Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, is a critical piece of Moscow's wartime economy.
Ukraine military aid surged in June, boosted by new EU fund
Russia's use of ballistic missiles has proven difficult for Ukraine to intercept, prompting Zelenskyy to call on allies to provide more air defence systems after warning that the country is facing a critical shortage.
Despite long-term shortages, military aid to Ukraine reached its highest level in June since the United States halted funding in February 2025, driven largely by new EU funding, according to data released by the Kiel Institute.
It found that in June, Kyiv was allocated €7.2 billion, the third-biggest monthly military funding boost from donors since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The EU's €90 billion loan was introduced to support Ukraine's budgetary and defence needs in 2026 and 2027.
On top of the loan support, Germany allocated €700 million, Denmark €600 million, and the Netherlands €500 million euros to support Ukraine's military.

Azerbaijan bets on the pomegranate as its next big export
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:14:53 UTC
21:14:53 KST

Azerbaijan is turning pomegranates, a fruit with 2,000 years of cultural history, into a global brand, with €48.2 million in exports and more than 200 cultivated varieties putting it in direct competition with Iran, Turkey and Spain
Azerbaijan exported €48.2 million worth of pomegranates and pomegranate products in 2025, making the fruit one of the country's fastest-growing non-oil exports.
Around 23,000 hectares of orchards now supply fresh fruit, juice, concentrate, wine and seed oil to 26 countries, from Gulf states to markets across Asia. That puts Azerbaijan up against established exporters such as Iran, Turkey and Spain, all of which sell pomegranates at scale.
"For Azerbaijan, the pomegranate is an integral part of our nation's cultural heritage, with a history spanning nearly 2,000 years, symbolising abundance, prosperity, and well-being," Farhad Garashov, chairman of the Pomegranate Producers and Exporters Association of Azerbaijan, told Euronews.
Azerbaijani producers point to a mix of indigenous varieties, EU-compatible phytosanitary standards and proximity to European and Gulf markets as their main advantages. More than 200 varieties are cultivated, concentrated in the Kur-Araz lowland and the Goychay district.
The best-known internationally is Guloysha, prized for its thin skin, high juice content and sweet-sour flavour. Other varieties, including Valas, Shah Nar, Nazik Gabig and Bala Mursal, offer distinct colours and flavours that producers use to stand out on supermarket shelves abroad.
"This rich heritage is one of the defining characteristics that distinguishes Azerbaijani pomegranates in international markets," said Garashov, whose organisation represents more than 500 farmers and exporters.
Longer shelf life a plus for exporters
Fresh fruit still dominates, but processed products, including juice, concentrate and oil, are giving producers a longer selling season.
Cold storage, processing plants and logistics infrastructure now let them supply buyers year-round rather than only during the autumn harvest.
Foreign buyers and large supermarket chains are demanding stricter phytosanitary standards, consistent fruit sizes and international packaging, requirements that are pushing smallholders toward new financing instruments and partnerships.
"Agriculture in Azerbaijan has entered a new stage of development that focuses not only on increasing production volumes, but also on branding high value-added agricultural products," the director of the Agrarian Innovation Centre under the Ministry of Agriculture, Anar Jafarov, told Euronews.
Climate change concerns
Yusif Lazgiyev, operations director at Az-Granata — a privately owned juice and beverage company that operates 332 hectares of its own orchards and supplies concentrate and bottled juice to export markets — said this year's harvest was significantly reduced after cold and rainy weather in late May and early June prevented the second of the pomegranate tree's three seasonal flowerings.
"Pomegranate trees normally blossom three times a season. This year, the pomegranates in our gardens blossomed only once due to climate change, and this has caused productivity and yield to drop," Lazgiyev told Euronews. "The rain washed the existing blossoms away."
He said yield losses from a single flowering cycle run to 15% to 20%, and that temperature swings between night and day were also causing disease to spread more quickly in orchards. Wine production this year was down 30% to 40% compared with 2025.
Garashov said the industry had identified drip irrigation, digital water management and improved water efficiency as priorities in response to higher temperatures and more frequent drought.
"Climate change, rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, and increasing water scarcity have become major concerns for all producers," he said.
The Goychay Pomegranate Festival, held each October in the district of Goychay, roughly 200 kilometres west of Baku, draws tens of thousands of visitors annually and serves as both a cultural celebration and a trade event where producers meet buyers, showcase new varieties, and negotiate export contracts.
It was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024, following an initiative led by First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva. It is organised by the Ministry of Agriculture and coordinated by its Agrarian Innovation Centre.
"This UNESCO recognition demonstrates the exceptional cultural value of the pomegranate for the Azerbaijani people while further enhancing the international visibility of the 'Made in Azerbaijan' brand," Garashov said.

Doors Open: Sofia Metro Expands with three new stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:13:52 UTC
21:13:52 KST

Author
Joan Kolev
Thursday 13 August 2026 14:45
Thursday, 13 August 2026, 14:45
General Vladimir Vazov metro station in Sofia
PHOTO Sofia Municipality
Font size
Starting August 14, the underground metro network in Bulgaria’s capital Sofia will expand by three kilometres and three new stations: “Stadion Georgi Asparuhov,” “Vitinia,” and “Gen. Vladimir Vazov.” This will allow residents of Sofia’s northeastern neighborhoods to reach the heart of the city - the National Palace of Culture - in around 12 minutes.
Some 45,000 passengers are expected to use the new metro extension each day, which should improve not only public transport connectivity but also road safety in the Bulgarian capital.
PHOTO BTA
“Thank you to the residents of the districts of "Hadzhi Dimitar", "Levski V", and "Levski G" for their patience, understanding, and cooperation during the construction of the metro line. With the opening of the new section, the results of years of work are now a reality - thousands of residents of these neighborhoods will have faster, more convenient, and environmentally friendly transport to different parts of Sofia. For us, this is an important step in the development of the Sofia Metro and in improving the city’s transport connectivity,” wrote Nikolay Naydenov, executive director of Metropoliten EAD, on the company’s Facebook profile.
Nikolay Naydenov
PHOTO BGNES
The expansion of the metro is a strategic priority for Sofia Municipality, and the newly opened section is part of a larger project. In 2027, another six stations are expected to open toward "Geo Milev" and "Mladost" neighborhoods, along with one additional station in "Obelya".
The first metro train in the Bulgarian capital began operating 28 years ago, serving just eight stations along a 6.4-kilometre route. From 1998 to the present, the underground railway has expanded to 52 kilometres, with the metro now the preferred means of transport in Sofia. 
Once the new stations are completed, the network will reach 61 kilometres, with approximately 650,000 passengers expected to use its 57 stations every day.
PHOTO Facebook / Sofia Metro
The first metro plans for Sofia date back to the late 1960s, but actual construction did not begin until the late 1970s. Progress was slow and fragmented, with construction repeatedly advancing and then stopping. Sofia residents were skeptical and often joked about the project and its future.
 The first metro section nevertheless became a reality: two years before the end of the 20th century, the underground railway connected Sveta Nedelya Square in central Sofia with Lyulin, one of the city’s large residential districts. The diagonal connection between the Obelya and Mladost 1 neighborhoods was completed in 2009.
“Citizens will understand the importance of the metro when it operates as a system, rather than as just one metro corridor,” architect Petar Dikov explained at the time. He became Sofia’s chief architect in 2006 and a member of the board of Metropoliten EAD. Today, he is chairman of the Union of Bulgarian Architects and recalls how rapidly the Sofia Metro map has changed over the past 20 years, eventually developing into a four-line network.
Architect Petar Dikov
PHOTO BTA
“After 2006, the major development of the Sofia Metro actually began. In September 2009, the section from Sveta Nedelya to Mladost metro station was opened - the first new section since the one inherited from the end of the previous century. That was when the most rapid development began, first toward the airport through Druzhba. Meanwhile, work on the second metro corridor also began.”
Gradually, residents came to appreciate the convenience of traveling underground - speed and predictability regardless of weather conditions. Nevertheless, some metro development projects have faced opposition, prompting routes to be reconsidered and changed. According to architect Dikov, these changes have often proved more cost-effective and beneficial. This was the case with the Third Metro Line, which is currently under construction.
PHOTO BTA
“The original project was developed by Metropoliten Prague. I want to emphasize that the first project for the Third Metro Line followed Sofia’s 2006 General Development Plan. It was supposed to run along Tsar Boris III Boulevard as a light, above-ground metro. After Pirogov Hospital, it would go underground, and then along Botevgradsko Shosse boulevard it would again run as a light, above-ground metro,” Dikov recalls.
That project, which envisaged a combination of underground and above-ground sections, was not implemented following protests by the civic organization “Save the Metro,” which prompted the designers to consider a different approach and completely change the route. This also required an amendment to the city’s development plan.
“We then decided to connect the Ovcha Kupel neighborhood with the two branches of the metro - the eastern and western ones. At the time, Ovcha Kupel was the most disadvantaged neighborhood of Sofia. The other branch would run along Vladimir Vazov Boulevard, where there are many densely populated residential complexes in need of better transport. We extended the route along Vladimir Vazov Boulevard and established a connection with the Gerena Stadium - every stadium needs good transport links.”
PHOTO Sofia Municipality
Thanks to European funding, the pace of construction has accelerated threefold. According to Sofia Municipality and Bulgaria’s Public Procurement Portal, the Second Metro Line was built with European funding under the Operational Programme “Transport,” receiving more than €500 million.
The Third Metro Line received funding in two stages - €185 million for the central section alone and another €68 million in grants for the second stage of construction. Total EU funding for the third line amounts to more than €350-400 million, including metro trains and extensions.
Stadium Georgi Asparuhov metro station
PHOTO Sofia Municipality
The construction of the new metro stations in Sofia is also being financed through European funds, together with co-financing from the municipal and state budgets. For the section along Vladimir Vazov Boulevard, the European Union is providing €144 million in funding.
It was recently announced that Sofia Municipality could receive another €265 million in European funding for public transport vehicles, part of which will be used to purchase 16 new metro trains.
As passengers travel comfortably and quickly, they will continue to hear the pleasant female voice announcing the stations of the Sofia Metro. It belongs to popular television journalist Nadya Obretenova.
Nadya Obretenova
PHOTO bnt.bg
“I have been recording the station announcements for the Sofia Metro since the very beginning. I don’t remember the year when I made the recording, but I was invited by the director of Metropoliten, engineer Stoyan Bratoev,” she told Radio Bulgaria.
Her professional interest in the development of the underground railway, however, goes beyond journalism. As an engineering student at Todor Kableshkov University of Transport, Obretenova completed an internship at the company responsible for designing the Sofia Metro. The political changes of 1989 and the suspension of work on this key infrastructure project forced her to turn toward journalism - a decision she says she has never regretted. Years later, however, she became the perfect person to announce the stations along the metro routes.
PHOTO BTA
“The most interesting thing is that when friends and acquaintances travel on the Sofia Metro and hear my voice, they think of me and realize that there’s something they haven’t told me or that we haven’t spoken recently. It’s very amusing that I often get calls from people I know, while in the background I can hear my own voice announcing the stations as they travel on the Sofia Metro. It was strange at first, but it doesn’t surprise me anymore.”
PHOTO BTA
The Sofia Metro is both a project and an achievement made possible by dozens of specialists - engineers, architects, geologists, and hydrotechnical engineers - people who create new connections and directions for the city. Their work is extremely demanding and risky, and the lives of thousands of people depend on its quality every day. Yet it is clear that the metro is much more than an engineering and transport structure: it shapes the way people live in a major city.

South Korea issues nationwide malaria alert after finding parasite in mosquitoes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:13:18 UTC
21:13:18 KST

Saadet Gökce
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
South Korean health authorities issued a nationwide malaria alert Thursday after detecting the parasite that causes the disease in mosquitoes.
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (KDCA) said genetic material from the Plasmodium vivax malaria parasite was detected in Anopheles mosquitoes collected in Paju and Yeoncheon County in northern South Korea between July 27 and Aug. 2.
"The detection of the parasite in vector mosquitoes means that the likelihood of contracting malaria from the bite of an infected mosquito has increased," the agency said in a statement.
The nationwide alert follows a malaria advisory issued June 22 due to an increase in vector mosquitoes. Alerts had subsequently been issued in five areas due to clusters of cases and increases in mosquito populations.
Despite the nationwide alert, South Korea recorded 201 domestically acquired malaria cases between Jan. 1 and Aug. 1, down 43.4% from 355 during the same period last year.
Malaria cases in South Korea have historically been concentrated in areas near the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) separating the country from North Korea, though risk areas have expanded in recent years.
The nationwide alert comes during an unusually hot summer in South Korea. However, the KDCA said malaria-vector mosquito density remains lower than last year, partly due to extreme heat.
Health officials warned that mosquito populations could rise again once the extreme heat subsides and urged authorities in malaria-risk areas to strengthen mosquito-control measures.
They also urged residents of and visitors to malaria-risk areas to avoid nighttime outdoor activities, wear long clothing, and use mosquito repellents, screens, and nets.
People experiencing suspected symptoms, including fever and chills, were advised to seek testing at a public health center or medical facility.

A senior Russian military officer was killed in a targeted bombing in annexed Crimea, Kremlin-installed officials and the Federal Security Service (FSB) said Thursday.
The explosion occurred around 10 a.m. local time on a street in western Sevastopol, the home port of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, according to the news outlet Ostorozhno Novosti.
Citing the FSB, the outlet reported that an explosive device was placed in a trash can and detonated when the officer walked by.
The FSB confirmed the death of a Russian Defense Ministry serviceman but did not disclose his identity, according to state news agencies.
The security agency announced the arrest of a 32-year-old Russian woman who they said was acting on the instructions of Ukrainian special services.
“Investigators established that she acted on instructions from Ukrainian special services and showed no remorse,” said Mikhail Razvozhayev, the Kremlin-installed governor of Sevastopol.
Unverified reporting by Ostorozhno Novosti claimed to identify her as Margarita Reutt, who lives in the southern Russian resort city of Sochi, volunteered to clean up oil from beaches in nearby Anapa and ran her own business.
The outlet previously reported that a court in August 2025 fined Reutt for “discrediting” the Russian military over public remarks on board a train in response to news of a Ukrainian drone strike.
Telegram channels with links to Russia’s security services claimed to identify the victim as Captain First Rank Robert Shageyev, who previously commanded the Ukrainian Navy’s only submarine before defecting to Russia during the 2014 annexation of Crimea.
Shageyev reportedly served as deputy commander of a Russian Black Sea Fleet submarine brigade.
The Moscow Times was unable to independently verify the details of those reports.
Razvozhayev said earlier that five people were killed overnight during an operation to dispose of an explosive device.

Israeli army seizes 16 Palestinian homes in West Bank's Qusra village, turns them into military posts: Official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:10:06 UTC
21:10:06 KST

Qais Omar Darwesh Omar and Rania Abushamala
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
The Israeli army has seized 16 Palestinian homes in and around Qusra in the northern occupied West Bank and converted them into military posts, a local official said Thursday.
Abdul Azim al-Wadi, head of the Qusra village council, told Anadolu that the army was continuing its military offensive in the town, south of Nablus, and had informed the council that it would last until Sunday morning.
Large Israeli forces, accompanied by infantry troops, military vehicles and bulldozers, entered Qusra and deployed across the town and its outskirts, he said.
Al-Wadi said the Israeli army told the council it was seeking to dismantle an illegal outpost established by occupiers near the town amid escalating tensions in the area.
He said three Palestinian families, including one with US citizenship, remained trapped inside their homes for a 4th consecutive day.
An Anadolu correspondent saw Israeli troops stationed inside several homes, while some families left their houses to stay with relatives.
Since Sunday, Israeli occupiers have erected a tent and temporary structures among Palestinian homes in the Ras al-Ain area on the outskirts of Qusra, according to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The occupiers also blocked roads leading to the area with rocks and surrounded three homes, the commission said.
It warned that the attacks could develop into a prolonged siege intended to isolate the families and force them from their homes.
The occupiers have obstructed the delivery of food, water and medicine to the homes, while water and electricity lines have also been cut, it added.
Earlier Thursday, large Israeli forces raided Qusra, imposed a curfew and ordered businesses to close amid a widespread deployment of infantry troops, military vehicles and bulldozers.
The developments come amid escalating occupier attacks in the area and Palestinian concerns that attempts to establish the outpost could become permanent and lead to the seizure of Palestinian homes and land.
The commission said occupiers had attempted eight times to establish an outpost in the Jabal Ras al-Ain area, citing its strategic location on high ground overlooking a large area.
Attempts to raid and seize the homes began about four months ago, prompting family members to take turns staying in them to prevent their takeover, it added.
The commission warned of a repeat of events in the nearby village of Jalud, where it said occupiers seized a home belonging to Mahmoud al-Tubasi’s family on July 22 after besieging it for more than three months.
According to the commission’s latest figures, occupiers carried out 12,506 attacks from October 2023 through June 2026, killing 52 Palestinians and setting 890 fires that damaged Palestinian property and farmland.
It also documented 2,256 attacks across the occupied West Bank in July, including 1,458 by Israeli forces and 798 by occupiers.

Lithuania’s justice minister revives call for public sex offender registry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:09:00 UTC
21:09:00 KST

Lithuania’s justice minister is calling for renewed efforts to establish a public registry of people convicted of sexual offenses against children after prosecutors announced cases against two priests this week.
Justice Minister Rita Tamašunienė said Thursday that such a registry could strengthen monitoring and prevention measures and help protect children from repeat offenses.
“In my view as justice minister, the time has come to return to this idea and look for solutions that would help protect children even better,” Tamašunienė said in a statement. “We fully support making such data public.”
She said authorities should continue monitoring people convicted of sexual offenses even after they have served their sentences, arguing that this would strengthen the state’s role in preventing repeat offenses.
Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė has also expressed support for the idea.
Lithuania’s parliament, Seimas, gave initial approval in 2024 to legislation that would establish a registry of suspects, defendants and people convicted of crimes against children’s sexual self-determination and inviolability.
Under the proposal, the registry would consist of a restricted database containing information that could be provided to courts, law enforcement agencies and other institutions when permitted by law, as well as a public database listing information about people convicted of the offenses. The public database would be available for viewing online.
The government issued a negative opinion on the proposal in March 2025.
The issue has returned to the spotlight after prosecutors announced this week that two cases involving priests accused of sexual offenses against children had been referred to court.
One priest is accused of sexual offenses against 11 minors. Law enforcement authorities allege 34 alleged criminal episodes committed over 23 years, from 2002 to 2025. His case was transferred to the Vilnius Regional Court.
In the second case, another priest is accused of possessing child pornography. There are no identified victims in that case, which was transferred to the Vilnius City District Court.
Tamašunienė said law enforcement authorities must fully investigate the circumstances and, above all, ensure that victims’ rights are protected and that they receive compensation for the harm caused.
She said the recent cases had shocked many people but urged the public to distinguish individual cases from the broader community of priests.

Lebanon has not agreed to shortlist of countries that could verify Hezbollah's disarmament, official says

A 26 June deal brokered by the US supposedly linked the progressive withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon to the "verified disarmament" of all non-state armed groups by the Lebanese government. Hezbollah, which is not a party to the agreement, has rejected disarming.

Israel has killed more than 4,300 people in Lebanon since March.

France accues Iran of 'bloodshed' over use of death penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:03:14 UTC
21:03:14 KST

After a statement condemning Iran's use of the death penalty, tensions rose between senior diplomats. Paris accused Tehran of 'bloodshed' and Iran called France's stance 'blatant hypocrisy.'
Following the publication of an international statement condemning the use of the death penalty in Iran, a war of words escalated between senior French and Iranian diplomatic officials. Paris played a central role in the international condemnation, accusing Iran of “bloodshed”, while Tehran in turn described France’s position as “blatant hypocrisy”.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot sharply criticised Iran’s actions in a post on X, writing: “Seven months after the widespread atrocities against the Iranian people who rose up to demand justice and dignity, this regime continues its bloodshed by carrying out an increasing number of executions.”
The French Foreign Ministry also confirmed Paris’s prominent role in the campaign condemning executions in Iran, saying that after the statement was initially signed by 26 countries and the EU’s foreign policy chief, additional countries joined, bringing the total number of signatories to 32.
In response, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi strongly rejected the criticism and accused the French government of applying double standards.
Araghchi wrote on X: "Countries like France should stop lecturing the world about “human rights” and international law. The hypocrisy is blatant and embarrassing."
Iran’s foreign minister added: "Your backing of Israel’s genocide in Gaza—and aggression against Iran—has destroyed whatever moral high ground you imagined you had."
Warnings from international bodies
The diplomatic tensions followed the publication of a joint statement on Wednesday.
More than 30 countries, including France, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Germany and Italy, along with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, condemned Iran’s use of the death penalty against protesters “in the strongest possible terms”.
The statement said the Islamic Republic was executing protesters in an attempt to “silence dissent”. The signatories said: “The use of the death penalty to intimidate communities and punish people for exercising their human rights is unjustifiable under any circumstances, and the people of Iran must be free to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly without fear.”
The involved countries called on Tehran to immediately end the executions and release those detained.
Economic protests to outbreak of war
The confrontation comes as warnings from the United Nations and human rights groups over a new wave of executions in Iran have intensified.
The latest wave of arrests and judicial sentences dates back to late December last year, when a protest movement initially centred on economic hardship, runaway inflation, the high cost of living and rising prices developed into widespread anti-government demonstrations.
While Iranian officials have reported that more than 3,000 people were killed and attributed the violence to “terrorist actions” organised by the United States and Israel, rights groups outside Iran have reported much higher casualty figures and said security forces opened fire on protesters.
Meanwhile, the joint US-Israeli attack on Iran on 28 February, which marked the beginning of a new Middle East war, further intensified the security crackdown. According to observers, the number of arrests and executions linked to the military conflict and protests has multiplied since then.
The United Nations and human rights groups have expressed concern over the escalation of judicial measures, citing the lack of fair trials and the extraction of forced confessions.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said earlier in August that Tehran was using executions to “spread fear and terror”. He reported that since March 19, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges, while more than 100 others remained at risk of execution.
According to Amnesty International, Iran executed more than 2,150 people last year, placing it a distant second to China among the world’s leading users of the death penalty.

Taipei's restored Toad Mountain military village fully opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:02:41 UTC
21:02:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — One of Taipei’s last intact Air Force military dependents’ villages will fully open Friday, capping nearly a decade of restoration and cultural preservation work.
Toad Mountain Huanmin New Village, in Daan District’s Gongguan area, will host an “A Village in the Mountain City” opening festival featuring a traditional banquet, market stalls, guided tours, and live music performances, according to a press release from the site’s management.
The settlement was designated a cultural landscape by Taipei City Government in 2014 and includes 39 former Air Force housing units. Phased repairs began in 2017, with the first section opening in 2020. The full site, divided into five zones for exhibitions, studios, and visitor services, officially opens Saturday.
The village traces its roots to 1949, when the Kuomintang retreated to Taiwan and established Air Force facilities on the strategically important hill. Dormitories were built for Air Force personnel and their families, forming one of Taipei’s few completely preserved military dependents’ enclaves.
Friday's official opening will feature an invitation-only “family banquet.” Public events Saturday and Sunday include a market with local foods and crafts, guided tours, and two themed music performances featuring songs from the 1940s through the 1980s, including music from the early years of Taiwanese television.
The site aims to become a long-term hub for historical memory, community programs, and cultural education, managers said.

Taiwan's AIDC, Vantor complete Presidential Cup drone flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:02:24 UTC
21:02:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Aerospace Industrial Development Corp. and US-based Vantor announced Thursday the completion of a 2-kilometer autonomous drone flight without satellite positioning, according to an AIDC press release.
AIDC said the joint demonstration was a follow-up test to see if drones can navigate independently with AI-backed visual navigation. The objective was to prove that the integrated system can function smoothly at long distances under demanding deployment conditions.
AIDC unveiled the drone visual navigation and positioning system at a flight demonstration in May. The company said Tuesday's Presidential Cup drone flight marked a milestone, as the drone completed its flight without GPS assistance.
The Global Positioning System is a satellite navigation system. Satellites in space send multiple signals to receivers such as smartphones, providing accurate coordinates in most parts of the world.
AIDC said regular drones rely on GPS for coordinates, which can be disrupted when signals are jammed or lost. AIDC integrated Vantor's upgraded software for better performance.
The company said the drone was able to determine its location by comparing ground imagery captured by its camera with a high-precision 3D database. AIDC said this enabled the drone to pilot itself.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) called for teams in the 2026 Presidential Cup Drone Competition to demonstrate precise, autonomous flight aided by AI target recognition in complex environments. AIDC noted that although it is not a competing team, it used the event as an opportunity for live validation.
AIDC said resistance to interference is becoming an important requirement for drones. The company is applying the integrated solution to military and civilian uses, ranging from patrols and search-and-rescue in difficult areas where signals are unstable to urban transport, factory inspections, and agricultural monitoring.
AIDC said that by reducing reliance on GPS, drones can better perform reconnaissance, rescue, and tactical autonomy with added resilience. The company said it will continue to research practical applications and seek more international collaboration.

Taiwan’s Compal posts NT$3.13 billion profit in Q2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:02:20 UTC
21:02:20 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Compal Electronics said Thursday its Q2 net profit rose more than fivefold year-on-year to NT$3.13 billion (US$97.41 million) as higher financial asset gains and stronger non-PC business boosted results.
Profit attributable to owners of the parent company rose 59% from the previous quarter, while earnings per share reached NT$0.73, per CNA. Non-PC products accounted for about 34% of revenue, up from 30% a year earlier, putting the company on track to reach its goal of 40% this year.
Compal’s gross margin fell to 4.6% from 5.3% in Q1 and 5.9% a year earlier, mainly because of higher component costs, including memory. Compal CFO Wang Cheng-chiang (王正強) said higher selling prices helped offset some of the impact, but the larger revenue base diluted margins.
Notebook shipments fell 13% year-on-year in the second quarter because of component shortages and higher prices, Compal President and CEO Anthony Peter Bonadero said. However, he said customers favored higher-end and AI PC models, lifting average selling prices and helping PC revenue rise 20% from the previous quarter and 23% from a year earlier.
Compal’s non-PC revenue rose 52% year-on-year in the second quarter, driven mainly by servers, with AI servers accounting for about 70% of total server revenue. The company is also adding NeoCloud customers, or emerging cloud service providers, as it expands its server business.
Compal’s new AI server manufacturing center in Daxi, Taoyuan, began operations this week and will now enter customer certification, with revenue contributions expected from Q4. The company reported Q2 revenue of NT$238.29 billion, up 18.38% from the previous quarter and 32.06% from a year earlier, per Anue.
