Israel trucks out Gaza’s rubble to ‘hide genocide’ and ‘redraw the map’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:29:32 UTC
20:29:32 KST

Israel trucks out Gaza’s rubble to ‘hide genocide’ and ‘redraw the map’
The Israeli military is carting away millions of tonnes of rubble – including from cemeteries and known locations of human remains – in what rights groups say is an effort to erase war crimes evidence.
Israel is carrying out a massive, organised operation to crush, mix and transport millions of tonnes of rubble out of the Gaza Strip, according to human rights groups and monitors.
The Israeli military’s systematic reshaping of the urban landscape comes against a backdrop of a staggering human toll, with at least 73,387 Palestinians – mostly children and women – killed since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 411-year-old boy shot by Israeli forces in Gaza
- list 2 of 4US strikes in Yemen killed 153 civilians in 2025, says Pentagon review
- list 3 of 4Israeli strikes in south Lebanon a ‘violation of international law’: PM
- list 4 of 4Palestinian women in Gaza face legal hurdles in divorce struggles
This removal of rubble could be an attempt at demographic engineering and erasing evidence of the genocide, the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor has said, in a report entitled Gaza Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment.
Obliterating the truth
The report estimates that there are approximately 68 million tonnes of rubble across the Gaza Strip, much of the result of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war on the enclave.
At least 10 million tonnes of rubble have already been removed, crushed or moved from their original sites within areas under Israel’s unlawful military control, which encompass about two-thirds of the enclave.
About 400 heavy pieces of excavation, crushing and transport machinery are also working to demolish the remaining structures in Gaza.
Debris is being loaded onto nearly 100 Israeli trucks daily, which are leaving the Gaza Strip for undisclosed sites within Israel and the occupied West Bank.
Budour Hassan, a researcher at Amnesty International, told Al Jazeera that this could be a calculated attempt to destroy evidence of crimes committed by Israel during the war.
“The bulldozing is an integral part of all attempts to destroy the lands in Gaza City and in the Gaza Strip in general,” Hassan said.
“The real fears are that these operations are taking place with the aim of obliterating and hiding evidence.”
Preventing access to evidence of crimes is a direct challenge to the International Court of Justice, Hassan said. The ICJ is currently overseeing a genocide case against Israel brought by South Africa and supported by numerous other nations.
“The occupation systematically works to obliterate evidence and destroy the features of the crime,” she added.
Mohammed Salha, director of the NGO Network in the Gaza Strip, believes the debris being moved out of the enclave contains missile fragments, ammunition, and personal belongings – crucial for future accountability.
“The occupation is moving the rubble, fragmenting it, and moving it into the Green Line to obliterate the evidence and facts,” Salha told Al Jazeera.
“Naturally, there are thousands of martyrs under this rubble, and moving this rubble with their remains means a deliberate destruction of the crime scene that contains the basic evidence that exposes the occupation’s commission of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.”
Urban engineering
The mass removal of rubble could serve a distinct military and colonial purpose. Euro-Med Monitor reported that the large-scale crushing and removal of rubble destroys land boundaries, house foundations and street networks, stripping Palestinians of the physical markers of ownership and deepening ethnic cleansing in Gaza. This sets the stage for efforts to re-establish Israeli settlements in Gaza.
Retired Brigadier General Elias Hanna, a military and strategic expert, explained to Al Jazeera how geography is being used against the population as an extreme form of collective punishment.
“The building and the geographical area have become part of the battle and part of the weapon itself,” Hanna said.
“When the Israeli enemy destroys and bulldozes, this bulldozing falls within the policy of collective punishment; that is, you create a new urban engineering and a new phase and a different shape for the social and security environment to punish those who resist and punish the civilian incubator at the same time,” Hanna said.
This strategy of urban engineering aims to permanently alter the ecosystem of the enclave by preventing the return of Palestinians to their homes and making the destroyed areas in Gaza unliveable or unbuildable, Hanna added.
The daily tragedy
The removal of ruins also means that the bodies of missing people, estimated by Gaza’s civil defence in July 2026 to number about 8,500, could be gone forever.
Using heavy machinery without prior forensic surveys risks crushing or scattering these remains, severely infringing on the rights of families to know the fate of their relatives.
Abu Asim, a Palestinian citizen whose family members remain buried in the eastern areas of the Gaza Strip, now designated as behind a military “Yellow Line“, shared his agony with Al Jazeera.
“My family’s story is that their body parts were scattered in the streets, and some of them are still to this day under the rubble of the house, and their remains have not been brought out,” he said.
“We lost them, and the first tragedy was their martyrdom, and the second and daily tragedy is the absence of these graves and the absence of the evidence with which we will try this occupation for these crimes and atrocities.”
Rescue efforts have been entirely paralysed in areas seized by the Israeli military.
Samir al-Mana’ama, a lawyer with the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, told Al Jazeera that during the war, Israeli authorities seized an area of approximately 70 percent of the eastern Gaza Strip.
“[The Israeli military is] preventing the access of rescue crews to recover the bodies of the martyrs, and it is also tampering with the rubble areas and moving them from one place to another, which leads to a clear and explicit violation of the provisions of international humanitarian law and international human rights law,” al-Mana’ama told Al Jazeera.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of civil defence in Gaza, highlighted the impossibility of their mission.
“In the available areas where we move now, things are very difficult and complex,” he told Al Jazeera. “So how about the situation if the matter requires coordination to enter the areas located inside the Yellow Line, which requires special equipment, coordination, and securing … the nature of our work there.”
Even known resting places of the dead have not been spared, Salha said, with historical burial sites included in this campaign of erasure.
“Reports and human rights documentation state that the occupation completely or partially destroyed more than 93 percent of the cemeteries in the Gaza Strip,” Salha said. “Neither stone, nor human beings, nor even the dead in their graves have been spared from the occupation.”

Guidance: Dartmoor firing times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:29:24 BST
20:29:24 KST

Dartmoor firing times
Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.
Documents
Details
Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.
Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

Brunei Capital Market seminar highlights sukuk as alternative financing instrument
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:28:23 CST
20:28:23 KST

BANDAR SERI BEGAWAN, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- The Brunei Darussalam Capital Market Development seminar, titled "An Introduction to Sukuk Issuance," was held on Wednesday near the capital.
In his opening remarks, Haji Asrul Adrain Haji Ahmad, Brunei's permanent secretary at the Ministry of Finance, emphasized the importance of strengthening the country's capital market ecosystem through greater collaboration, capacity building and broader participation from the corporate sector.
He also encouraged participants to leverage the seminar as a platform to deepen their understanding of sukuk and gain exposure to international best practices.
The seminar aimed to enhance participants' understanding of alternative financing options, particularly sukuk as an instrument for raising financing through the capital market.
The seminar brought together nearly 100 participants, comprising policymakers, regulators and potential issuers from Brunei Government-Linked Companies and private sector corporations. ■

====================================================================================================

China extends anti-dumping duties on Indian optical fiber for five years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:28:17 CST
20:28:17 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- China will continue to impose anti-dumping duties on imports of single-mode optical fiber originating from India for five more years starting Aug. 14, 2026, the Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday.
This decision was made following a review of the anti-dumping measures, which was initiated in August 2025 at the request of China's domestic industry, the ministry said in a statement.
If the anti-dumping measures were terminated, the dumping of single-mode optical fiber from India would likely continue or recur, potentially causing ongoing or renewed harm to China's domestic industry, according to the ministry's expiry review investigation.
Under the extended measures, anti-dumping duties on the imported products range from 7.4 percent to 30.6 percent.
China imposed anti-dumping duties on single-mode optical fiber imports from India in 2014 and extended these duties for another five years in 2020.
Single-mode optical fiber is mainly used in high-speed, long-distance and access network transmission, and is widely applied in long-haul trunk lines, metropolitan area networks, cable television and fiber-optic access networks. ■

Malaysia sees more areas reporting unhealthy air quality
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:28:14 CST
20:28:14 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Unhealthy air quality was detected across 11 areas in Malaysia on Thursday, according to data from the country's air quality monitoring system.
The northern Borneo state of Sarawak was badly affected, with the Semarahan district recording the highest air pollutant index (API) of 183, followed by Serian (182), Kuching (176), Sarikei and Sri Aman (158), and Mukah and Sibu (152), according to data from the Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System.
In Peninsular Malaysia, four areas recorded unhealthy readings: Johan Setia (154) and Shah Alam (101) in Selangor state, as well as the capital Kuala Lumpur (131) and administrative capital Putrajaya (104).
Fifty-five areas recorded moderate API readings.
According to the country's air quality rating, an API reading of zero to 50 is "good," 51 to 100 "moderate," 101 to 200 "unhealthy," 201 to 300 "very unhealthy," and 301 and above is "hazardous."
Meanwhile, the Malaysian Meteorological Department National Weather and Earthquake Operations Centre senior director Maqrun Fadzli Mohd Fahmi told Bernama that although rain is forecast to occur in several places, it is not yet able to restore air quality on a large scale. ■

====================================================================================================

Chinese researchers uncover "ripple" structures in Milky Way
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:27:56 CST
20:27:56 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Chinese researchers have identified widespread corrugated structures in the Milky Way for the first time, offering fresh observational evidence for understanding the galaxy's three-dimensional architecture and dynamic evolution.
The finding, from a team at the Purple Mountain Observatory (PMO) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was published on Aug. 7 in the journal Nature Astronomy.
The Milky Way's overall shape resembles a warped record, with one side bent upward and the other downward, a large-scale deformation known as the "warp." However, systematic observations and quantitative studies of finer vertical structures within the galaxy have long been lacking.
The team analyzed more than 30,000 molecular clouds in 3D, using carbon monoxide (CO) spectral-line survey data from the PMO's 13.7-meter millimeter-wave telescope, said Sun Yan, associate researcher at PMO and the paper's first and co-corresponding author.
CO is a key tracer of cold molecular gas, the raw material for star formation. The sample covers about half of the Milky Way's outer disk, reaching up to roughly 26 kiloparsecs from the Galactic center.
Based on these samples, the team constructed the first global warp model of the molecular gas outer disk. After subtracting the large-scale warp background, they detected clear, wave-like vertical undulations, or corrugations, in the residual structure.
"These corrugations appear as large-scale vertical deviations of the disk, likely originating from bending waves excited by external gravitational perturbations," Sun said.
"They may well be the 'ripples' propagating through the outer disk as a result of gravitational disturbances caused by satellite galaxies, such as dwarf galaxies, flying past the Milky Way," Sun added. ■

La Liga game between Celta Vigo and Osasuna postponed until August 27
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:27:50 CST
20:27:50 KST

MADRID, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- Sunday's la Liga game between Celta Vigo and Osasuna has been postponed after a fungal outbreak has affected the playing surface at Celta's Balaidos Stadium.
Officials from La Liga decided to postpone the match until August 27th after a pitch inspection to see if the game could proceed or not.
Celta is reported to have requested the game to be postponed, whereas Osasuna had indicated it would prefer for it to proceed.
Ironically, Celta could have asked for the game to be postponed a month ago given that the club's striker, Borja Iglesias formed part of Spain's World Cup winning squad and teams which have players who reached the last four of this summer's competition, don't have to start their season until the weekend of August 22nd and 23rd.
However, the fact Celta is playing in this season's Europa League means the club originally preferred to play Osasuna on the scheduled date rather than postpone it and face a fixture pile-up.
The change means Celta will now have games on August 22nd, 27th, 30th, as well as September 3rd and 7th.
The opening matches between FC Barcelona and Athletic Bilbao, Real Madrid and Real Sociedad and Valencia and Betis have all been postponed, while Atletico Madrid will play Malaga on August 19th because of players involved in the World Cup. ■

Who is Mohsen Rezaei, Iran's new security chief with an Interpol Red Notice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:27:40 UTC
20:27:40 KST

Mohsen Rezaei is one of the Islamic Republic's founding military figures, a four-time failed presidential candidate and the subject of an Interpol Red Notice over the 1994 Buenos Aires bombing that killed 85 people. Here is what we know about Iran's new security council chief.
One of the founding figures of Iran's IRGC Mohsen Rezaei has been appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council — giving one of the country's most controversial senior figures formal authority over the institution responsible for Tehran's strategic decisions.
The appointment was made in a presidential decree signed by Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday.
Hours earlier, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had separately appointed Rezaei as his personal representative on the council.
With nearly five decades at the top of the Islamic Republic's security and military apparatus, Rezaei, 71, succeeds Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a veteran IRGC commander who resigned after around four months in the post and was appointed as a political adviser to Khamenei.
Right after his appointment was announced, Rezaei has said publicly that Iran will not open a second shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz, that US warships entering the strait will be targeted, and that the war must end and Iran's frozen assets must be released before Hormuz can be reopened.
Who is Mohsen Rezaei?
Rezaei, whose birth name was Sabzvar, was born in 1954 in Khuzestan province into a Bakhtiari tribal family.
Initially a political activist against the rule of Shah Reza Pahlavi in the early 1970s, Rezaei was arrested by the shah's intelligence agency SAVAK and imprisoned in Ahvaz.
He was one of the founders of the Mansouroun militant group, which helped lay the groundwork for the Mojahedin of the Islamic Revolution Organisation.
After the 1979 revolution, Rezaei joined the central council of the Islamic Republic and served on a 12-member committee that drafted the IRGC's constitution.
In September 1981, at the age of 27, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appointed him commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Guards.
Rezaei held the position for 16 years — making him one of the longest-serving military commanders in the history of the Islamic Republic — before stepping down in September 1997.
He then became secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council, the body that resolves disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council and sets broad state policy, for nearly 24 years.
He was appointed deputy president for economy under President Ebrahim Raisi in 2021, a post he left in June 2023.
Despite this record of institutional prominence, Rezaei has run for president four times and lost each time. In the 2021 election, he received 3.4 million votes — fewer than the number of ballots deemed invalid in the vote.
The bombing of the Jewish centre in Argentina
Rezaei's name has been associated internationally with the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people and injured hundreds in the deadliest terrorist attack in Argentina's history.
In 2007, Argentine prosecutors sought arrest warrants for nine people in connection with the attack, including Rezaei, then IRGC commander. Interpol issued a Red Notice against him that remains in force.
Tehran and Rezaei have consistently denied any involvement in the attack, describing the allegations as politically motivated.
The case has nevertheless had practical consequences: Argentina protested his appointment as deputy economic president in 2021, previously objected to his attendance at the inaugurations of Nicaraguan presidents, and asked Qatar to arrest and extradite him during a visit to Doha — a request that was not carried out.
Operation Karbala-4
The most controversial episode of Rezaei's military command domestically was Operation Karbala-4, a December 1986 assault during the Iraq-Iran war intended to retake parts of the Faw area that was detected and repelled by Iraqi forces, resulting in heavy Iranian casualties, including frogmen units.
In 2015, the remains of 175 divers who had participated in the operation, reportedly buried with their hands tied, were discovered and identified.
Rezaei's subsequent claim that continuing the operation after it had been compromised was a deliberate deception ahead of the larger Operation Karbala-5 — or the siege of Basra, the largest military offensive of the war — drew sharp criticism from former officials, journalists and social media users.
Qassem Soleimani, then Quds Force commander, contradicted the account by saying Karbala-4 had been the primary operation all along.
Another controversy surfaced in November 2011, when Rezaei's eldest son Ahmad, who had previously defected to the US and given media interviews criticising senior Islamic Republic officials, was found dead in a Dubai hotel room.
Dubai police attributed the death to an overdose of antidepressants. Rezaei's family and the Expediency Council secretariat rejected that conclusion and described the death as suspicious. The cause of Ahmad Rezaei's death has never been conclusively established.
War, succession and regime in flux
Rezaei's appointment comes after one of the most turbulent periods in the Islamic Republic's history.
The US and Israel launched broad strikes against Iranian military targets on 28 February, killing Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Defence Minister Mohammad Reza Ashtiani and around 40 senior military and security commanders.
Ali Larijani, who had been secretary of the Supreme National Security Council since August 2025 and was regarded by many analysts as Iran's most powerful figure on the eve of the war, was killed in a subsequent wave of Israeli strikes on Tehran.
Zolghadr then succeeded Larijani in that role. Under the constitution, an interim council of President Pezeshkian, judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Ejei and a Guardian Council-appointed cleric managed the country's leadership functions until Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as the third ayatollah on 9 March.

Indigenous rangers, scientists map vulnerable reefs in northern Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
19:27:37 CST
20:27:37 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- A two-year collaboration between Indigenous rangers and scientists has produced the first comprehensive scientific baseline of coral reefs around the Groote Archipelago in Australia's Northern Territory.
The study documented the seafloor composition of five reefs surrounding Groote Eylandt using underwater remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) in waters that can be challenging to access due to saltwater crocodiles and marine stingers, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
The surveys found coral cover ranging from 5 to 47 percent across the sites, with reefs dominated by hardy massive corals rather than branching varieties more common on other reefs, said the study co-authored by Anindilyakwa Land and Sea Rangers and UTS researchers.
Fieldwork in early 2024 coincided with an environmental stress event. Satellite data showed elevated sea temperatures before the event, although they were not at levels typically associated with severe coral bleaching. Ranger surveys subsequently identified mass coral bleaching at several sites.
The findings challenge assumptions that remote or marginal reefs are naturally resistant to heat stress, said UTS Associate Professor Emma Camp, senior researcher of the study published in the journal PLOS One.
"Remote reefs like these have too often been treated as an afterthought in conservation, despite how important they are to the communities who rely on them," Camp said.
The project combined traditional Indigenous knowledge with modern technology, with local rangers guiding scientists to key reef sites and receiving training to operate ROVs and drones, researchers said. ■

US-China, the economy, and a burial dispute: What is at stake in Zambia’s election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:23:03 UTC
20:23:03 KST

US-China, the economy, and a burial dispute: What is at stake in Zambia’s election?
Zambians are voting in presidential, parliamentary, and local elections on Thursday, with incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second five-year term as a bitter dispute over the burial of his predecessor and longtime rival, Edgar Lungu, continues to overshadow the campaign.
Although 14 presidential candidates are in the race, the contest is widely seen as primarily pitting Hichilema against opposition figure Brian Mundubile, a former senior member of the government of late President Lungu.
Nearly 8.8 million people are registered to vote, according to the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ). Under the Constitution, a presidential candidate must receive more than 50% of valid ballots to win outright; otherwise, the two leading candidates proceed to a runoff.
What has happened since Zambia's 2020 default?
Following the country’s 2020 debt default, Zambia signed a $1.3 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) debt restructuring program though it is reported to owe China, Lusaka’s largest creditor, some $6 billion. However, the standard of living for ordinary citizens remains heavily strained due to painful fiscal austerity measures, high inflation, and severe climate shocks like regional droughts.
Speaking after casting his ballot in central Lusaka, Kantumoya Derrick Mpaka, a Zambian national who studied at the Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia (RUDN University), told RT that voting there had been peaceful and orderly.
“People are very civil. Everyone is calm. There is no chaos whatsoever,” he said. Mpaka described the election as highly unpredictable but said he expected Hichilema to prevail by a narrow margin, stressing that this was his “personal assessment” rather than an “endorsement of the incumbent.”
Who is Hakainde Hichilema?
Hichilema, 64, is a businessman and leader of the United Party for National Development (UPND). He won the presidency on his sixth attempt in 2021, defeating Lungu by nearly one million votes.
His first term has focused on repairing an economy damaged by Zambia’s 2020 sovereign default. The International Monetary Fund says agreements cover approximately 94% of the external debt targeted for restructuring and that Zambia has made substantial progress toward macroeconomic stability.
Who is Hichilema’s main challenger, Brian Mundubile?
Hichilema’s main rival Mundubile, 55, is an accountant, lawyer, and former lawmaker. Under Lungu, he served as Northern Province minister and government chief whip. He later became leader of the opposition in parliament.
Mundubile has criticized Hichilema’s economic and human rights record and promised Zambians a larger share of the country’s copper wealth. His political background suggests greater continuity with the China-friendly policies of the Lungu era, during which Beijing financed major infrastructure projects.
He is running for the presidency under the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity banner while leading the Tonse Alliance. The coalition was originally formed around Lungu and brought together several parties seeking to remove the UPND from power.
Mundubile’s most notable political achievement has been reaching an agreement with part of the divided Patriotic Front movement. Makebi Zulu, an ally and former lawyer of Lungu, is his running mate. However, several other opposition figures, including Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe, are running separately, meaning the anti-government vote remains fragmented.
How is Zambia’s economy performing?
On Wednesday, the Ministry of Commerce, Trade and Industry said investment in critical sectors has increased gross domestic product (GDP) from $19 billion to $40 billion since 2021, generated 7.8% growth, and produced a positive trade balance. The Zambia Statistics Agency, however, put annual growth at 3.8% in 2025, followed by a 7.7% year-on-year expansion in the first quarter of 2026.
Mpaka told RT that the figures do not reflect many voters’ circumstances. “On paper, our economy is doing okay, but in reality people are suffering, especially in rural Zambia, where people are living in poor conditions,” he said, citing a wide gap between rich and poor. High food costs, unemployment, and electricity shortages remain major concerns.
How important is Zambia to the global copper industry?
Hichilema has also introduced free primary and secondary education, recruited tens of thousands of teachers, and attracted billions of dollars in mining investment. A February 2026 World Bank Group report ranks Zambia as Africa’s second-largest and the world’s ninth-largest copper producer. Rising demand for minerals used in electric vehicles and clean-energy technology has intensified international interest.
In May, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe accused Washington of linking a proposed five-year health package worth up to $2 billion to a critical-minerals agreement favoring US companies.
What’s Hichilema’s foreign policy about?
In foreign policy, Hichilema has strengthened relations with the US and Europe while maintaining extensive economic ties with China. Beijing remains a major creditor and investor in Zambia’s mines and infrastructure, including a planned $1.4 billion renovation of the Tanzania-Zambia Railway.
Relations with Moscow have also continued. In a December interview with RT, Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe described Russia as an “all-weather” friend and characterized bilateral ties as a “strategic partnership,” highlighting cooperation in education, energy, and trade.
Does Zambia favor the East or the West?
Andrey Maslov, head of the Center for African Studies at Moscow’s Higher School of Economics, told RT on Thursday that regardless of the election results, any leader of Zambia will follow a multilateral policy.
“Larger than any country in Europe, Zambia anchors two rival transport, logistics, and resource strategies: The US seeks to draw Zambia’s resources toward the Atlantic Ocean via Angola, while China finds it more advantageous to develop the Tanzania-Zambia corridor,” he said. “The country itself is attempting to balance these interests and benefit from these contradictions.”
Maslov noted that Washington might view Hichilema as capable of containing China’s expansion and preventing Zambia from aligning with alternative centers of power. However, the expert predicted that any Zambian leader would pursue a multilateral foreign policy while remaining mindful of public opinion, including opposition voters.
"Zambia is traditionally perceived as a source of copper and cobalt for global markets. Its role is, however, gradually evolving – for instance, the country has already become an exporter of electricity," Maslov adds.
Why is the burial of Edgar does Lungu’s controversial?
Former President Edgar Lungu died while receiving medical treatment in South Africa in June 2025, but his remains have not been buried following a dispute between his family and the Zambian authorities.
The government sought to repatriate him for a state funeral at which Hichilema would preside. Lungu’s family opposed the plan, saying the former president did not want his longtime rival involved in his funeral.
In June, South Africa’s Supreme Court of Appeal ruled that the government had not established a legal right to override the family’s wishes. Lusaka subsequently said it would not appeal.
The dispute has nevertheless entered the election campaign. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, who previously acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson, have promised to give the former president a dignified burial if elected.

Human Rights Watch says the Taliban detained 6 staff of a women’s and children’s rights group

The reported detentions come as Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers prepare to mark the fifth anniversary of their return to power on Saturday.
The six men — employees of the Women and Children Legal Research Foundation — were detained on July 18 after they were told to come to their office to retrieve confiscated laptops and phones, Human Rights Watch said in a statement released late Wednesday. Their families were given no information about their whereabouts, their condition or possible charges.
Human Rights Watch called on the Taliban to allow family and lawyers to visit the detained and for them to be “immediately released unless they have been charged with a recognizable offense.”
The statement came after the U.N. said two Afghan members of its political mission were detained on Sunday in the western city of Herat by the Taliban’s General Directorate of Intelligence. The U.N. mission has not been informed of the charges against the two men or been able to visit them, U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq told reporters.
The mission has called on the Taliban “to ensure compliance with the privileges and immunities of the United Nations and its officials,” Haq said.
There was no immediate comment on the two incidents from the Taliban, which seized power on Aug. 15, 2021, as U.S. and NATO forces withdrew from the country after two decades of war.
Shortly after taking power, it barred girls from secondary schools and later extended the restrictions to higher education, employment and other sectors, effectively excluding women and girls from public life.
“The Taliban seems to consider any effort to assist women and girls a threat to their abusive rule,” said Macarena Sáez, women’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “They should immediately provide information on the six staff members’ whereabouts and release them if held unlawfully.”
Human Rights Watch said the detention of the six employees came a month after the security forces searched and sealed their office in Kabul and interrogated staff members about their work.
The U.N. mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, said Thursday it had no information on the reported six detentions or whether the two incidents were connected.
The detentions come as a humanitarian crisis in the poverty-stricken Asian nation is worsening and as Taliban forces are engaged in cross-border fighting with Pakistani forces. Clashes escalated sharply in February when Afghan forces launched a raid into Pakistan in retaliation for Pakistani airstrikes inside Afghanistan. Islamabad later declared it was in “open war.”
The U.N. mission’s mandate from the U.N. Security Council includes promoting and supporting humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people, promoting human rights, equality for women and girls, inclusive governance and economic stability.

As Abdul El-Sayed breaks a barrier, anti-Muslim vitriol surges on multiple fronts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:23:02 UTC
20:23:02 KST

As Abdul El-Sayed breaks a barrier, anti-Muslim vitriol surges on multiple fronts
Abdul El-Sayed made history this month in Michigan by becoming the first Muslim nominated by the Democratic Party to run for the U.S. Senate. But elation among many of his fellow Muslim Americans was tempered by awareness of persisting and widespread anti-Muslim sentiment across much of the nation.
Some Republicans, including President Donald Trump, swiftly began referring to the nominee by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, while depicting him as a danger to America. “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic,’' said U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., in a post on X.
El-Sayed says such attacks betray a weakness in those who launch them.
“We all pray for the same things. ... We want what’s good for our kids and our families,” he told MS NOW after his primary victory. “They’re going to use Islamophobia, because their ideas are tired.”
The vitriol extends far beyond the political class. Tensions related to anti-Muslim sentiment have heightened in several communities around the country, where some residents have bitterly opposed proposals to build new mosques.
“American Muslims have made incredible political and societal progress in recent years,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, national deputy director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR. He cited increased visibility in entertainment and sports and the election of Democrat Zohran Mamdani as New York City’s first Muslim mayor.
“But there also is a very concerted backlash to this progress,” Mitchell said. “You’ve seen this in the resurgence of anti-Muslim hate and rhetoric, the targeting of mosques.”
A Dallas suburb is a flashpoint
McKinney, Texas, a large suburb in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, is one of the flashpoints. Despite angry anti-Islam remarks at a heated city council meeting on Aug. 4, the council voted unanimously to approve a site plan for the McKinney Islamic Association’s proposed new mosque, classroom building and gym.
Among those urging the council to give the plan fair treatment was George Fuller, a former mayor of McKinney, a nonpartisan position. Opponents of the mosque project booed him, and some shouted “traitor” as he left the council chamber. One woman could be seen on video physically accosting him.
“I have never witnessed so much hate, anger and lack of humanity in our beautiful community gathered in one place as I did today at City Hall,” Fuller later wrote on Facebook.
During the hearing, which lasted more than four hours, the speakers included U.S. Rep. Keith Self, a Republican whose district includes McKinney. To loud applause, he urged the council to reject the mosque proposal.
“I know you’re in the accommodation phase, but the intimidation phase follows quickly,” Self said. “Child marriage. Honor killings. Don’t tell me it can’t happen here.”
Fuller also went to the microphone, evoking the broader phenomenon of divisive political rhetoric.
“Sadly, we live in a time when some have discovered that the easiest way to gain attention or win elections is not by offering solutions but by manufacturing fear, dividing communities, demonizing neighbors and turning misinformation into a political strategy,” he said.
In North Carolina, anger flares over approval for a new mosque
The scenario was similar in Mooresville, North Carolina, when town commissioners held a public comment session on Aug. 3 about a proposed mosque that had already been approved, with early phases of construction underway.
Angry residents at the meeting voiced hostility to Islam and assailed the commissioners for not being more forthcoming about the project as it took shape over previous months. One speaker cited violence in Nigeria by Islamist extremists as a reason for concern in Mooresville. Another depicted Islam as “a political regime with the ultimate goal of takeover in regions and nations.”
CAIR’s regional manager, Al Rieder, issued a statement denouncing “the hateful and conspiratorial anti-Muslim rhetoric” that surfaced at the meeting and expressed concern about the safety of Muslims in the area about 25 miles (40 kilometers) north of Charlotte.
“Muslims are your neighbors, your doctors, your teachers, your local politicians, your police,” he said.
A few hours after the public meeting, the town commissioners released a summary of the mosque project, which calls for a two-building Islamic center on a parcel acquired in 2019 by a local Muslim organization.
The commissioners said that the parcel is in an area zoned to allow religious assembly and that the mosque proposal was handled the same way as a proposal for a new church.
“All decisions must be based on adopted ordinances, objective standards and legal requirements, which do not allow for different rules for different religious groups,” the commissioners said. “We encourage all members of our community to remain respectful in their discussions and interactions as this project moves through the appropriate processes.”
In Oklahoma, Muslim leaders fight against the rebuff of a new mosque
A mosque controversy has been raging for many months in Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, Tulsa’s largest suburb.
Back in January, at a stormy meeting attended by hundreds of people, the city council voted 4-1 to reject a rezoning proposal by the region’s Islamic Society to build Broken Arrow’s first mosque. Before the vote, dozens of residents voiced anti-Muslim views while opposing the project.
Council members who rejected the mosque had raised concerns about its potential impact on infrastructure such as roads, sewers and flood plain management.
But the Islamic Society is persisting with its quest. On Aug. 3, it filed a lawsuit against the mayor and four councilors, alleging that the vote reflected “a wave of bigoted opposition from members of the community and local politicians.” The lawsuit contends that the council violated state and federal laws governing religious land use, treating the mosque proposal differently from other comparable rezoning requests.
“They did not want a mosque in their city. They did not want Muslims here,” said Meghan Murphy, an attorney with CAIR’s Legal Defense Fund, at a news conference announcing the lawsuit. ”So they made up a reason, and in doing so they violated the law.”
Some see a terrorism threat while others see baseless scaremongering
Opposition to mosque construction isn’t a new phenomenon: In Murfreesboro, Tennessee, an effort launched in 2010 to block a mosque project dragged on for more than three years. The mosque was built anyway as the case moved through the courts, but members of the Muslim community faced public protests, vandalism, arson and a bomb threat during that span.
The latest anti-mosque campaigns coincide with a broad wave of anti-Muslim rhetoric from Republican officeholders over the past year. In Congress, several bills were introduced targeting sharia, the moral and spiritual framework that guides Muslims in prayer and ethical conduct. Some Republicans say they’re concerned about growing Muslim populations in major cities and potential ties to terrorism — fears that CAIR and other civil rights groups say are unfounded and being exploited for political purposes.
Republican governors in Texas and Florida have endorsed efforts to shut down CAIR, saying it has ties to terrorism. CAIR has denied the allegations and filed lawsuits calling the governors’ efforts unconstitutional.
Muslim American leaders view the vitriol as political scaremongering.
“Every election year, we expect a rise in anti-Muslim hate,” said CAIR’s Mitchell. “It’s been worse this year than it has been in years.”

6 Arab football federation chiefs back FIFA President Infantino amid calls to resign

Dilara Hamit
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
The heads of six Arab national football associations expressed support Thursday for FIFA President Gianni Infantino as he faces mounting pressure to resign over an abandoned plan to sell a stake in the commercial rights to FIFA competitions.
The joint statement backing Infantino was signed by the presidents of the football federations of Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt and Mauritania. Four of the signatories are also members of the FIFA Council.
“We express our full support for Mr. Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide,” they said.
The declaration follows calls from European governing body UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (Concacaf) for Infantino to resign.
The three confederations, representing 136 of FIFA’s 211 member associations, accused Infantino of a breach of trust over his attempt to attract private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.
The plan proposed transferring commercial rights to a separate company and selling a 20% stake to private investors to raise approximately $4.2 billion.
It also included $20 million in development funding for each member association during the next FIFA Forward funding cycle, with the possibility of doubling the amount if the proposal was approved.
FIFA later withdrew the plan following widespread opposition from confederations, national associations and other football stakeholders.
The federation chiefs from the six Arab countries praised Infantino’s efforts to expand opportunities across different regions and strengthen football’s role in bringing communities together.
“We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world football,” they added.
Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is expected to seek reelection in March next year.
Despite the revolt by the three confederations, he retains significant support, particularly in Africa, where the Confederation of African Football’s Executive Committee recently reaffirmed its backing for him.

Estonia's State Fleet takes delivery of cutting-edge cow dung-powered vessel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Estonia's State Fleet takes delivery of cutting-edge cow dung-powered vessel
Estonia's State Fleet took delivery Wednesday of a new €22 million compressed biomethane vessel to be used to install navigational aids, conduct research and respond to marine pollution.
In fact, it could be said that Estonia has a new Kratt as of Thursday. That is the name given to the State Fleet's new multifunctional work vessel at Baltic Workboats' shipyard in Nasva. The unique vessel, powered by renewable biomethane, is technologically ahead of the global state of the art and could become an export product featuring technology developed in Estonia.
"The State Fleet's task is also to show the market which technologies are reliable and which can be used in the maritime sector. I think that is our role. It is equally important for us to demonstrate that fuel production has a future in Estonia, and this vessel is a perfect example of that. Compressed biomethane has proven itself on land, but not yet at sea. Our job is to serve as something of a testing ground while also showing the market where technology can go," State Fleet Director General Andres Laasma said.
"I think that both Estonia as a country and Baltic Workboats have once again proven that we can develop and build complex projects, and that we can sell this vessel in Norway and anywhere else in the world where green solutions are a priority," Baltic Workboats CEO Margus Vanaselja said.
One of the vessel's captains, who has effectively held the position on land and alongside the quay for the past year, is now eager to get out to sea.
"I've previously done buoy work aboard the Sektor, a buoy tender that is more than 30 years old. This vessel definitely has many more amenities, is much more technologically advanced and is something Estonia needs. It will make our work considerably easier," Kratt captain Sander Laus said.
"On August 12, a naming ceremony was held for a very important vessel. It is the latest innovation from Estonia's marine engineers. The vessel runs on alternative fuels — methane gas extracted from cow manure and electricity," said shipping enthusiast and Kratt spokesperson Marko Matvere.
According to Matvere, the fuel should be slightly cheaper than diesel, which is part of the point, as ships consume large amounts of fuel and place a considerable burden on the environment. "What could be more ingenious than taking literal crap and using it to run an engine? To me, that's the height of innovation," Matvere said with a smile.
While the State Fleet's previous vessel was completed eight years ago, the next new ferry serving Estonia's major islands is expected to be completed in two years. It, too, will use an alternative energy source: electricity.

Tree lines out, swamps in—Lithuania rethinks how to stop Russian armor at the border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:20:24 UTC
20:20:24 KST

Lithuania's government approved an expanded plan on 12 August to fortify its borders with Russia and Belarus against a possible attack, LRT reports. Lithuania, a Baltic state and NATO member, sits wedged between Russia's Kaliningrad exclave and Belarus. The decision opens a new counter-mobility belt reaching inland from the border, a 20-meter strip that widens to 150 meters where the army marks out areas for operations.
The buildout answers a fear that has gripped the Baltics since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022: that a Russia left unchecked in Ukraine could turn on them next. Western intelligence agencies have warned for years that Moscow could eventually threaten NATO itself, and former CIA director David Petraeus has singled out Lithuania as the likeliest first target, pinned between Kaliningrad and Belarus and sitting beside the Suwałki Gap, the thin land corridor that is NATO's only overland route to the Baltic states.
The decision raises the number of engineering parks, storage depots for obstacles like concrete blocks and roadblocks, from 27 to 50, and gives that work until the end of 2028, more than three years past the original April 2025 target. The state rail company LTG Infra is to store the equipment. The changes could cost an extra €50 million ($58 million) from the State Defense Fund between 2026 and 2030.
Of the Baltic states and Poland fortifying their eastern borders, Lithuania is the most at risk yet the least fortified, according to a satellite review by open-source analyst Clément Molin, even as Belarus keeps testing that border with engineered migrant crossings. The plan is Lithuania's share of the Baltic Defense Line, the joint barrier it launched in 2024 with Latvia and Estonia, alongside Poland's parallel East Shield.
The design comes straight from Ukraine. Lithuania began building counter-mobility parks in 2023, drawing on Russia's war against Ukraine, and much of what it is now putting into the ground, the swamps, ditches, and obstacle fields, was tested first on Ukrainian battlefields, where mud, water, and simple barriers have repeatedly stalled armored advances.
The restored swamps should make some ground impassable to heavy military vehicles within a few years, the Defense Ministry says, with that work due by the end of 2030. Plans for defensive ditches and streams in the Marijampolė municipality were dropped, and the ministry found better sites in the Vilkaviškis and Šakiai districts. Deadlines for obstacles on roads and bridge approaches, and for fitting bridges with holders for explosives, were also moved to the end of 2028.
"Military counter-mobility is an important part of Lithuania's defence preparedness," Deputy Defense Minister Tomas Mikelkevičius said. "We seek to make the best possible use of Lithuania's terrain and engineering measures to impede an adversary's movement if necessary and create more favorable conditions for our armed forces to operate."
Lithuania approved its first counter-mobility plan in July 2024. The plan's original 2024 estimate put the full system at around €600 million ($690 million) over the decade.
Russia's pressure on the Baltic borders
The buildout lands amid steady friction along NATO's eastern edge. Latvia has absorbed the bulk of the migrant crossings funneled from Belarus, and this week found its first used smuggling tunnel under the border. Estonia has switched on the first sensors of a planned drone wall along its Russian frontier and is reallocating €500 million ($575 million) toward air defense and long-range strike. Russia, for its part, has shut seven rail crossings with Latvia, Estonia, and Finland without explanation.
The fortification drive is a bet on time. Estonia's military chief has set a two-year clock, warning Russia could be combat-ready again by 2027, and ISW analysts assessed in May that Moscow was manufacturing pretexts for aggression against the Baltics. Poland's parallel East Shield, meanwhile, has gone up far slower than promised, leaving the region's defenses still thin where the threat is judged greatest.

Finland breaks new ground with English-language upper secondary curriculum
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:19:13 EEST
20:19:13 KST

The first students to study Finland's upper secondary school curriculum entirely in English began classes on Thursday in six cities across the country.
The new track follows a law change introduced last year, which permits upper secondary school students to take all subjects and sit the end-of-school matriculation exams in English.
The reform is aimed at attracting foreign skilled workers with families to Finland, as well as encouraging Finnish expats to return to the country with their children.
The first cohort of English-language curriculum students is due to take the matriculation exam in English in 2028.
"I've been struggling quite a bit"
The new English-language tracks are being rolled out initially in six cities: Vantaa, Helsinki, Tampere, Jyväskylä, Oulu and Pori. Espoo will join the list next year.
At the Aviapolis upper secondary school in Vantaa, 17-year-old Aakash Gamage told Yle that the option to study the upper secondary school curriculum in English is a very welcome development for him.
"I've been struggling quite a bit when I've been doing my studies in Finnish, and it will be much, much easier when I do it in English, and I hope to get better grades," he said.
Gamage moved to Finland with his parents from Sri Lanka less than two years ago, and he completed ninth grade at a Finnish secondary school. The English-language track is open to students who have studied in a Finnish school for less than three years.
Gamage's classmate, 24-year-old Eoghan Donnelly, wants to study at a Finnish university — but he must first sit and pass the Finnish matriculation exam.
"There are a few paths I want to go down. It will be either history, philosophy, or engineering. They are my main choices at the moment," he said.
Donnelly is originally from Ireland but went to school in the UK, and he moved to Finland about 18 months ago.
"If this option hadn't been available, I would have had to completely learn the Finnish language first," Donnelly said.
Lack of material concerns teachers
Although classes have now started, the teachers responsible for providing the curriculum in English have expressed concern about the lack of study materials in English.
Juho-Kustaa Mäkinen, who teaches history, social studies and ethics at Aviapolis, noted that education publishers have seemed reluctant to produce English-language materials that cover the Finnish curriculum.
"Publishers have settled for translation tools. I'd prefer the material to be in English from the start," he said, adding that he has translated the existing material into English himself and finds articles from English-language media to support it.

Russia returns bodies of 261 fallen Ukrainian soldiers to Ukraine
The Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported this on Telegram, according to Ukrinform.
"As a result of the repatriation process, the bodies of 261 people who were killed and who, according to the Russian side, are Ukrainian service members have been returned to Ukraine," the agency said.
Law enforcement investigators, together with experts from specialized institutions, will carry out all necessary procedures to identify the repatriated remains.
The Coordination Headquarters said the repatriation was made possible through joint efforts by representatives of the Coordination Headquarters, the Joint Center under the SBU, the Ukrainian Armed Forces, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Office of the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing under Special Circumstances, the State Emergency Service and other bodies within Ukraine's security and defense sector.
The Coordination Headquarters expressed its sincere gratitude to the International Committee of the Red Cross for facilitating and supporting the repatriation process.
The agency also separately thanked personnel of the Joint Center for Civil-Military Cooperation Support of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, which transports the repatriated remains to specialized state institutions and organizes the transfer of the fallen to law enforcement agencies within the Interior Ministry system, forensic medical examination institutions within the Health Ministry system, and representatives of the Armed Forces' civil-military cooperation structures, which provide overall coordination.
On July 16, the Coordination Headquarters said that the remains of 501 people killed in the war had been returned to Ukraine as part of repatriation efforts. According to the Russian side, they may belong to Ukrainian service members.

Pro-Palestinian campaigners in Lebanon, Jordan and elsewhere in the Arab world have called for a boycott of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” over producer Avi Arad’s support for Israel and his rejection of criticism directed at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during the war on Gaza.
The Campaign to Boycott Supporters of Israel in Lebanon urged audiences not to purchase tickets for the film, arguing that financially supporting a production involving figures who have publicly backed Israel amounts to “cultural normalisation.”
“Do we want to support a production involving individuals who have publicly expressed political support for Israel?” the group said in a social media statement ahead of the film’s release.
The campaign called on the public to avoid paid screenings and said its position reflected its opposition to normalising Israel or its policies.
In Jordan, the Taharrak anti-normalisation group issued a separate statement calling for the film to be boycotted and excluded from the schedules of Jordanian cinemas.
The group also urged the Jordanian Artists Syndicate, cinema operators and other relevant bodies to take a position against its screening. The calls have since been amplified by activists and content creators in other Arab countries.
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” released internationally on July 31, stars Tom Holland as Peter Parker and is directed by Destin Daniel Cretton. Marvel lists Arad as one of its four producers alongside Kevin Feige, Amy Pascal and Rachel O’Connor.
Arad served in Israeli army
The campaign focuses on Arad’s political record rather than the film’s plot or its other cast and crew members.
Arad, a former Marvel Studios chief who holds Israeli and US citizenship, served in the Israeli military between 1965 and 1968 and was involved in the 1967 Six-Day War.
In a 2024 letter published by entertainment news outlet TheWrap, Arad rebuked then-US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer after the senator described Netanyahu as an obstacle to peace and called for Israel to hold new elections.
“It’s not your war. It is not your country. And it is not you who is at risk,” Arad wrote, arguing that Schumer had no right to influence Israel’s electoral process. He also described himself as a proud former member of the Israeli military and rejected Schumer’s position on a ceasefire.
Campaigners say those statements demonstrate Arad’s support for Israel’s conduct during its genocidal war on Gaza and argue that ticket purchases contribute financially to a production associated with him.
The effect of the campaign on attendance remains unclear. The film continued to screen in Lebanon despite the boycott call, with a representative of the Grand Cinemas chain telling Lebanese publication L’Orient Today shortly after its release that demand remained high.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine in July hit highest level since May 2022: UN
At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said.
The United Nations has reported that civilian deaths in Ukraine have reached their highest level in July since the opening months of Russia’s invasion in 2022.
“At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July, a 30 percent increase compared with the previous month and a 70 percent increase compared with July 2025,” the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission said in a statement.

The UN said it has verified the deaths of 16,874 civilians since Russia’s invasion, but warned that this is likely a significant underestimate since it cannot confirm casualties in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces.
That figure includes the port city of Mariupol, which Russia laid siege to at the start of the war and where thousands are widely thought to have died.
At least 54 civilians were killed in Kyiv during the month – “one of the hardest hit cities”, the UN said.
Russian authorities, for their part, reported an increase in the number of civilians killed to 79 in July.
Russian military official ‘killed in blast’
On Thursday, Russian news agencies, citing the country’s Federal Security Service (FSB), said a Russian military official was killed in an explosion in Russian-annexed Crimea.
Also on Thursday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train in southern Ukraine’s Odesa region, killing two of the train’s crew, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of continuing a campaign of “terror” by attacking the train on Thursday, which he said was carrying 340 people.
“Whoever was operating that drone certainly could not have been unaware that the target was entirely civilian,” said Zelenskyy in a post on X.
While two crew members were killed, including the train’s driver, none of the passengers was harmed, said the chairman of the state railway operator, Oleksandr Pertsovskyi.
Video published by Ukrainian emergency services showed a bright fire raging in the train cab, the front of which was blown out and mangled.
Moscow’s forces have repeatedly hit trains throughout the war in what Kyiv claims is an effort to disrupt its logistics and hit civilians.
Zelenskyy said Russia also fired more than 130 attack drones into 11 regions of Ukraine overnight Wednesday into Thursday.
The Russian attacks hit several businesses in Ukraine’s Chernihiv, damaging them, reported Ukraine’s state news agency.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces also seized control of the Ukrainian village of Petrivka in the eastern Donetsk region.
Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said “asymmetric warfare” that has gone beyond the battlefield to affect logistics lines “has taken its toll on people both in Russia and Ukraine”.
Russia attacks grain export port
Elsewhere , Russia struck Ukraine’s largest grain export port on the Danube, causing damage and starting a fire, authorities said.
The port of Izmail, near the Romanian border in Ukraine’s southern region of Odesa, handles exports of grain and other commodities.
The Izmail regional state administration said on Telegram the overnight strikes had damaged port infrastructure and taken out power in the southeast of the city.
The attack on Izmail and record-low Danube water levels could complicate Ukraine’s plans to use the river to ship grain to Europe.
‘More air defence needed’
Zelenskyy has pleaded with allies to deliver more advanced air defence systems – particularly United States Patriots – to fend off intensifying attacks by Russia’s super-fast ballistic missiles, whose trajectory and speed make them hard to stop.
He repeated that plea on Thursday, saying “more air defence support and more pressure on Russia are needed if the world is serious about stopping this war in Europe.”
In Russia, Ukraine’s military struck an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in the republic of Bashkortostan, causing a fire, Ukraine’s military said on Thursday.
It said the complex supplies the Russian military and pledged to continue hitting “key enemy targets”.
Ukraine has increased its own long-range attacks on Russia in recent months – justifying them as retaliatory strikes designed to hit Moscow’s war machine and dent its vital energy revenues.

Number of MPs backing Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president rises to 62
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:13:00 UTC
20:13:00 KST

Number of MPs backing Ülle Madise as Estonia's next president rises to 62
Sixty-two MPs have signed in favor of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise as a candidate at next month's presidential elections, up from the 55 received as of yesterday.
While 21 signatures are required to nominate a candidate during the registration process next week, the 62 in favor received at the time of writing is only six votes short of the 68 votes needed to get the next head of state elected at the Riigikogu.
Madise, who has not yet publicly given her consent to run, was backed by 61 coalition MPs from the Reform and Eesti 200 parties, plus MPs from the opposition Social Democrats (SDE).
This is not quite a clean sweep of all members of those parties — three MPs had yet to give their signatures: Mart Võrklaev, Margit Sutrop (both Reform) and Züleyxa Izmailova (SDE) were yet to sign in favor of Madise at the time of writing.
Võrklaev told ERR that he was still weighing up the matter. "For now, I would prefer to keep those reasons to myself," he said when asked why he had not yet signed in Madise's favor, and mentioned Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) rector Tiit Land as an alternative potential candidate. The Reform Party is to meet with Madise next Tuesday.
In response to ERR's inquiry about whether or not she plans to sign her support signature in the near future, Izmailova also said she will decide on giving her signature to Madise, or not, following a meeting between Madise and the SDE Riigikogu faction set for Monday.
Following departures from parties and their Riigikogu groups, the current Riigikogu has a large number of independent MPs, now 20, none of whom have given their signature in favor of Madise yet.
Some have declared that they will not vote at all, while others have promised to form their position after meeting Land and Madise.
The two newest independent MPs, Kalev Stoicescu and Meelis Kiili, who at the start of this week left Eesti 200 and Reform respectively, have stated they may instead back Land, in the interests of providing a choice and a debate, though Stoicescu added that this would not necessarily mean withdrawing his support for Madise.
As a reminder, as recently as July 23, Stoicescu wrote on his social media account that he was awaiting Madise's consent to run and for the collection of signatures in support of her nomination, and that he would back her.
Isamaa (eight seats) and the Center Party (seven seats) have both said they would potentially sign in favor of Land as a candidate, but they are also due to meet Madise too, and will make their decision after that meeting. With 15 seats combined, however, they lack the number of signatures to nominate Land or any other candidate alone, even if the four independent MPs who vote with those parties are factored in — though Stoicescu and Kiili would hold the balance then and could provide the required 21.
The actual nomination process is open Friday, August 21, the day after the Restoration of Independence Day, and runs to Monday, August 24. The Riigikogu voting takes place Wednesday, September 2 and Thursday, September 3.
Madise's name has been mentioned in connection with a potential presidential bid since the start of July. She would likely need to rescind her role as justice chancellor before running for president, due to conflict of interest issues.
You can read more on the proposed candidates here.

Russia&apos;s economy continues to weaken, with production, domestic demand and investment declining in July — the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:12:28 EEST
20:12:28 KST

Russia's economy continues to weaken, with production, domestic demand and investment declining in July — the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
In July 2026, Russia's economy deteriorated: oil and gas production fell by 9.3%, domestic demand grew by only 1.5%, and investment declined by 2.1%. A downturn was recorded in most regions.
In July 2026, the Russian economy showed a further deterioration in financial activity. The main blow hit the extractive sector, petroleum product manufacturing, and public administration. But the problem is no longer limited to export commodities—domestic demand and investment are also weakening. The Foreign Intelligence Service reports, UNN writes.
The largest decline in revenues occurred in export-oriented industries. In the extraction of oil, gas, and other minerals, they were 9.3% below the average level for the second quarter. In August, pressure will be intensified by settlements for June exports, when global prices for oil, metals, and mineral fertilizers were falling
At the same time, domestic demand is losing momentum. In trade, financial services, insurance, real estate, telecommunications, and other sectors focused on the domestic market, revenues increased by only 1.5%, compared with 6.9% in the second quarter. Support came from financial services, insurance, and real estate. Agriculture and telecommunications, on the contrary, reduced their payments.
Industries dependent on state funding declined even more sharply. In July, their revenues fell by 15.4%, following a 12.6% decline in the second quarter. The largest drop occurred in public administration
Investment activity is also falling. Payments in construction, machine building, equipment manufacturing, and scientific research declined by 2.1%. The largest drop was recorded in electronics, machinery and equipment manufacturing, transport engineering, and specialized construction.
Demand within production chains is also weakening. Revenues from intermediate demand—goods and services that enterprises use in their own production—decreased by 0.9%. The main negative contributions came from agriculture and oil and gas extraction.
Problems are already apparent in most regions. Excluding extraction and public administration, a decline was recorded in the Northwestern Federal District, by 1.5%; the Southern Federal District, by 14.1%; the North Caucasian Federal District, by 4.9%; and the Siberian Federal District, by 3.2%. At the same time, the extractive sector contracted in virtually all federal districts. The commodities-based model that for years ensured the main inflow of money into the Russian economy is beginning to fail across the country

WSJ: Ukrainian drone operators defeat US unit during exercise in Germany
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:11:00 EEST
20:11:00 KST

WSJ: Ukrainian drone operators defeat US unit during exercise in Germany
During the Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, Ukrainian drone operators from the Nemesis unit – the 412th Brigade of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces – quickly detected and simulated strikes on vehicles belonging to a US mechanised brigade, demonstrating their advantage in the use of drones.
Source: European Pravda, citing The Wall Street Journal
Details: The Combined Resolve exercise in Germany, held in April and May, showed that the US troops from Texas taking part were unprepared for the capabilities of Ukrainian drone operators.
Under the exercise scenario, troops from a US mechanised brigade were advancing on the positions of a simulated enemy. Sources told the WSJ that the opposing force included Ukrainian drone operators from the 412th Nemesis Brigade of the Unmanned Systems Forces alongside various other units.
The Americans had standard electronic warfare and counter-drone systems. During the mechanised "assault", the Ukrainian pilots easily detected US vehicles and simulated attacks using drone-dropped munitions and FPV kamikaze drones. No live munitions were used, with a "hit" recorded when a drone manoeuvred extremely close to its target.
Ultimately, the attacking force was "destroyed" so quickly that troops deemed to have been hit were brought back into the exercise as reinforcements to keep the war game going.
Meanwhile, the exercise showed that the US drone operators lacked the skills to troubleshoot problems quickly and prepare drones in conditions resembling actual combat.
The exercise scenario was subsequently repeated, and the US troops learned to disperse more effectively, improve their camouflage and make better use of electronic warfare systems.
During subsequent iterations, the Ukrainian drone operators were moved to the other side and demonstrated how uncrewed technologies could be used in offensive operations.
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said that this kind of training experience cannot be replicated in the United States and that the changes seen after NATO exercises involving Ukrainians are significant.
According to one US source, this was not the first time Ukrainian troops had demonstrated an advantage while training against US forces. In 2023, one US officer involved in an exercise acknowledged that the US already had much to learn from Ukrainian forces about the use of drones and developed a training programme that was subsequently introduced in US units.
Background:
- In May 2025, Ukrainian drone operators defeated a simulated enemy during exercises in the Baltics, with British, Estonian and US troops on the opposing side (apparently referring to Hedgehog 2025).
- In spring 2026, Ukrainian UAV operators taking part in NATO exercises on Gotland "defeated" the Swedish troops tasked with opposing them.

Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:44 UTC
20:10:44 KST

Amsterdam researchers find remedy for fatal child brain disease
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Researchers from the Emma Children’s Hospital at Amsterdam UMC have for the first time found a way to treat a rare genetic brain disease found mostly in children – vanishing white matter, or VWM.
According to The Lancet Neurology, which published the findings, VWM is a neurodegenerative disease “with onset mostly in children aged 1–6 years that causes early death and has no effective therapy.” It’s caused by a genetic defect and occurs in 1 in 100,000 people in the Netherlands.
But now the blood pressure drug guanabenz has been found to inhibit the disease.
In a trial at Amsterdam UMC, 33 children from various countries received guanabenz for four years, while the comparison group included 66 children who did not receive it. Children who received the drug stabilised and ended up needing a wheelchair less often and less quickly.
They also lived – as compared to five patients in the comparison group who died.
“We saw that the disappearance of the white matter in the brain slowed down or even stopped,” chief researcher Marjo van der Knaap told broadcaster NOS.
Moving forward, “the disease-modifying effect of guanabenz should be confirmed in a long-term extension study,” wrote the researchers. The drug also needs the approval of the European Medicines Agency to be used as a treatment for VWM.

Unknown Publisher

PAS’ latest sharia law push signals its Malaysian federal power ambition
The move aims to signal to Malay voters that PAS is committed to Islamic values ahead of the next general election, analysts say
In 2024, the country’s apex court ruled that 16 provisions in an earlier raft of amendments to the northern state’s sharia law were unconstitutional as the offences – ranging from sodomy to incest and intoxication – overlapped with common law, the latter of which takes precedence in criminal cases.
The latest amendments work around certain points raised by the federal court. For example, they replace specific descriptions of sexual acts such as sodomy with broader terminology to say that Muslims are prohibited from using their limbs or intimate parts for sexual purposes that run contrary to Islamic law.
But a successful implementation of the new amendments by PAS is less important than ensuring its target audience knows it has strived to broaden sharia law ahead of the next general election, according to analysts.
“PAS knows that Islamic sharia law cannot be implemented by the state as long as the Malaysian constitution is not amended,” said Mazlan Ali, a political analyst with Universiti Teknologi Malaysia.

Türkiye plans lunar mission launch in early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:22 UTC
20:10:22 KST

Türkiye plans to launch its lunar spacecraft in the first months of 2027, equipped with a domestically developed hybrid propulsion system, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said.
Kacir told reporters during the Turkish Scientific and Technological Research Institution's (TUBITAK) Sky Observation Event in the western province of Afyonkarahisar that Türkiye had finalised the launch schedule for its Moon mission.
He said the spacecraft's homegrown hybrid propulsion system had completed all testing phases and that the mission would give Türkiye technological capabilities possessed by only a handful of countries.
Building independent access to space
Kacir said space infrastructure had become a strategic pillar of Türkiye's defence capabilities, pointing to recent satellite projects including Turksat 6A, Imece, Bilsat, Rasat and Gokturk-2.
Türkiye is also working to establish independent and cost-effective access to space through the construction of its own equatorial spaceport in Somalia.
The facility is intended eventually to support launches of domestically developed satellites and spacecraft.
"We're reaching the point where these efforts will enable Türkiye to produce rockets capable of launching our own satellites into space entirely through our own means," Kacir said.
"Equatorial regions offer the opportunity to access space through more cost-effective means, taking advantage of the Earth's rotational speed," he added.
Growing space ecosystem
Kacir said the country's advances were supported by a growing domestic space ecosystem, while a planned space technopark at Middle East Technical University (METU) would bring institutions and companies together for research and development.
Türkiye is also preparing to sign international cooperation agreements to develop and manufacture components for new space stations and is seeking to participate in additional crewed space science missions, he said.
The developments come as the southwestern province of Antalya prepares to host the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) from October 5-9, with around 10,000 participants expected from more than 100 countries.
Kacir said the congress had already broken previous records for pre-registration and paper submissions and was expected to become one of the largest scientific gatherings ever held in Türkiye.
The congress will include a section dedicated to next-generation space startups, while a meeting of parliamentarians and government representatives is expected to culminate in the Antalya Declaration, which will emphasise peace, security and stability amid global geopolitical divisions.
