Putin draws Tokyo's ire over 1st visit to contested island
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:10:00 UTC
20:10:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island near Japan Thursday, drawing a strong reaction from Tokyo, which said the move made improving relations between the two countries more difficult.
The island, known in Russia as Iturup and in Japan as Etorofu, is one of four in the Kuril chain, close to Japan's main islands, that Moscow seized in the days after Japan's surrender in World War II.
Tokyo has maintained its claim to them, making their return a condition for concluding a formal peace treaty that would unlock closer economic ties.
It "hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in a televised statement.
"We hope that the Russian side will take the seriousness of this matter fully to heart," she added.
Ties between Moscow and Tokyo soured after Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Japan joined other nations in condemning the attack and imposing sanctions on Russia.
Putin's visit to the island comes two days before Japan marks 81 years since its surrender ended World War II and a day after North Korea fired a missile into the sea separating it from Japan ahead of major joint military exercises by Seoul and Washington.
Dmitry Medvedev was the first Russian leader to visit the disputed territory in 2010.
On Thursday, the Russian and Chinese ambassadors to Japan, Nikolai Nozdrev and Chinese Ambassador Wu Jianghao, issued a joint statement pledging to oppose attempts to revise the results of World War II.
They also warned against remilitarization in the Asia-Pacific, language that echoes Moscow's rejection of Japan's claim to the islands.
On the trip, which state news agency TASS described as Putin's first to the island chain, he visited the Yasny fish-processing plant on the island, after overseeing navy drills in Russia's Far East.
Vesti TV channel images showed Putin in a dark suit, beside two large tuna and a halibut laid out on a table, as two officials spoke about fishing and the migratory behavior of fish. He also stopped to try local fish roe.
"What lovely weather you have there, just like a resort!" Putin told a group of locals.

====================================================================================================

Europe facing strain on resources and services due to heatwaves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:09:59 UTC
20:09:59 KST

Britain is set to face it's fifth heatwave this summer while France has put 80 départements on orange alert.
Large parts of western Europe, especially Britain and France, will be sweltering under another heatwave this Thursday as countries feel the strain on resources, the economy and services.
Forecasters are predicting the mercury to rise as high as 38 Celsius in central and southeast England, falling just short of the August record of 38.5 C, set in 2003.
This will be the country's fifth heatwave this summer.
The Met Office said earlier this week that only average conditions were needed for the rest of August to beat last year's record for the hottest year.
For a country that's largely not equipped to deal with these levels of heat, it's been a particularly uncomfortable few weeks. Air conditioning is a rarity outside of shops and offices.
Working has been particularly difficult in hospitals, where nurses have been known to collapse from heat exhaustion, according to the Royal College of Nursing.
“When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed,” said RCN chief executive and general secretary Professor Nicola Ranger.
The bulk of the country is now officially in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment to mitigate, all of whom have to look for mitigations both in the short-term and in the long-term in the face of human-caused climate change.
Most of France on orange alert
In France, the heatwave has placed 80 départements under orange alert until Friday, as the government estimates these successive extreme heat events this summer could cost between 10 and 15 billion euros.
Except for part of the northeast, three Pyrenean départements, Lozère and Haute-Loire (under yellow alert), the rest of France is under orange alert with another day of very high heat. This heatwave episode "is reaching its peak on Thursday and Friday," estimates Météo-France.
The highest temperatures will be recorded from Centre-Val de Loire to Nouvelle-Aquitaine, where highs will range "between 38 and 40°C, or even a bit more at peak points. In Île-de-France they will be close to 38°C," it said.
Access to water is also on the agenda given this extremely hot and dry summer.
"Our first priority remains obviously drinking water supply, which is already under strain in several areas, more specifically today in 50 French départements," said Monique Barbut, the Minister for Ecological Transition.
"More than 40,000" people are affected by tap water cutoffs, according to the government.
Europe is the planet's fastest-warming continent and in some places is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather. Repeated heatwaves have fuelled a historically hot summer of drought and wildfires, and contributed to the deaths of thousands of people so far.
Scientists blame growing heatwaves on human-caused climate change.

On December 4, 2024, Badal was attacked inside the Golden Temple during a penance ordered by the Akal Takht.
NEW DELHI: Sukhbir Singh Badal’s Thursday attack in Nanded marks the second serious attempt on the Shiromani Akali Dal leader’s life. The SAD leader was also attacked two years ago at the Golden Temple when a gunman opened fire at him while Badal was serving religious punishment at the shrine.On December 4, 2024, Badal was attacked at the entrance of the temple, where he was seated in a wheelchair because of his fractured leg, during a penance ordered by the Akal Takht. Video footage from the incident shows the moment the attacker overpowered him within seconds.The footage showed him dressed in a blue sewadar uniform. He was stationed at the temple entrance as part of the punishment pronounced by the Akal Takht over alleged misconduct during his tenure from 2007 to 2017.As Badal sat with a placard around his neck, a man who was later identified as Narayan Singh Chaura approached him and opened fire. The attempt, however, was foiled almost immediately.In the clip, right after the gunman pulled out the weapon, an alert sewadar, believed to be a volunteer associated with an Akali leader, intervened and pushed the assailant’s arm upward as he attempted to fire. The bullet was discharged harmlessly into the air, and the attacker was quickly overpowered by volunteers and others present at the scene.
Police personnel stationed at the shrine also moved in and apprehended Chaura on the spot. Confirming the swift response, ADCP Harpal Singh said, “No one was injured in the attack.”It was not long after the attempted attack that other sewadars present at the scene assembled together to create a human shield around Badal.Despite the dramatic shooting attempt, Badal remained calm.Still seated in his wheelchair, he continued performing his duties as a sewadar, holding a spear and staying at the temple entrance after the assailant had been detained.In a separate clip, the shooter could be seen being overpowered by the crowd. The people holding the man can be heard asking him his motive for opening fire on the SAD leader.
The religious punishment had been announced on December 2, 2024, by Sikh high priests for Badal and other Akali leaders in connection with incidents of sacrilege and the pardon granted to controversial Dera Sacha Sauda chief Gurmeet Ram Rahim. The tankhah was part of a reconciliation process led by Sikh religious authorities to address long-standing grievances within the community.
With Wednesday’s attack once again putting security arrangements at the Golden Temple under scrutiny, the earlier firing incident has returned to focus as a reminder that this was not the first time Sukhbir Singh Badal was targeted while performing religious service at Sikhism’s holiest shrine.

A suspected explosive device was found on railway tracks in the southern German town of Treuchtlingen, Bavaria, on Thursday, local media reported.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to examine the object and determine whether it contained explosives.

Lithuania Fortifies Borders With Belarus and Russia With New Defensive Zones and Barriers
Unknown

2026-08-13

- Category

Lithuania Fortifies Borders With Belarus and Russia With New Defensive Zones and Barriers
Lithuania’s government has approved a package of measures to strengthen border defenses, including the creation of counter-mobility zones, the restoration of wetlands, and the installation of engineering barriers at key infrastructure.
The announcement was made by Lithuanian Deputy Defense Minister Tomas Mickelkevičius on August 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the plan, Lithuania will establish designated areas for military counter-mobility engineering measures. A 20-meter-wide strip will be created along the borders with Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region, while the designated areas in operational zones identified by the Lithuanian Armed Forces will extend up to 150 meters. The measure is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.
The plan also calls for restoring wetlands in areas where natural terrain could serve as a barrier to advancing heavy military equipment. Once their hydrological systems are restored, the areas could remain difficult for heavy vehicles to cross without specialized engineering equipment for several years. The work is expected to be completed by the end of 2030.
The measures extend to critical infrastructure. Reserve barriers are being installed along sections of national roads and at bridge supports identified by the Lithuanian military, while bridges will be equipped with structures that can accommodate explosives if their destruction becomes necessary during a conflict.
Lithuania also plans to amend its bridge-design regulations by the end of this year. New and reconstructed bridges would have to include designated points for attaching explosives and structural features that would facilitate their demolition in a military emergency.
The government is further updating plans for restoring drainage ditches and regulating waterways, adding another layer of obstacles that could slow or restrict the movement of potential enemy forces.
The measures come as Lithuania continues to face security concerns along its border with Belarus. Lithuanian border guards recently discovered an unfinished underground tunnel near the village of Latežeris in Druskininkai municipality.
The passage had been dug from Belarus beneath the border fence and was about 4 meters long and 1.5 meters deep.

Russia’s Starlink Rival Faces Rocket Bottleneck as Rassvet Satellite Network Expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:07:12 UTC
20:07:12 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Starlink Rival Faces Rocket Bottleneck as Rassvet Satellite Network Expands
Russia is continuing to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink. However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
According to Defense Express on August 13, the production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Soyuz-2.1b rockets are manufactured at the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara. The facility is located in a large industrial area on the southwestern outskirts of the city. Its production complex consists of workshops with a combined length of about one kilometer.
The facility manufactures rocket fuselages and individual components and also carries out final assembly. According to the information provided, Progress can produce up to 20 carrier rockets annually, the outket reported. Production follows an assembly-line process, with several rockets simultaneously undergoing different stages of assembly. The facility also conducts bench testing of individual components and assemblies.
The assembly of the Soyuz-2 relies heavily on manual labor and the qualifications of its personnel. The rocket is an evolution of the Soviet Vostok launch vehicle and consists of three stages powered by liquid-fuel engines, along with a payload fairing.
The Soyuz-2 is more than 50 meters tall and has a launch mass of about 313 tons. The rocket is currently produced in two main versions: the Soyuz-2.1a, designed to launch Soyuz spacecraft, and the Soyuz-2.1b, used to place satellites and other spacecraft weighing up to 7.4 tons into orbit, according to Defense Express.
After all rocket components are manufactured and tested, they are loaded onto seven freight railcars and transported to the designated spaceport. There, the components are assembled, the payload is integrated, and the rocket is installed on the launch pad, fueled, and prepared for launch.
Since 2022, Russia has conducted an average of six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches per year. In 2026, according to the information provided, four such launches had been conducted so far.
Russia has announced that the Rassvet constellation will require at least 288 satellites for full operational capability. Since one Soyuz-2.1b can launch 16 of these satellites at a time, 18 launches would be required to reach that number.
At the same time, four months passed between the first two launches of Rassvet satellites.
Rockets of the Soyuz family are used not only to launch Rassvet satellites but also to deploy other military, civilian, and scientific spacecraft.
Russia also has another launch option for satellites: the Angara family of carrier rockets, which are manufactured at the Polyot plant in Omsk.
The planned expansion of Rassvet has also prompted discussion over how the constellation could be countered. However, Defense Express reported on August 5 that targeting individual satellites would likely be an ineffective and potentially counterproductive approach.
Unlike earlier military space systems that depended on a limited number of high-value spacecraft, modern satellite constellations are built around hundreds of interconnected satellites. As a result, the loss of individual Rassvet satellites would have a limited effect on the network as a whole.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Putin Lands on Disputed Kuril Island for First Time, Triggering Sharp Protest From Japan

Putin Lands on Disputed Kuril Island for First Time, Triggering Sharp Protest From Japan
Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to Iturup, one of the disputed southern Kuril Islands claimed by Japan, prompting Tokyo to lodge a strong protest.
Released footage showed Putin visiting the island, known in Japan as Etorofu, where he toured the Yasny fish-processing plant and was shown products including tuna and halibut, according to the Kremlin press service on August 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He also visited the Kuril Central District Hospital and a local school before meeting Sakhalin regional governor Valery Limarenko.
After leaving Iturup, Putin traveled to Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, where he met residents.
The trip drew an immediate response from Japan, which regards Iturup and several neighboring islands as sovereign Japanese territory.
Japan’s foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo had lodged a formal protest, according to Japan Wire.
“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu, are an inherent part of the territory of Japan both historically and under international law. Japan strongly protests this visit,” he said.
Japan claims Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets, collectively referred to in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russia currently controls all four.
The dispute has remained one of the principal obstacles preventing Moscow and Tokyo from signing a formal peace treaty more than eight decades after World War II.
The Soviet Union seized the islands at the end of the war. In 1956, Moscow and Tokyo signed a joint declaration under which the Soviet Union agreed that Shikotan and the Habomai islets could be transferred to Japan after the conclusion of a peace treaty.
The two countries never reached such an agreement, however, while Japan later continued to press its claim to all four disputed territories.
Russia maintains that the outcome of World War II settled its sovereignty over the islands and cannot be reconsidered.
Speaking shortly before his visit during Russian Pacific Fleet exercises, Putin claimed Moscow previously had constructive relations with former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and other Japanese leaders over the territorial dispute but accused Tokyo of changing its position.
Relations deteriorated sharply after Russia launched its full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine in 2022 and Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow.
Russia subsequently suspended negotiations with Japan over a peace treaty.
Japan, in turn, returned in 2022 to describing the disputed islands as territory “illegally occupied” by Russia, terminology Tokyo had not officially used since 2003.
Earlier, the Japanese government had lodged a formal protest after Russia announced plans to conduct live-fire exercises near the disputed Northern Territories from August 1 to September 1.

====================================================================================================

Lesson of the UAE, Abraham Accords: Lasting peace begins in the classroom - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:07:01 UTC
20:07:01 KST

Today, six years ago, on August 13, 2020, the Middle East changed. US President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Mohamed bin Zayed, announced an agreement for full normalization between Israel and the United Arab Emirates.
For the first time in more than a quarter-century, another Arab country chose to establish full relations with the State of Israel. A month later, the Abraham Accords were signed at the White House.
At the time, most of the attention was focused on the political breakthrough – and rightly so. The agreement broke a concept that had dominated Middle Eastern diplomacy for decades: the claim that Israel could not reach true peace with the Arab world before resolving the Palestinian conflict.
But six years later, after the Middle East has gone through one of the most turbulent periods in its history, a deeper lesson can be identified. The UAE’s lesson is that true peace does not begin at a signing ceremony. It begins in the classroom.
Since August 2020, relations between Israel and the Emirates have faced intense tests that none of the signatories to the agreement could have predicted. The October 7 massacre, the war in Gaza, and the regional turmoil created immense pressure on Israel’s relations with the Arab world.
The UAE sharply criticized Israeli policy on various issues. There were disagreements, tensions, and periods in which the warmth that characterized the beginning of the relations was replaced by caution.
But relations were not severed.
The embassies remained open, channels of dialogue were maintained, and economic and institutional ties continued to exist. It is precisely the disagreements that illustrate the importance of the achievement.
Peace is not measured when everything is quiet. It is measured at the moment when the sides disagree, the public is agitated, and the political cost of maintaining relations rises.
Here lies the first lesson of August 13: an agreement that holds up only during periods of quiet is a temporary arrangement. True peace is tested by its ability to survive a crisis.
Peace cannot be built on decades of education toward hatred.
For decades, the international community in the Middle East focused almost entirely on leaders and agreements. Presidents met. Diplomats drafted. Governments signed. International money flowed. Institutions were established.
But the most important question was asked too rarely: What does the Muslim child learn in the classroom the morning after the agreement is signed?
You can bring a leader to the negotiation table through interests and pressure. You can establish an embassy by a government decision. You can even create security and economic coordination mechanisms.
But if the education system continues to teach the next generation that the Zionist entity is an eternal enemy, that its history is forged, that its religion is inferior, and that its very existence is illegitimate, an agreement has been signed between governments, but peace has not been built between peoples.
The UAE offers a different model.
On my visits to the UAE, I found an extensive emphasis on tolerance, coexistence, and acceptance of other cultures and religions – including a magnificent synagogue in the Abrahamic Family House complex in Abu Dhabi.
Studies by the IMPACT-se research institute that examined the Emirati education system also found positive changes regarding Judaism and Israel, and the Abraham Accords themselves were integrated into the learning materials.
This does not mean that all disagreements have disappeared, but it teaches that a country seeking to create long-term peace cannot settle for changing its foreign policy. It must gradually create a cultural infrastructure that allows the next generation to accept peace itself as legitimate. This is a strategic lesson, not just an educational one.
The Palestinian comparison that cannot be ignored
And here lies the difference that the State of Israel and the West must learn from.
Since the Oslo Accords, vast sums have been invested in building Palestinian institutions. Governance and security mechanisms were established, agreements were signed, and international aid was transferred on a massive scale. The assumption was that building institutions, improving the economy, and political progress would gradually create an incentive for peace.
But for years, research and reviews pointed to inciting content in the Palestinian education system, including the glorification of “martyrs,” content hostile toward Israel, and a consistent absence of education that recognizes the State of Israel and the Jewish people as legitimate neighbors with a historical connection to the land.
The West sometimes sought to build peace from the top down, while beneath it, mechanisms continued to exist that passed the conflict on to the next generation.
You cannot expect a child who is educated for years to view Israel as an illegitimate entity to become a natural partner for reconciliation at age eighteen just because leaders signed a document.
The Emirates teaches the other side of that same equation.
When leadership changes the public discourse, encourages religious tolerance, recognizes Judaism, and presents cooperation with Israel as part of a possible future, it creates an additional protective layer for relations even when severe political disagreements arise.
Peace through strength, interests, and awareness
The Abraham Accords also proved another principle: Peace does not have to be born out of weakness or out of giving up national interests. On the contrary.
The agreements were born out of a recognition of shared interests. Israel and the Emirates identified shared regional threats and understood the benefits inherent in cooperation in the fields of security, technology, trade, energy, innovation, and tourism.
Instead of the old concept according to which the parties must first resolve all disagreements and only then start cooperating, the Abraham Accords offered the opposite logic: cooperation itself can become an engine of stability.
But the past six years add a third layer to the equation.
Strength creates deterrence.
Interests create profitability.
Education creates resilience.
All three components are necessary.
Peace that is not backed by strength is liable to invite aggression. Peace that lacks shared interests is liable to become an empty document. And peace that is not supported by an educational and cultural infrastructure is liable to collapse when the first crisis arrives.
The lesson for the day after
This lesson has special meaning right now.
In any future discussion on regional arrangements, on expanding the Abraham Accords, on relations with the Palestinians, and on the future of Gaza, the State of Israel and its partners must not repeat the mistake of measuring peace through signatures alone.
Textbooks must also be measured.
When the international community invests billions in reconstruction, it must ask not only how many schools were built, but also what is taught inside them.
When new institutions are established, one must examine not only who runs them, but what worldview they convey to the next generation.
Does Israel appear on the map?
Is the Jewish people presented as a people with a history and a right to self-determination?
Is terrorism presented as heroism or as a disaster?
These are not marginal questions. These are questions of national security.
You can defeat an army on the battlefield. You can dismantle a terrorist organization. You can eliminate commanders and destroy infrastructure. All of these are necessary for the defense of the state. But long-term victory also requires preventing the ideology that birthed the war from passing intact to the next generation.
This is the greatest lesson of August 13, 2020.
The achievement of the Abraham Accords is not only that Israelis fly to Dubai, that Israeli and Emirati companies do business, and that an Israeli flag flies over an embassy in an Arab country.
The more important achievement is proving the possibility of creating a different model in the Middle East.
A model in which countries do not have to agree on everything to live in peace. A model in which shared interests replace the politics of boycott. A model in which tolerance is not just a diplomatic slogan, but a value that a country seeks to pass on to the next generation as well.
Leaders can sign a peace agreement in one day.
Strength and interests can preserve it in times of crisis.
But for peace to last for generations, it must be taught in the classroom.
This is the lesson of the United Arab Emirates, and it should also be the lesson for any future arrangement in the Middle East.
The writer is the deputy head of the Security Policy Institute of the Israel Defense and Security Forum (IDSF/Habithonistim), and former policy adviser to strategic affairs minister Ron Dermer.

NATO to Deploy Battle-Tested AI Drone Fleet From Ukraine to Defend Eastern Flank Against Russia
NATO is shifting its approach to future warfare by prioritizing drones, satellites, sensors, and artificial intelligence, Bild reported on August 12.
The alliance’s push for automation draws from the battlefield in Ukraine, where forces have already begun deploying AI-guided drone swarms capable of identifying targets, communicating with one another, and executing strikes autonomously—even when Russian electronic warfare severs human control.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
To protect against potential Russian aggression, NATO plans to establish a unified surveillance and defense system along its eastern flank—stretching from Finland to the Black Sea. The system is designed to quickly detect and help repel incoming attacks.
The development of these new technologies is heavily influenced by Ukraine’s battlefield experience. Bild notes that the Ukrainian military is already actively using AI for drone control, navigation, and precision strikes.
US Army Major Ben Schiff, who oversees NATO's digital systems, explained the pressing need for automation to Bild.
“Humans decide what the drone does. But they don’t necessarily have to fly it themselves, because we don’t have a million pilots. We can’t launch a million drones simultaneously,” Schiff told the publication.
In the future, autonomous machines are expected to take over various battlefield tasks. Aerial drones will independently search for targets, while ground robots will handle supply deliveries and perform dangerous missions instead of deploying human soldiers, Bild wrote.
However, NATO emphasized that the ultimate goal of this automation is not to replace humans in warfare. Instead, the focus is on reducing the physical risks to military personnel while maintaining strict human oversight and control over the deployment of weapons.
Demonstrating how Ukrainian tactics are already shaping defenses along NATO's eastern flank, Germany’s 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania recently equipped its Leopard 2 tanks and Fuchs armored personnel carriers with improvised anti-drone screens.
Spotted during the Freedom Shield 2026 military exercises near the Belarusian border, the vehicle crews designed the protective cages directly from Ukrainian combat experience to defend against FPV drones and dropped munitions.

Polls open in Clacton, as research shows Farage has spent more than £10,000 in byelection fight against Count Binface
Good morning. In the media, August is known as the “silly season”. With parliament not sitting and many people on holiday, there is less proper news than normal, which means the nonsense stories get (even) more attention than usual. We are almost slap bang in the middle of the month, and today we’ve got a silly season classic in Clacton, where Nigel Farage, the Reform UK candidate, is fighting a byelection in which his main opponent is a joke candidate who dresses up as a dustbin.
Farage is not inherently silly. Few politicians have been more consequential over the past quarter of a century (because he did more than any other single individual to make the Brexit referendum happen); for most of the past 16 months his party has had a big poll lead and he has a very realistic chance of being the next PM; and even if he doesn’t become PM, his hard-right, anti-migrant, crass, crypto-friendly populism will have changed British politics significantly.
But this byelection is rather absurd because it is essentially pointless; all it will do is postpone, not resolve, the verdict on the financial sleaze allegations that Farage is facing (his alleged failure to properly declare donations, including a £5m gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire).
Here is Alexandra Topping’s story.
Voting started in Clacton about two hours ago.
Normally there is not much new to report on polling day. But Politico has published a good story by John Johnston and he reveals that Reform UK has spent more than £10,000 during the election campaign on social media adverts designed to help it see off the threat from Count Binface. Johnston says:
POLITICO analysis of the Reform UK leader’s digital campaign messages shows that Farage has run a twin-track strategy in the seaside seat as polls open Thursday. The two key themes of the digital air war have been painting Farage as a champion for local residents — as well as an insurgent leader harried by the “establishment” machine.
Farage and his party have spent more than £10,000 pushing those messages via ads on Meta’s platforms — which include Facebook and Instagram — in the campaign so far.
Johnston says Farage is the only candidate in the byelection using “paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign”. He says:
Almost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”
The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.
“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

Even allowing for the investigations into Farage by the Guardian (which he would always dismiss on account of the paper’s politics), to what extent is his decline in popularity shaped by the fact that his supporters amongst the right-wing press appear to have turned on him in favour of the so-called ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories? And why has it only happened now?
I think there are many reasons why Nigel Farage, and Reform UK generally, are less popular now than they were at the end of 2025 and the start of 2026. Here is a rough list, which is more chronological than in order of importance.
1) Kemi Badenoch’s approval ratings as Tory leader improving a lot over the past 12 months. This has not helped the party’s overall ratings much, but she is more popular with Reform-leaning voters than she was, and there is less talk now of the Tories disappearing as a major political party.
2) Small boat arrival numbers going down. Migration is Reform’s key issue; without it, they don’t have a distinctive message. It has not disappeared as a political topic, but the fall in small boat arrival numbers has made it less salient.
3) The revelations about Farage’s undisclosed £5m donations, and other undeclared support he has received from George Cottrell. These reports have probably had more impact on voters who already disliked Farage than on his supporters. But they have made him wary of media scrutiny, because when asked about these issues in interviews he inevitably looks shifty and evasive. At one point Reform UK’s most popular salesman went into hiding. In this sense, the ‘opportunity cost’ is significant.
4) The rise in Restore Britain. Rupert Lowe’s far-right Restore Britain party is still, in most respects, electorally irrelevant. But it is eating into the Reform UK vote a lot. Lowe also benefits from the backing of Elon Musk who promotes Restore Britain on his X platform.
5) Rightwing papers being less supportive. This is a consequence of Farage becoming less popular as much as a cause; these papers like to back a winner. But there has been a definite shift in tone.
6) Andy Burnham becoming PM, and Labour support rising as a result.
Of all these factors, 3) and 6) are probably the most important.
Reform UK infighting is probably a factor too – although every party led by Farage has been plagued by this problem.

The number of households in temporary accommodation in England has risen to a new record high, after a slight fall at the end of last year, the Press Association reports. PA says:

What happens to Farage if he loses?
I have a question about Nigel Farage’s political future. If he were to lose his seat as an MP (or step down) would he still be able to lead the Reform party and contest the next general election?
First, I should stress that I don’t know anyone who thinks there is even a slight chance of Farage losing. But it is a quiet afternoon in August – so let’s indulge in a hypothetical.
Yes, Farage could remain as Reform UK’s leader, and yes, he could fight the next election. Zack Polanski has led the Green party to its highest ratings ever without being an MP. Reform UK would have to choose a parliamentary leader, but being in parliament does not automatically allow you to overshadow a charismatic, non-MP leader. (Just ask the Greens’ parliamentary leader – if you can remember who she is.) Farage has never liked speaking in parliament much anyway.
Whether Farage would want to stay in politics or not is another matter.
Is the byelection a ruse to stymie the parliamentary inquiry into claims Farage broke rules by not declaring donations?
Readers have asked various versions of this question.
If Farage loses, does the inquiry wind up? No. The parliamentary commissioner for standards can continue inquiries into people who are no longer MPs, and has done so in the past.
If Farage is re-elected, does the investigation process have to start again from scratch? No. The current investigation can continue.
If Farage declares the £5m loan from Christopher Harborne, does that make up for the fact that he did not declare it after being elected in 2024? No. But, in the court of public opinion, that might be seen as a mitigating factor. If/when a report comes out saying he broke the rules by not declaring the donation, Farage would be able to argue this was ‘old news’ because he had already put the matter right. But his decision to try to neuter the inquiry by holding the byelection is likely to be seen as an aggravating factor – because it implies he does not respect the disciplinary process.

There are 34 candidates in the Clacton byelection. This is the most ever, and easily beats the previous record – 26 candidates in the Haltemprice and Howden byelection in 2008. That was quite similar to this one because it was triggered by an MP resigning to make a point (David Davis, who wanted to register opposition to Labour’s plan to allow terrorist suspects to be held for up to 42 days before being charged), and the other main parties chose to sit it out.
Andrew Teale has written a wonderfully detailed history of the constituency in a byelection preview in a post on his Substack blog. He says the number of candidates is causing considerable practical problems.
He explains:
The last time the record for candidates in a parliamentary by-election was broken was in Haltemprice and Howden in 2008, with 26 candidates standing then. That should have resulted in a ballot paper around 70 centimetres long, but the returning officer for Haltemprice and Howden couldn’t find a printing firm which could handle that. The election staff then had to seek emergency permission from the Electoral Commission to redesign the ballot paper with the 26 candidates arranged in two columns.
This time the Clacton returning officer has found a printer who can handle sheets of paper which are 90 centimetres long, but at a price: the printing costs for this by-election are far higher than normal. There are also going to be all sorts of issues at the count: apart from the difficulties in physically handling such a volume of paper, the ballot is simply too long to fit on Tendring’s normal counting tables. Tables are having to be doubled up to counter this, which will reduce the space available in the hall and lead to a slower count.
Extreme heat contributes to record 2.5m people visiting A&E in July, NHS England figures show
The number of patients in England being cared for in hospital corridors or makeshift areas has remained above 3,000 a day for the second month in a row, as the NHS experiences a “summer surge”, the Press Association reports.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, warned yesterday the health service must start planning for summer pressures in the same way as winter.
However, the data shows overall waiting times for treatment fell slightly in June after rising for two months in a row.
An average of 2,300 patients received corridor care in A&E departments in England each day in July, along with 728 patients elsewhere in hospital wards, totalling 3,028.
This is down slightly from an average of 2,439 patients in A&E departments and 749 in hospital wards each day in June, totalling 3,188.
It is the third time corridor care figures have been published by NHS England, and the second consecutive month they have remained above 3,000 a day.
The data covers patients who have been receiving corridor care for at least 45 minutes.
This means care did not take place in a clinically appropriate and safe setting where patients have privacy, access to food, water and toilets, and lights can be turned off and noise levels minimised to allow sleep.
Nuffield Trust deputy director of research, Sarah Scobie, said: “The fact that we even need a proper definition and data for corridor care in the NHS shows just how far A&E performance has spiralled out of control, with very long waits now the norm.
“The data from the last few months shows huge variation from day to day, so patients will be having very different experiences depending on which day they end up in hospital.
“But corridor care and long waits are not just a problem for A&E departments.
“What’s especially saddening in July’s data is that on almost every day of the month, there were cases of corridor care for children in other areas of hospitals while they waited for a proper bed on a ward.”
Elsewhere, the monthly performance figures also show the overall NHS waiting list fell after rising consecutively for two months.
An estimated 7.27m treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of June, relating to 6.15m patients, down from 7.28m treatments and 6.16m patients at the end of May.
Commenting on why A&E attendance figures have been so high, NHS England said:
The NHS normally experiences spikes in demand during the summer months, as the public spends more time outside which can lead to a rise in accidents. But this summer has seen unprecedented pressure, with the heat contributing to an increase in admissions caused by more outdoor activity and respiratory issues linked to dry weather, as well as worsening of underlying medical conditions.

Those who question Kuril Islands’s belonging to face dire consequences — Medvedev
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:03:10 UTC
20:03:10 KST

MOSCOW, August 13. /TASS/. Japan can declare the Kuril Islands its territory as much as it likes; this idle talk will change nothing, and anyone who fails to understand this will face dire consequences, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev said in a statement on his English-language X page.
Commenting on Tokyo’s protests and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s statements over Russian President Vladimir Putin’s first-ever visit to Iturup in the Sakhalin Region, the security official said: "Japan’s Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi can prattle on all she likes about the Kuril Islands being ‘historically Japanese,’ but this chatter won’t change a thing. They were, are, and will remain Russian land. Anyone who fails to understand this will face the monstrous consequences of their delusion."
On August 13, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup in person for the first time. Prior to that, Medvedev himself had traveled to the Kuril Islands as head of state in 2010. He also visited the islands in 2012, 2015, and 2019 as prime minister. In 2021, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited Iturup.
Moscow and Tokyo have been in negotiations on a peace treaty based on the outcome of World War II since the mid-20th century. The main obstacle to such an accord remains the disagreement over rights to the southern part of the Kuril Islands. After the war, the entire archipelago was incorporated into the Soviet Union, but Japan disputes the ownership of the islands of Iturup, Kunashir and Shikotan, as well as several small uninhabited islands. The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly stressed that Russia’s sovereignty over these islands is based on a firm legal foundation and is indisputable.

EXPLAINER – Putin’s 1st Kuril Islands visit: What is the territorial dispute between Japan, Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:02:52 UTC
20:02:52 KST

Burc Eruygur
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
- Territorial dispute ongoing surrounding 4 southernmost Kuril Islands, including Iturup and Kunashir, which Tokyo calls Etorofu and Kunashiri, respectively
- Unresolved territorial dispute has prevented signing of a peace treaty between Tokyo, Moscow since World War II
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday made his first in-person visit to the Kuril Islands, which have been the site of an ongoing dispute between Japan and Russia for over 80 years.
According to the Kremlin, Putin visited the island of Iturup while accompanied by Valery Limarenko, governor of Russia’s Sakhalin region in the country’s Far East, where he visited a fish processing complex, as well as a local hospital and school.
While this was Putin’s first visit, Russian government officials have previously visited the islands, most recently Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin in 2021.
Dmitry Medvedev, deputy head of Russia's Security Council, was the first Russian president to visit the Kuril Islands back in 2010
Putin’s visit was strongly protested by Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the disputed islands as “inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law.”
What are the Kuril Islands?
The Kuril Islands are an archipelago of numerous volcanic islands and islets that separate the Sea of Okhotsk from the northern Pacific Ocean.
The island chain lies between the southernmost point of the Kamchatka Peninsula in the Russian Far East and the northeastern point of Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaido, stretching approximately 1,300 kilometers (807 miles).
Along with the island of Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands currently make up Russia’s Sakhalin Oblast, one of the country’s 83 federal subjects.
Why are Russia and Japan fighting?
The territorial dispute surrounding the Kuril Islands emerged during World War II, when the Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 and then seized the island chain.
Among the territories it seized include the archipelago’s four southernmost islands: Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets, as referred to by Russia.
However, Japan disputes Russia’s sovereignty over the four islands, which it defines as its “Northern Territories.” It also calls the islands of Iturup and Kunashir as Etorofu and Kunashiri, respectively.
Tokyo says that the four disputed islands are an “inherent territory of Japan” under Russian “occupation.” Meanwhile, Moscow says that its sovereignty over the Kuril Islands was determined by the results of World War II
The unresolved territorial dispute has prevented the signing of a peace treaty between the two countries since World War II.
Have there been efforts to resolve the dispute?
Despite Moscow and Tokyo having yet to sign a formal peace treaty, both capitals signed a joint declaration in 1956 that ended their state of war and restored diplomatic relations.
As part of the declaration, the Soviet side agreed to transfer Shikotan and the Habomai Islands to Japan once a formal peace treaty was concluded, though little meaningful developments occurred on the issue during the Cold War era.
Negotiations continued after the Cold War, producing results such as the 1993 Tokyo Declaration and 2001 Irkutsk Statement, the latter of which reaffirmed the 1956 declaration as the baseline legal foundation for peace talks.
Talks intensified under the administration of then-Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who agreed with Putin to intensify negotiations to draft a peace treaty, based on the 1956 declaration, back in 2018.
However, the process collapsed with the start of the Ukraine war in 2022, when Russia suspended peace-treaty negotiations due to Tokyo’s sanctions against Moscow.

Tehran Has to Make a Choice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:01:57 UTC
20:01:57 KST

Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
When the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey got together last week to forge a new defense agreement, they emphasized that their pact wasn’t aimed at any particular country. But one country was surely on everybody’s mind: the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Iran has positioned itself as the most overtly anti-Western state in the region, and the coming together of three prominent Muslim-majority countries aligned with the West, two of which have land borders with Iran, signals its isolation. Iran has endured months of war with Israel and the United States without losing, but it has done so in part by repeatedly attacking neighboring countries that house U.S. military bases. Now these countries are among those closing ranks against Iran in an agreement signed in and named for Mecca, Islam’s holiest city.
The symbolism can’t be lost on Tehran. The parties to the Mecca pact include some of the world’s most powerful Muslim-majority countries: the two with the biggest economies in the region (Turkey and Saudi Arabia, which also spend the most on their militaries), and the Muslim world’s sole nuclear power (Pakistan).
Iran has traditionally maintained good relations with Turkey and Pakistan; its cultural bonds with these two countries are strong and go back centuries. More recently, the Islamic Republic has worked to improve its relations with Saudi Arabia, particularly since reestablishing diplomatic ties with Riyadh in 2023.
Even so, Iran’s regional policies have put the country at odds with these and other neighbors. Tehran gave its full support to the regime of Bashar al-Assad in Syria, which rebels who were backed by Ankara and Riyadh overthrew in 2024. The Iranian military exchanged strikes with Pakistan in 2024 and attacked Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Iranian missiles were intercepted over Turkish airspace earlier this year. Tehran-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq have attacked Saudi interests. More broadly, Iran’s anti-American stance clashes with the official orientations of all three signatories of the Mecca agreement.
Skeptics will point out that the new defense pact might not mean much in practice. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a similar deal last year but did not invoke it when Saudi Arabia came under attack during the current conflict. But the language of the Mecca accord is stark: “Any armed attack against any of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” The arrangement includes a new organization, to be overseen by a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, and regular meetings among the foreign and defense ministers of the three countries, along with their military chiefs. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, has compared the new organization to NATO and suggested that Egypt, the most populous Arab state, is likely to join. Altogether, the pact suggests a significant improvement in relations between Turkey and the Arab states—a development that could help stabilize the entire region.
Iranian officialdom has mostly greeted the news of the Mecca pact with studied nonchalance. A spokesperson claimed to welcome the arrangement as evidence that the member countries would no longer rely on the United States. A reformist civil-society activist suggested to me that the Mecca agreement could be “an opportunity, not a threat,” insinuating that Iran could one day join it. But some hard-line politicians are less sanguine. Ebrahim Azizi, the head of the Parliament’s foreign-policy committee, posted on Saturday that the Mecca three “haven’t found the right path yet. We warn them about miscalculations. No mistake will go unanswered.”
Washington has long encouraged its allies in the Middle East to work together. Throughout much of the Cold War, regional alliances held off both Soviet communism and Arab radicalism, which meant that the United States felt the need to intervene only rarely and briefly. Iran was a crucial part of this architecture—intervening, together with Saudi Arabia, in civil wars in Oman and Yemen to help defeat Communist-backed rebels, and helping to found the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in 1969. President Richard Nixon so relied on Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi to help keep the U.S. out of Middle Eastern affairs that in 1972 he told Pahlavi, “Protect me.” Then came the Iranian Revolution of 1979, and with it, a new era of chaos and discord.
Iran is not the only Middle Eastern country excluded from the emerging security arrangement that Mecca portends. Israel, too, is absent. The 2020 Abraham Accords normalized Israel’s relations with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan, but the big prize was always Saudi Arabia, which has conditioned recognition of Israel on progress toward the formation of a Palestinian state. Israel is currently moving away from this prospect rather than toward it. Pakistan doesn’t recognize Israel either. Turkey has diplomatic and military relations with Israel, but the two countries have drifted apart in recent years.
If Israel still wants to work toward regional recognition, it may find that its best course is to patch things up with Turkey and try to meet the Saudis halfway. At least these two countries don’t share the depth of Iran’s animus against Israel.
Iran, too, will be faced with a choice. It can go on supporting militias and destabilizing the region, which will further isolate it. Or it can embrace the regional consensus on economic development, diplomatic reconciliation, and a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict. The Islamic Republic can either militate against Mecca, in other words, or give up its revolutionary ambitions at last.

AOC and Mamdani wanted to defund the police. Their backtracking puts organizers at risk | Derecka Purnell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:00:57 UTC
20:00:57 KST

The north may not remember, but 9 August this year marked the 12th anniversary of the police killing of Michael Brown Jr in Ferguson, Missouri. That day, the US representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez reassured an ABC news anchor that she, like other progressive politicians and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates, had “moved away” from statements they made during the pandemic, particularly on police and prison abolition. Questioned further, she explained:
“I have a local city councilman that has this saying: ‘Woke 1 was crazy’… especially during Covid, I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place. And I actually think that the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful. I think that when we talk about crime today, it’s fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down. And I think that we all share in the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible. I think that, you know, during lockdown, of course, rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today. And I’m grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they’re campaigning on in this moment.”
A few days later, on Wednesday, Zohran Mamdani, the progressive New York mayor, who has previously stated that his pandemic-era tweets supporting the defund movement were “out of step” with where he is now, chimed in on Ocasio-Cortez’s comments, saying: “Sometimes what you believe in can change. I know there are some for whom they still believe in that. I’ve made very clear that I do not believe in defunding the police and that to me, delivering critical public safety also looks like working with our police department alongside many other partners.”
The New York City councilman to whom Ocasio-Cortez was referring, Chi Ossé, was actually inspired by the abolition movement to run for office. But earlier this week, he was quick to proudly claim coinage of the term “woke 1”, which has been used by people who seek to minimize statements they made in the aftermath of George Floyd’s murder by police in May 2020.
In one sense, these politicians are absolutely correct. If “woke 1” represents a political baptism in shallow waters, then I have met many who were swept up in an emotional online conversion toward the radical, romantic rhetoric of “defund the police”. I know the power of the feeling of being connected to an idea that can offer relief and salvation. Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani and Ossé appeared at an altar of abolition during a global movement that condemned policing. It was a vibe. Sure, they may have even been earnest at the time. But as the abolitionist Mariame Kaba has said about centuries of organizing: abolition is not about your feelings or how you identify. It’s what you do.
During the pandemic, I was a couple of years off from an ongoing campaign to close a jail and about to enter a campaign to prevent another one from opening. I wrote my book, Becoming Abolitionists, in that time partially because of how quickly some conversions happened – through charismatic check-marked profiles and inspirational protests, rather than through an organization or collective. Many people were just beginning to understand how abolition was connected to other movements, including those against capitalism, imperialism, racism and ableism. I wanted to focus on centuries of abolitionist resistance that gave rise to contemporary abolitionist demands. “Defund” wasn’t simply a new idea about removing dollars from a budget (though we’d take it!) and leaving everything in society the same. Rather, it was and is a personal and political commitment and strategy to eliminate carceral, communal, colonial, capitalist and climate-based violence while building the people, practices and institutions to help us thrive.
This fact is what makes Ocasio-Cortez’s comments additionally troublesome. Even by her own logic, “crime” is largely a product of exploitative, unequal social relations, such as economic inequality, and democratic socialism would produce more equal social relationships and reduce crime. So if democratic socialism is effective, then why keep funding the New York police department at $11bn? And why dismiss taking money away as “rhetoric”?
Because: the police were not created for public safety. They were created to keep property owners and slaveowners safe. The abolitionist geographer Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes in Geographies of Global Change that “the best estimate for crime as a driving force of prison expansion shows it to account for little more than 10 percent of the increase. Rather, it is a greater propensity to lock people up, as opposed to people’s greater propensity to do old or new illegal things, that accounts for about 90 percent of US prison and jail growth since 1980.” The rhetoric of public safety obscures this history and protects the institution as a heavily unionized, violent jobs program. This does not mean the police never show up when someone needs help, or that people become cops because they only want to hurt others. What it does mean is that historically, cities are willing to rely on the poverty that capitalism creates to fill its carceral ranks with people looking to enter the middle class.
Seeing progressive politicians move away from their earlier feelings poses a question about what they’re moving toward. Ossé and AOC did not introduce any “woke 1” legislation or resolutions that they now have to retract. Mamdani actually attempted the opposite: the racial justice working group of DSA, among others, successfully pressured him to reverse his commitment to add almost 600 more officers and $70m to the NYPD, against his campaign promise to maintain the headcount of the force. He was positioning this move while boasting historic lows for crime in the city. So unlike the students, artists, congregants and organizers I met and know, the politicians prioritized political office over political homes. Because these figures represent more than their political ideas, I understand. But the dismissal is the problem. The ideas rooted in the defund movement that got them the spotlight were not polling well by the time their volunteers were canvassing for their political campaigns. As a result, they dismissed those ideas as something to grow and learn from, not to publicly explore and explain.
By contrast, for example, upon receiving pushback from the “defund” framing, activists in North Carolina chose “refund Raleigh” instead as an organizing campaign strategy to explain abolition to the community, develop a public services investment strategy and secure policies that decouple public safety and police. Even decades before abolition entered a mainstream branding debate, Wilson Gilmore said that she and others organizing through Californians United for a Responsible Budget chose a “deliberately bland name” to attract community members to the campaign. Still, other organizers chose more explicit “defund” campaign names as clear sites of struggle, sacrificing public palatability for political clarity.
These efforts are equally important: people, politicians and corporations weaponized the ambiguity of “Black lives matter” toward everything, including more police funding and hires. So whether explicit in naming “defund” or not, abolitionist organizers across the country have been spearheading electoral campaigns, mutual aid efforts, disaster recovery, anti-immigrant detention networks, stopping jails and more. It is not always successful and apparent, but the commitment remains because the struggle continues.
Right now, DSA members like AOC, Ossé and Mamdani feel refreshing because electoral politics have been captured for so long by Democrats and Republicans. And the state has done such a horribly impressive job at exhausting, shackling, killing and exiling actual revolutionaries that politicians who repeat the slightest radical rhetoric can start to feel like revolutionaries. What remains, though, is that the very movements producing that rhetoric, from abolition to Free Palestine, also produced the possibilities of their elections. And downplaying those movements puts organizers who continue this work at risk, especially right now.
What time is it when politicians across the political spectrum, from AOC and Ossé to Marco Rubio and Donald Trump, suggest that progressive and left organizers are “woke” and “crazy”? It is the time when those who have not yet realized that the demonization of people, organizations and ideas about justice – regardless of where they come from – leads to targeting, surveillance, deportation, imprisonment and death.
If leaders of DSA, an organization of which I am also a member, want to continue to grow as an electoral political home for people who believe these ideas are not only possible, but also worth pursuing, they must know that they are subject to the same lessons they are teaching establishment Democrats right now: do not laugh off the political demands of those who put you in office. For all of what their constituents, canvassers and staffers did as part of a fight on our behalf, is it worth treating years-long radical, Black and multiracial pursuits of freedom as mere pandemic pandemonium? No, it’s not. But more than what we are called by any of them is what we continue to call ourselves. Our own histories, convictions and clarity, not politicians, lead the way.

How Trump’s order on vaccines is sowing confusion, doubt and fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:00:56 UTC
20:00:56 KST

Donald Trump’s executive order on vaccines does not change the US recommendations for the shots – but experts say it does create confusion and doubt about vaccines, which will lead to more illness and possibly deaths among children and will make it harder for families and pediatricians to protect them.
The executive order was an attempt to reinstate sweeping changes to the vaccine schedule made earlier this year by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services and a longtime vaccine opponent – changes that were later halted by a federal judge.
But an executive order can only offer guidance to agencies; it doesn’t change laws or set recommendations. Recommendations from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the federal agency that sets vaccine guidance, remain the same.
“Nothing’s changed,” said Noele Nelson, a public health professor at Cornell University and former pediatrician. The primary effect of the order has been “adding unnecessary confusion” and “undermining trust in vaccines without any change in the scientific evidence”, she said.
While the science and the recommendations are unchanged, “what is going to change is more people are going to be confused and scared”, said Vincent Iannelli, a pediatrician near Dallas and founder of Vaxopedia, a resource on vaccines.
The president is an influential figure, and his inaccurate comments about the dangers of vaccines and a long-disproven connection to autism can have resounding effects, said Wendy Parmet, faculty co-director of the Center for Health Policy and Law at Northeastern University.
“People hear Trump is doing this and they think, ‘My God, he’s powerful. He’s doing it. Nobody will be able to have hepatitis B vaccines.’ That isn’t true, but it’s confusing, and it can sow more distrust,” Parmet said.
Trump also lacks the authority to recommend spacing doses, she said: “The president can’t tell doctors to say to parents: ‘Why don’t you come back in a week and have the second shot?’ But saying it can certainly lead some parents, maybe many parents, to start asking their doctors for multiple visits.”
Adding four or five visits for every round of vaccination will make pediatricians’ schedules even busier, and insurance frequently does not cover additional vaccination visits. It opens up the possibility for errors as pediatricians struggle to understand which vaccines have and haven’t been administered.
“It also means that they have to come back to the office more, which means they might be exposed to more illnesses,” Iannelli said. “The biggest risk is they’re going to delay getting protected from that illness that the vaccine protects them from.”
Vaccines are spaced the way they are based on decades of evidence, Nelson said: “It provides the best immune response to the vaccine, and the spacing is not arbitrary. For some vaccines that are considered to have lifelong immunity – like hepatitis A, hepatitis B, measles – spacing is critical.”
Trump’s rhetoric also increases the stigma around autism and may encourage families to seek out dangerous treatments.
“Nobody talks enough about how much it hurts kids with autism,” Iannelli said. “Their whole framing about how vaccines cause autism – it makes people think that their kids are damaged. It pushes them into trying unproven and dangerous therapies.”
Trump also invoked religious freedom, indicating that the executive order may put pressure on states to reduce vaccination mandates for school attendance. The administration has previously pushed its priorities around “parental authority” on vaccines in communication with states, and it has placed religious freedom at the heart of its health policies.
There are no federal mandates on vaccination outside of the military, and states set vaccination requirements for school attendance. Forty-six states and the District of Columbia already have religious exemptions for vaccine requirements; all states have medical exemptions.
“This potentially could put pressure on states that don’t have [religious] exemptions right now,” Nelson said. But there would probably be pushback and legal challenges if the administration tried to push states to change its vaccine laws, she said.
The few states that don’t have religious exemptions have already litigated the issue, Parmet said. “New York and California and Connecticut, in particular, have been litigating and litigating and litigating, and they’ve been winning and winning and winning on these vaccine cases. And I don’t see those states suddenly folding,” she said. “If Trump tries to coerce the states more, it will get litigated again.”
There have been people opposed to immunizations since they were created, and it goes in a cycle, Iannelli pointed out. As soon as a disease is controlled by vaccines, people forget why the vaccines are needed; immunization rates drop, diseases resurge and people rush to vaccinate once again. “It happens every time,” he said. But in the meantime, children suffer.
With announcements like Trump’s, “people are primed to listen because they’re already scared”, he said. “Then they hear something like this, and it reinforces the idea that they should be scared.” Frequently, Iannelli said, they don’t even know why they’re scared; they just know that they are.
Recently, he had a visit with parents who said they didn’t think they would get their child vaccinated that day. He asked what their concerns were; they were worried about the information they had seen online, and they thought it might be better to split up the shots. Iannelli listened and told them he could do that, but they would need to schedule several follow-up visits. Tetanus is all around, he added, and there has been an increase in measles. The parents said: “Oh – let’s just get them,” Iannelli said.
“It helps you to address it and reassure them, and you just keep asking questions and talking,” Iannelli said. Pediatricians shouldn’t lecture their patients or kick them out of their practices, he said; they should do something called “motivational interviewing”, where they determine the reasons for a patient’s hesitation and help them find the reasons to change.
“As pediatricians, that’s our lane,” he said, before adding: “Parents don’t need a lecture; they just want to talk about their concerns.” Concerns, he notes, that are being amplified by misinformation spread at the highest levels of US government. And it doesn’t take much time to listen and respond, he said. “You don’t want to spend a half hour on it. You want to spend a couple minutes on it. And then, after a couple visits, it works.”

Baby pulled alive from Colombia earthquake rubble as rescue window closes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:00:22 UTC
20:00:22 KST

Rescue teams in Colombia were making desperate efforts Thursday afternoon to find survivors of the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck the country Monday, before the critical 72-hour window for locating survivors closes. The official death toll stands at 265, with more than 3,500 injured and nearly 500 people still missing. In recent days, authorities had reported 3,000 to 4,000 people missing or out of contact, but after cross-checking and further inquiries, officials said the number is lower.
Search-and-rescue experts say the chances of finding survivors drop sharply three days after an earthquake, although past disasters have shown that people can still be found alive beyond that point, especially if they have access to food and water. The earthquake struck Colombia on Monday at 7:34 a.m. local time, meaning the most critical phase of the rescue effort ends Thursday afternoon.
In Cali and Pereira, two of the cities hit hardest, rescue teams worked through a third consecutive night, clearing rubble with their bare hands and using cranes and search dogs. From time to time, they stopped — not to rest, but to create silence so they could listen for cries for help or signs of life beneath collapsed buildings.
Marta Pérez, a Cali resident, said overnight that two of her relatives were trapped under the rubble and that she felt helpless. “We will hold on to hope until the very last moment,” she said.
Fernando Loaiza, a rescue volunteer, said he and his colleagues had no intention of stopping. “As you can see, we are all here, the whole city of Cali, hoping to find more survivors,” he said.
Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder also said overnight that rescue efforts were entering their final stage.
Meanwhile, the rescue of Salomón, a 3-month-old baby pulled alive from the rubble of a five-story building that collapsed in Cali, continued to draw attention around the world.
The infant was rescued several hours after the earthquake after a passerby heard the weakening voice of Salomón’s father calling from beneath the debris: “I’m here. I’m with a baby.”
Video of the rescue showed the infant, dressed in a dust-covered onesie, being carefully pulled from the rubble. His father, Juan David Gómez, could be seen lying at an awkward angle, one arm covered in blood, while still trapped beneath a slab of concrete.
He, too, was eventually rescued. Both father and son were taken to a hospital and are in stable condition. The baby suffered only scratches and a minor head injury, while Juan underwent surgery and is recovering.
The baby’s mother, 29-year-old Valentina, however, remained trapped in the rubble with her younger brother. It was unclear whether they had survived.
In Pereira, rescuers focused overnight on a collapsed bakery where they believe a vendor, Pablo Loaiza, may still be alive beneath the debris. Rescue teams used equipment capable of detecting slight movements and found signs suggesting he was alive and waiting to be rescued.
Loaiza’s relatives gathered at the scene, anxiously awaiting updates. “They’re telling us it could be him,” said his 16-year-old niece, Sara. “My heart is about to explode.”
Family members said rescuers asked Pablo to knock twice and then three times from beneath the rubble, and it appeared he responded. People at the scene applauded excitedly.
Pro-Israel government: ‘We did not reject aid for political reasons’
More than 11,000 homes were destroyed in the earthquake, leaving thousands of families homeless. For many residents, Wednesday night was their third consecutive night outdoors, either because their homes had been damaged or because they were afraid to return amid continuing aftershocks. More than 100 aftershocks have been recorded since Monday’s main quake.
In the town of Roldanillo, Juliana Méndez sifted through the ruins of the beauty supply store where she worked, one of many businesses damaged in the earthquake. “It’s like starting everything over,” she said of the destruction.
In Pereira’s Providencia neighborhood, residents were seen removing furniture and household belongings from damaged buildings. One of them was Ana Paulina, whose apartment is now unsafe. “We’re in shock,” she said. “We are not prepared to tell our children that we have to pack whatever we can and start a new life.”
Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office just three days before the powerful earthquake, declared an economic state of emergency and three days of national mourning. Citizens across Colombia mobilized to help, bringing water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods. Long lines formed outside blood donation centers.
Over the past day, Colombia began approving and receiving international aid missions, including one from Israel. The United States announced immediately after the earthquake that it was allocating $15.5 million in emergency assistance to the government in Bogotá, while the European Union committed 2 million euros.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday night that he had ordered an aid delegation to leave for Colombia “immediately.” After years of strained ties with Israel, Colombia is now renewing relations and plans to open an embassy in Jerusalem following the election of the new, pro-Israel president, de la Espriella.
At the same time, criticism of Colombia’s new government has grown over what critics describe as poor preparedness and delays in accepting international assistance during the crucial hours after the earthquake, in what is being seen as the administration’s first major leadership test.
Among the accusations is that the tense transition between de la Espriella and the outgoing left-wing administration of former President Gustavo Petro — marked by the absence of an orderly handover and the late appointment of the head of the national disaster management agency — led to administrative breakdowns and confusion over the official channels for receiving aid, even as the 72-hour rescue window was closing.
The government has also been accused of showing deep suspicion toward parts of the international community, refusing certain aid offers and turning away trained rescue teams from countries including Mexico.
Colombia’s new government and its Foreign Ministry strongly rejected claims that aid offers had been refused for political or ideological reasons, saying no country or organization had been deliberately excluded.
Officials said the government specifically requested rescue teams from only four countries — the United States, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel — based solely on professional considerations, because teams from those countries hold the required international certifications. Other organizations, they said, were provided with a specific list of humanitarian equipment and supplies that were needed.

Foreign minister to warn 'monoculturalism' a threat to national security
