Foreign Minister Penny Wong to warn monoculturalism a threat to national security
In short:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will deliver the annual Gyngell Lecture at the Lowy Institute in Sydney on Friday.
She will use the opportunity to warn that the rise of populism threatens Australia's national security and that "denigrating our region and neglecting our partners" is not in our interests.
She will argue that the push for "monoculturalism" will leave the nation "lonely in a dangerous world".
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will use a high-profile speech on Friday to declare that the rise of populism threatens Australia's national security, saying the "melancholic fantasy of monoculture" risks making Australia "lonely in a dangerous world".
Senator Wong will deliver the annual Gyngell Lecture — which is named after the revered policy stalwart Allan Gyngell who died in 2023 — at the Lowy Institute in Sydney.
It comes as Labor continues to struggle in the polls, with Pauline Hanson and One Nation remaining politically ascendant, despite increasingly sharp scrutiny from other political parties and the media.
One Nation has vowed to slash foreign aid and withdraw Australia from multilateral institutions if it wins power, while Senator Hanson has taken aim at corruption among Pacific leaders.
Senator Wong will not mention the party by name in her speech, but will make multiple clear references to One Nation's core policies, arguing that isolationism will impoverish and isolate Australia.
"Denigrating our region and neglecting our partners is no way to secure Australia's interests," she will say.
"Neither is encouraging some kind of retreat from the world and the institutions that go with it."
Most Australians say diversity positive
This year's Lowy Institute poll shows Australians are increasingly unhappy with migration levels, with 55 per cent saying the total number of migrants coming to Australia is "too high" — as well as a sharp drop in the number of Australians who support cultural diversity.
But 73 per cent of those polled still said they see diversity as "entirely" or "mostly" positive, which Senator Wong will say shows the nation still retains faith in the multiculturalism, even if social cohesion is "under pressure".
Senator Hanson has called for a return to "monoculturalism", although she insists that the term is not racially discriminatory and simply requires migrants of all faiths and backgrounds to embrace Australian values.
Senator Wong will argue this vision is not just at odds with the reality of modern Australia but will also leave the nation adrift in Asia, and "lonely in a dangerous world".
"I've always believed the ability of Australians to connect with people from every part of the world is a national asset … an asset that expands our choices in the world," she will say.
"The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and cut off our connections … to look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, no opportunities to grow from."
She will also argue that a poisonous debate over diversity could also stoke social resentments and division in Australia.
"Well before we could ever realise this melancholic fantasy of monoculture, there is a lot of damage that can be done," she will say.
"Because Australians would be turned against each other. Australia would be a more hostile place. Harder to be family, harder to be a friend, colleague, or neighbour."
A warning against division
The foreign minister will also suggest that fuelling division will make Australia more vulnerable to disinformation campaigns from "external" forces — although she will not point the finger at any foreign states.
Researchers have previously accused some authoritarian states — including China and Russia — of running disinformation campaigns aimed at fracturing social trust in Australian democracy and driving narratives more favourable to them.
"At a time where external and internal forces are seeking to divide us, turning Australians against each other makes us more vulnerable," Senator Wong will say.
"Division makes us easier to exploit, it doesn't make us stronger."

A Community Leader Fights for Haitians in Ohio, While Worrying About His Own Fate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Viles Dorsainvil doesn't have time to think about his own future.
His days are filled with responding to increasingly frantic calls from fellow Haitians in Springfield, Ohio, where he is a community leader known for helping make sense of immigration issues. Then he spends his evenings up late, often until midnight, working on his own schoolwork, as he pursues dual master's degrees in public administration and international relations at Wright State University near Dayton.
Amid this hectic pace, Dorsainvil, 40, is grappling with the same situation as many of those around him. He came to the U.S. in 2020 under what’s known as Temporary Protected Status, or TPS. Last week, a federal court confirmed that the Trump administration's bid to end TPS for Dorsainvil and roughly 330,000 other Haitians had succeeded, setting the stage for scores of deportations in the coming months.
In recent weeks, Haitians across the country have received a stark warning from the Department of Homeland Security: accept $2,600 and return to Haiti, or refuse and be fitted with an ankle monitor, allowing Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to easily detain them for deportation at any point in the future. Some Haitians are preparing to flee to another country. Others are resigned to returning to Haiti.
Dorsainvil has yet to receive a letter from DHS. He is trying to keep from becoming overcome by fear, especially while others in the community still depend on him. But his precarious situation feels untenable.
"I don't know which plan I should have," he says.
In Springfield, fear of this moment has been rooted deeply in the community's psyche since the last presidential campaign, when Donald Trump and JD Vance helped spread false rumors about Haitian migrants eating residents' pets in Springfield. Last June, then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem first announced that TPS for Haitians would be terminated.
That set off a monthslong legal fight that officially ended this month, with a federal judge affirming the Supreme Court's decision from June. “These individuals can either self-deport or we'll arrest you and send you back,” Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told NewsNation last week.
The Haitian Support Center in Springfield that Dorainvil co-founded in 2023 has seen calls spike from Haitians worried about their future in the wake of the Supreme Court ruling. On the other end of each line is another Haitian immigrant trying, like him, to rebuild a life in America after leaving a home country torn by deadly earthquakes and endless gang violence.
Since late July, at least 50 people in Springfield have received a DHS letter about their deportation status, according to the center's own tally. The letters instruct them to come to the nearest local ICE offices for a check-in appointment and preview the choice they will be asked to make.
Dorsainvil, who has accompanied some Haitians to provide translation, says most check-ins unfold the same way: after immigration officers confirm an immigrants' identity and status, they offer the $2,600 payment and deportation, which the immigrant usually refuses. Then they are outfitted with an ankle monitor, despite objections from their lawyer who often argue for less intrusive measures.
None of the court rulings can alter the chaotic reality that still engulfs Haiti. The State Department continues to warn American citizens not to travel to the country, citing the risk of “crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care.” The Department also recommends U.S. citizens who need to travel to Haiti leave DNA samples and dental records with trusted people to make it easier to identify their remains.
Dorsainvil stresses that many Haitians in the U.S. would love to return to their homeland if that was a viable option. “So far, we just don't have a country to come back to,” he says.
Haitian migrants scared to leave their homes
Two weeks ago, Dorsainvil made the difficult decision to close down the Haitian Support Center for two days over fears of a rumored ICE operation in Springfield. He feared ICE agents might stake out the center’s office to catch Haitians coming there for help. The heightened vulnerability has left Springfield’s Haitians in a state of panic. Many of those who haven’t fled their homes are staying indoors and keeping their kids home from school.
The anxiety among Haitian immigrants isn't confined to Ohio, where Gov. Mike DeWine has limited state cooperation with ICE and praised Haitians for helping revitalize Springfield’s economy. In Florida, home to the nation's largest Haitian population, immigrants face intensified enforcement as the Republican-controlled state government closely aligns itself with Trump's mass-deportation agenda. Last year, Governor Ron DeSantis mandated all local officials work with ICE operations, and the state government has threatened officials who hesitate to do so with criminal penalties.
State authorities in Florida are now required to make immigration-related arrests on behalf of ICE. It’s a dynamic that has left the state’s Haitian immigrants "paralyzed," says Anne Piervil, an immigration attorney based in Orlando.
“People aren't driving. People aren't taking public transportation. People are scared to go to the airport,” she says, adding that some TPS holders have lost their driver’s license because renewal was tied to their immigration status.
An ICE spokesperson said in a statement that TPS had been allowed to function as a de facto amnesty program and that the program was always intended to be temporary.
“What we would say now is it’s closing time which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here,” the spokesperson said in an unsigned statement. “The good news is it’s not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home.”
Scores of Haitian immigrants have also reportedly lost their jobs. Piervil said large amusement parks, hotels, and nursing homes in Orlando have begun dismissing hundreds, if not thousands, of Haitian workers since the Supreme Court ruling.
The fraught situation in the U.S. is prompting some Haitians to contemplate fleeing to a third country, despite the obstacles. Aside from the costs and a possible language barrier, many Haitian immigrants are also concerned about their own safety if they move to a third country, according to Felipe Sousa-Lazaballet, a community organizer in central Florida. That fear was heightened after reports in February that four decapitated Haitian women were found in the Dominican Republic—Haiti's neighbor—after they had been deported from Puerto Rico. The Dominican Republic has also been deporting hundreds of thousands back to Haiti each year.
The option to move to Canada is also becoming increasingly infeasible. Earlier this year, Canada tightened its immigration laws in response to an influx of migrants. Any TPS holders who try to cross the border risk being returned immediately to the United States and into ICE custody.
For many Haitians in the U.S., the only realistic option is to simply wait for what comes next. The community in Springfield is left collectively holding its breath, wondering if a rumored mass deportation operation will come to pass.
For now, Dorsainvil, along with many volunteers in the community, continues to provide as much support as he can, from daily transportation and translation to grocery shopping. Like many other Haitians living in Springfield, he also finds solace in prayer and meditation.
“I meditate to reboost my system and mental health,” he says, “just so that I can continue to serve my community again tomorrow, and the next day.”

Religious leaders sign interfaith peace accord in Abuja to launch national harmony initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:59:19 UTC
19:59:19 KST

More than 50 Muslim and Christian leaders have signed an interfaith peace accord in Abuja, launching a new body to promote religious harmony across Nigeria.
Nigeria's more than 200 million population is roughly evenly divided between a predominantly Muslim north and a largely Christian south, with other groups practicing traditional religions.
Focus on the religious divide was heightened last November when US President Donald Trump called Nigeria a "disgraced country" and threatened military action over what he said was the treatment of Christians by "Islamic Terrorists."
Islamist insurgents such as Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province have wrought havoc in the country for more than 15 years, killing thousands of people, but their attacks have been largely confined to the majority Muslim northeast.
While Christians have been killed, the vast majority of the victims have been Muslims, analysts and rights groups say.
Accord welcomed by faith leaders
No mention was made of Trump's comments in the official statements about the accord signed on Wednesday at a conference organized by the Muslim World League, an Islamic non-governmental organization based in Saudi Arabia.
But the government and various other groups have been working to show progress on security since his remarks.
Muslim World League Secretary-General Mohammad Al-Issa said there was enthusiasm among the two faiths to "turn a new page."
"We do not deny that extremist ideas have harmed everyone; all have been affected by it," he said.
Christian and Muslim leaders from Nigeria described the pact as a turning point.
John Praise Daniel, chairman of the Northern Christian Religious Leaders' Assembly, said he hoped it would curb divisive rhetoric by clerics.
"No hate speech, and no disrespect for other religious groups, no calling of people as infidels," he said.
Khalid Abubakar, secretary-general of Jama'atu Nasri Islam, said: "It is not a call to leave your own religion, but a cooperation of working together in harmony."
Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin represented President Bola Tinubu at the signing ceremony. Three northern state governors were also present.
Jibrin said on the opening day of the two-day event: "The government is determined to make sure that we remain united as a country, despite our differences, whatever the differences may be."
The accord comes ahead of the January 2027 election, when religion will again be a factor in Nigerian politics.
Tinubu's ruling All Progressives Congress is running on the same presidential ticket of two Muslims that it fielded in 2023, breaking Nigeria's long-standing practice of balancing presidential tickets between the country's two main faiths.

USS Abraham Lincoln conditions under scrutiny after reports sailors attempted to jump overboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:58:45 UTC
19:58:45 KST

US Senator Richard Blumenthal (Connecticut) has demanded a formal inquiry into the conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln in a letter sent Wednesday to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao.
Blumenthal, who himself served in the US Marine Corps Reserve, sent the letter following reports of several US Navy service members stationed aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln attempting to jump overboard as the aircraft carrier enters its ninth month of deployment at sea.
The Navy later confirmed that a sailor went overboard earlier in the month but that the circumstances around the incident were still under investigation.
Two American newspapers that cover matters related to the US military, Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, originally reported on the matter earlier this week.
“The Lincoln’s extended deployment raises broader questions about the Navy’s ability to sustainably generate carrier forces while preserving service member well-being, maintenance, schedules, fleet readiness, and the capacity to respond to future contingencies,” wrote Blumenthal in his letter.
Blumenthal gives US Navy two weeks to provide answers
Citing reports of supply shortages, water contamination, and several other issues that have arisen over the past months, Blumenthal granted the US Navy two weeks, until August 27, to provide answers.
In his questions posed to the naval force, Blumenthal requested details surrounding Lincoln’s extended deployment, how the Navy assesses the mental health and morale of its soldiers, and how it has worked to solve the quality-of-life problems that have been reported on board the carrier.
Further, Blumenthal asked the Navy to explain what military objective Lincoln’s ongoing deployment is meant to achieve and how the US Defense Department “assess[es] whether the carrier’s continued presence is necessary to accomplish that objective.”
US Senator Ruben Gallego (Arizona) echoed Blumenthal in a post to X/Twitter on Thursday, saying that he is looking into conducting an official oversight visit with a bipartisan Senate Delegation due to the reports.
“Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty. The way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it’s dangerous,” Gallego wrote. “These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home.”
“The stories of crew members threatening to jump off the ship are a frightening alarm bell as to how bad the situation has become: moldy showers, sporadic hot water, rationed meals and soap, broken toilets, and grueling 12- to 16-hour shifts with no days off.”
“Congress must do its duty to provide oversight and hold the administration accountable for these actions,” he said.
Later on Thursday, Hegseth rejected the claims, saying that the reports about Lincoln's conditions are "misrepresented."
USS Theodore Roosevelt to reportedly relieve Lincoln
Late last week, Cao and several other senior Navy officials had reportedly held a town hall-style meeting with the families of the service members aboard the Lincoln.
One of the spouses told Cao and the other officials that her husband had sent her a message on Thursday saying that “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow,” reported Stars and Stripes, citing one of the meeting attendees.
According to the spouse, officials didn’t directly address that or other similar statements presented to them by concerned family members, but did affirm that those aboard Lincoln had access to mental health professionals, chaplains, and doctors.
Navy Times reported that Cao said that the US Navy is preparing the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group to relieve Lincoln, but could not provide a timeline due to “operational security.”
Later on Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the USS George Washington aircraft carrier is being sent to replace Lincoln as part of a "previously scheduled rotation plan," citing US officials familiar with the matter.
Annabelle Loma, the wife of one of the service members who tried to jump from the aircraft carrier, told Navy Times that her husband had been repeatedly overextended before his attempt.
“He’s scared,” Loma told Navy Times. “He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out, his 13-year career is ruined, just like that. That’s not fair, that’s not right. That’s not what he should be worrying about right now.”
According to Navy Times, the Lincoln’s ombudsman had initially called Loma to inform her of the incident and that her husband was put on medical hold.
She has not heard anything else from the US Navy “in recent weeks,” Navy Times reported.
Both papers gave details of several other attempts made by service members to jump overboard, including an incident where the jumper was restrained by other soldiers who happened to be on watch.
“When she can email me, she’s definitely down,” Shelby Sander, whose mother is stationed on Lincoln, told Navy Times. “I think they’ve had five weeks of non-stop combat operations or something like that, so that makes it really tough to communicate consistently or even know if we’ll be able to. It sucks.”
“I don’t know how to enjoy starting my senior year when my mom isn’t here, you know?” Sanders said. “Will she be back before homecoming? My birthday? Christmas? I have no idea, and that’s all that I think about.”
Manuel Guevara, the father of a soldier serving on Lincoln, told Navy Times that his son had sounded “exhausted, down and worried the last time they spoke.”
“Us being out there keeps wars out of our country, but it sucks having your family away. It makes the homecoming that much sweeter, but the uncertainty of when that day will come starts to eat away at you,” Guevara shared with Navy Times.
“I don’t want to worry that the circumstances of this deployment will get the best of my son, and he doesn’t make it back home,” Guevara said. “That’s an unbearable burden on my heart.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

China's lead in orbital data centres risks leaving Europe behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:56:50 UTC
19:56:50 KST

China is racing ahead on orbital data centres while Europe still debates the concept, a new policy brief warns, and the gap is starting to widen.
China's push into orbital data centres risks leaving Europe behind, according to a new policy brief from the European Space Policy Institute (ESPI).
Orbital data centres are increasingly seen as key strategic assets for processing the vast amounts of data generated by AI and satellite systems.
The brief, titled "Constellating Compute: China's Domestic Policy Towards Orbital Data Centre Leadership," warns that if the technological gap widens significantly, Europe risks having to compute its own space data through third-party actors and losing access to orbital information.
European efforts are under way but remain limited in scale.
The EU-funded research project ASCEND, backed under Horizon Europe since 2023, found that orbital data centres could strengthen European digital sovereignty.
The European Space Agency (ESA) has also worked with UK firm Open Cosmos on the Φ-sat-2 satellite, which carries AI capabilities for Earth observation.
French start-up ALATYR has also announced plans to manufacture robotically assembled orbital data centres. Even so, compared with developments in China and the US, the gap in Europe is starting to widen.
Why is China ahead in the orbital data centre race?
China has treated space-based computing as a national strategic priority, giving rise to a wave of state-backed initiatives and policies to support the goal.
Central to this effort is the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which first formalised orbital data centres in a new strategy, alongside the Beijing Municipal Government and the Zhongguancun Science Park.
China has combined top-down policy drafting, private and state-owned industry adaptation, municipal and provincial government incentives, and support for non-state actors and working groups, according to the brief.
High-profile prototype constellations have driven early implementation. The Three-Body Constellation, launched by start-up ADAspace in May 2025, marked the first operational example of space-based computing.
In a joint laboratory with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ADAspace has since used the constellation's in-orbit computing power to control a robot on the ground, one of several technical trials the company has run since the satellites reached orbit.
Other companies have followed. Beijing Orbital Twilight Technology Co., Ltd. (Orbital Chenguang) announced an undisclosed equity round alongside €7.4bn worth of debt financing in April 2026.
Nayuta Space unveiled its ALAYA supercompute constellation, planned to deploy 12,500 computing satellites. Shanghai Xingshu Tiansuan Space Technology Co. unveiled its Xingshu Plan at the World AI Conference in July 2026, envisioned to grow to 1,000 satellites.
China Mobile, Zhejiang Lab, Bailing Aerospace, Zhongke Tiansuan Technology and Interstellar Glory Space-Based Computing Technology (iSpace) have also announced their own constellations.
Beijing's municipal government has moved to incubate the sector further, issuing a call for orbital data centre project proposals in June 2026 alongside the Zhongguancun Science Park, and launching a space computing innovation centre bringing together rival companies including GalaxySpace and Landspace under a company-plus-alliance model.
According to state broadcaster CGTN, the centre's priority areas include space-based computing chip design, high-performance computing payloads and integrated space-ground cloud computing technologies.
CASC has also outlined a five-year plan for the sector, agreed with the Chinese Society of Astronautics in January 2026 under the guidance of state bodies including the China National Space Administration.
According to CGTN's reporting on the plan, it includes building gigawatt-level space digital infrastructure combining cloud, edge and terminal technologies, though the underlying policy documents do not appear to have been formally published, and Euronews could not independently verify the claims.
The brief recommends that the EU establish coordinated political guidance, investment support and a regulatory framework for orbital data centre development, that a flagship initiative be included in the Horizon Europe Moonshot Projects under the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, and that European space actors convene working groups with international counterparts on standards and data sovereignty.

What would a North Korean troop surge mean for Ukraine war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

What would a North Korean troop surge mean for Ukraine war?
August 13, 2026
North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine, with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict.
In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.
North Korea has suffered thousands of casualties in the Ukraine war
Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analysts believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region.
Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.
On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.
Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'
South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.
Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.
"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.
Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.
"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."
Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?
Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution.
"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.
"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.
"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine."
Russian officials praise North Koreans
"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.
The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean casualties, some 2,000 may have been killed.
"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.
"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."
North Korean women also moving to Russia
Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."
"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.
"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.
"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."
Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military
According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."
"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.
"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.
North Korea has suffered thousands of casualties in the Ukraine war
Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analysts believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region.
Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.
On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.
Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'
South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.
Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.
"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.
Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.
"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."
Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?
Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution.
"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.
"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.
"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine."
Russian officials praise North Koreans
"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.
The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean casualties, some 2,000 may have been killed.
"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.
"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."
North Korean women also moving to Russia
Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."
"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.
"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.
"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."
Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military
According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."
"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.
"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

Colombia makes final push to find survivors with quake toll at 265

2026-08-13

19:54:00 KST

Colombian rescuers mounted a final push Thursday to find earthquake survivors as the crucial 72-hour window for rescue operations neared its end.
The magnitude 7.4 quake, the strongest to hit Colombia this century, has killed 265 people, injured more than 3,500 and left almost 500 missing, according to local authorities.
In cities such as Cali and Pereira, emergency crews worked through a third night with their bare hands, cranes and sniffer dogs, stopping not to rest but to listen for signs of life.
Thursday morning will mark 72 hours since the quake, a period when survivors are considered most likely to be found alive beneath collapsed buildings.
Cali resident Martha Perez said she felt "helpless" as two relatives were thought to still be trapped under rubble.
"We will hold on to (hope) until the very end," Perez told AFP on Wednesday night.
"As you can see, all of us here – the entire city of Cali – are hoping to find more survivors," volunteer rescuer Fernando Loaiza said.
Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said Wednesday that rescue efforts were "entering the final phase."
Colombia's newly installed President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared the disaster an "economic emergency" and announced three days of national mourning.
"We will do what is necessary," he said in a statement, vowing to "emerge again as a country and as a society."
More than 11,000 dwellings have been destroyed and thousands of families have been rendered homeless, according to official figures.
In Pereira, crews focused on a collapsed bakery where they believe a street vendor trapped since Monday's earthquake may still be alive beneath the rubble.
Rescuers using equipment that detects vibrations said they had picked up possible signs of life from Pablo Loaiza, prompting anxious relatives to gather near the wreckage.
"They tell us it could be him," said his 16-year-old niece, Sara Loaiza. "My heart is about to burst out of my chest."
Relatives said the trapped man appeared to respond when rescuers asked him to knock twice, then three times from beneath the rubble, drawing applause from those gathered at the scene.
"Every half hour we make everyone be quiet to see if we can find people alive," volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez told AFP.
"So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead."
Many have already spent consecutive nights outdoors, either because their homes were damaged or because they feared aftershocks.
In the town of Roldanillo, Yuliana Mendez picked through the wreckage of the beauty products store where she worked, one of many businesses damaged in the disaster.
"It's like starting over from scratch," she said.
In Pereira's Providencia neighborhood, residents hauled furniture and household items from damaged buildings. Among them was lawyer Ana Paulina Crosthwaite, whose apartment block was left unsafe by the quake.
"We're in a state of shock," she told AFP. "We're not prepared to tell our children that we have to pack whatever we can and start a new life."
Many Colombians have mobilized to help, bringing water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods, while long lines formed outside blood donation centers.
"It's about wanting to help your community, your city and your country," said blood donor Ferney Cabrera.
The United States announced $15.5 million in emergency aid to Colombia, and the European Union pledged two million euros ($2.3 million).

Rights Group Urges Taliban To Free 'Disappeared' Aid Workers

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

19:53:55 KST

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on Afghanistan's Taliban rulers to release several international aid workers who were "forcibly disappeared" from their offices last month and are still missing without word on their location or condition.
HRW said in a statement that the Taliban, which seized power five years ago, has provided no information on the whereabouts of the leadership team of the nongovernmental group Women and Children Legal Research Foundation (WCLRF), who were arrested in Kabul on July 18.
Taliban security forces on June 21 raided the office of the NGO, which delivers assistance programs and conducts research and advocacy on women's and children’s rights, and confiscated laptops and phones from staff members.
They later sealed the office and launched an investigation against the staff members.
HRW said that on July 18 Taliban officials ordered six male staff members to return to the office to collect their confiscated devices. Instead, all six were taken into custody.
“The Taliban seems to consider any effort to assist women and girls a threat to their abusive rule,” HRW’s Women's Rights Director Macarena Saez said in a statement.
“They should immediately provide information on the six staff members’ whereabouts and release them if held unlawfully.”
Two UN Staffers Detained
Separately, the United Nations confirmed the detention of two of its staffers earlier this week, saying it has not been informed of any charges, nor has it been granted access to the two detained aid workers. The UN's political mission in Afghanistan, UNAMA, is involved in human rights monitoring and data gathering.
While seizing Kabul on August 15, 2021, the Taliban pledged, among other things, that "women will be very active in society," though a clause adding "within the framework of Islam" brought some skepticism regarding how strictly or restrictively that framework would be interpreted.
Since then, the Taliban have sharply curbed women's rights, including banning them from most jobs and public appearances. Some 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan are barred from attending secondary school, according to the United Nations cultural agency UNESCO.
Afghanistan is the only country in the world to ban females from attending secondary schools and universities, leading to what the UN has called “gender apartheid.”
Quoting Zarqa Yaftali, director of the WCLRF, said the families of the staff members who disappeared are “living in constant fear and uncertainty.”
The Taliban has also tightened the noose around independent media and journalists’ rights organizations since seizing Kabul five years ago.
Nai Supporting Open Media in Afghanistan (Nai SOMA), a journalists’ rights body, says the Taliban have converted Afghanistan into an open prison for media and freedom of expression.
In its report encompassing the five-year Taliban rule, the organization says at least six journalists have been killed in incidents of violence relating to members of the Islamic State militant group and the Taliban.
Sidiqullah Tawhidi, a senior Nai SOMA official, told RFERL’s Azadi Radio that 700 incidents of violence against journalists were registered in the past five years.
The Taliban has also revoked the licenses of several media outlets in Kabul and other provinces over the past five years accusing them of “unprofessional” journalism.

Eurovision music contest will take place in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas next year

Eurovision music contest will take place in Bulgaria’s Black Sea city of Burgas next year
SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Next year’s Eurovision Song Contest will take place in Burgas, a port city on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, organizers said Thursday.
It’s the first time the music extravaganza is held in the Balkan country, which scored its first-ever victory in the contest in May, when Bulgarian singer Dara beat 24 other competitors with her infectious party anthem “Bangaranga.”
Bulgaria’s public TV broadcaster BNT, which will organize the largest live music event, and the European Broadcasting Union announced the location on Thursday. The two semifinals will take place on May 11 and 13, 2027, while the final will be held on May 15.
Bulgaria’s capital city, Sofia, also had applied to host the event.
Eurovision director Martin Green said “Burgas will bring something truly special to Eurovision.”
“It is a dynamic and welcoming city on the Black Sea coast with a strong musical and cultural identity, which possesses the ambition, infrastructure, and passion needed to welcome the big Eurovision family,” he said in a statement.
Milena Milotinova, head of BNT, told a news conference that together with the EBU and Burgas they “will face intensive joint work to organize a contest that will live up to the high expectations of millions of viewers around the world.”
Burgas Mayor Dimitar Nikolov said hosting the contest was a major honor for the city.
On Wednesday, Eurovision organizers introduced new rules barring countries affected by an armed conflict or other security risks from hosting the contest. Under the new rules, the winning broadcaster will be ineligible to host if an armed conflict, sensitive geopolitical situation or other circumstances threaten the security, safety or stability of the country or surrounding region.
The contest has faced security concerns in recent years as tensions rose over the participation of Israel over its conflicts in Gaza and elsewhere. Five longtime participants — Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia — boycotted in protest.
The new rules also raised the minimum age for competitors from 16 to 18. Organizers say the change aims to boost safeguarding and protection of younger artists from the pressures associated with competing.

Trump’s vaccine plan would require millions of individual shots last used decades ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:53:02 UTC
19:53:02 KST

Trump’s vaccine plan would require millions of individual shots last used decades ago
WASHINGTON (AP) — Public health experts have been quick to condemn an executive order from President Donald Trump aimed at upending childhood vaccinations in the U.S., but the biggest obstacles may be the unprecedented financial and logistical challenges it would impose on parents, health providers and drugmakers.
Monday’s announcement by the Republican president calls for separating combination shots — including the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine — into separate injections. Appointments for that and other vaccinations should be spaced out whenever possible, the order states.
To accomplish that, drugmakers would need to revive a slate of individual vaccines that have not been widely used in the U.S. for decades. They would also have to build new manufacturing plants capable of producing millions more vaccine doses than the nation currently uses.
For parents, unbundling the MMR vaccine and spacing out the shots would mean returning to the doctor’s office many more times than is currently needed. Those appointments could also strain pediatricians who typically administer the shots, while driving up costs tied to syringes and other medical supplies.
Studies in the U.S. and other countries have shown that combination vaccines increase the likelihood that children will be fully protected from infectious diseases before starting school.
Health experts say there is no scientific basis for changing course.
“We do things that are less convenient and more expensive if there’s a good reason to do it,” said Dr. Anna Durbin, of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “There is no good justification for this. I think it’s very bad public health policy.”
Trump’s plan would require vaccine manufacturing overhaul
Under Trump’s executive order, federal officials are instructed to develop within 90 days plans for breaking up the MMR shot and spacing out other vaccines.
But pharmaceutical scientists and former regulators say those changes would likely take years and require drugmakers to spend tens of millions of dollars on new studies and manufacturing facilities.
Currently, there are no individual vaccines in the U.S. for measles, mumps or rubella. All the vaccines approved for those viruses by the Food and Drug Administration are combination shots. That three-in-one approach has been the standard in the U.S. since the 1970s.
Dr. Jesse Goodman, a former FDA vaccine chief, said companies would have to conduct large studies showing new individual shots produced immune system-boosting reactions in children similar to the current versions.
Companies might also have to demonstrate the safety of new manufacturing facilities and procedures, given that individual measles shots haven’t been widely produced in the U.S. for roughly a half-century.
“The question is how much has changed since then and how comfortable will the FDA and the companies be relying on those comparisons?” said Goodman, who is now a professor at Georgetown University.
Designing, constructing and getting federal sign-off for new vaccine plants typically takes about five years, according to industry experts.
Additionally, Goodman said the FDA would have to review and license each unbundled vaccine separately, a process with no precedent.
“I don’t think there’s any comparable example of removing hugely effective public health measures that protect babies for no documented scientific reason,” he said.
Individual shots for measles and related diseases tend to be used by lower-income countries that can’t afford the MMR shot. Merck, GSK and the handful of other companies that supply U.S. childhood vaccines make only the combination shot.
In separate statements, Merck and GSK said they stand by the safety and effectiveness of their products. Neither discussed plans to unbundle their shots.
“To date, there has been no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots,” Merck said in an emailed statement.
Parents would need to make many more trips to the doctor
The MMR shot is currently delivered in two doses — the first at the age of 1 and the second dose after age 4. Splitting up the shot into its three separate components would mean six office visits. Spacing out other shots for pertussis and other infectious diseases could multiply the number of visits many more times.
As the number of visits goes up, parents are more likely to miss appointments or stop making them, according to Durbin.
“It’s going to be less convenient, more expensive and you’re going to have fewer people getting vaccinated,” she said.
For well over a decade, Trump has expressed his view — against medical groups’ guidance — that childhood vaccines should be administered in smaller doses over a long period of time. Last year he called on called on Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to look at reducing the number. Kennedy and other officials have pointed to smaller countries, such as Denmark, that recommended slightly fewer vaccinations than the U.S.
But breaking up combination shots will result in kids receiving many more individual shots than other comparable nations, Durbin notes.
White House spokesman Kush Desai said the Trump administration’s efforts on the MMR vaccine “will give parents more options on timing and frequency for their children, which ultimately will increase vaccination rates for all three diseases.”
Vaccine order is not legally binding
Despite the precedent-breaking nature of Trump’s order, some experts are skeptical it will result in meaningful changes.
Neither the White House nor the FDA can compel drugmakers to develop and seek approval for new vaccines. And from a business perspective, companies have little incentive to develop individual versions of vaccines they already sell in combination shots.
“They’d be competing against themselves, and there’s no reason to do that,” said Dr. Paul Offit, a Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia vaccine researcher and former government adviser.
While Trump’s order calls for more federal research and recommendations, only state governments have the legal authority to require vaccinations for schoolchildren. The order simply advises states to consider updating their laws to reflect the Trump administration’s approach.
“I think states will ignore this,” Offit said. “I think that bottom line is that we don’t need to look to Donald Trump for our medical advice.”

Tropical Storm Lala forms in the Pacific and hurricane watch is issued for the Big Island of Hawaii
HONOLULU (AP) — Tropical Storm Lala formed Thursday in the Pacific Ocean and a hurricane watch has been issued for the Big Island of Hawaii, where it could bring heavy rain and flooding this weekend, forecasters said.
The storm is forecast to bring rain to the Hawaiian Islands starting late Friday as well as high winds and dangerous surf, the National Hurricane Center said.
Lala was about 700 miles (1,127 kilometers) east-southeast of Hawaii with maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (64 kph), the Miami-based center said. It’s moving west.
Strengthening is forecast, and Lala could be near hurricane strength as it approaches the Big Island. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible, and it is typically issued 48 hours ahead of potential tropical-storm-force winds.
The system could bring rainfall totals of 5 to 10 inches (13 to 25 centimeters) in the island chain, with up to 20 inches (51 centimeters) possible, forecasters said. That could produce flooding and mudslides, the center said.
Also in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Hernan formed Thursday but that storm wasn’t threatening land.
Hernan was about 1,460 miles (2,350 kilometers) west of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico, the center said. Maximum sustained winds were around 45 mph (72 kph) and it was moving west-southwest.
In the Atlantic Ocean, former Tropical Storm Cristobal weakened and degenerated into a post-tropical remnant low on Thursday, the center said. It was about 500 miles (805 kilometers) west of the Azores and didn’t threaten land.

Iran-backed Houthis clash with Yemeni forces and other Mideast developments
Clashes between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and government forces in Yemen raged overnight and into Thursday, raising fears that the country’s civil war could reignite and open another front in the Middle East.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Yemeni soldier killed in clashes with Houthis
At least one government soldier was killed and another critically wounded in clashes with the Houthis in the mountainous province of Taiz, Yemeni military officials told The Associated Press.
The fighting came as part of a spate of recent Houthi attacks on government-held areas across the country. Dozens of government troops have been killed since last week, the Yemeni military said.

Yemen faces “catastrophe” from rising hunger and from health services crumbling amid the fighting, said U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher. He said 6 million people in Yemen face emergency levels of food insecurity bordering on famine, “the highest number globally.”
Iran and Oman working to clean oil spills off their coasts
Oil spills spreading off the coasts of Iran and Oman are raising concerns about environmental damage as oil shipments have come under fire in the Iran war.
Iran said Thursday it’s working to clean up an oil spill off Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Images distributed by Iran’s semiofficial news agency ISNA showed oil fouling the island’s beaches.
While Iran hasn’t said what caused the spill, the firm TankerTrackers.com says it appears to have started with an Iranian attack on a bulk carrier off Oman. Iran has repeatedly attacked shipping in the strait since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
Oman is responding to another spill in the Arabian Sea, coming from a tanker grounded off its southern coast. The tanker Caroline Bezengi — a sanctioned vessel believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” — has been grounded since reporting an explosion in June. No party has claimed responsibility and the cause is unknown.
A British maritime risk and response company said Thursday it has been hired to salvage the tanker and stop the oil leak off Oman. Oil from the ship has been spreading for weeks, reaching shores hundreds of kilometers (miles) north of the vessel.
Israeli strikes kill 2, including a police chief, in Gaza
Israeli strikes killed at least two people in the Gaza Strip on Thursday and wounded several others, health officials said.
Jamal Abu Kamil, a Gaza governorate police chief, was killed when his vehicle was struck southwest of Gaza City, according to the territory’s interior ministry and Shifa Hospital, where his body was taken along with a person wounded by the same strike.
The Israeli military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about that strike.
A separate Israeli strike killed a man and injured another person in Khan Younis, according to Nasser Hospital, where both were taken.
The Israeli military said it struck a Hamas company commander in Khan Younis who “planned to execute terror attacks” against troops.
American ambassador to Israel condemns settlers’ siege of Palestinian homes
The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned a siege by Israeli settlers of a Palestinian-American family’s home in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, calling it a “horrific act of terror.”
Mike Huckabee’s remarks on X represented an unusually sharp rebuke from the Trump administration as settler violence against Palestinians has surged in recent years.
Starting Sunday, settlers targeted three homes in the village of Qusra, preventing occupants from leaving despite dwindling supplies.
Qusai Abu Rida was holed up inside with his teenage son when settlers cut the water and electricity, leaving them to drink well water as dozens of Israeli settlers erected tents outside. His Palestinian American brother in Ohio, who owns the house, watched the siege unfold on security cameras and called for updates.
Israeli troops have intervened multiple times, but the settlers keep returning, said Loui Ridi, the homeowner in Ohio.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli settlers and members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Cabinet on Thursday celebrated Israel’s return to Ganim with a ceremony in front of new homes.
Ganim was evacuated in 2005 as Israel withdrew from settlements in Gaza and parts of the West Bank. Last year, Netanyahu’s Cabinet approved the return of settlers to Ganim and another former settlement near the Palestinian city of Jenin.
“The era of withdrawals and expulsions has ended,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said. “The era of construction and Zionism begins.”

SBU uncovers Russian spies gathering intelligence on F-16 and Mirage jets at Ukrainian airfields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

SBU uncovers Russian spies gathering intelligence on F-16 and Mirage jets at Ukrainian airfields
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
"The SBU's military counterintelligence, under the personal coordination of SBU chief Oleksandr Poklad, has neutralized a large-scale agent network of Russian military intelligence, better known as the GRU, through which the enemy could have carried out missile strikes on Ukrainian Armed Forces air bases," the statement said.
The investigation found that the suspects' activities enabled Russian forces to plan and conduct attacks on airfields hosting F-16 and Mirage 2000 aircraft.
According to the case materials, the Russian-recruited group consisted of 14 people living in different regions of Ukraine.
Investigators established that the Russian GRU initially recruited a resident of Lviv who administered a Telegram channel about aviation. He attracted the Russians' attention after posting photographs of Ukrainian Armed Forces fighter jets in pro-Kremlin chats.
To carry out the assignments, the agent recruited 13 of his subscribers "in the dark" – people who owned high-quality cameras and lived near the Ukrainian Defense Forces' aviation infrastructure. They were instructed to photograph Ukrainian airfields, military aircraft, their crews and technical personnel, as well as record the time intervals between aircraft takeoffs and landings, allegedly for the Lviv blogger's Telegram channel, the SBU said.
The suspects used professional cameras and concealed themselves in abandoned buildings or in open areas near air bases while taking the photographs.
The images were stored in an online repository to which the agent had provided them with access in advance. He then forwarded the photographic material to a Russian handler, whose identity has already been established by the SBU.
The agent also passed the Russians schedules for military helicopter takeoffs and landings. He obtained this intelligence from a Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation squadron commander who provided the information on his own initiative.
During searches of the suspects' homes, investigators found smartphones and digital photography equipment containing evidence of their work for Russia, as well as photographs of Ukrainian forces' aviation facilities.
In addition, SBU officers blocked four Telegram channels and ten thematic groups where photographs and other information about Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation units were being distributed.
Investigators served the detained agent, his accomplice and the military officer with notices of suspicion of crimes against the foundations of Ukraine's national security.
The investigation is ongoing to bring all those responsible to justice.

From regional to international: The birth and evolution of Call of Polesie festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

An archive photo
                    
                    GOMEL, 13 August (BelTA) – The Call of Polesie festival has steadily gained momentum over the years and has now reached an international scale, BelTA has learned.
The Gomel Oblast Center of Folk Art has traced the origins and evolution of Call of Polesie festival.
Its roots lie in the very heart of the Pripyatsky National Park – the agrotown of Lyaskovichi. The event was conceived to introduce thousands of people to the unique culture and traditions of the Poleshuks (the inhabitants of the historic Polesie region), featuring ancient holidays and rituals, songs and dances, legends and folklore, as well as the exceptional skill of artisans and arts and crafts masters.
A decision of major regional significance to organize the festival was made right there in Polesie, by a sturdy, centuries-old oak tree. The head of state greenlit the birth of a new tradition – the Call of Polesie festival of ethnocultural traditions. Soon it became clear that the decision made by the president at the time served as the very foundation for creating such centers of attraction. Call of Polesie rapidly gained momentum, evolving into a large-scale festival now widely known far beyond the region and the country.
The first open festival of ethnocultural traditions Call of Polesie took place in 2010. It became a trademark event, showcasing the region’s ethnocultural traditions on a grand scale, while also helping to strengthen creative ties among the people of Polesie across Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine. Judging by the immense interest it garnered, it was already clear back then that the brand had a bright future, and the fest would become a new driver for the development of cultural, historical, ethnographic, and ecological tourism.
That was when the tradition was born: creative groups, artisans, and arts and crafts masters set up traditional homesteads in Lyaskovichi to showcase their land. They represented eight districts of Gomel Oblast (Yelsk, Zhitkovichi, Kalinkovichi, Lelchitsy, Mozyr, Narovlya, Petrikov, and Khoiniki), three districts of Brest Oblast (Luninets, Pinsk, and Stolin), and the team from the Pripyatsky National Park. Visitors could also sample regional Poleshuk cuisine. These locations became the main Polesie trademark and have remained the highlight of the event for many years.
Back then, the lumberjack competition featuring contestants from the Polesie districts sparked great interest among the spectators. Fishing competitions were also held for both adults and youth. Visitors thoroughly enjoyed carriage rides along the waterfront, as well as boat and cruise ship excursions down the Pripyat River. Meanwhile, a mini-train proved to be a popular way for both children and adults to tour the agrotown of Lyaskovichi.
In 2010, the Call of Polesie festival welcomed more than 500 performers and keepers of Belarusian folk culture, around 100 artisans and arts and crafts masters, and hundreds of honored guests from Belarus, neighboring countries, and further abroad.
The Call of Polesie festival gained such momentum that it was granted national status as early as 2012, with a schedule established to hold the event once every two years.

The head of state greenlit the birth of a new tradition – the Call of Polesie festival of ethnocultural traditions. Soon it became clear that the decision made by the president at the time served as the very foundation for creating such centers of attraction. Call of Polesie rapidly gained momentum, evolving into a large-scale festival now widely known far beyond the region and the country.
The first open festival of ethnocultural traditions Call of Polesie took place in 2010. It became a trademark event, showcasing the region’s ethnocultural traditions on a grand scale, while also helping to strengthen creative ties among the people of Polesie across Belarus, Russia, and Ukraine. Judging by the immense interest it garnered, it was already clear back then that the brand had a bright future, and the fest would become a new driver for the development of cultural, historical, ethnographic, and ecological tourism.
That was when the tradition was born: creative groups, artisans, and arts and crafts masters set up traditional homesteads in Lyaskovichi to showcase their land. They represented eight districts of Gomel Oblast (Yelsk, Zhitkovichi, Kalinkovichi, Lelchitsy, Mozyr, Narovlya, Petrikov, and Khoiniki), three districts of Brest Oblast (Luninets, Pinsk, and Stolin), and the team from the Pripyatsky National Park. Visitors could also sample regional Poleshuk cuisine. These locations became the main Polesie trademark and have remained the highlight of the event for many years.
Back then, the lumberjack competition featuring contestants from the Polesie districts sparked great interest among the spectators. Fishing competitions were also held for both adults and youth. Visitors thoroughly enjoyed carriage rides along the waterfront, as well as boat and cruise ship excursions down the Pripyat River. Meanwhile, a mini-train proved to be a popular way for both children and adults to tour the agrotown of Lyaskovichi.
In 2010, the Call of Polesie festival welcomed more than 500 performers and keepers of Belarusian folk culture, around 100 artisans and arts and crafts masters, and hundreds of honored guests from Belarus, neighboring countries, and further abroad.
The Call of Polesie festival gained such momentum that it was granted national status as early as 2012, with a schedule established to hold the event once every two years.
The president arrived in Polesie for the opening of the celebration. It was then that the head of state spoke the words that would define the festival’s future: “This is a colorful rural holiday that will live on for centuries.” Aleksandr Lukashenko proposed upgrading the festival to international status.
 
Year after year, interest in the festival events grew noticeably. By the second Call of Polesie, an international scientific and practical conference Traditional Culture of Polesie and the Modern World was held with the participation of scholars from Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Poland. For the first time, an exhibition of works by artists from Gomel and Gomel Oblast, a mini open-air painting session, and performances by poets and writers from the region, among other events, took place on the banks of the Pripyat for festival guests and participants. People of all ages took part in the second edition; the youngest participant was 6 years old, the oldest was 85.
A new feature of the 2012 festival was the official opening of the Nature Museum, which was visited by the head of state.
The third edition of the Call of Polesie was held in 2014, now with international status. For the first time, an art plein air, Land Under White Wings, featured artists from Gomel and Brest. An ethnographic camp, Summer Camp in Petrikov District, presented a program that included expeditionary work to collect folklore material from local tradition bearers, workshops, and a round table on the region’s traditional folk culture.
For the first time, the central concert venue hosted the award ceremony for the Honorary Poleshuk commemorative badge, which is still presented to distinguished residents of Polesie, as well as the ceremonial cancellation of a special postage stamp, during the opening of the 3rd International Festival. A new festival tradition was the Paleskaya Prygazhunya [Polesie Beauty] beauty contest.
The festival stage featured performances by groups from Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, Poland, and Moldova. Later, artists from Lithuania and Latvia also joined the Call of Polesie.
In 2016 and 2018, Polesie revealed itself ever more brightly and broadly. Every year, the Call of Polesie resonates in the hearts of tens of thousands of admirers of authentic, original folk culture.
The 6th International Festival of Ethnocultural Traditions, Call of Polesie, took place on 29 August 2020. The unique culture of Belarusians was showcased through homestead displays, exhibitions, workshops, and concerts. The main festival venue was upgraded and visitors could explore the open-air historical and ethnographic complex, Museum Under the Open Sky. The season’s concept was dedicated to the Year of Native Land, featuring the region’s ethnic mythology and revealing the Secrets of the Poleshuks. For the first time, diplomats from Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Iran, Lithuania, Pakistan, Palestine, Russia, Sudan, and Uzbekistan were among the festival’s guests. On the eve of the event, during the Trade Advisor Day, they explored the potential of Pripyat Polesie at the Mozyr Economic Forum.
Tens of thousands of guests responded to the Call of Polesie in 2022 and 2024. Each festival season remained in people’s hearts for a long time.
On 15 August, the Call of Polesie gathers friends for the 9th time. In the Year of the Belarusian Woman, the festival is dedicated to the theme of the female image. Its leitmotif is The Female Voice of Polesie: A Living Heritage. The large-scale celebration will take place over an area of more than nine hectares. Two concert venues will be used - the main stage and a smaller stage. The festival will feature 13 hospitable homesteads, which will introduce guests to the authentic creativity and culinary heritage of eight districts of Gomel Oblast, four districts, and Pinsk of Brest Oblast. Each homestead will present vivid female images, both historical and contemporary.

Putin's Kuril Islands visit does little to normalize bilateral relations — Japanese PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:52:23 UTC
19:52:23 KST

TOKYO, August 13. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to Iturup has hindered the normalization of relations between Moscow and Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters.
According to her, the trip "has complicated the medium- and long-term restoration of relations." "We would like the Russian side to fully appreciate the seriousness of this matter," she said. Takaichi noted that since Putin announced in January 2024 that he planned to visit the "Northern Territories," as Tokyo calls the southern part of the Kuril Islands, including Iturup, Japan had "urged the Russian side not to make this trip."
"We strongly protest this," she said. Takaichi stressed that all the "Northern Territories," including Iturup, are "inherent [Japanese] territory from historical and legal perspectives." The Japanese prime minister also said that Putin's visit to the Kuril Islands "completely runs counter to Japan's position" and that it had "hurt the feelings of the Japanese people."
Japan's Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador to Tokyo Nikolay Nozdrev over Putin's visit to Iturup, Kyodo reported.
The Russian Embassy in Tokyo told TASS that it would issue an official comment on the matter later.
Since the middle of the last century, Moscow and Tokyo have held talks aimed at drafting a peace agreement following World War II. The main obstacle remains their differences over sovereignty of the southern Kuril Islands. Following the war, the entire archipelago became part of the Soviet Union, but Japan disputes Russia's sovereignty over Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and a group of small uninhabited islands. The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly stressed that Russia's sovereignty over these territories, which has been formalized under international law, is beyond doubt.

EU budget: Sweden, part of the 'frugal' camp, is about to turn even more hawkish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:50:37 UTC
19:50:37 KST

Sweden is part of the EU's so-called "frugal" bloc, alongside Germany and the Netherlands - net contributors pushing to rein in the bloc's next long-term budget and limit the cost for national taxpayers. But a shift to the left in Stockholm is unlikely to soften its position.
The leader of Sweden's Social Democratic Party, Magdalena Andersson, is set to become the country's next prime minister. But her centre-left credentials won't make her any less of a "frugal" hardliner in the upcoming EU budget negotiations.
The Swedish Social Democratic Party (S) is on course to win the 13 September election, currently polling at 32%, well ahead of the national-conservative Sweden Democrats on 20% and the centre-right Moderate Party of current Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson on 17%, according to the latest data.
That would make Sweden one of the few EU countries turning towards a progressive government, as centre-left executives now remain only in Spain, Denmark and Malta, with electoral trends elsewhere in Europe generally favouring the radical right.
But anyone expecting Stockholm's next government to soften its stance in the EU's sensitive long-term budget talks will be disappointed, as Andersson's administration is shaping up to be even more hawkish than the current one.
"The next Swedish government is likely to be much tougher," a Swedish official told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to comment publicly. "During the parliamentary hearings they always ask why the current government is not doing more to oppose the budget proposal."
Sweden belongs to the so-called "frugal" bloc, alongside Germany and the Netherlands — net contributors that pay far more into the EU budget than they get back.
Stockholm has been particularly hostile to the scale of the European Commission's €2 trillion proposal, even in the reduced form put forward by the Cypriot presidency, and is pushing to keep the overall budget down to limit the impact on Swedish taxpayers.
Swedish officials estimate the Commission's original proposal would increase the country's contribution by around 60%, just as public finances are already strained by surging defence spending and military aid to Ukraine.
At a March hearing of the Committee on EU Affairs, Social Democrat MP Matilda Ernkrans said the current government had depleted the country's finances, severely limiting the scope for reform in the next mandate.
"Against this background, an increase in the EU fee of the magnitude now being discussed is completely unacceptable," she said, pointing in particular to the need to maintain the so-called rebate: a discount Sweden secured in the previous budget negotiations.
Andersson served as Sweden's finance minister from 2014 to 2021 — spanning the negotiations of the previous seven-year budget — when she personally secured an annual rebate of more than €1bn, one she now appears determined to preserve.
"The Social Democrats are focused on domestic policies and do not want to sacrifice their social agenda to Brussels," the Swedish official said, adding that some form of rebate will likely be necessary to reach a final agreement.
This push to shrink the EU budget in order to protect fiscal space for domestic social policy puts Sweden's Social Democrats at odds with their centre-left peers in the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group in the European Parliament, where they are regularly sidelined in budget discussions.
The S&D has also backed extending common borrowing at EU level, following the model of NextGenerationEU, Europe's post-pandemic recovery fund. Andersson, by contrast, initially opposed the scheme while in office, even though her government ultimately signed up to it.
On EU-level debt more broadly, her position has shifted: she has backed joint borrowing to build up Europe's defence and support Ukraine militarily, arguing "this needs to happen at a furious pace and all countries must do it, even those with worse economic conditions," as she said in 2025.
Still, Stockholm is set to remain wary of EU-level borrowing, since the interest rates involved are higher than Sweden's own borrowing costs — making it economically unattractive.
"Sweden has long adhered to the mantra of being 'the most frugal in Europe'. This negotiating position yielded particularly good results in the negotiations on the EU's joint pandemic recovery fund," reads an S-sponsored report on the EU budget.
"Sweden succeeded in limiting the level of grants to member states, securing a Swedish rebate of around 11 billion Swedish krona per year and establishing a conditionality mechanism based on the principles of the rule of law," the report continues.
Finally, the future Swedish government is unlikely to shift the country's sceptical stance towards EU "own resources" — Europe-wide taxes to directly finance Brussels — with the report noting "there is a traditionally critical attitude on the part of Sweden towards the introduction of new own resources."
