Ukraine brings home 261 bodies in latest repatriation, as Russia claims the dead are Ukrainian soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:49:56 UTC
19:49:56 KST

The Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said the remains arrived on 13 August, and that investigators will now work to establish the identities.
Ukraine recovered the 261 bodies as part of repatriation measures carried out with Russia, the Coordination Headquarters reported. Russia claims the dead are Ukrainian servicemen, but law enforcement investigators and forensic experts will conduct the identification before any confirmation.
The return of the dead remains one of the few channels that still functions between Kyiv and Moscow during Russia's war against Ukraine. Each handover lets families of the missing bury their relatives, and it again relied on the International Committee of the Red Cross, which helped coordinate the exchange.
Ukraine's Interior Ministry, the Security Service of Ukraine, the Armed Forces, the Office of the Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, the State Emergency Service, and the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Missing Persons under Special Circumstances all took part, the Coordination Headquarters said. Units of the Armed Forces transported the remains and passed them to police and to medical examiners under the Health Ministry for identification.
Previous exchanges
The handover is the latest in a long series of transfers Russia has carried out during its war against Ukraine, and in each case it has claimed the dead were Ukrainian servicemen or citizens, an account Ukrainian forensic experts verify independently. The exchanges have followed the Istanbul agreements that Kyiv and Moscow reached on 2 June 2025. Over the course of that June, Russia returned 6,057 bodies, and on 17 July 2025 it handed over another 1,000. Further transfers of 1,000 followed on 19 August, 18 September, 23 October, and 20 November 2025, before Russia returned 1,003 bodies on 19 December. The exchanges continued into 2026 with 1,000 bodies on 26 February and another 1,000 on 9 April, after which the totals fell to 522 on 18 June and 501 on 16 July, ahead of the 261 returned on 13 August.
Taken together, the transfers have returned thousands of the dead since mid 2025, which makes the repatriation of remains one of the most consistent forms of contact that still survives between Kyiv and Moscow.

Expert urges people to keep expectations low in the garden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:49:00 UTC
19:49:00 KST

Expert urges people to keep expectations low in the garden
Eva Luigas says that she failed this year with growing zucchini and her outdoor cucumbers also struggled, but her tomatoes did very well.
Luigas said the most important thing in gardening is not putting too much pressure on yourself, because everything should be done with joy and curiosity.
"This year I failed at growing zucchini. I have three plant varieties that have produced only female flowers. So I have to go buy zucchini to make soup," said rural lifestyle journal Maakodu managing editor and gardening expert Eva Luigas. "My outdoor cucumbers also struggled this year."
Luigas said she took especially good care of her tomatoes. "I am very excited about the Estonian tomato variety 'Siive.' I sowed the seed on April 11, planted it outside in June, and on August 5 I got my first outdoor tomatoes without any covering," she said.
"The most important thing in gardening is not putting too much pressure on yourself. You cannot do everything anyway. Do not set demands too high. Everything should be done with joy and curiosity," the gardening expert said with a smirk.
In August, she said, you should collect your own seeds and look around to see who has good peas, cucumbers or tomatoes. Perennial beds should be tidied, and garlic should be lifted from the ground, otherwise the cloves will separate. "I even plan to prune apple trees a little," Luigas said. "Summer pruning is also done when you have made a hard cutback in spring."
Luigas also tidies garden edges in August. "At the beginning of August you start applying fall fertilizer. It is a very good time for planting and propagation, a good time to sow something edible again — lettuce, dill and radish. If you do not have free space, then sow for pre‑growing. Just put them in pots and later place them in free spots," Luigas advised.
Knowing a plant variety, she said, gives information about its different characteristics — growth, height, fruit and flower color, flowering and germination time. "It is not hard to keep the seed packets and write things down somewhere. Today you can take a picture with your phone right away," the expert said. "A gardener's life is full of excitement."

Meta 'systematically' suppresses Palestinian voices on Facebook, Instagram: study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:48:09 UTC
19:48:09 KST

Meta’s content moderation practices have systematically restricted Palestinian voices on Facebook and Instagram, according to a report by Palestinian digital rights group 7amleh and a researcher at Utrecht University.
The Platformicide of Palestine 2021-2025 examined 3,520 cases submitted to 7amleh’s Palestinian Observatory for Digital Rights Violations from January 2021 to December 2025.
The cases included account suspensions, post removals, restrictions on livestreaming and reduced content distribution.
The report uses the term “platformicide” to describe what it considers the structural erasure of Palestinian visibility and participation on social media.
While it does not conclude that Meta deliberately censored individual users, the report argues that the repeated restrictions cannot be explained solely as isolated technical or moderation errors.
Only 32.5 percent of the documented cases involved an identifiable policy violation.
Among cases where a reason was provided, Meta’s Dangerous Organisations and Individuals policy accounted for 57.2 percent of restrictions, a figure that rose to 71.1 percent in cases involving journalists.
Account suspension most common practice
The policy is intended to prevent support for terrorist and violent organisations, but the report argues that it has been applied too broadly to journalists, media organisations, activists and civil society groups covering Palestine and Israel’s war on Gaza.
Account suspensions were the most common enforcement measure, affecting about one-third of the documented cases.
The research also identified less visible restrictions, including reduced reach and recommendation filtering, which users commonly describe as “shadow banning.”
Nearly half of the 2,828 appeals submitted by 7amleh on behalf of affected users received no response from Meta, according to the report.
Meta has previously said it was working to improve the accuracy of Arabic-language moderation, route content to reviewers familiar with relevant Arabic dialects and provide users with clearer explanations of enforcement decisions.
The report calls on Meta to commission an independent human rights audit, reform its application of the Dangerous Organisations and Individuals policy and strengthen protections for journalistic and public-interest content.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US accuses Chinese exporters of masterminding ‘Great Transshipment Scam’
White House alleges that companies are systematically routing trade through third-party nations to evade US tariffs
The Trump administration on Thursday released a sharply worded report accusing Chinese exporters of orchestrating a system of “illegal transshipment” through more than 40 third countries to dodge US tariffs, branding the practice “The Great Transshipment Scam”.
It alleges that exporters use limited assembly, relabelling, repackaging, re-invoicing and false country-of-origin declarations to disguise Chinese-origin products and secure more favourable tariff treatment on entry into the US.
The White House report says that Chinese exporters have “increasingly routed goods through third countries … where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabelling or documentation changes could create the appearance of a different national origin.”

Turkey lays out plans for defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:45:09 UTC

Turkey lays out plans for defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia
- Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement to strengthen military cooperation and treat an attack on one as an attack on all.
- The pact includes plans for senior minister meetings, joint military exercises, and deeper defence industry collaboration focusing on advanced technologies.
- Turkey aims to expand the alliance, possibly including Egypt, and is also involved in forming a coalition to protect Red Sea shipping.
AI generated
ANKARA – Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will group senior ministers, hold joint exercises and deepen defence industry cooperation under a military pact signed between the regional powers last week, Turkey’s defence ministry said on Aug 13.
The three Sunni Muslim US allies, alarmed by a regional conflagration that has brought Iranian missile fire onto Gulf oil exporters, signed the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement” on Aug 7.
They said the accord stipulates that an armed attack against any member would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO’s Article 5 collective defence clause.
At a weekly briefing in Ankara, the defence ministry said the pact’s fundamental goal was to ensure defence and military ties were put on a “more institutional and sustainable” footing.
“Under the accord, strategic political and military mechanisms plan to be established involving the Defence Ministers, Foreign Ministers, and Chiefs of General Staff/Armed Forces Commanders, and that coordination among the three countries will be conducted at the highest level,” it said.
The ministry added that joint military exercises involving land, naval, and air forces, as well as air defence and unmanned systems were planned, in addition to deeper defence industry cooperation.
“The aim is to provide not only product and system supply, but also joint development and production, technology cooperation, and sustainable maintenance and logistics support,” it said, adding that unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence capabilities would be prioritised.
Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion – with Egypt as a potential candidate – and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
The ministry also said Turkey was participating in meetings in Jeddah aimed at establishing an international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping. REUTERS

Sudanese paramilitaries renew assault – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Sudanese paramilitaries renew assault – Reuters
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have renewed their assault on the strategically important city of El Obeid, while drone strikes have been reported in several parts of the country, including the capital region, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing witnesses and local sources.
Eight drones targeted El Obeid, prompting the Sudanese military to activate its air defenses, according to the news agency. Medical sources cited by Reuters said two people were killed and several others wounded.
Drone attacks were also reported in Khartoum, Bahri, Atbara, and other locations, with witnesses saying one UAV crashed into the courtyard of a mosque in Bahri. The report said neither the RSF nor the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had immediately claimed responsibility for the strikes.
El Obeid has become a key flashpoint in the battle for Sudan’s Kordofan region. The city is home to roughly half a million people, including around 100,000 displaced by the conflict, according to Reuters.
The latest escalation is part of Sudan’s ongoing civil war between the SAF and RSF, which erupted in April 2023.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The aerial campaign continued on Thursday, with Sudan Tribune reporting a second consecutive day of drone attacks on the Khartoum area. Military sources told the outlet that air defenses intercepted multiple UAVs over northern and western Omdurman, while residents reported explosions as low-flying drones approached the city.
Fighting has also intensified hundreds of kilometers to the southeast in Sudan’s Blue Nile region. RSF forces and their allies from the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) launched an assault on the border town of Geisan this week, triggering clashes with the Sudanese army.
The latest fighting follows a series of battlefield gains by the SAF. The Sudanese army recently recaptured Kurmuk in Blue Nile state and, in late July, regained several areas in North Kordofan from the RSF, including Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh, and Um Sayala. Army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan subsequently visited frontline positions in the region.

Water levels fall to record lows in Switzerland amid drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:44:46 UTC
19:44:46 KST

Burak Bir
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
Rivers and streams across Switzerland have fallen to exceptionally low levels as an drought grips the country, according to media reports on Thursday.
The ongoing drought has caused water levels across Switzerland to fall to record lows, with the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) registering historic lows at 11 monitoring stations, news outlet Swiss Info reported, citing the Keystone-SDA news agency.
The FOEN said that between April 1 and July 31, around a fifth of monitoring stations saw their lowest water levels on record for this time of year.
Water levels in many watercourses north of the Alps are so low that such levels occur only once every two to 10 years, and in some cases only once every 30 to 100 years or even less frequently, according to the FOEN.
Along with rivers and streams, lakes are also being affected by the heat wave and drought, with water levels exceptionally low, in Lake Constance, Lake Walen, Lake Zurich, Lake Zug and Lake Maggiore.
Switzerland still has "abundant water resources," the FOEN said, but warned that climate change will alter their availability.

Italian Embassy Guide on the Rights and Duties of Foreign Workers in Iceland
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
12:44:10 CEST
19:44:10 KST

The new digital guide published by the Italian Embassy in Norway and Iceland, titled “Rights and Duties of Foreign Workers in Iceland,” aims to clearly and systematically outline the steps Italian workers must take to fully integrate into the Icelandic labor market. This was announced by the Italian Embassy in Norway and Iceland. 
   The publication addresses the main aspects of the Icelandic labor system, including collective bargaining agreements and minimum wages, vacation time and pay, sick leave, working hours and overtime pay, types of employment contracts, procedures for posted workers and non-EEA citizens, the tax system, and the relevant authorities to contact in case of need.
                                    
                                       
				   Particular attention, the embassy explains, is given to the procedures required to work legally in the country, including obtaining a kennitala (the Icelandic national identification number) and, where required, a residence and work permit.
                                    
                                       
				   The initiative stems from a growing trend: according to the Registry of Italians Residing Abroad (AIRE), nearly a thousand Italian citizens are registered in Iceland, in a context where the Icelandic labor market—characterized by high wages, one of the highest unionization rates in the world, and collective bargaining coverage extending to approximately 90% of workers—offers 
concrete opportunities, particularly in the tourism, construction, and healthcare sectors.
                                    
                                       
				The ebook can be accessed in digital format on the embassy’s webpage dedicated to thematic guides.

Russian drone strikes passenger train in Odesa region, killing driver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:43:26 UTC
19:43:26 KST

Footage filmed in Ukraine’s Odesa region on Thursday 13 August 2026 by the national emergency services shows a severely damaged passenger train locomotive, as firefighters extinguish the flames. A nearby carriage has shattered windows, while passengers board evacuation buses with their luggage.
A Russian jet-powered Shahed drone struck the locomotive of the Odesa-Dnipro passenger train in the Berezivka district on Thursday morning, killing the driver and his assistant, Ukrzaliznytsia chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said. A monitoring team had detected the drone and ordered the train to stop near a station, but the drone's sudden manoeuvre left the crew too little time to evacuate after stopping the train. All 340 passengers were evacuated safely and taken to Odesa by 21 buses.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the operator could not have been unaware the train carried civilians and renewed calls for stronger air defences. Russia launched 133 drones at Ukraine overnight, with 111 intercepted, the air force said, as strikes also wounded six people elsewhere in the country.

Eurovision to bar countries at war from hosting: What that means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:41:47 UTC
19:41:47 KST

Eurovision to bar countries at war from hosting: What that means
Israel, which hosted the contest in 2019, will no longer be allowed to do so – but can still compete, protesters say.
The organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have announced that any country involved in an “armed conflict” or “sensitive geopolitical situation” will no longer be allowed to host the annual tournament.
The announcement on Wednesday by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises Eurovision, comes as Russia’s war on Ukraine and Israel’s war on Iran, genocide in Gaza, occupation of Lebanon and raids and arrests in the occupied West Bank continue.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli minister blasts Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal for Palestinian flag wave
- list 2 of 3Eurovision braces for new protests over Israel’s participation
- list 3 of 3Where did Eurovision go wrong?
While Russia was barred from competing in the contest at all in February 2022 over its invasion of Ukraine, Israel was permitted to continue both hosting and competing despite multiple protests and the boycotting of the contest by several countries last year.
Now, while Israel may not be able to host the event – which it did in 2019 as winner of the 2018 contest – it can still take part.
Here’s what we know about what this all means.
What is Eurovision?
The Eurovision Song Contest, which began in 1956, is an annual event co-produced by EBU and its member broadcasters, “most notably the public broadcaster of the preceding winning country, the Host Broadcaster”. Next year, Bulgaria, which won the 2026 contest in May, will host.
Ukraine won the contest in 2022 but was unable to host the following year amid the war with Russia.
Despite its name, the contest is open to any country which has broadcasting operations in Europe and is a member of the EBA. Israel was the first non-European country to participate in 1973.
What has Eurovision announced and why?
On Wednesday, EBU said that under new rules, “the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.”
If necessary, EBU said it will commission “an independent security assessment of the winner’s region” and hold consultations to decide if the winning country may still host.
If the winning country is not allowed to host, then the contest’s organisers will find an alternative host broadcaster.
The organisers of the contest have come under increasing pressure to exclude Israel from the contest since its genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023. Some participant countries refused to take part last year, and several protests have taken place.
It is, however, unclear if the change in the contest’s rules is due to the boycotts and Israel’s participation.
Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement on Wednesday: “The Eurovision Song Contest is constantly evolving, and our annual review of the rules is an important part of making sure the contest remains fair, transparent and consistent for all those who participate, including the millions who engage with the event globally.”
He noted that the rules are guided by feedback from EBU members.
“These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” he added.
Why have some countries boycotted Eurovision in recent years?
As soon as Israel’s participation in the 2026 contest was confirmed by EBU in December last year, several countries, politicians and artists began calling for a boycott of the contest.
On December 4, the Netherlands, Slovenia, Spain, Iceland and Ireland said they would boycott the contest if Israel took part.
Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS, representing the Netherlands, accused Israel of “proven interference” in the previous year’s contest while also noting its “serious violation of press freedom” during the Gaza war. It said “under the current circumstances, participation cannot be reconciled with the public values that are fundamental to our organisation.”
Ireland said it would not take part either, with its broadcaster RTE citing “the appalling loss of lives in Gaza and humanitarian crisis” as the reason for its boycott.
Slovenia’s national broadcaster said it would boycott participation “on behalf of the 20,000 children who died in Gaza”, while Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE also announced it would not participate.
“The situation in Gaza, despite the ceasefire and the approval of the peace process, and the use of the contest for political goals by Israel, make it increasingly difficult to keep Eurovision a neutral cultural event,” RTVE’s secretary-general, Alfonso Morales, said in a statement.
On December 10, Iceland’s broadcaster RUV said the Nordic nation would also not participate in the 2026 competition. “It is clear from the public debate in this country and the reaction to the EBU’s decision last week that there will be neither joy nor peace regarding RUV’s participation,” the broadcaster’s Director-General Stefan Eiriksson said in a statement.
Despite the boycotts, the contest took place in May this year, in Vienna, and 35 countries participated.
Has there been any response from countries affected?
Not from Israel, which last hosted the event in 2019. It came second place in the 2026 tournament and thus very close to hosting it again in 2027.
Last year, amid widespread protests over Israel’s confirmed participation in the contest, Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrote in a post on X on December 4: “Israel deserves to be represented on every stage around the world, a cause to which I am fully and actively committed.”
Russia is already barred from hosting or participating, and Ukraine would be unable to host the event even if it could.
Ukraine has never hosted Eurovision. In 2023, when it was meant to host the contest, the United Kingdom did so instead.
EBU told Al Jazeera: “The rules of the Eurovision song contest apply to all participating broadcasters and any assessment of the ability to host would be made much closer to the time of the event.”
Will countries that boycotted this year return?
There has been no response so far from Spain, the Netherlands, Slovenia or Ireland about the contest’s new rules.
However, given that they staged their 2026 boycott over Israel’s participation in the contest, not just whether it would be permitted to host, it seems unlikely they will change their stance.
Many critics have stressed that Israel’s participation in the contest signals EBU’s hypocrisy given its stance on Russia.
In an interview with Al Jazeera in May, Sven Kuhn von Burgsdorff, former European Union representative to the occupied West Bank and Gaza, said the actions of both Russia and Israel against Ukraine and the Palestinian people have been found to be in violation of international law and human rights.
“It would be only consequential to also suspend Israel’s participation in the Eurovision song contest as long as the country maintains its illegal occupation of Palestinian land, thereby not only suppressing Palestinian rights but also entrenching a regime with characteristics of segregation or apartheid, as ruled by the International Court of Justice (ICJ),” he said.
In April – one month before the contest final took place in Vienna – more than 1,000 musicians and people working in the cultural sector signed a letter calling on nations to boycott the contest and accused the EBU of hypocrisy over its refusal to allow Russia to take part because of its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“The EBU’s hypocritical responses to Russia’s and Israel’s crimes have removed any illusion of Eurovision’s claimed ‘neutrality’. In 2022, the EBU said that Russia’s presence would ‘bring the competition into disrepute’,” the letter stated.
“Yet more than 30 months of genocide in Gaza – alongside ethnic cleansing and land theft in the besieged West Bank – aren’t considered sufficient to apply the same policy to Israel.”

Bodies of 261 fallen returned to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:40:28 EEST
19:40:28 KST

The bodies of 261 fallen, said by the Russian side to be Ukrainian servicemembers, have been returned to Ukraine, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said.
"As a result of repatriation measures, the bodies of 261 fallen, which the Russian side claims belong to Ukrainian servicemembers, have been returned to Ukraine. Law enforcement investigators, together with representatives of expert institutions, will carry out all necessary measures to identify the repatriated dead," the Coordination Headquarters said on Telegram on Thursday.
The repatriation was carried out as a result of joint work by the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the Joint Center under the Security Service of Ukraine, the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Ukraine’s Interior Ministry, the Office of the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, the Secretariat of the Commissioner for Persons Missing under Special Circumstances, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service, and other Security and Defense Sector agencies, according to the statement.
"We express our sincere gratitude to the International Committee of the Red Cross for its assistance and support in carrying out the repatriation measures. Special thanks to the personnel of the Joint Center for Support of Central Military Medical Directorate Measures of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, which transports the repatriated dead to specialized state institutions, arranges the transfer of the bodies of the fallen to law enforcement and forensic medical examination authorities under the Health Ministry, and to representatives of the Armed Forces’ civil-military cooperation structures, who provide overall coordination," the statement said.

This boutique hotel in Lisbon has an in-house library, rooftop sunset sessions and a pillow menu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:40:09 UTC
19:40:09 KST

Villa Dorothéa is designed as a private micro-neighbourhood within Lapa, threaded through with passageways that give it the feel of a village.
For travellers to Lisbon, a new boutique hotel has opened offering a different kind of hospitality from most city centre accommodation.
Villa Dorothéa lies in the Portuguese capital’s Lapa district, occupying a carefully restored 19th-century hamlet. It is spread across five interconnected houses set between cobbled pathways, quiet courtyards, and terraces scented with jasmine and bougainvillaea.
The hotel has no formal lobby. Instead, guests follow footpaths paved with traditional Portuguese stonework, passing ceramic tributes to the area’s fishing heritage and historic tiled plaques that connect the house, hotel, and surrounding city.
A micro-neighbourhood in busy Lisbon
Villa Dorothéa is designed as a private micro-neighbourhood within Lapa, threaded through with passageways that give it the feel of a village.
The houses date back to 1878 and were originally home to the families of the city’s fishermen.
The interiors, by LACASTA Interior Design Studio and Carla Kottmann, combine architectural details with contemporary furnishings that sit alongside collected objects, books and decorative pieces to create the familiarity and character of a private residence.
At the heart of the property is The Secret, a 25-seat gastrobar extending between a secluded courtyard and a rooftop overlooking the city. It is open to both guests and external diners and draws inspiration from the city’s culture of long evenings, shared plates and conversation.
It also serves signature cocktails inspired by Luís de Camões’ Os Lusíadas, a 16th-century epic poem about maritime exploration.
As for breakfast, there’s specialty coffee from nearby award-winning roastery Filtrô and bread delivered fresh each morning by local artisan bakery Pão do Pastor.
Enjoy Lisbon’s slower side
Villa Dorothéa encourages guests to take life slowly. The hotel is home to a library curated in partnership with the Lisbon bookshop Salted Books.
Launching later this summer, Villa Suppers will bring guests and Lisbon locals together around long communal tables, drawing inspiration from the tradition of Portuguese family lunches.
Its ongoing social calendar will also include a series of events throughout the year such as sunset DJ sessions on the roof terrace, Champagne rituals and wine tastings with local producers.
As for wellness, each room has its own yoga mat and accessories, while group classes are available in partnership with LX Portal Yoga Studio across the street. In-room Swedish massages by wellness pioneer Cristina Lobo can also be arranged on request.
The property has introduced a dedicated pillow menu, with a choice of a cooling gel pillow, an ergonomic memory foam pillow, and an aromatherapy memory foam pillow infused with CBD, lavender, essential oils and chamomile.
Why you should stay in the Lapa neighbourhood
Lapa is one of Lisbon’s most distinguished residential neighbourhoods, known for its graceful architecture and colourful streets.
From the 16th century onwards, the area became known for the palaces and estates of noble families and prosperous merchants, later attracting the Portuguese aristocracy and bourgeoisie.
The arrival of embassies and diplomatic residences in the early 20th century further shaped the discreet, cosmopolitan character that Lapa retains today.
The neighbourhood houses some of the city’s most talked-about restaurants – including Skizzo, Da Noi and Familjen – alongside a host of independent design shops, artists’ studios and artisanal coffee spots.

German police evacuate buildings, rail traffic suspended after suspected explosive device found on train tracks in Bavarian town
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
August 13, 2026
Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.
Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene.
A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.
Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.
Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.
Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.

Ukrnafta ready to deploy mobile gas stations if needed – CEO
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:40:00 EEST
19:40:00 KST

Ukrnafta already has fuel trucks that can be used as mobile gas stations and plans to purchase several more units so that it can be ready to promptly supply consumers with fuel if it becomes impossible to do so at stationary filling stations, the company’s Chairman of the Board Bohdan Kukura said.
"Our UKRNAFTA network has several small-capacity fuel trucks (up to three cubic meters) that can be used as mobile, movable complexes. We plan to purchase several more units. We need to have them on hand so that we can respond promptly to the situation if necessary," he said in an exclusive interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
"Taking into account all the nuances and risks, we definitely need to be ready to use mobile filling stations," the CEO of Ukrnafta said.
At the same time, he pointed out that changes to legislation are necessary for mobile filling stations to operate.
"At present, a mobile filling complex can be used exclusively within the boundaries of an existing filling station and under an existing license, for example, if the station has been destroyed. But the security situation must be taken into account, because we are talking about a fuel tanker and a gathering of people," Kukura explained.
He also noted that the operation of mobile filling complexes increases the risk of the emergence of a shadow segment that could appear uncontrollably in different locations.
"And this is primarily a risk for consumers, because in the event of a shadow market, fuel quality would be highly questionable," Kukura said.
As reported, over the first seven months of 2026, Russia destroyed 37 filling stations belonging to the Naftogaz group. Some have been restored, while the rest sustained critical damage and ceased operations.
The Finance Ministry, together with relevant agencies and the fuel business, is drafting a bill on mobile excise warehouses that would allow fuel to be sold when stationary filling stations are unavailable. According to Deputy Finance Minister Svitlana Vorobei, the document could be ready within a week.
She added that, for example, in Sumy and Chernihiv regions, there are already communities where 100% of filling stations have been destroyed by Russian strikes, while the fuel companies operating there are refusing to rebuild them "because it makes no sense."
For her part, Tetiana Dumenkova, deputy head of the Association of Fuel and Energy Businesses, drew attention to the fact that local authorities, in the absence of stationary filling stations, have already been forced to make decisions to sell fuel on a mobile basis, but, according to her, "they are not legal."
In early July, the Trostianets City Council in Sumy region, due to damage to stationary filling stations caused by Russian shelling, informed residents of the community about the deployment of mobile filling points, emphasizing that fuel would be dispensed only for cash.
Local authorities recently reported the destruction of all filling stations in the Opishnia community of Poltava region.

Israel's army and settlers clash in Qusra. But is it theatre?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:39:40 UTC
19:39:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli soldiers clash with settlers in Qusra. But was it for show?
A rare confrontation between Israeli soldiers and settlers in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday has raised questions among Palestinians over whether the clash marked a genuine attempt to restrain settler violence or a carefully staged show of enforcement amid mounting international pressure.
The confrontation unfolded on Wednesday morning in Qusra, south of Nablus, where settlers had erected a tent just metres from the home of the Abu Rida family. The family says settlers have besieged the property for four days in an attempt to seize it.
The scene was unusual in a territory where the Israeli military has for years been accused of protecting settlers during attacks on Palestinians, including assaults in which homes and property have been torched and Palestinians have been killed.
But shortly after 7am on Wednesday, Israeli soldiers arrived and attempted to dismantle the settlers' tent.
"The occupation army arrived at around 7am today, attempting to dismantle the tent that several settlers had set up in front of our home to seize it," Qusay Abdulmunim Abu Rida told The New Arab. "But what happened was strange, as the settlers attacked the soldiers, who responded by firing tear gas and stun grenades."
Soldiers dismantled the tent and confiscated a car and an off-road vehicle belonging to the settlers, Abu Rida said. The settlers then confronted the soldiers, recovered the car and fled along bypass roads used by settlers.
The confrontation lasted about an hour and a half. But any reprieve for the Abu Rida family proved short-lived.
"It is true that the army left after an hour and a half of clashes, but the number of settlers continued to increase until it reached more than 100 settlers at the site of the same tent that the soldiers had confiscated," Abu Rida said.
A family under siege
For four days, settlers have maintained a tent about four metres from the Abu Rida home, according to the family, as part of what they describe as an escalating effort to force them from the property.
The settlers began digging around water networks before removing electricity poles and destroying cables supplying the house. They also smashed surveillance cameras and blocked the road leading to the property, preventing residents of Qusra from bringing the family food, water and medicine.
For Abu Rida, the tactics bear an unsettling resemblance to what happened about two weeks earlier to the Tubasi family in nearby Jaloud, where settlers seized a Palestinian home after Israeli soldiers intervened and helped remove the family.
"They want to repeat what they did to the Tubasi family's homes in Jaloud," Abu Rida said.
He said the pressure began months earlier, after settlers erected additional tents at an outpost established at the beginning of the year.
Abu Rida, his brothers, their wives and children subsequently moved into the threatened house, which belongs to his brother Murad, who lives and works in the United States and returns to the village for annual visits.
The Israeli army's sudden confrontation with the settlers therefore left the family puzzled.
Just two days earlier, Abu Rida said, soldiers had prevented foreign activists from reaching the family with food and water, telling them that the surrounding area had been declared a closed military zone for six months.
The family says the designation is particularly difficult to understand because the house is in Area B, which under the Oslo Accords is under Palestinian civil administration and joint Palestinian-Israeli security control.
"We do not understand how Mount (Ain Ainya), where our home is located, can be turned into a completely closed military zone," Abu Rida said. "The settlers want to seize the entire mountain, so they have made our lives unbearable through their attacks and siege on us day and night."
The group immediately surrounding the house was initially small, he said, numbering no more than 10 settlers, most of them between 17 and 18 years old.
But larger groups have repeatedly joined them.
"Two days ago, they held a fire party at night, attended by dozens of settlers wearing white and black clothes, and they were armed," Abu Rida said.
Pressure on Israel
The confrontation came as Israel faces growing international scrutiny over escalating settler attacks against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier, the UN Security Council had discussed the violence at a meeting requested by France, Britain, Greece, Denmark and Latvia, which cited a "significant escalation" in settler attacks in recent months.
Muawiya Musa, a researcher specialising in Israeli affairs, said the timing was significant.
Israel's government and state institutions have openly overseen and supported the expansion of settlements, he said, while the military has provided settlers with security cover during attacks on Palestinians.
The growing international criticism, he argued, had created pressure for Israel to demonstrate that it was capable of restraining the settlers.
"These international protests have finally begun to bother the Israeli government and army, requiring them to take a step that appears more serious, especially after the latter was accused of colluding in these attacks," Musa told The New Arab. "Therefore, today's campaign in Qusra was aimed at giving the impression that the army is enforcing order and the law."
The soldiers' relatively forceful response, including the use of tear gas and stun grenades against settlers, could reflect the need for a more visible display of enforcement, Musa said.
"Its use of a relatively higher degree of violence this morning may indicate an urgent need for a demonstrative display by the army in which it presents itself as more serious than at previous times," he said.
But Musa cautioned against interpreting the confrontation as evidence of a fundamental rupture between the Israeli state and the settlement movement.
Settlers and the religious Zionist movement have become deeply embedded in Israeli political and military institutions, he said, while support for settlement expansion has spread more broadly through Israeli society.
How powerful are the settlers?
Asked whether settlers had grown beyond the Israeli military's control, Musa said it was still "too early" to reach such a conclusion.
What was clearer, he said, was the extent of their influence.
Settlers, particularly members of the religious nationalist movement driving the current expansion campaign, wield considerable power across Israeli state institutions, including the military and security services, Musa said.
That influence makes any sustained confrontation between the state and the settlement movement difficult, he argued, because attempts to restrain settlers could produce far-reaching political consequences inside Israel.
There are nevertheless divisions within the Israeli military and political establishment over how far settlement expansion should go.
According to Musa, some of that concern centres on the expansion of settlements and outposts into Areas A and B of the occupied West Bank, which under the Oslo framework were intended to remain distinct from the territory under full Israeli control.
Expanding deeper into those areas would dramatically increase contact and friction between settlers and Palestinians, Musa said, further eroding any remaining physical separation between the two populations.
That trajectory, he argued, could ultimately force Israel towards either a binational political reality or an increasingly explicit system of apartheid.
Israel's right wing, however, has shown little concern about that prospect, Musa said, seeing the current moment instead as an opportunity to accelerate demographic changes across the occupied West Bank through sustained pressure on Palestinians.
For the Abu Rida family, those larger political questions are playing out immediately outside their home.
The soldiers who dismantled the settlers' tent on Wednesday eventually left. The settlers did not.
Within hours, their numbers had swelled to more than 100.
For Musa, the episode therefore offered little evidence that Israel's broader approach to the settlement movement had changed.
Instead, he said, the struggle over the West Bank was increasingly becoming "a race against time" before the United States determines what final political reality it wants to see there.

NEW DELHI: Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) chief and former Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhbir Singh Badal was injured after being attacked at a gurdwara in Maharashtra's Nanded on Thursday. The assailant, identified as 62-year-old Jaspal Singh, had been working at the same gurdwara for the past two years as a 'sevadar' (volunteer/attendant).According to police, the attack took place when Badal was visiting Mata Sahib Gurdwara in the Hazur Sahib area. The attacker allegedly tried to stab the Akali Dal leader in the stomach, news agency IANS reported quoting sources.
"... Near the stairs, a 'sevadar' (volunteer/attendant) suddenly approached and attempted to attack with his 'kirpan'... Immediately following the incident, we took the attacker into custody, and interrogation is currently underway. He is approximately 60–62 years old and has been working as a 'sevadar' at the Gurudwara for about two years," Nanded Police SP Nilabh Rohan said. "Initially, he himself stated that he was angry about the drug issue in Punjab... No connection to any gang has been established ... The exact reason is not yet clear. We are currently interrogating him ... The Nanded Police and the ATS are collaborating on the case," he added.
Security personnel accompanying Badal intervened immediately and overpowered the attacker before he could inflict more serious injuries.Police later identified the accused as Jaspal Singh, son of Teja Singh and a resident of Solapur Bazaar in Pune. Investigators said he had been residing at Mata Sahib Gurdwara for the last two years.Badal sustained an injury to his hand and was rushed to Yasho Sai Hospital in Nanded for treatment. Officials said that he received stitches on his hand and is in stable condition.Inspector Santosh Kendre of the Maharashtra Police's Special Protection Unit (SPU), who was deployed for Badal's security, was also injured while trying to stop the attacker.The SPU is a specialised unit tasked with providing security to VVIPs during their visits and movements.Badal was accompanied by his wife, SAD MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal, during his visit to Takht Sri Hazur Sahib. Punjab security personnel and Maharashtra Police officers were also present when the attack took place.Maharashtra CM Devendra Fadnavis has sought a detailed report from the Nanded Superintendent of Police and ordered an inquiry into the motive behind the attack. He also spoke to Badal over the phone to inquire about his condition.
Police have detained the accused and launched an investigation into the circumstances that led to the attack. Security has been tightened in and around the gurdwara premises.This was not the first attack on the Akali Dal leader.In December 2024, Badal survived an assassination attempt outside the Golden Temple in Amritsar while performing 'sewadar' duties after the Akal Takht had pronounced religious punishment on him and several other party leaders over decisions taken during the SAD government's tenure between 2007 and 2017.

Missed the eclipse? Here’s where to travel to see 2027’s ‘eclipse of the century’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:38:51 UTC
19:38:51 KST

Gibraltar, Marbella and Lampedusa all lie in the path of totality for the eclipse on 2 August, 2027.
Missed this year’s eclipse and have serious FOMO? Don’t worry, because there’s another one coming up in 2027 – and it’s being described as the ‘eclipse of the century’.
Taking place on 2 August 2027, this eclipse will be the longest on easily accessible land until 2114, with totality lasting six minutes and 23 seconds at the point of the greatest eclipse in Egypt.
For context, yesterday’s eclipse lasted for two minutes and 18 seconds at its maximum point.
You don’t have to travel all the way to Egypt to see it either, as the path of totality will pass through the Strait of Gibraltar before continuing through parts of North Africa and the Middle East.
Where in Europe and beyond to see the 2027 eclipse
It’s another big one for Spain, although the cities in the path of totality are different to this year’s eclipse.
In Marbella, totality will last for three minutes and 21 seconds, while in Cádiz, it will be dark for two minutes and 56 seconds.
Ceuta and Melilla, Spain’s exclaves on the coast of North Africa, will also see the totality for four minutes and 49 seconds, and four minutes and 34 seconds, respectively.
The British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar is another European option, with totality lasting four minutes and 28 seconds.
Lampedusa, one of Italy’s Pelagian Islands, will see totality for two minutes and 56 seconds.
In Morocco, Tangier will see totality for four minutes and 51 seconds. Several cities in Tunisia lie in the path of totality, with the southeastern port city of Sfax descending into darkness for two minutes and 56 seconds.
Given the fact that the greatest eclipse is in Egypt, it’s unsurprising that many umbraphiles (aka eclipse chasers) are headed there for the big day.
In the Siwa Oasis, it will last five minutes and 33 seconds; in Asyut, six minutes and seven seconds; and in Luxor, six minutes and 22 seconds.
In Saudi Arabia, totality will last five minutes and 53 seconds in Jeddah, and five minutes and 10 seconds in Mecca.
If you are planning a trip, I suggest booking a hotel ASAP as many properties are already fully booked, and those that aren’t are seriously pricey.
Worried about the heat in some of these cities? I chatted to Dr. Kelly Korreck, a programme scientist for eclipses at NASA Headquarters, earlier this year, who told Euronews Travel that the temperature could drop as much as 10°C.
Other eclipses to make a note of
An annular solar eclipse – where the moon doesn’t completely cover the sun, leading to a “ring of fire” effect – is coming up on 26 January, 2028.
It will start in South America before passing through Portugal, including Madeira, and cities in Spain including Barcelona, Córdoba, Cádizm and Seville. The maximum coverage is around 84%.
Australia and New Zealand will next see a total solar eclipse on 22 July, 2028. Cities in the path of totality include Sydney, Queenstown and Dunedin.

A network of Russian GRU agents hunting for F-16s and Mirage 2000s was uncovered in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
13:37:49 EEST
19:37:49 KST

A network of Russian GRU agents hunting for F-16s and Mirage 2000s was uncovered in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU neutralized a Russian intelligence agent network consisting of 14 people who collected data on Ukrainian air bases. The enemy planned to use this information for missile strikes against F-16 and Mirage 2000 aircraft.
An intelligence network of the Russian military intelligence agency was exposed in Ukraine. It included 14 people who were "hunting" for F-16s and Mirage 2000s, the SBU reported on Thursday, UNN writes.
Details
"The military counterintelligence of the Security Service of Ukraine, under the personal coordination of SBU Chief Oleksandr Poklad, neutralized a large-scale agent network of Russian military intelligence (better known as the GRU), through which the enemy could launch missile strikes on the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ air bases. The investigation established that the suspects’ activities enabled the enemy to plan and carry out attacks on the airfields of Ukrainian forces equipped with F-16 and Mirage 2000 combat aircraft," the SBU reported.
According to the case materials, "the group recruited by the enemy consisted of 14 people who lived in various regions of Ukraine."
"Countering Russian special services seeking to destabilize the situation in Ukraine from within is one of the SBU’s top priorities today. We are actively strengthening the counterintelligence regime because we understand that the enemy continues to seek to damage our country’s defense potential and destabilize the Ukrainian rear, having no notable successes on the front. This operation is another example of our systematic work in this area. Everyone who agrees to work in the interests of Russia should realize: the SBU will definitely bring you to justice," said Head of the Security Service of Ukraine Oleksandr Poklad.
It was established that "the Russian GRU initially recruited a Lviv resident who administered a Telegram channel about aviation." He came to the attention of the Rashists when he published photographs of Ukrainian Armed Forces combat aircraft in pro-Kremlin chats.
"To carry out the enemy’s assignment, the agent, without revealing the true purpose, involved 13 of his subscribers who had high-quality photographic equipment and lived near the Defense Forces’ aviation infrastructure. They were to photograph Ukrainian airfields, military aircraft, their crews and technical personnel, as well as record the time intervals between aircraft takeoffs and landings, allegedly for the Lviv blogger’s Telegram channel," the SBU stated.
According to the SBU, the suspects used professional cameras for this purpose, concealing themselves in abandoned buildings or in open areas near air bases. "They stored the photographs taken in an online storage facility, access to which they had previously received from the agent. He then passed the photographic materials to his handler from Russia, whose identity has already been established by the Security Service," the statement said.
"The agent also ‘leaked’ the schedules for the departures and landings of combat helicopters to the Rashists. He received such intelligence from a commander of a Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation squadron, who provided the information on his own initiative," the statement said.
During searches of the suspects’ residences, the SBU reported, officers found smartphones and digital photographic equipment containing evidence of work for the enemy, as well as photographs of Defense Forces aviation facilities.
In addition, SBU officers blocked four Telegram channels and 10 thematic groups where photographs and other data about Ukrainian Armed Forces aviation units were distributed.
"Investigators of the Security Service have now notified the detained agent, his accomplice and the serviceman of suspicion of committing crimes against the foundations of national security," the statement said.
The investigation is ongoing to bring all those responsible to justice.

Huanggang port drill smooth: Chris Tang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:36:33 UTC
19:36:33 KST

Around 1,000 civil servants on Thursday took part in a stress test at the new Huanggang port public transport interchange, the first large-scale drill conducted at the Hong Kong side of the facility.
Participants from more than 20 government departments travelled to the interchange using various modes of public transport, including buses, cross-boundary coaches, minibuses and taxis. They then made their way through the departure hall and arrival hall of the port building, before heading back to the interchange to leave by public transport.
The process was repeated in loops to simulate pedestrian and vehicle traffic, involving more than 120 vehicle trips.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang said the drill went smoothly and was "meticulously arranged", according to a government statement.
He noted that the drill covered passenger boarding and alighting, pedestrian and vehicle traffic management, terminal passageway capacity, signage clarity and barrier-free facilities. There were also simulations for passengers boarding and getting off taxis, buses and minibuses at the same time.
The security minister also said some participants pointed out issues regarding unclear signage and queue control. Tang said officials have taken note of the feedback and will follow up with improvements.
He added that stress tests will continue at the border checkpoint almost daily to ensure safe and smooth operations when the port officially opens to the public.  
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan was also there to inspect the drill. 
She said her bureau will review and improve the transport arrangements, to ensure a highly efficient transport network once port operations begin.

Snow cannons and reservoirs: How Swiss resorts' winter equipment could help put out wildfires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:35:50 UTC
19:35:50 KST

Kilometres of underground water pipes could prove useful beyond the winter months as the risk of wildfires grows even in places like Switzerland.
There's barely any snow in sight above Adelboden in the intense August sunshine, never mind skiers. But the Swiss resort may have a new way to put its snowmaking equipment to work as Europe bakes through hot summers: helping douse forest fires.
Glaciers in Switzerland and around the Alps have been retreating rapidly in recent years, among other changes attributed to the impact of climate change caused by human activity. Snowfall has become less frequent and reliable over recent decades.
That's a big issue for a mid-altitude ski resort like the Adelboden-Lenk area, whose roughly 200 kilometres of slopes span an altitude between 1,000 and 2,300 metres. These days, an estimated 70 per cent of the snow on its slopes is made artificially.
Snow cannons and lances are the visible part of the snowmaking network. But much of it is out of sight: dozens of kilometres of underground water pipes that could prove useful beyond the winter months as the risk of wildfires grows even in places such as Switzerland’s Adelboden-Lenk ski area.
How reservoirs of melted snow could be used to douse wildfires
“We can help firefighters with our infrastructure," says Jürg Klopfenstein, who is responsible for the resort's snowmaking operations. "Not primarily with our snow cannons, which can mainly be used to water the fields or aim them at surrounding infrastructure. But firefighters can use our infrastructure, and helicopters can refill their tanks using our water reservoirs.”
Those reservoirs collect rainfall and melting snow in the warmer months, and the water is used to produce snow during the ski season. The pipes and pumps connect 210 snow cannons and 50 snow lances in the Adelboden-Lenk area. In case of fire, the system could be used to create wet buffer areas, slowing the advance of flames and buying time until emergency services and air support arrive.
So far this year, Switzerland hasn’t experienced large-scale fires, unlike some of its neighbours. But the country is suffering from drought and the authorities assess the risk of wildfires as high across almost the entire nation, including the Bern region where Adelboden is located.
Lack of humidity is 'a real problem' – even in spring
Like many other mountain areas, the Bernese Oberland isn't just a winter destination but attracts many mountain bikers, hikers, runners and paragliders in summer.
Stefan Buchs, the operations manager at the Adelboden-Lenk resort, says that different types of vegetation and different levels of soil humidity mean the large and frequent forest fires seen in southern Europe can't be extrapolated directly into a similar risk in the Alps.
But even so, “widespread wildfires are a likely scenario," he says. “We discussed this with the firefighters, and they recognised it already. They see that humidity is a real problem. It gets really dry even in the spring. Not just in the summer.”
Adelboden Mayor Willy Schranz says that “we must be prepared, because I am sure it won’t be the last summer like this one.”
A climate change expert with environmental group Greenpeace, Nathan Solothurnmann, cautions against overestimating what putting a snowmaking system to work against wildfires can achieve in the long run and in a wider context.
“This watering system that they’re planning in Adelboden might for sure help for a while," he says. “But of course the changes we're facing [are] much worse. All those types of adaptations, they just help for a while.”
"In most parts of Switzerland, there are no pipes buried underground that we can use when a forest is burning,” he adds.

Meta removes 756,000 accounts belonging to under-16s in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:34:58 UTC
19:34:58 KST

Meta said on Thursday it had deactivated 756,000 Facebook and Instagram accounts in Australia that it assessed as belonging to users under the age of 16.
462,000 Instagram accounts and 294,000 Facebook accounts were deactivated as of June 30, Meta said in a statement.
Australia was the first country in the world to introduce a nationwide minimum age of 16 for social media accounts, with the restrictions taking effect in December 2025.
More than 500,000 accounts were removed in the lead-up to the law taking effect, with additional accounts removed in subsequent months, Meta said.
Other countries are also moving to tighten social media access for children. France has introduced a nationwide ban for users under 15, while Spain, Malaysia and several other countries are considering similar age restrictions.
Meta said enforcement remains ongoing and that the number is expected to rise.
The company said it uses artificial intelligence to analyse posts, comments, biographies and captions for indications that an account holder may be under 16, including references to birthdays and school grades.
Meta has also simplified the process for parents and other users to report suspected underage accounts and introduced AI-assisted reviews of such reports.
It has strengthened measures designed to prevent removed users from registering new accounts and changed the Australian Apple App Store age rating for its platforms to 16+.

German shipping giant Hapag-Lloyd takes $600M hit from Middle East conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
10:34:02 UTC
19:34:02 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
German container shipping company Hapag-Lloyd incurred around $600 million in additional costs in the second quarter due to the conflict in the Middle East, the company said Thursday.
Hapag-Lloyd's group profit fell to $83 million in the April-June period from $306 million a year earlier, according to its quarterly earnings statement.
Group earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) edged up to $829 million from $820 million, while operating profit declined to $176 million from $189 million.
The company said strong exports from Asia and improved demand in the US helped partially offset cost pressures stemming from the Middle East conflict.
In its Liner Shipping segment, operating profit fell to $153 million from $167 million, primarily as the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz generated additional costs for bunker fuel, insurance, storage, service rerouting and inland transportation.
Segment revenue rose to $5.7 billion, supported by higher transport volumes and freight rates.
Transport volume increased to 3.5 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) from 3.4 million a year earlier, while the average freight rate climbed 9% to $1,475 per TEU.
"The second quarter was better than the first, driven by significantly higher spot rates and robust demand," CEO Rolf Habben Jansen said.
The company raised its full-year outlook in July, forecasting group EBITDA of between $2.7 billion and $3.7 billion and operating profit of $100 million to $1.1 billion.
Hapag-Lloyd cautioned that its outlook remains subject to considerable uncertainty due to volatile freight rates and the Middle East conflict.

Police in Ecuador seize 1,000 pounds of cocaine bearing the face of soccer star Erling Haaland; woman arrested
Norway's soccer star Erling Haaland's face has appeared on billboards, trading cards and television screens, becoming a social media phenomenon for scoring seven goals across four World Cup matches in July.
Now, police in Ecuador have found it in an unexpected place — printed on green rectangular packages that made up a stunning cocaine shipment seized in a truck near the Colombian border.
The driver of the vehicle was arrested following the seizure of the stash of 469 kilograms (1,034 pounds) of cocaine on Wednesday, police said in a statement.
A news release said anti-narcotics agents were conducting an operation following an anonymous tip received early Tuesday morning on the Pan-American Highway when they noticed a suspicious truck. After searching it, they found 370 packages hidden in a false bottom of the truck.
Police released a video showing the packages spilling out from the truck's false bottom, with the stickers of Haaland — often called a "pretty princess" and "babygirl" by his fans — clearly visible.
Haaland was one of the top scorers and most charismatic players at the World Cup held in Mexico, the United States and Canada, and his imposing stature, goofy sense of humor and seemingly endless appetite sparked a wave of creative viral videos and memes.
Ecuador is considered to be a logistical hub for drug trafficking, where drugs are stockpiled, stored and distributed via Central American routes mainly to the United States, though narcotics are also shipped to Europe.
Police said a woman identified only as María R., with Colombian identity documents, was arrested in Wednesday's operation in the area of Guagua Negro, near the border city of Tulcan, 246 kilometers (153 miles) north of the capital Quito.
The estimated value of the shipment is nearly $842,000 on the domestic market, and more than $11 million in the U.S. and more than $19.6 million (17 million euros) in Europe.
In Ecuador, local criminal gangs allied with Colombian and Mexican cartels manage the routes and ship the narcotics, 80% of which originate in Colombia and the rest in Peru.
In the first half of this year, police reported seizing 80 tons of drugs, while in 2025 authorities confiscated nearly 215 tons, primarily cocaine. In 2024, the amount reached almost 295 tons.
Cocaine with creative packaging
Police provided no explanation for the stickers with the image of the golden-haired Norwegian striker. However, it is common practice for drug traffickers to label their shipments with the names of well-known sports figures and other celebrities as a way of signaling which criminal network produced the merchandise and which client it belongs to.
 Haaland is not the only soccer star apparently favored by drug smugglers —   the image of Argentine national team captain Lionel Messi has also appeared on another seized package.
 
Packages of drugs are often packaged with other distinct designs. Last year, a beachgoer in Florida found nearly $500,000 worth of cocaine wrapped in "Yosemite Sam" packaging washed up on shore.
In August 2024, tourists on a Florida beach found a package with 16 bricks of suspected cocaine wrapped in packaging depicting a dune buggy.
In June 2024, boaters off the coast of the Florida Keys found 65 pounds of cocaine — in packages emblazoned with bald eagles —floating in the ocean.
Just weeks earlier, divers found about 55 pounds of cocaine about 100 feet underwater off Key West. Images released by the sheriff's office showed packages marked "Nike SB," with imitations of the footwear brand's iconic swoosh logo on the front.

Ukraine's Air Force faces backlash over decision to stop publishing Russian ballistic missile figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ukraine's Air Force faces backlash over decision to stop publishing Russian ballistic missile figures
A Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile is launched at the Kapustin Yar proving ground, Astrakhan Oblast, Russia on March 2, 2018. (Wikimedia)
Ukraine's Air Force will cease publishing the exact number of Russian ballistic missiles launched and shot down in its daily morning updates, spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed on Aug. 13 after several days without the figures appearing.
The move, while publicly explained as being made for security and communications reasons, has been criticized for reducing overall transparency between the military, the media, and Ukrainian public as a whole about an issue that directly affects them.
The last daily report to state a concrete number of Russian ballistic missiles was published on Aug. 8.
By Aug. 11, when Russian Iskander missiles, North Korean KN-23 missiles, and Zircon cruise missiles struck Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, killing seven people and injuring dozens more, the types of missiles were disclosed but not the exact number.
First and foremost, Ihnat said, the decision was connected to a series of negative headlines about the Air Force's failure to down any ballistic missiles.
"I understand that everyone already knows everything and sees that the topic is very sensitive, especially for the capital," the spokesperson wrote.
"But when we put an official message - 28/0 (ballistic missiles intercepted), the result is that all our media write 'The Air Force did not shoot down a single missile,' and amplify it throughout the country. Meanwhile, enemy media will only copy all this and replicate it for themselves, giving a standing ovation!"
"Honesty and transparency in communication are what advantageously distinguished our Armed Forces from the Russian ones."
Critics of the announcement said that the move could lead to a slippery slope where more and more information important for the public interest could be withheld for communications reasons.
"When some communication disappears, the vacuum can be filled with suspicions and rumors, and distrust may, on the contrary, increase," Oksana Romaniuk, director of Ukraine's Institute of Mass Information (IMI), told the Kyiv Independent.
"The state during wartime really does have the right to conceal information for security reasons, but it should not conceal socially important data simply because they create unpleasant headlines," she added.
The sentiment was repeated by many in the comments section under Ihnat's Facebook post.
"Honesty and transparency in communication are what advantageously distinguished our Armed Forces from the Russian ones," commented Taras Yemchura, Defense Sector Lead at Ukraine's Better Regulation Delivery Office.
"Citizens understand that there is nothing to shoot them (ballistic missiles) down with. I believe that the best way to build the stability of society is an honest conversation between adults, and not silencing reality."
"When some communication disappears, the vacuum can be filled with suspicions and rumors, and distrust may, on the contrary, increase."
Responding to criticism in the comments to his post, Ihnat said the total numbers of ballistic missiles launched would still be published on a monthly basis, and that nothing would change with the real-time warnings of launches published by the Air Force on Telegram.
For most of 2026, Ukraine has struggled with a dire shortage of interceptors for the advanced U.S.-built Patriot surface-to-air missile system, which remains Ukraine's only system capable of shooting down Russian Iskander and Kinzhal ballistic missiles.
But with the U.S. war in Iran severely depleting Washington's interceptor stocks while increasing demand for the Patriot worldwide, Ukraine's hopes of consistently defending itself from ballistic missiles remain slim in the near term.
On Aug. 13, President Volodymyr Zelensky claimed that just 10% of U.S. stocks of Patriot interceptors would be enough to destroy "all" Russian ballistic missiles launched at Ukraine, and that only 5% would be enough to get through the winter, when a new Russian strike campaign against civilian energy, heating, and water infrastructure is expected to begin.
Ukraine receives the missiles either in small quantities from European nations, or through deliveries from the U.S. paid for by partner countries, after the Trump administration agreed to the NATO-led PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List).
The release of more Patriot missiles to defend Ukraine's skies has since become the front-and-center issue of Zelensky's diplomatic efforts with Trump, but with mixed results.
In late July, Trump seemingly agreed to provide Kyiv with the license to produce Patriot interceptors domestically, but later backtracked on his decision.
Meanwhile, Kyiv, together with defense giant Fire Point, has announced work on a homegrown anti-ballistic missile project dubbed Freyja, to be developed in collaboration with European partners as a long-term alternative to dependence on the Patriot system.
But given the advanced technological requirements — from engineering to software — of creating such a system, the program is unlikely to produce results before winter.

19:32:05 KST

Democratic senators demand answers about conditions aboard USS Abraham Lincoln
Washington — Senate Democrats demanded answers Wednesday about conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises during the aircraft carrier's record-setting deployment.
In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, of Connecticut, called for the Navy to account for conditions aboard the carrier, which he said "has been deployed more than 250 days" without coming ashore "in over 200 days, setting a record for consecutive days at sea."
Blumenthal voiced concern over such extended deployments, noting "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" and other problems aboard the Lincoln.
A Navy official told CBS News that the "Lincoln is operating in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions. In response, leadership prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail. Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC, and healthy meal options."
The Navy confirmed in a statement to CBS News that a sailor assigned to the air wing attached to USS Abraham Lincoln went overboard from the ship earlier this month and was recovered safely. The sailor was quickly picked up by an air wing search and helicopter, treated by the ship's medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The sailor's family was notified.
The circumstances are under investigation, the Navy said. CNN was first to report the sailor overboard.
In two recent meetings, family members clashed with Navy leadership over the difficult conditions — including food shortages — faced by the 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard the Lincoln and demanded to know when loved ones would return home, MSNOW reported.
Some families reported severe mental health issues and attempted suicides on board.
Citing a report in the Military Times that said several sailors had tried to jump overboard or were prevented from trying to in recent months, Sen. Ruben Gallego, of Arizona, said in a social media post Wednesday that the Navy "must allow a bipartisan Congressional Delegation to visit the USS Lincoln to conduct (an) oversight investigation into this horrible situation."
The Navy official told CBS News,"Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship. ... (The) Lincoln is providing a comprehensive support network, including onboard deployment-resilience counselors, chaplains, Fleet and Family Support Center services, Military OneSource, and medical professionals."

Details

-  the job functions of a counter-technical intelligence specialist; 
-  the necessary professional competencies; 
-  requirements for education, knowledge, practical skills, and more. 
The new professional standard will be used to train personnel at educational institutions, assess professional qualifications, and enable employers to formulate clear requirements for employees. This will unify approaches to the training and certification of specialists, improve the quality of personnel training, and ensure that their competencies meet current security challenges in the security and defense sector, public administration, and business

A man was killed in an explosion in occupied Sevastopol on the morning of 13 August, according to the Russian outlet ASTRA and the local Telegram channel Emergency/Sevastopol.
The man's identity has not been officially confirmed, but Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels are circulating claims that he is Robert Shahieiev, deputy commander of the 4th separate submarine brigade of Russia's Black Sea Fleet — a former Ukrainian Navy officer who sided with Russia after the occupation of Crimea.
What happened
According to preliminary information from Russian sources, the man was walking down a set of stairs with a friend when the explosion occurred. He died of his injuries at the scene. The device is believed to have been planted in a trash bin next to a bench, per preliminary reports cited by Ukrainska Pravda.
The Russian Telegram channel "Baza" reported that the blast took place in a park behind a residential block on Stoletovsky Avenue and that forensic investigators were working at the scene. The channel said local residents were being urged to stay alert and avoid approaching suspicious objects.
Some witnesses initially believed a drone had struck a nearby building because of how loud the blast was, according to accounts circulating on Telegram.
Unverified claim about a suspect
The pro-Kremlin channel Mash claimed a woman carrying a backpack may have been involved, alleging she stood between two residential buildings — numbers 28 and 30 — and watched the man before the explosion. Ukrainska Pravda noted this claim has not been confirmed.
No source has provided official confirmation of the victim's identity or a motive for the attack.
