Total eclipse plunges Spain’s Segovia into darkness for 59 seconds of wonder (4/4)
From our special correspondent in Segovia – A total solar eclipse on Wednesday plunged Spain’s Segovia into daytime darkness for 59 seconds. Perched high up on the city's iconic cathedral bell tower, locals and visitors from and wide watched, in awe, as the moon’s shadow blotted out the sun.
Issued on: Modified:
There are rare occasions in life when time is seemingly suspended by an extraordinary event, unleashing a whirlwind of emotions that, in the moment, transform us.
The total solar eclipse that covered swaths of Spain late on Wednesday offered one such moment – particularly for the lucky few gathered atop Segovia’s majestic Cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin and San Frutos overlooking the Castile and Leon region's rugged landscape.
Only a handful of people had the privilege of climbing up the 16th-century bell tower, passing through gates and doors that are usually closed to the public at this time of day. And because a view like this must be earned, they climbed the 190 steps leading to the lofty summit on foot.
The 90-metre ascension was a mere formality for Minos, who travelled from Malmö in Sweden with his sister Michelle to witness “the eclipse of a lifetime”.
Read moreEclipse chasers: When chasing totality becomes a way of life (1/4)
As the moon began to hide the sun, the astronomy enthusiast eagerly counted down the minutes leading up to totality – the moment when the sun’s face is entirely hidden from view.
“Ten to go,” he announced, proudly pulling out a state-of-the-art camera fitted with a solar filter, a gift from their father for this very special occasion.
‘Dios mio!’
Like countless other eclipse chasers, the Swedish pair travelled from Madrid through the breathtaking Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range to reach Segovia, known for its iconic Roman aqueduct and majestic Alcazar castle, which is said to have inspired Snow White’s castle in the eponymous Disney movie.
As mainland Europe witnesses its first total solar eclipse since 1999, FRANCE 24 is dedicating a series of articles to this astronomical event – one of the continent’s most anticipated of the decade – with reports from the path of totality in Spain.
• Eclipse chasers: When chasing totality becomes a way of life (1/4)
• From Solar corona to human emotions: What can we learn from eclipses? (2/4)
• ‘First of our lives’: Thousands race for best spot in Spain to watch total solar eclipse (3/4)
Such architectural gems are part of everyday life for locals in the know, who made up the majority of the privileged few gathered at the top of the cathedral. They included Segovian couple Kelly and Yago, who watched the spectacle alongside relatives, strangers and a priest, their eclipse glasses firmly in place and their eyes fixed on the shrinking sun.
Read moreIn pictures: Partial to total eclipse sweeps across much of Europe
At 8:30pm, chiming bells heralded the moment when the moon would completely blot out the sun. “It’s Jesus ringing for us!” joked the priest, provoking a general burst of laughter.
“Dios mio… Dios mio!” (My God!) Kelly repeated as darkness and an eerie silence descended on this ancient city, soon giving way to applause from the crowd gathered at the foot of the tower.
Wonder and fear
As the fifty-nine seconds of total eclipse lapsed, it was hard to recall whether the moment had passed quickly or whether every second had been felt as a unique experience.
It was equally difficult to interpret the passing emotions on people’s faces as they gazed at the celestial alignment.
There was shock and awe as the solar corona appeared in all its glory, but also apprehension at the thought of damaging one’s eyesight, and the fear of missing even part of a fleeting moment that many will never experience again.
“I’ll remember this for the rest of my life,” said Yago as his awestruck partner wiped away the tears welling up in the corners of her eyes. “It’s something you can’t imagine until you’ve experienced it,” he added.
Read moreFrom Solar corona to human emotions: What can we learn from eclipses? (2/4)
Yago spoke of ancient people who would have viewed eclipses as a bad omen or a sign of the gods’ wrath, and for whom such experiences were often a source of both thrill and fright.
Science now offers a simple explanation for why the sun briefly disappears. But gazing at a total solar eclipse for 59 seconds, one can only understand the vertigo experienced by our ancestors who once looked up at the sky without knowing whether our star would return.

Inside Minsk – by all means, there are plenty of places where we are building,” he emphasized. 
 
 
                    
                    
                                        
                                    
                                                        The president suggested finding a more targeted approach to distributing agricultural subsidies, emphasizing that the invested money must yield an appropriate return. At the same time, there is no question of completely abandoning subsidies. “In some areas, we must provide help, otherwise it will be like in Western Europe: they stopped providing support, and agriculture collapsed,” he added.
The field visited by the head of state belongs to the Zdanovichi agricultural enterprise in Minsk District. Aleksandr Lukashenko inquired in detail about the state of affairs with the enterprise’s head, Grigory Chuiko. According to him, while the farm has enough land, “the city is still encroaching.” In this regard, the president raised the issue of the impermissibility of residential development on agricultural land once again. “We need to densify and build in empty spaces, on small pockets of land. Inside Minsk – by all means, there are plenty of places where we are building,” he emphasized.

ARKHANGELSK, August 13. /TASS/. Under the pretext of "mythical threats from the East," NATO is militarizing the Arctic region and intensively strengthening its offensive capabilities along Russia’s northern borders, Russian Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Department Director Vladislav Maslennikov said.
According to the diplomat, Western countries' approaches toward the Arctic region have increasingly been dominated by a confrontational mindset and scenarios involving the use of force to secure their interests in recent years. "As a result, the high latitudes, which were characterized exclusively by peaceful and constructive cooperation for decades, are now witnessing a rise in military and political tensions and an increased risk of unintended escalation," he noted while speaking at the 4th Arctic Regions Forum.
"Under the pretext of countering mythical threats from the East, NATO is pursuing a course of active militarization of the Arctic Region and is intensively strengthening its offensive capabilities along our northern borders. Large-scale exercises aimed at rehearsing offensive scenarios are regularly held in the region, and non-Arctic member states of the alliance are actively involved in these activities," the diplomat emphasized.
Maslennikov stressed that reducing the overall potential for conflict in the region and committing to international cooperation and law are among Russia’s primary and unwavering priorities. "At the same time, Russia is taking the necessary measures to ensure its national security by developing an appropriate response to emerging challenges and threats, which are growing by the day," he added.
TASS is the forum’s general media partner.

====================================================================================================

Xi Story: The rain, the caves and the quest to preserve Mogao Grottoes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:52:05 CST
17:52:05 KST

LANZHOU, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- In Dunhuang, an ancient Silk Road city in northwest China, even rain has caught the attention of Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The city is home to the Mogao Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage site dating back to the 4th century. The region's arid climate has helped preserve the murals, sculptures and a vast trove of Buddhist art in hundreds of grottoes carved into cliffs on the edge of the Gobi Desert. But increased rainfall and rising humidity, particularly in summer, can accelerate the deterioration of the fragile heritage.
During a visit to the caves in August 2019, Xi asked experts whether Dunhuang had been seeing more rain in recent years. He then turned to another challenge: how to balance growing visitor numbers with the need to protect the grottoes.
"His questions addressed the most pressing challenges facing the heritage," Fan Jinshi, honorary president of Dunhuang Academy, recalled.
Since the Mogao Caves were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987, visitor numbers have risen steadily, increasing the strain on the environment inside the grottoes.
"For a World Heritage site, conservation comes first. Tourism comes second," Xi said, emphasizing that economic benefits should never take precedence over preservation.
The attention Xi has paid to Dunhuang is part of a broader commitment to protecting China's millennia-old cultural heritage. Over the years, he has repeatedly called for the protection of cultural relics, archaeological discoveries and traditional culture, while visiting heritage sites across the country to witness conservation efforts firsthand.
"Protecting and passing on our historical and cultural heritage is a responsibility to history and to the people," Xi has said.
To Xi, China's cultural legacy is not simply a glimpse into the past. It continues to shape the present and inspire the future.
For centuries, Dunhuang stood at the crossroads of the Silk Road, where merchants, monks, artists and travelers converged, bringing with them ideas, faiths and artistic traditions from across Asia.
Standing before a mural in Mogao Cave 323 depicting Zhang Qian's journey to the Western regions, Xi was drawn to a scene of openness and exchange dating back more than two millennia. The Tang Dynasty (618-907) artwork tells a story not only of diplomacy, but also of the encounters and exchanges along the Silk Road.
"Dunhuang culture reflects the cultural confidence of the Chinese nation. Only a civilization that is confident in itself can preserve its own identity while embracing, learning from and drawing on the best of other civilizations," Xi has said.
During his visit to Dunhuang, Xi called for Dunhuang Academy, which oversees the conservation and study of the Mogao Caves and other major grotto sites in the region, to become a model for World Heritage conservation.
Years later, that vision has been transformed into a comprehensive approach that combines craftsmanship, science and technology.
Inside Mogao Cave 454, conservator Yin Zhihong works with meticulous care to remove soot stains from a mural. The burning incense and candles have left the soot deeply embedded in the paint, so even the smallest mistake could cause damage.
Researchers are testing a flexible cleaning technique that uses a nanoscale sponge to lift the soot without harming the pigments. The technology is now moving from the laboratory into the caves, showing how scientific innovation is providing new tools for preserving cultural heritage.
But for Dunhuang, the focus is increasingly shifting from repairing damage to preventing it.
At the grottoes' monitoring center, a wall of screens offers a real-time picture of the caves and the environment around them. Temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels inside the grottoes are tracked alongside visitor numbers. Rainfall and blowing sand are monitored across hundreds of kilometers, helping conservation teams spot potential threats and act before damage occurs.
Smart cave doors turn that data into action. They automatically seal the grottoes when heavy rain approaches or sandstorms threaten, and open in fine weather to allow fresh air to circulate.
Digital technology is opening another path to protect and share the heritage. Dunhuang Academy is building high-resolution digital records that allow the murals, sculptures and manuscripts to be preserved and studied remotely, while online exhibitions allow more people to experience the heritage without adding to the pressure on the sites.
Dunhuang is part of a broader nationwide effort. Under Xi's leadership, China has increasingly prioritized the protection of cultural heritage, while promoting responsible use and minimal intervention. Years of investment, technological advances and painstaking conservation work have strengthened China's capacity to safeguard its cultural and historical legacy.
That expertise is also being introduced beyond China's borders.
In Uzbekistan's ancient city of Khiva, a major Silk Road hub, Chinese heritage experts worked with local counterparts to restore historical sites, helping bring the once-weathered city back to life. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Public Security (MPS) said on Thursday that Chinese and Thai police recently worked together to bust a major cross-border credit card fraud ring targeting Chinese citizens, arresting nine suspects.
The operation, jointly carried out by the MPS and Thailand's Royal Thai Police headquarters, resulted in the arrest of four Chinese nationals and five Thai nationals, the ministry noted in a statement.
The two sides coordinated the timing of the crackdown and dismantled several criminal sites, arresting the suspects, the ministry said.
According to the statement, Chinese police uncovered the transnational criminal ring in 2025 and promptly shared information about the case with their Thai counterparts and sought their assistance.
Investigations found that two of the suspects had conspired, with one allegedly operating a shop in Thailand as a front for illegally obtaining victims' credit card information, while the other allegedly used the stolen data to make counterfeit cards and recruited people to use the cards for fraudulent transactions and launder the illicit proceeds for profit. Authorities have so far identified more than 5 million yuan (about 736,500 U.S. dollars) in financial losses linked to this case.
The operation marked the first coordinated joint law enforcement action by police from the two countries in recent years targeting economic crime, the ministry said.
It added that the two sides will explore establishing a regular cooperation mechanism to combat cross-border economic crimes, with plans to deepen collaboration in areas including information sharing, exchange of expertise, joint analysis, the pursuit of suspects, and the recovery of illicit proceeds. ■

British firm Inzpire to train Ukrainian pilots in air tactics
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:49:43 BST
17:49:43 KST

The Ministry of Defence is to award Inzpire a contract worth £502k to deliver air warfare education and training to the Ukrainian Air Force, covering roughly 20 weeks of instruction a year, the department stated in a contract award notice.
The contract runs for a year from 26 August 2026, with a single 12-month option period available, and the earliest date for signature is 26 August.
According to the notice, the work covers an air tactics and planning course, including the setting of training objectives, course development and delivery. The contract was placed directly rather than through competition, and is classified under the common procurement vocabulary code for technical training services.
The supplier is Inzpire Limited, a company based at Alpha Court in Lincoln and recorded as a small or medium-sized enterprise.
Inzpire was founded in 2006 by former RAF aircrew and has built its business around mission planning software and the provision of experienced military personnel as instructors and advisers. Its GECO mission system is used on British and export aircraft, and the company has held training and evaluation contracts across the RAF and Royal Navy, including work supporting fast jet and rotary wing crews.
Britain has trained Ukrainian personnel continuously since 2022, most visibly through Operation Interflex, the infantry training programme run in the UK with contributions from more than a dozen partner nations, which has put tens of thousands of recruits through basic soldiering courses. Air training has been a smaller and less publicised strand.
Ukrainian pilots began elementary flying training in the UK in 2023 as part of the international effort to prepare crews for the F-16, with the aircraft themselves supplied by Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium since Britain does not operate the type. Language training and ground school ran alongside, with conversion to type handled elsewhere.
Tactics and planning instruction of the kind covered by this contract addresses a different problem from flying the aircraft. Soviet-derived air forces were built around close ground control, with controllers directing aircraft onto targets, while NATO practice places far more responsibility on the aircrew to plan missions, interpret the air picture and make decisions in flight.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:48:44 UTC
17:48:44 KST

Berlin-based nonprofit HateAid has filed a criminal complaint against Meta’s AI-powered smart glasses, saying the device violates Germany’s strict privacy laws and should be banned, Politico reports.
In recent months, the Meta glasses have been the subject of a flood of complaints, with reports of people being filmed without consent or having intimate footage captured without the knowledge that Meta’s contractors could be reviewing them.
HateAid has argued that selling Meta’s smart glasses in Germany is a criminal offense because the device allows people to secretly film others. The lawsuit claims that selling the glasses in Germany violates the Telecommunications, Digital Services and Data Protection Act. HateAid’s complaint is against Meta, Ray-Ban, and Oakley, as well as several retailers.
Meta spokesman Matthew Pollard said the smart glasses were approved by German watchdog BNetzA in 2022 and
are designed to be more secure than any smartphone.
Security measures include an LED light that turns on when the glasses are recording video, and technology that prevents the light from being changed.
Meanwhile, HateAid said the glasses should only be marketed if they are clearly identifiable and there should be clear restrictions on where they can’t be used.
European privacy watchdogs have commissioned a report on smart glasses, which is expected to be ready by the end of the summer.

Photos: Hope fades in Colombia as teams dig for earthquake survivors
Colombian rescuers battle time to save lives after deadly 7.4 earthquake, as hopes dwindle in search for survivors.
Colombian rescuers are racing against time to find survivors of Monday’s powerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake, as search operations stretch into a fourth day across the country’s west.
Authorities say at least 265 people have been killed and more than 3,500 injured, while close to 500 remain unaccounted for in the strongest quake to hit Colombia this century.
In the city of Pereira, crews are focusing on a collapsed bakery where they believe street vendor Pablo Loaiza may still be trapped.
Specialist teams using vibration sensors and sniffer dogs have reported intermittent signs that someone could be alive beneath the concrete.
Outside, relatives keep vigil. “My heart is about to burst out of my chest,” said his niece, 16-year-old Sara Loaiza.
Rescue workers in Cali and Pereira are digging through unstable rubble with cranes and hand tools, frequently ordering silence to listen for voices.
President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared an “economic emergency” and three days of national mourning, as thousands of people sleep outdoors in makeshift shelters and volunteers organise food, water and blood donations for the worst-hit communities.

Sweden's right-wing government lags in poll, but gap narrows
STOCKHOLM, Aug 13 - Sweden's ruling right-wing coalition government is lagging centre-left opposition parties ahead of an election for parliament next month, but the gap between the two sides has narrowed since June, a new opinion poll showed.
The July 29 to August 10 survey, published by the daily Svenska Dagbladet, showed Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson may again become prime minister after four years in opposition, replacing Ulf Kristersson of the right-wing Moderates.
Swedes go to the polls on September 13 and the election campaign focuses on cost of living, security, immigration, crime and energy supply.
Support for the four opposition parties, of which Andersson's Social Democrats is the biggest by far, stood at 50.6%, up from the 48.9% they won in the 2022 election, according to the survey of 2,016 voters by pollster Demoskop.
The backing for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's governing bloc, including the closely aligned far-right Sweden Democrats, stood at 46.9%, down from the 49.6% they won in the last election four years ago.
In a blow to the government's chances of staying in power, junior coalition member the Liberals polled just 2.4%, well below the 4% threshold to win Riksdag seats.
Andersson's Social Democrats, Sweden's largest party, was set to win 30.2%, the poll showed, against 30.3% four years ago, while the Moderate Party could see a decline to 16.8% from 19.1% over the same period.
It remains unclear with which opposition parties Andersson would form a government, but a shift in power is likely to entail more welfare spending with no big changes on immigration, defence or support for Ukraine.
The Sweden Democrats, who plan to join the cabinet for the first time if the right-wing bloc wins, had 20.2% support, down from 20.5%. Its leader, Jimmie Akesson, has said his party aims to hold several major ministerial posts. REUTERS

Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

17:45:25 KST

Your takeaway habit is feeding Dutch inflation, says DNB
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch households are spending so much on takeaway meals that it is impacting national inflation, the Dutch central bank DNB has reported.
Delivery meals have nearly doubled as a share of the average shopping basket, from around 1.6% in 2015 to just over 3% today, DNB said on Thursday.
Prices have climbed fast. With more people spending, delivery firms have also passed on higher wage, energy and ingredient costs, and between 2020 and 2023 the category went from adding less than 0.1 percentage point to inflation to a full 0.35 point.
It has since eased back to 0.13 point – but only because prices stopped rising so fast, not because anyone is ordering less, DNB said.
The bank traces consumer habits back to the Covid pandemic, when locked-down households began using ordering apps much more, especially while working from home.
Dutch inflation has sat above the European Central Bank’s 2% target for years, driven mainly by rents and food prices. The pizza and sushi deliveries are now also hitting the figures.

Drought amid the heat may damage crops and the sowing of winter crops - Ukrhydrometeorological Center

Unknown Publisher

Drought amid the heat may damage crops and the sowing of winter crops - Ukrhydrometeorological Center
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported that the heat at the beginning of August was caused by African air and broke records in the west. The drought may damage late-season crops and soil preparation for winter crops.
The heat at the beginning of August in Ukraine was caused by African air masses and reached record levels in the western regions, while the intensification of drought against this backdrop could threaten the sunflower, corn, and buckwheat harvests, as well as create unfavorable conditions for preparing the soil for sowing winter crops for the 2027 harvest, the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center reported, according to UNN.
Details
"The first ten days of August in Ukraine, compared with the climatic norm, proved to be among the warmest in the western regions in terms of the average ten-day and maximum air temperatures for the entire observation period," the report said.
Average daily air temperatures on the hottest days, as noted, "exceeded the climatic norm by 4-9 ℃".
"This temperature pattern was caused by the arrival in Ukraine of hot air masses of African origin. In the second half of the ten-day period, the movement of an active cold front through the western and northern regions caused a brief cooling in this area, uneven rainfall, and locally heavy showers accompanied by hail and squalls," the report said.
During the first ten days of August, as a result of hot weather on most days and predominantly dry conditions, atmospheric and soil drought spread and intensified, creating unfavorable agrometeorological conditions for the completion of the growing season of late agricultural crops throughout the country. In areas where reserves of available moisture had already been depleted, the growing season of late agricultural crops ended prematurely. This was also facilitated by dry winds observed across most of the country
"Such a high-temperature regime may have a particularly negative impact on the yield of sunflowers, which are in the mass flowering phase; on the formation of corn ears and grain filling; and on the amount of grain in buckwheat, which is undergoing grain formation," the report emphasizes.
In the southern regions, as noted, "premature ripening of corn grain and sunflower seeds was observed, resulting in a reduction in the weight of the grain and seeds (a decrease in productivity)".
"As a result of the adverse effect of the heat on late agricultural crops, loss of turgor (wilting of plants) during the daytime and drying of plants were observed; leaves and ovaries fell off, while sunscald appeared on the leaves and fruit," the report states.
In most regions, the prolonged precipitation deficit throughout the summer created unfavorable conditions for preparing the soil for sowing winter crops for the 2027 harvest. First and foremost, winter rapeseed, whose optimal sowing period falls between August 10 and 25

Six Arab football federations back FIFA's Infantino

Breadcrumb
Six Arab national football associations back FIFA's Infantino
Six heads of Arab national football associations, including Qatar and 2030 World Cup co-hosts Morocco, backed FIFA President Gianni Infantino on Thursday, with football's world governing body in crisis following a failed private investment plan.
Infantino, who is seeking reelection next year, has faced open revolt after three confederations—UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF—called for him to quit over his aborted bid to bring private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.
The Swiss administrator had proposed carving off the commercial rights to the World Cup and selling 20% to private investors to raise about $4.2 billion.
"Recognising the important role of Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening cooperation among football associations across the Arab world, we ... express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide," the heads of the six federations said in a joint statement.
The statement was signed by the heads of the national federations of Qatar, Lebanon, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt and Mauritania. Four of the six signatories are also FIFA Council members.
"We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together," they said.
"We look forward to continuing our close cooperation with him towards a stronger and more prosperous future for world football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to the global game."
Infantino’s withdrawn proposal came with a $20 million grant for member associations for the next funding cycle, an amount that could have been doubled if they signed the deal.
Despite the opposition of the three confederations, which represent 136 of the 211 member associations who will vote in the FIFA presidential election in March, Infantino still has plenty of allies in the game.

Lockheed calls its GRIZZLY containerized launcher production-ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:39:45 UTC
17:39:45 KST

- Lockheed Martin posted video Tuesday describing its GRIZZLY containerized missile launcher as production-ready and reloadable.
- GRIZZLY completed its first Hellfire missile live-fire test in March 2026 and intercepted a Group 3 drone using a JAGM missile in June 2026.
Lockheed Martin posted a new video of live-fire testing for GRIZZLY, its containerized missile launcher, describing the system as production-ready and built to add mobility to distributed weapons.
“Built fast. Built flexible. Built for the mission. GRIZZLY is an affordable, reloadable and production-ready containerized launcher designed to bring mobility and adaptability to the fight. The future of defense is here, and it’s containerized,” Lockheed Martin said in the post.
GRIZZLY packages a missile launcher inside a standard 10-foot Tricon shipping container, a size small enough to move by truck, rail or ship without specialized transport equipment. Lockheed Martin built the system using existing weapon and launcher architecture, including the fielded M299 launcher, completing development in about six months through internal company investment rather than a government contract.
The company completed its first integrated live-fire test of GRIZZLY in March 2026, firing a Hellfire missile from the container in both vertical and angled launch configurations. That test validated the launcher’s ability to load and fire a missile directly from the containerized format, according to Lockheed Martin. The system uses commercial off-the-shelf materials, which the company says lowers logistics costs and shortens acquisition timelines compared with custom-built launcher hardware.
Lockheed Martin expanded GRIZZLY’s role in June 2026, when it used the launcher to intercept a Group 3 one-way attack drone with a Joint Air-to-Ground Missile, or JAGM, for the first time. JAGM is a Lockheed Martin-built precision missile designed to replace both the Hellfire and the TOW anti-tank missile, combining a dual-mode seeker that can lock onto a target using laser guidance, radar, or infrared imaging depending on conditions like weather, smoke, or enemy jamming.
The missile was originally developed for use on helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft to strike armored vehicles, but its guidance flexibility has made it increasingly attractive for counter-drone missions, where a target’s small size and fast, erratic movement make a single-mode seeker less reliable. That June test paired GRIZZLY with the company’s Sanctum counter-unmanned aircraft system, showing the launcher can function for defensive point-defense missions as well as offensive strikes. Group 3 drones generally weigh between 55 and 1,320 pounds (25 to 600 kilograms), covering midsize unmanned aircraft that fall between small commercial drones and larger military systems.
The choice of Hellfire as GRIZZLY’s original interceptor has drawn some skepticism online, where critics have questioned whether a missile originally built as an anti-armor weapon, and one that costs roughly $150,000 per unit, makes sense as a counter-drone tool against targets that can cost a few thousand dollars to build. That criticism echoes a broader debate in air defense circles over cost-per-kill economics, the same imbalance that has driven interest in cheaper interceptor drones and directed-energy weapons. But the case for using an already fielded, thoroughly proven missile family is straightforward from a logistics standpoint. Both Hellfire and JAGM have extensive combat reliability behind them, and pairing either with GRIZZLY means a unit defending a rear base or an expeditionary staging area does not need to stock a separate munition, train a new crew, or add personnel to operate a dedicated interceptor system. That modularity also positions GRIZZLY against one of the cheaper interceptor options on the market today, Russia’s Pantsir-based systems, whose interceptor missiles are estimated to start around $200,000 per unit, putting Lockheed Martin’s missile costs in a comparable range rather than a clear disadvantage.
Lockheed Martin has said GRIZZLY is designed to work with different command, control and sensor systems rather than a single dedicated network, allowing it to integrate into a range of operational setups. The company has also developed a related containerized launcher called Kodiak, which completed its first live-fire test earlier this month using a Reduced-Range Practice Rocket to demonstrate offensive fires with GMLRS-family munitions.
The M299 launcher architecture GRIZZLY draws on is already fielded on Apache helicopters and other aircraft, giving Lockheed Martin an established design base rather than a clean-sheet launcher build. Tricon containers, the standard shipping format GRIZZLY uses, are a military logistics standard already used to transport ammunition, vehicles and equipment worldwide, which is part of why a container-based launcher can blend into existing supply chains without drawing attention as a distinct military system.
U.S. and allied interest in similar containerized systems has grown alongside concerns that fixed launch sites are increasingly vulnerable to satellite tracking and long-range precision strikes, a lesson reinforced repeatedly during the war in Ukraine.

US diplomat calls Israeli settler siege of West Bank homes ‘act of terror’
Israeli settlers have blocked the homes of three Palestinian families in Qusra, cutting them off from food and supplies.
The United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has said a days-long siege of Palestinian homes by Israeli settlers amounts to “terror”.
Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has voiced support for Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, made the unusually critical comments on Thursday, after Israeli settlers besieged three Palestinian homes in the village of Qusra near Nablus, including one belonging to a dual US citizen.

Palestinian residents say they have been cut off from water, electricity and other critical supplies during the siege, which they describe as an attempt by the settlers to seize their land.
“Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting,” Huckabee wrote in a post on X. “No excuse for such thuggish behaviour.”
The Times of Israel reported that Israeli forces and police attempted to “evacuate the settlers” early on Thursday after a previous failed effort the day before. The settlers, who have used rocks and tents to block the Palestinian homes, remained in the area as of Thursday morning, according to the report.
Loai Ridi, an American-Palestinian who owns a house in the village, said his brother Qusai Abu Rida and 18-year-old nephew, Ahmed, were among those trapped.
Speaking to Al Jazeera from Toledo in the US, he said the family was relying on a temporary solar power system and leftover well water from the winter after supply lines were cut.
“He [Qusai Abu Rida] does not want to leave the home. Because if he leaves the home, the settlers will take over immediately,” Ridi said.
Aisha Abu Rida, a Palestinian besieged in the town, vowed “not [to] leave our home, no matter what happens”, in comments to Al Jazeera.
Nida Ibrahim, Al Jazeera’s correspondent in the occupied West Bank, said the village of Qusra “in general is under siege”.
“We are trying to get to Qusra through the roads. But every single entrance to Qusra is blocked by the Israeli army. And that is usually done to prevent other Palestinians from trying to come and offer help to these families,” she said.
“So not only are we talking about three families trapped in their homes, but we are also talking about a whole village that is under siege because of something they did not do.”
Israeli military claims to dismantle ‘illegal outposts’
Huckabee, however, also defended Israeli authorities, saying they had gone to Qusra at the request of the US embassy “to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this”. The US ambassador shared footage appearing to show Israeli tanks rolling into the West Bank town.
Israel’s military on Thursday said its forces had dismantled “two illegal outposts … on the outskirts of the Qusra and Jalud areas” of the occupied West Bank, confiscated equipment and detained one Israeli.
Israeli settlers regularly attack Palestinians and their property in the occupied West Bank, sometimes in the presence of Israeli forces who have been accused of backing the settlers.
Violence and land seizures in the Palestinian territory have intensified in recent months, with settlers emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which has overseen a rapid expansion of settlement construction in the territory.
Qusra sits in Area B of the occupied West Bank, nominally under Palestinian civil administration. The village has faced a string of recent attacks, including the burning of a newly built mosque last month.
In the neighbouring village of Jalud, a similar two-week siege in July forced two Palestinian families off their land before settlers took over the property.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in the occupied West Bank in settlements that are considered illegal under international law, alongside roughly three million Palestinians. Israel has occupied the territory since 1967.

Millions witnessed the most significant eclipse in Europe for decades yesterday evening as the Sun disappeared behind the Moon. Here are some of the best shots taken from the celestial event.
Parts of mainland Europe experienced its full solar eclipse in two decades yesterday evening, with the moon passing directly between the Earth and the Sun.
Considering the next total solar eclipse is not due to occur until 2081 for France, 2090 for the UK and not until the next century for Germany (Spain, on the other hand, get to see one next year), it was an event not worth missing.
Here are some of the best shots from yesterday's historic celestial event.

Why Islamophobia in Germany is a structural problem at the heart of society
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

While Islamophobic crimes in Germany are decreasing, it's important not to become complacent.
In the first half of 2026, authorities recorded 231 offences, a significant decrease from 489 in the same period last year.
However, the federal government notes that these are preliminary figures and may increase with subsequent reports.
Thirty-three of the recorded cases were committed online, 44 were classified as incitement to hatred, and 13 involved the use of symbols of unconstitutional organisations.
In addition, there were 11 violent crimes, nine cases of coercion or threats, and three cases of property damage.
But the official figures represent only the tip of the iceberg.
The CLAIM alliance, a coalition of more than 50 civil society organisations, recently documented 4,096 anti-Muslim incidents nationwide in 2025 – both criminal and non-criminal.
This amounts to over 11 incidents on average each day, representing a 33 percent increase from 2024.
The number of unreported cases is likely to be far higher: According to a study by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, only four percent of those affected in Germany report experiencing discrimination.
Seventy-five percent of Muslims surveyed reported experiencing racist discrimination in government agencies. Therefore, CLAIM emphasises: "Anti-Muslim racism is not a fringe phenomenon, but a structural problem".
A closer look at the figures reveals that women are particularly affected: In 64.5 percent of documented cases, women were the target. Women, especially those wearing headscarves, are particularly vulnerable to insults, threats, and physical assaults.
In Dresden, for example, a senior citizen attempted to forcibly rip the headscarf off a 14-year-old girl. In Düsseldorf, an unknown assailant punched a woman wearing a headscarf in the face, causing her to briefly lose consciousness.
A Muslim family in Berlin-Zehlendorf has been terrorised for years by their neighbour, who has sent racist hate messages; at least 15 police reports have gone unanswered.
In North Rhine-Westphalia, several mosque communities have received bomb threats with explicitly anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian content.
These cases are not fringe events. They are representative of a development that demonstrates that Islamophobia has long since become a structural problem and has arrived in the mainstream of society.
Whether it's the Motra Monitor, the "Independent Expert Group on Islamophobia" dissolved by the CDU/CSU, the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's studies on the centre of society, or other studies, they all confirm what many don't want to hear: anti-Muslim prejudice is not confined to the extreme fringes.
It is an integral part of the mainstream of society. A significant portion of the population sees Islam not as an enrichment, but as a threat, and in some cases, acts accordingly.
Statistics often differ
Attacks on mosques, their documentation, and statistical recording are part of this development. For example, the police recorded 79 attacks on mosques in 2024.
However, even here, the figures vary depending on the recording method: The organisation #brandeilig documented 96 attacks for the same year, while the Islamic religious community Turkish-Islamic Union for Religious Affairs, in its own survey, counted a total of 175 attacks for 2024.
This discrepancy highlights a problem: Official statistics record incidents only according to a narrow definition of criminal law, while the lived reality of those affected is often quite different.
Beyond physical violence, it is primarily everyday discrimination that shapes the lives of many Muslims. The Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency recorded 175 inquiries about Islam-based discrimination in the first half of 2025 alone.
Islamophobia is omnipresent: the labour market is currently the most frequently affected area.
Ali Pasa Akbas, chairman of the Union of Turkish-Islamic Cultural Associations in Europe (ATIB), is particularly concerned about structural disadvantages.
Muslims are not only harassed on the street or online, he told TRT Deutsch. Discrimination also occurs daily in the workplace, when searching for housing, and in educational institutions.
Akbas therefore advocated for a more intensive dialogue with security authorities and politicians in order to develop joint strategies against Islamophobia and exclusion.
Organisations that have been committed to social cohesion for decades should be perceived as trustworthy partners in this process.
However, all social actors are called upon to combat structural disadvantage.
"Only through cooperation between the state, politics, civil society, and the media can we succeed in sustainably combating exclusion and racism," said Akbas.
At the same time, he emphasised his organisation's willingness to contribute to a cooperative partnership based on trust.
Kenan Aslan, chairman of the Union of International Democrats (UID), also views this development with great concern. The figures are an alarming sign of the growing threat Muslims face in their daily lives, the 45-year-old told our editorial team.
Incidents in the workplace, in education, and in public services are particularly worrying and pose a lasting threat to social cohesion.
Aslan emphasised that as a multi-religious society, we share the responsibility to uphold human dignity and protect life. Mosques and places of worship are "symbols of peace, tolerance, and religious freedom".
Their protection must therefore be a top priority for government action.
The chairman of the UID expects significantly stronger, preventative, and visible protection of mosques and other places of worship from the security authorities.
At the same time, political leaders must prosecute Islamophobic hate crimes consistently, effectively, and transparently.
"Because a society in which religious freedom is respected and protected is a society with a future," Aslan tells TRT Deutsch
How media contribute to exclusion
A key factor in the spread of anti-Muslim sentiment is the media. Studies show that reporting on Islam and Muslims is often stereotypical and negative.
Islam is frequently associated with terrorism and threats, while Muslims are portrayed as backward, foreign, or homogeneous.
This media bias contributes to the normalisation of exclusion and provides an additional platform for positions that have long since become socially acceptable in political debate.
On the streets, in government offices, when searching for housing, at work, in the media, and in the minds of many people.
The actual number of unreported cases is often greater than what official figures show. Ignoring the problem only deepens its roots. However, giving in to despair would be a mistake.
The task for the coming years will be not only to document Islamophobia but to counter it with all available means.
This includes education, protecting those affected, and fostering a culture of cooperation and respect that enables participation and leaves no room for hatred and exclusion.
This article was first published on TRT Deutsch

‘Successful in business, not debate’: Parliament Monsoon Session ends with 12 Bills passed, Lok Sabha productivity at 19%
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 13, 2026, 14:05 IST

Union minister Kiren Rijiju targets opposition
NEW DELHI: Parliament’s Monsoon Session ended on Thursday with both the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha being adjourned sine die, bringing to a close a session marked by repeated disruptions and protests by opposition parties.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said the session was successful in terms of legislative business, with 12 Bills passed, but criticised the quality of debates and discussions.Addressing a press briefing, he said the government was not satisfied with the level of parliamentary discussion during the session.
Rijiju said Lok Sabha productivity stood at 19% of the total allotted time, while Rajya Sabha recorded 39%.“The Monsoon Session concluded today. We view it from two perspectives. In terms of business, it was a very successful session; we passed a total of 12 bills. However, from the perspective of debate and discussion, it was not as successful,” Rijiju said.
He alleged that opposition parties repeatedly disrupted proceedings and avoided discussions offered by the government.“Based on my parliamentary experience and what I have seen in my life, this is the first time the Opposition was running away from discussions,” he said.
According to Rijiju, 11 Bills were passed in the Lok Sabha without discussion, while one Bill underwent discussion. He said the Bills were discussed in the Rajya Sabha, although Congress and some other Opposition members staged a walkout.
Public Examinations Bill was discussed in both Houses
Rijiju said the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Bill was the only legislation to undergo a full discussion in the Lok Sabha during the session.“Only one bill, addressing the issue of paper leaks and unfair means in examinations, underwent a full discussion in the Lok Sabha,” he said.The legislation, which seeks to prevent unfair means in public examinations, was also discussed in the Rajya Sabha before being passed during the session.
Opposition protests continued through the session
The Monsoon Session, which began on July 20, witnessed prolonged disruptions in both Houses.Opposition protests initially focused on the NEET paper leak and alleged irregularities involving donations to the Ram temple in Ayodhya.The opposition later sought discussions on police action against students protesting over the NEET issue and demanded statements from Prime Minister Narendra Modi and home minister Amit Shah.The government offered a discussion on the NEET paper leak and related issues, along with a reply from Shah, but the proposal was rejected by the Congress. A similar proposal made on Wednesday also failed to break the deadlock.Congress leader and leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said the Opposition wanted answers over allegations concerning police action against protesting students and criticised the prospect of a speech by Shah.
Rijiju accused Congress MPs of reducing their parliamentary role to sloganeering and creating disruptions.“Another observation I have made is that Congress MPs seem to believe their primary role is merely to raise slogans and create a ruckus with placards and banners,” he said.
He also said disruptions had particularly affected newly elected MPs by limiting opportunities for debate and discussion.“As the minister of parliamentary affairs, I feel genuinely sorry for the Congress MPs, especially the new ones,” Rijiju said. “How can they learn if there are no debates or discussions?”He expressed hope that opposition parties would reflect on their conduct and participate in more substantive debates when Parliament reconvenes for the Winter Session.The session also saw counter-protests between BJP and INDIA bloc MPs at the Makar Dwar steps of the Parliament complex.

Latvian State Forests fined 7.86 million euros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:34:48 UTC
17:34:48 KST

Latvia’s Competition Council (KP) has imposed a 7.86 million euros fine on state-owned forestry company Latvijas valsts meži (LVM) for creating unjustified competitive advantages for companies holding long-term logging agreements, Competition Council chairwoman Ieva Šmite announced at a press conference on Thursday.
The authority found that LVM’s long-term logging agreement partners – AS Pata Saldus, AS Pata Strenči, SIA Pata Jēkabpils, SIA Berivs, SIA Krebsar and SIA ACA Timber – were granted access to specific timber resources and logging rights without having to participate in public auctions or compete for those resources with other market participants.
Other companies, meanwhile, could obtain the same types of resources only through public auctions, where they had to compete for limited supplies and did not enjoy equivalent access.
For the infringement, the Competition Council imposed a 7.86 million euros fine on LVM and ordered the company to fulfil two legal obligations: end the advantages arising from the long-term logging agreements and introduce timber sales procedures that provide all interested market participants with equal opportunities to purchase timber.
According to the Competition Council,
the arrangements gave certain long-term agreement partners unjustified competitive advantages
and reduced their business risks, while discriminating against other companies.
The authority also found that the volume of softwood sawlogs available to other market participants was reduced. The infringement distorted competition in the timber market over a prolonged period and also had negative effects on related markets.
In total, the Competition Council found that 11 long-term logging agreements remained in force in 2023, with the longest running until 2096. The Competition Council opened its investigation into LVM implementation of long-term logging agreements after the 1st of January 2020 in February 2026.
Before formally opening the case, the Competition Council began negotiations with LVM on 14 December 2024 in an attempt to address the company’s non-compliance with Latvia’s Competition Law. During the negotiations, the authority met and corresponded with LVM several times, repeatedly calling on the company to find a solution to the long-term logging agreement issue.
In June 2025, the Competition Council sent a letter to LVM and the Ministry of Agriculture warning about the negative impact of the agreements on competition and asking the two institutions to jointly develop proposals to eliminate the competition law concerns.
The ministry said it was working with LVM and planned to submit proposals by August 2025.
However, no proposals were received by the deadline, and in September the Competition Council again reminded the parties of the need to ensure free and fair competition in the timber market.
In November 2025, Competition Council representatives met then-Agriculture Minister Armands Krauze to discuss the issue and possible solutions. According to the authority, the minister considered proposing legislative amendments that would ensure fair competition not only in the use of forest resources but also in relation to other environmental resources. However, no concrete proposals followed.
On the 5th of December, 2025, the Competition Council again wrote to LVM, reiterating that the long-term agreements violated the principle of competitive neutrality and giving the company until the 23rd of December to submit concrete proposals.
The authority also warned that if no proposals were submitted,
it could launch formal proceedings and impose sanctions if a violation of competition law was established.
The Competition Council noted that negotiations giving LVM an opportunity to address the competitive neutrality concerns lasted for more than a year before the case was formally opened.
The Competition Council also referred to a December 2022 letter from the Prosecutor General’s Office. Following an investigation, prosecutors had issued a warning to LVM concerning procedures for restructuring the long-term logging agreements, drawing attention to legal requirements applicable to state-owned companies and questioning the justification for the procedure used.
The Prosecutor General’s Office also sent a letter to the Ministry of Agriculture, as Latvia’s highest authority responsible for the forestry sector, calling for regulations governing the operation of long-term logging agreements and preventing unequal treatment of market participants.
Thus, according to the Competition Council,
both LVM and the Agriculture Ministry had been aware since the end of 2022 that the issue required a solution.
In early February this year, LVM informed the Competition Council that it had filed court claims seeking the termination of the long-term agreements. However, citing restricted-access information, the company did not provide further details about the claims.
As LVM failed to demonstrate within the deadline set by the Competition Council that the competition concerns had been eliminated, the authority formally opened proceedings.
LVM has previously said that, taking into account the Competition Council’s position on ensuring free and fair competition in the timber market, it had applied to Riga City Court seeking to have the agreements declared invalid. The company also asked the court to suspend the agreements until a final ruling enters into force.
LVM has stressed that the long-term logging agreements predate the company itself and were originally concluded by the State Forest Service. According to LVM, when the company was established 26 years ago, legislation required it to assume obligations arising from those agreements.
LVM maintains that it has not concluded any new long-term logging agreements during its existence
and has merely administered historical contracts inherited from the State Forest Service.
The company has also said that since the beginning of its operations it has sought ways to terminate the agreements, considering both their disproportionately long duration and the manner in which they had been extended by regional State Forest Service structures to be problematic.
The issue gained wider public attention in September 2025, when TV3 programme Nekā personīga, citing the Competition Council’s assessment, reported that LVM’s long-term agreements did not comply with competitive neutrality requirements.
The historical agreements were signed after Latvia regained independence and were originally intended to provide a degree of stability to state-owned companies involved in primary timber processing during the privatisation process.
LVM later inherited the long-term contracts but did not terminate them,
as a court had ruled that it could not do so.
Some of the exclusive agreements were restructured by LVM beginning in 2013. Others remained unchanged and are still valid for several decades. These arrangements continue to grant certain market participants special rights to purchase roundwood without participating in the state-owned company’s auctions, while the guaranteed timber supplied to these partners is unavailable to their competitors.
LVM reported revenue of 604.585 million euros in 2025, up 3.2% year-on-year, while profit increased by 37.7% to 206.73 million euros.
Latvijas valsts meži was established in 1999 and has share capital of EUR 525.989 million. The company manages state-owned forest land. LVM is wholly owned by the Latvian state, with the Ministry of Agriculture acting as the shareholder.

Unknown

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US and 40 other countries have urged the global community to follow stricter advance-notification procedures when conducting long-range missile launches.
In a joint statement issued Tuesday, the signatory countries said recent missile tests in the Pacific did not follow standard procedures for advance launch notification. “Conducting nuclear-capable ballistic missile tests without sufficient advance notice and detail is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests,” the statement said.
The statement applies to intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and space launch vehicles. It called for at least 24 hours’ advance notice and information including the missile class, launch window, launch area, and planned direction.
“Countries should also provide clear notices for airmen and mariners consistent with international standards to reduce risk, including in expected impact or landing areas,” the statement said.
Though the statement did not name any specific country, China fired a submarine-launched ballistic missile carrying a training warhead from the South China Sea into the Pacific Ocean in July, per USNI News. Taiwan’s National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said at the time that the action was “a provocation that destabilizes the Indo-Pacific.”
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) welcomed the joint statement. China has continued to bolster its military capabilities and use gray-zone tactics in an attempt to unilaterally alter the status quo in the Taiwan Strait and Indo-Pacific region, Lin said, per the foreign ministry.
“These actions not only threaten Taiwan but also pose serious challenges to the security and peace of neighboring countries and the region as a whole,” he said.
The foreign ministry emphasized that maintaining peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and Indo-Pacific has become a global consensus and serves the common interests of all parties.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s container shipping companies reported strong second-quarter profits Wednesday as an earlier-than-usual peak season helped support freight rates.
Yang Ming Marine Transport Corp. posted net profit of NT$5.7 billion (US$178.2 million) for the second quarter, up 4.82-fold from the same period a year earlier. Wan Hai Lines Ltd. reported net profit of NT$11.5 billion, up 9.71-fold year-on-year, according to CTEE.
Wan Hai said continued instability in the Middle East has disrupted some shipping routes and pushed up fuel costs, while congestion at several major ports has reduced available shipping capacity. The tighter supply has helped keep container shipping rates high, with the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), a key measure of shipping rates, remaining well above its level at the beginning of the year despite recent fluctuations.
Rates for shipments to the US have been particularly strong, while a shortage of available vessels has provided further support for prices.
Looking ahead to the third quarter, Yang Ming said European and US routes are entering their traditional peak season. Higher shipment volumes are expected to provide further support for the market.
At the same time, port congestion could pose a challenge to shipping operations. Major ports in Shanghai and Europe experienced heavier congestion in the second quarter due to weather, a temporary increase in shipments, and operational bottlenecks.
Yang Ming said it remains unclear whether the situation will improve in the third quarter.
With US tariff policies becoming clearer and supply chains gradually returning to normal, Wan Hai expects the market to strengthen toward the fourth quarter. Holiday-season restocking and inventory replenishment are expected to provide further support for freight rates and shipping volumes.

Japanese oak grows in cool northern Japanese forests and often requires more than a century before it can be crafted into casks. Its porous grain makes coopering exceptionally difficult, contributing to the wood’s rarity, according to the press release.
When Kavalan’s new-make spirit matures in Taiwan’s warm, humid climate, the whisky is said to develop notes of sandalwood, incense, and coconut alongside the distillery’s signature tropical fruit aromas.
King Car Group Chair Y.T. Lee (李玉鼎) was quoted as saying, “Mizunara oak is one of the rarest and most demanding casks in whisky making … Through Takahide Komatsu’s butterfly artwork, this release also celebrates the richness of Taiwan’s natural world.”

Students set new records for A-level grades in bumper year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:32:37 UTC
17:32:37 KST

Sixth-formers have basked in a summer of record-breaking exam results in academic and vocational subjects, allowing more than a quarter of a million 18-year-olds to go on to higher education.
The proportion of students in England gaining the highest grade of A* in A-level subjects rose to 9.7%, up from 9.4% last year, setting a new record outside the pandemic era, when exams were scrapped.
Northern Ireland was the best-performing country, with 30.7% of grades being As and A*s, followed by 29.6% in Wales and 28.7% in England.
The A-level results followed last week’s improved results in Scotland, where the proportion of students awarded Highers and Advanced Highers qualifications rose above 2019 pre-pandemic levels, and a record 18,000 Scottish school-leavers gained higher education places.
The bumper crop of results means nearly 263,000 UK pupils have already been accepted on to university courses starting this autumn, driven in part by the rising number of 18-year-olds in the population.
The results were boosted by improved results across the board, but mathematics in particular showed a strong improvement despite a rise in the number of candidates taking the subject.
Among the most striking trends this year was the surge in popularity of economics, which jumped from 10th most popular position last year to fifth, with more than 47,000 exam entries.
Myles McGinley, the managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, speaking at a briefing by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), said: “The students getting their A-level results today were born around 2008.
“So they’re the children of the financial crisis [and they] will have experienced the implications and impacts of that through Covid and beyond, and those forces that really shape the world.
“So I think it feels natural that they should be interested in that. And of course we know that economics provides excellent career options.”
As the Andy Burnham government focuses more closely on vocational subjects, examination boards published detailed results for level 3 qualifications, including BTecs and Cambridge Technicals, showing that just under 10% of the 300,000 candidates gained top grades.
Ian Bauckham, the head of England’s Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation (Ofqual), said the improved results could be trusted by employers.
“A-levels are trusted because they are awarded to rigorous and consistent national standards. Universities, employers and students can have confidence that an A-level grade represents what students know and can do.
“Vocational and technical qualifications are equally important. They help students develop the knowledge and skills needed for apprenticeships, employment and further study.
“When an employer or university sees these qualifications, they can be confident they demonstrate students’ genuine achievement.”
Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said: “A record 262,820 of UK 18-year-olds have earned a place at a university this year, including an increase in students from the most disadvantaged backgrounds. These students will go on to gain new skills and experiences that will benefit them throughout their whole lives.
“To those who have not got the results they were hoping for, don’t panic. There are still 26,000 courses available through clearing.”
The improvements in maths and further maths helped boys carry off a higher proportion of top grades. McGinley said: “The gap between boys and girls has widened: at A* and A grades in England boys are now a full percentage point ahead. However, with more girls taking A-levels the absolute number of girls achieving these grades is higher.”
But substantial regional disparities persist, with the East Midlands in particular missing out on the otherwise positive national trend. While nearly a third of candidates in London gained A*s and As in their A-level subjects, only 23.1% in the East Midlands did so, dropping to last place among England’s regions alongside the north-east.
Pepe Di’Iasio, the general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “These results are clearly affected by relative levels of socioeconomic disadvantage and reflect the structural inequalities which exist in our nation. Every year we say that we cannot go on like this and that as a society we must do more to support communities which often feel abandoned and neglected. When will we actually do that?”
Exam boards pushed back on any suggestion of grade inflation. Presenting the results at the JCQ briefing, Richard Harry, the director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board, WJEC, insisted grades could be trusted.
“What grade inflation really means is not outcomes going up. It really means that the grades no longer mean what they used to mean in terms of the level of attainment. The methods that we use to award qualifications are designed to ensure that those grades do mean the same thing.
“So that a learner in 2026 getting an A or an A* or a C can be confident that means the same thing in terms of the underlying knowledge, skills and understanding that those learners have, compared to those learners in previous years.”

Polish Armed Forces Operational Command confirmed the occurrence of a dangerous situation.

Eurovision to bar countries at war from hosting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:31:53 UTC
17:31:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Eurovision to bar countries at war from hosting, which includes Israel
Eurovision Song Contest organisers announced Wednesday that they were excluding any country in an armed conflict from hosting the competition and increased the mininum age of competitors.
While they did not mention any country by name, Israel, which has been at war in Gaza since 2023, came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.
Under the old rules, the winning country normally hosts the following year's competition.
Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region", they said in a statement.
In a first, five countries—Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland—boycotted the 2026 competition in Vienna over Israel's participation.
They said they could not take part alongside Israel because of its genocidal war on Gaza, ongoing since October 2023.
Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said in a statement that the changes had been guided by feedback from member countries.
"These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special," he added.
Minimum age requirement
The organisers also announced that competitors must be at at least 18, up from 16, on the day of their first rehearsal.
"This change continues the work already undertaken by the contest to strengthen safeguarding and protect younger artists from the pressures associated with competing at the Eurovision Song Contest," they added in the statement.
The youngest person to win the contest was 13-year-old Sandra Kim from Belgium in 1986, according to Eurovision records.
Eurovision is a co-production of public broadcasters belonging to the European Broadcasting Union. Since the EBU includes members from outside Europe, the contest is not limited to European countries.
The EBU said it could commission an independent security assessment before deciding whether a winning country is capable of hosting the event safely.
If a winning country is found unable to host the contest, the EBU will appoint another host nation.
Under the new rules, that country will organise the concert "in its own right" and "will not be required to stage the event on behalf of another member".
Ukraine hosted Eurovision in 2017 despite the conflict in the country's east between Ukrainian forces and Moscow-backed separatists.
But after Ukraine won the contest in 2022, it was unable to host the following year's edition because of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Eurovision 2023 was instead held in Liverpool in Britain on Ukraine's behalf.

Opinion
Beijing’s offshore insurance tax tests Hong Kong wealth management
While markets initially fell, more transparent cross-border oversight could strengthen the city’s credibility as a wealth management centre
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Matteo Giovannini is a finance professional with extensive experience in private and state-owned enterprises, specialising in Asian markets and cross-border project financing. 
Financial markets have been gripped by concern in recent days over reports that China was introducing a new tax on returns from offshore insurance policies. The significance of the episode could prove more complex than the initial market reaction suggests.
According to a report from Caixin, Chinese tax authorities have sought to collect tax on investment returns generated by offshore insurance policies held by mainland residents, with early enforcement cases reportedly emerging in Beijing and Hangzhou. The report unsettled financial markets, sending shares of Prudential, HSBC, AIA and other firms lower as investors reassessed businesses exposed to mainland demand.
According to China’s State Taxation Administration, the 20 per cent tax rate on relevant insurance investment income is not new and does not specifically target Hong Kong. The authority also urged the market not to overreact, seeking to correct the impression that China had launched a sweeping crackdown on Hong Kong insurance.
Therefore, the question is: are existing tax rules being enforced more systematically as authorities gain greater visibility over offshore financial assets?
For years, offshore insurance has occupied a distinctive place in mainland China’s wealth management landscape. To many affluent Chinese families, policies purchased in Hong Kong were never simply insurance products.
They also served as long-term investment vehicles, US dollar savings instruments, estate planning tools and a means of diversifying assets beyond the mainland financial system. By combining financial returns, protection, succession planning and access to international currencies, they offered several benefits in one product.

How Hong Kong can protect manual workers bearing brunt of heatwave
Heatwave has taken toll on indoor and outdoor workers, triggering calls for authorities to review heat stress prevention measures
At a bustling fruit store in Hong Kong’s Causeway Bay, a crowd of workers sporting damp towels around their necks or fan vests buy up chilled drinks to stay hydrated as temperatures hit 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 Fahrenheit) on a busy weekday morning.
Soaked in sweat, 29-year-old construction worker Yau is among the crowd, buying a litre of water to help beat the heat on Wednesday.
“I spend at least HK$100 a day on water lately. It is expensive, and I get poor just drinking water to survive the heat,” said Yau, who works without shade for a few hours every day.
At some stores, a one-litre bottle of cold water can set a busy worker back as much as HK$20.
The recent heatwave has also taken a toll on indoor workers. Cleaner Zoe Ip, who keeps the back staircases, car parks and outdoor areas at a private estate tidy, described the weather this summer as particularly “stifling” compared with past years.
Thanks to limited indoor ventilation, Ip said the air felt “thinner”, leaving her low on energy and her mouth feeling dry after just 20 minutes of sweeping the floors.

Monument against violence in youth care system vandalised
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Just two months after it was unveiled, the national youth care monument (Nationaal Monument Jeugdzorg) commemorating violence against young people in the system was vandalised in Apeldoorn.
“This feels like a new attack,” Naomi van Aggelen told broadcaster NOS. She worked for years on the monument and was herself wrongly sent to live at a youth care institution when she was 12 years old.
“It is a very sad sight,” she said of the monument meant to acknowledge the suffering of young people in care homes. “Actually, [it’s] a denial of that recognition.”
 Located in Apeldoorn’s Zuiderpark, the wings of the monument – titled De Erkenning (The Recognition) – were broken off and are now missing while scratches and dents are visible on what remains.
“Who does such a thing? We have no idea,” said Van Aggelen. “We don’t know where the wings are.”
The council has filed a police report and is said to be reviewing if additional security measures are needed.
The monument was commissioned after a 2019 report by De Winter Commission that found since WW2, some 20,000 children were the victims of violence in youth care. The organising foundation calls it a place of reparation, remembrance and “of vigilance: all current forms of violence must also stop.”
The future of the monument is still unclear. “I have no idea if we should leave the work for what it is,” said Van Aggelen. “Maybe we should glue it, then it symbolises another broken child in youth care.”

Rheinmetall test-fires kamikaze drone from truck-mounted launcher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
08:29:25 UTC
17:29:25 KST

- Rheinmetall launched its FV-014 loitering munition from a Containerized Missile Launcher mounted on an HX truck for the first time in July 2026.
- The FV-014 has a range of up to 100 kilometers, a flight duration of up to 70 minutes, and weighs about 22 kilograms at launch.
Rheinmetall launched its FV-014 loitering munition from a Containerized Missile Launcher mounted on an HX truck for the first time, the company said, completing both stationary and moving launches during a customer demonstration.
The test took place in July 2026 at the National Test Centre for Unmanned Aerial Systems at the German Aerospace Centre in Cochstedt, Saxony-Anhalt. The system carried out simulated operational profiles and attack flights during the demonstration. Both the FV-014 and the Containerized Missile Launcher are Rheinmetall in-house developments.
Rheinmetall first unveiled the Containerized Missile Launcher publicly at the Eurosatory defense exhibition in Paris in June 2026. The company has said the launcher, built from a standard 20-foot ISO shipping container, can hold up to 18 FV-014 munitions and can be deployed statically or mounted on platforms including Rheinmetall’s HX-series truck, rail cars or naval vessels. The July test at Cochstedt marked the first time the system launched from a truck while both stationary and in motion.
The FV-014 has a launch weight of about 22 kilograms (49 pounds), including a payload of roughly six kilograms (13 pounds). It carries a High-Explosive Dual Purpose warhead capable of penetrating more than 600 millimeters (24 inches) of solid armor steel, and Rheinmetall said the weapon is effective against both armored and unarmored targets as well as infrastructure.
The munition has an operational range of up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) and a flight duration of up to 70 minutes. Rheinmetall said an electrically powered propeller keeps the aircraft quiet during approach, and the system is designed to reduce its radar and infrared signature. After launch from the container using a booster, the FV-014 unfolds its wings and transitions into aerodynamic flight.
An operator controls the FV-014 from a ground station with what Rheinmetall calls permanent human-in-the-loop control, meaning a person must authorize each strike and can abort a mission if conditions change. Rheinmetall said the system is built to withstand GNSS interference through a high degree of autonomy, allowing it to operate in contested electronic warfare environments. Beyond individual strikes, the FV-014 supports swarm operations, letting operators engage multiple targets simultaneously or overwhelm enemy air defenses by forcing them to respond to more threats than they can track.
Rheinmetall said the Containerized Missile Launcher connects to command, control, communications, computers and intelligence systems, allowing launches to be triggered locally, by radio link or by satellite communication. The launcher includes its own power supply for extended operation in remote areas and uses commercial off-the-shelf components to reduce lifecycle costs. Rheinmetall also said the system includes a “sleeper” capability that allows it to be activated remotely after being positioned in the field.
Germany’s Bundeswehr has already ordered FV-014 systems, which are expected to equip Panzerbrigade 45, Germany’s armored brigade stationed in Lithuania, starting in 2027, according to Rheinmetall’s April 2026 contract announcement. The brigade is Germany’s first permanent combat formation deployed abroad since the Cold War. Rheinmetall said it plans to expand FV-014 deployment to mobile land vehicle platforms and seagoing units in the future.

By the end of the year, legislation will require bridges, already at the design and renovation stages, to include structures for rapid demolition, as well as to restore defensive trenches and river channels.
