Putin pays his first visit to Pacific island chain claimed by Japan, drawing a protest from Tokyo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:53:01 UTC
16:53:01 KST

Putin’s first trip to the Pacific island chain claimed by Japan draws a protest from Tokyo
MOSCOW (AP) — Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday made his first visit to the Kuril Islands, a Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that also is claimed by Japan, which voiced a diplomatic protest over the trip.
Putin visited a fish plant, a hospital and a school on Iturup, one of the volcanic chain’s southern islands. He also briefly spoke to local residents and met with the governor of Russia’s Sakhalin region, Valery Limarenko.
Japan asserts territorial rights to the four southernmost islands of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories. The Soviet Union took them from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the dispute kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.
Decades of diplomatic efforts to negotiate a settlement haven’t produced any visible results. Moscow over the years has also bolstered its military presence on the Kurils in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance in the dispute.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin’s visit to Iturup, which Japan calls Etorofu.
“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu (Iturup) Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.
He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he “promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterward.
Later Thursday, the Russian Embassy in Japan called Tokyo’s protest “unfounded” and said Nozdrev had explained that “the southern Kuril Islands are an integral part of the Russian Federation and became part of it following World War II on legitimate international grounds.”
Putin’s travels are “sovereign decisions of the Russian leadership and can’t be subject to discussion with foreign states,” the statement added.
Japan also protested in 2021 when Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited Iturup.
Putin in recent days has visited several regions in Siberia and the Far East. Before coming to Iturup, he stopped on Sakhalin Island to attend the final part of drills by Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
Speaking aboard a warship that was participating in the naval exercises, Putin said Wednesday that the current status of the Kuril Islands “is enshrined in international documents as a reality that arose following the outcome of World War II.”
“But even here, Russia was prepared to seek a solution with the goal of concluding a peace treaty with Japan,” he said.
Putin said that in the past, Moscow “had developed constructive relations with a number of Japanese leaders, including the tragically deceased former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who did much to bring Japan and Russia closer together, to align our positions.”
Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after it sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022 and “listed Russia as a source of primary threats,” a change in that constructive relationship, he added.
Russia remains ready “to cooperate with all its neighbors, including Japan and other states in the region,” Putin said.
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Putin’s visit is “incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories” and is “absolutely unacceptable.”
She said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.
“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said. “We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”
One of the reasons Japan has made the effort to maintain ties with Russia is to allow former Japanese residents to return to the islands and pay tribute at their graves as a humanitarian consideration.
Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s former president and prime minister who now serves as deputy chair of the country’s Security Council, responded to Takaichi’s remarks on X by saying, “This chatter won’t change a thing.”
The Kuril Islands “were, are, and will remain Russian land,” Medvedev, who himself visited the Kuril Islands four times as president and prime minister, wrote. “Anyone who fails to understand this will face the monstrous consequences of their delusion.”

Associated Press writer Mari Yamaguchi in Tokyo contributed.

Beyond ordinary volunteering: The story of Belarus’ Angel rescue team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:53:00 UTC
16:53:00 KST

News of the story 
        
                "Belarusians in the focus"
        
    
                                                              
            
                                                                              
            
                                    For the Angel search and rescue team, finding missing people is a finely tuned system where every minute counts, and high-profile stories are backed by strict protocols and grueling physical and mental demands. The group’s leader and founder, Sergei Kovgan, shares how a heartfelt impulse grew into a massive organization, explains why thermal-imaging drones and simple human empathy are crucial, and highlights what makes volunteering with the Angels so unique.
 
The Angel search and rescue team was officially registered in 2015, but its true birth date is 15 June 2012, when its first social media group was created. According to Sergei Kovgan, it all started with a heartfelt impulse. As a child, he dreamed of working in law enforcement, but it wasn’t meant to be. One weekend, while spending time with friends at a country house, he saw a woman on live television pleading for help because her father was lost. Realizing he was in nearly the exact same area where the man had gone missing, Sergei decided to help and invited a friend to join him.
“My friend and I arrived at the police station, and I was shocked that, apart from us, no one else had responded to that woman’s plea on a nationwide broadcast,” he said.
Back then, he thought it would be great to build a database of like-minded volunteers ready to help out in such situations. Initially, he planned to focus solely on wilderness searches. However, just a couple of days after the social media group was set up, a young woman went missing in Minsk, forcing them to take on urban searches as well. Gradually, a team took shape, search and rescue equipment was acquired, and a division of responsibilities by area was established.
Volunteering with the Angels is not a one-off act of help in one’s spare time, Sergei Kovgan admited with a smile. Here, everything is urgent, like living on a powder keg. A message comes in, and you have to respond immediately. The top priority is the search for young children. In such cases, Red Shield Operation is activated: all searchers, rescuers, and volunteers, upon seeing the information, switch their focus to supporting the unit conducting the operation.
Over the 14 years of the Angel search and rescue team’s existence, volunteering has become practically a full-time job for Sergei Kovgan, with no vacations and often around the clock. He simply cannot allow himself to ignore a call.
“An important goal for the Angel is not to lose the accumulated strength,” Sergei Kovgan said. “I want the team to grow and strengthen. To do this, we need to attract new volunteers, train them under the guidance of experienced ones, and maintain the momentum of helping people. I would also like to strengthen regional branches and upgrade equipment. We also need to scale up our educational work: hold meetings, seminars, and produce informational materials for children.”
Sergei Kovgan is the featured guest of our project Belarusians in Focus. We sat down with him to discuss volunteering in the Angel teams and learn what Red Shield Operation means.

Parliament Monsoon Session concludes: Key takeaways from the final day of proceedings

Parliament Monsoon Session concludes: Key takeaways from the final day of proceedings
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 13, 2026, 13:21 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Monsoon session of the Parliament concluded on Thursday
NEW DELHI: Parliament’s Monsoon Session concluded on Thursday with both Houses adjourned sine die after weeks marked by legislative business, opposition protests and repeated disruptions over the Jantar Mantar protest and other political flashpoints.The Lok Sabha’s final morning was strikingly brief. In just three minutes and 10 seconds, members assembled, all six stanzas of Vande Mataram were rendered, MPs including Prime Minister stood to attention, and Speaker Om Birla adjourned the House sine die.The closing proceedings unfolded amid familiar slogans, with the Opposition shouting “apologise, apologise” and “who ordered the lathi-charge?” as home minister Amit Shah entered. Birla also skipped his customary valedictory remarks on the House’s performance, underscoring a session dominated by disruption. Rajya Sabha witnessed Mallikarjun Kharge remarks over Haldwani 'Suddhikaran' row followed by JP Nadda's clarification and condemnation of the event.Meanwhile, in Rajya Sabha, leader of opposition Mallikarjun Kharge raised the Haldwani ‘suddhikaran’ row, alleging that a havan was conducted at the venue after his rally. Leader of the House JP Nadda condemned the incident and assured Kharge that the matter would be investigated.
Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha adjourned sine die
The Lok Sabha was adjourned sine die by Speaker Om Birla at 11.06 am, followed by the Rajya Sabha, bringing the 19-sitting Monsoon Session to an end. The session had been scheduled from July 20 to August 13. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju had said before the session that the government wanted the Houses to see “meaningful debate, discussion and decisions on issues of National importance”.The closing proceedings, however, came amid a continuing logjam over the opposition’s demand for a government response to the police action against students protesting the NEET controversy.
Rijiju flags low Parliament productivity
Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said 12 Bills were passed during the Monsoon Session, but acknowledged that parliamentary discussion remained limited. “It was a good session…we have passed 13 bills; but it was not a good session in terms of discussion,” he said. Lok Sabha productivity stood at 19%, compared with 39% in Rajya Sabha, he added. He also accused the Opposition of avoiding debate despite the government’s willingness to discuss issues.
On the last day of the Monsoon Session, Lok Sabha proceedings opened with all six stanzas of Vande Mataram on Thursday, marking a first for Parliament. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and other senior leaders were present. The move followed fresh Union home ministry directions on the National Song’s protocol. During the session, Parliament also passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, providing statutory protection around national symbols.
Kharge raises ‘purification’ row in Rajya Sabha
Congress president and leader of opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge used the final day to raise an alleged “purification” ritual at the Ramlila Maidan in Haldwani after his public meeting there.Kharge said, “I was in Haldwani where I made a public speech at Ramlila Maidan. Lakhs of people were there. At that time, I did not mention the name of any community or religion; I only reiterated the issues of the Govt. But after my speech, people of BJP performed a ‘havan’ there to ‘purify’ that stage...Is this the way in a democracy? How are you protecting the Constitution? I am the LoP.”Union minister JP Nadda responded that the BJP did not support such an act and said it would be investigated. “BJP does not subscribe to such activities. Never. But we will investigate this. I assure you that whatever happened there will certainly be investigated,” Nadda said, adding that he condemned the incident.
Modi and Shah present as session closes
PM Narendra Modi and Union HM Amit Shah were present during the closing proceedings, as the student protest controversy remained the dominant unresolved political issue. The Opposition had demanded Shah’s statement and his presence in the Houses over the police action during the July 20 march by students towards Parliament.On Wednesday, Shah said the government was prepared for a detailed discussion. “As far as the discussion is concerned, Kiren Rijiju, who is our parliamentary affairs minister, has made it very clear that the government is ready to discuss every aspect of the student protests regarding NEET,” Shah said.He added, “On my part, I have also said that I am ready to answer any question in Parliament. But they don't want the discussion to happen at all. Now let the public decide who is running away.”Rahul Gandhi rejected the offer, saying the Opposition was not interested in an “Amit Shah lecture” and questioning who ordered the use of force against protesting students.
Bills: 12 introduced, 11 passed by both Houses
The Monsoon Session saw 12 Bills introduced, with 10 cleared by both Houses, according to PRS Legislative Research. Key legislation covered public examinations, national honour, birth and death registration, the Supreme Court, MSMEs, taxation, tribunals, cooperative development, Kerala’s name and mining.The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill received the most debate, 17 hours and 34 minutes across both Houses. Several other Bills passed with limited discussion, including four minutes each for the birth and death registration and Supreme Court judges Bills.
NEET protests and the political battle that dominated the session
The NEET controversy and police action against student protesters dominated the Monsoon Session, with the Opposition demanding a debate on alleged examination irregularities, education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation and accountability for the July 20 crackdown. Repeated protests led to adjournments, while the government said it was ready for discussion.The Opposition, however, linked any debate to accountability over the alleged police action. The issue remained unresolved at the session’s close. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi asked, “Who shot the students? Who gave the order to beat up the students with lathis with nails?”
The wider legislative and political legacy
Beyond the NEET confrontation, the session produced a broad legislative package. Parliament cleared the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, raising the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges other than the Chief Justice from 33 to 37; the MSME Development Amendment Bill; taxation amendments; the Tribunals Reforms Bill; the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill; the National Cooperative Development Corporation Amendment Bill and the Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill.
The Kerala Bill was among the final measures passed, clearing the Lok Sabha on August 11 and the Rajya Sabha on August 12. The Mines and Minerals Amendment Bill cleared the Rajya Sabha on the final day.The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill became another major political flashpoint. Instead of being passed, it was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee for detailed scrutiny amid Opposition demands that it be withdrawn.

Iran to join BRICS development bank soon, central bank governor says

Iran to join BRICS development bank soon, central bank governor says
DUBAI, Aug 13 - Iran will soon join the New Development Bank, the development lender established by the BRICS group of nations, central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in a state media report published on Wednesday ahead of a BRICS finance meeting in India.
Iran remains under sweeping U.S. and international sanctions, and it has yet to reach a peace deal to end the current conflict with the U.S. and Israel, giving Tehran added incentive to seek alternative financial channels outside the dollar system.
The NDB's corporate communications division told Reuters it could not confirm information regarding Iran's membership.
Iran joined BRICS in 2024 as the group expanded, in a move aimed at deepening economic ties among emerging economies, and it has since made clear its desire to become a member and shareholder of the NDB.
The bank was set up by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa in 2015 to finance infrastructure and sustainable development projects. It has since expanded its membership to include the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and other emerging economies.
"The most important result of cooperation among BRICS member countries is the establishment of the New Development Bank, and our country will soon become a member of this bank," Hemmati said, according to state media.
Hemmati is attending the first meeting of BRICS finance ministers and central bank governors, hosted by India, which holds the rotating BRICS chairmanship this year.
BRICS members have sought to reduce reliance on the U.S. dollar by promoting trade and financial transactions in national currencies.
Hemmati said Iran believed BRICS members could conduct trade using their national currencies and was seeking bilateral and trilateral monetary cooperation with other members.
NDB membership is open to members of the United Nations, as well as to borrowing and non-borrowing member countries, the bank said. Uzbekistan became its 10th member on June 5. REUTERS

Ukraine blocking prisoner swaps with Russia – human rights commissioner
Ukraine has been blocking Russian proposals to exchange certain prisoners while publicly accusing Moscow of holding up the process, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova has said.
Lantratova, whose office is directly involved in prisoner swaps, criticized the Ukrainian authorities on Wednesday, accusing them of misrepresenting Russia’s position on a group of detainees captured between 2014 and 2022 who are from Donbass and Crimea.
“The Ukrainian side published lists of our guys… claiming Moscow refuses to include them in exchanges,” Lantratova wrote.
“Those are our lists,” she added. “We compiled them based on conversations with their mothers, families, and loved ones, and we are fighting for each of them. These are the same names Ukraine cynically publishes while claiming they have been ‘abandoned,’ despite knowing that in reality we are waiting for Kiev to formally respond to our proposal.”
Lantratova also pointed to a list of 224 Ukrainian citizens whom she said Russia is prepared to release in exchange for prisoners held by Kiev, but whom the Ukrainian government has declined to accept.
“Ukraine refuses to take them back. They don’t want those 224 people. They value publicity, not human life,” she stated.
On Thursday, Lantratova released another list containing the names of 273 Ukrainians whom she said could also be included in a prisoner exchange.
Last week, several pro-Ukrainian Telegram channels published the personal data of around 150 prisoners from Donbass, alleging that Russia regarded them as “expendable.”
The Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics broke away from Ukraine after the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev, which overthrew the country’s elected government and brought anti-Russian forces to power. The ensuing conflict saw Kiev launch a military operation against the two Donbass republics. Russia initially pushed for their peaceful reintegration into Ukraine under the Minsk agreements, which envisaged special status for the region.
Former Ukrainian and Western leaders later acknowledged that the Minsk process had bought Kiev time to strengthen its military with Western support. After the conflict escalated in 2022, Donetsk and Lugansk held referendums on joining Russia and were subsequently incorporated by Moscow.
Kiev officials have at times openly disparaged the population of Donbass. Maj. Gen. Mikhail Drapaty, who later became commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces, described the region in a 2023 interview as heavily populated by “settlers and criminal elements” who “do not want to work, want handouts, and do not care which country they live in.”

He made the remarks in an interview with CNN, Ukrinform reports.
Zelensky said his days are spent in "millions" of phone calls, in opaque deal-making with allies for more interceptor missiles.
"This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025. Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before. Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired," he said.

"This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can't even share. It doesn't mean that it's outside of the law. But I can't speak about it," he said.

He also rejected the idea of Ukraine conceding the remaining territory in the Donbas that Putin seeks to conquer, saying that security guarantees remained key for Kyiv.
"Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?"
He added that he agreed with some Western assessments that Putin may seek to escalate the war against NATO, possibly attacking the smaller NATO Baltic states.
"He doesn't know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It's more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in NATO or not in NATO. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control," Zelensky said.

Train crew killed as Russian attacks kill at least 8, injure 50 across Ukraine over past day
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured 50 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Aug. 13.

Pertsovsky said the train was entering a station so passengers could be evacuated after a drone threat was detected.

Russian forces attacked Ukraine overnight on Aug. 13 with 133 Shahed-type drones, the Air Force said.

In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces targeted 28 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, killing three people and injuring 19 others over the past day, the local military administration said.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks injured seven people, according to the local military administration.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian forces killed two people and injured six others across the eastern region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four others over the past day, according to local authorities.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, eight people were injured in Russian attacks, including a 15-year-old boy, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In northern Chernihiv Oblast, a 10-year-old girl was injured in Russian drone attacks over the past day, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, five people were injured in more than 10 drone and artillery attacks, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

Justice minister rejects UK's plan of sending its prisoners to Estonia
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta rejected the idea of taking in prisoners from the United Kingdom to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British prisons.
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC that Estonia does not rent prison cells to other countries, even as Swedish prisoners are set to be housed at the half-empty Tartu Prison starting in August under an agreement already signed.
Both the Conservatives and Reform UK have proposed renting cells in prisons abroad, including in Estonia, to address a shortage of space in British prisons and prevent offenders in England and Wales from being released early.
The Labour Party also explored the idea in 2024, but talks with Estonia went nowhere.
Pakosta said Estonia had not received any proposal from the United Kingdom to rent prison space, adding that if such a proposal were made, "our answer would be unequivocal — in the famous words of Margaret Thatcher: No. No. No."
"Such a proposal would not merely be misguided, misleading or unacceptable; it would deserve outright rejection," Pakosta told the BBC.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government plans to release thousands of prisoners early this October in a desperate attempt to free up space in prisons that are operating at nearly 100 percent capacity.
Downing Street on Monday did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons when reporters asked whether the government was considering the option. A spokesperson for the prime minister's office said the government was focused on "creating additional capacity within the domestic system."
"As for renting prison places abroad, it simply isn't a quick solution," the spokesperson added. "It would require initial legislative changes based on a complex international agreement that would take several years to negotiate."

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova reported that the target was the Salavat refinery. Russian residents also reported a large column of black smoke rising over the facility, according to the Astra news outlet.
Major Russian Refinery Targeted Again
The Salavat complex is Gazprom’s largest petrochemical facility and one of Russia’s major oil-processing sites. It can process up to 7.5 million metric tons of crude annually, accounting for about 2.7% of Russia’s total refining capacity.
The plant produces gasoline, diesel, kerosene, liquefied gases, ammonia, urea and other petrochemical products.
The refinery was already hit by Ukrainian drones on July 14. Reuters, citing informed sources, reported that the attack damaged two primary oil-processing units, forcing the facility to halt operations.
Repairs were expected to take anywhere from several weeks to several months, according to Reuters sources.
Russian Fuel Shortages Mount
The latest strike comes as Ukraine has sharply stepped up attacks on Russia’s oil-refining infrastructure.
Russia Produces 3,000 Geran-4/5 Drones a Month, Ukraine Says
Since the beginning of August, at least four Russian refineries have stopped processing crude following Ukrainian attacks, including facilities in Orenburg, Tyumen, Saratov and Volgograd regions.
An S&P Global analysis cited by The Moscow Times found that Ukrainian attacks had disrupted operations at at least 26 Russian oil-processing facilities in 2026. Seven had yet to restore production by the end of July.
Russia’s refining output has subsequently fallen to around 3.6 million barrels per day, according to EA Analytics – its lowest level since May 2002.
The disruptions have contributed to a growing fuel shortage across Russia.
Although gasoline shortages eased toward the end of July, problems resurfaced in August. Residents of at least 16 Russian regions have again reported long lines at gas stations and restrictions on fuel sales.
In some regions, Gazprom and Lukoil stations have stopped selling AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline.
The repeated strikes are putting increasing pressure on Russia’s already strained fuel supply as Ukraine continues targeting energy infrastructure deep inside Russian territory.

Rents fell in July in more than half of Swiss cantons

Rents fell in July in more than half of Swiss cantons
In 15 out of 26 Swiss cantons, proposed rents fell in July, whereas the opposite usually happens, according to the property platform Homegate.
Overall, however, the national average has remained stable compared with June, while asking rents continue to rise year-on-year.
The Homegate index thus remains at 134 points, according to a press release published on Thursday. Compared with the same period in 2025, asking rents have risen by 2.4% across Switzerland.
This index, compiled in collaboration with Zurich Cantonal Bank (ZKB), measures the quality-adjusted monthly change in rents for new and re-let flats, based on current market offers.
+ Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
Rental offers fell most sharply in Nidwalden, by 4.0%, followed by Schwyz (-1.9%) and Geneva and Uri (both -1.5%). The sharp decline observed in Nidwalden can be explained by several increases in recent months, which now appear to have been corrected. Generally speaking, Homegate has observed a widespread downward trend in Central Switzerland.
In Zurich, rents also fell by 0.4%. By contrast, asking rents rose in St Gallen (+0.7%) and Ticino (+0.6%).
These declines were not enough to reverse the annual trend, with all cantons continuing to record an increase compared with July 2025 – particularly in Graubünden (+7.1%), Zug (+5.0%) and Lucerne (+4.2%). The other cantons in Central Switzerland also recorded above-average rent growth, regardless of the fluctuations observed in July.
As regards cities, Lugano is the only city surveyed where asking rents rose month-on-month in July, by 1.9% – a significantly sharper increase than in the canton of Ticino as a whole. The situation is the reverse in Lucerne: asking rents in the city fell by 2.4%, a decline twice as steep as that recorded in the canton (-1.2%).
The trend observed in Lugano is also continuing year-on-year, with a rise of 6.3%. As with the cantons, all the other cities surveyed also show a positive trend compared with the previous year.

Colombia earthquake: Rescue operation enters 'final phase'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:45:00 UTC
16:45:00 KST

Colombia earthquake: Rescue operation enters 'final phase'
August 13, 2026
Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water.
"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital."
The latest on the Colombia earthquake
The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday.
De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said.
The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo.
In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP.
Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.
Families grapple with human toll
In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby."
A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better."
Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks.
Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake.
International aid set to pour in
Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river.
"This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.
And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief.
The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June.
Quake response provides test for new Colombian president
De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure.
"This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve.
Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort.
Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned.

Romania scrambled two F-16s because of a group of drones near the border. One target entered the country's airspace for 10 minutes, after which explosions occurred on Ukrainian territory.
Romania once again scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after a group of drones was detected during russia's attack on Ukraine near the border; an aerial target was detected entering Romanian airspace for approximately 10 minutes, the country's Defense Ministry reported on Wednesday, according to UNN.
Details
As stated, the Romanian Ministry of National Defence's radar surveillance system, at 01:27 local time on the night of August 12–13, "detected a group of five aerial targets in the area of Izmail, over Ukrainian territory, near the river border with Romania."
Measures were taken to alert the population in the northern part of Tulcea County, and an RO-Alert message was sent at 01:30.
"Two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force from the 86th Air Base in Borcea were scrambled to monitor the situation. Ground-based radars detected an aerial target entering national airspace approximately 2 km south of the town of Pardina. The target remained in national airspace for approximately 10 minutes along the Chilia branch, after which it left Romanian territory in the direction of Ukraine approximately 13 km southwest of the settlement of Chilia Veche," the Romanian Defense Ministry stated.
"Shortly after leaving Romanian airspace, reports of explosions were received on Ukrainian territory," the statement said.
The air raid alert issued for the north of Tulcea County ended at 02:42.
"The Ministry of National Defence is continuously monitoring the situation and informing allied structures in real time about such events," the statement said.
Later, Romania's Defense Ministry issued a new statement: "On Thursday morning, August 13, at 09:02, the radar surveillance system of the Ministry of National Defence detected an aerial target near the river border with Ukraine. Two F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force from the 86th Air Base in Borcea were scrambled at 09:20 to monitor the situation."
The population in Tulcea County was alerted again, with an RO-Alert message issued starting at 09:13.

Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, has sparked disquiet within the Prison Service after questioning why the murderer and serial sex offender Simon Levy was released from jail after sexually assaulting a female prison officer.

But Whitehall sources have hit back saying that it is “inaccurate” because the Prison Service had no legal power to keep Levy in jail.
Levy, 40, was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.
Rowley acknowledged mistakes over the force’s handling of Levy but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were “just not true”, following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.
Rowley questioned why the Prison Service released Levy after he sexually assaulted a female prison officer in HMP Brixton in April 2022. The Met questioned him in June 2023, five months after he was released from prison.
Levy was not charged with the prison offence until October 2025 – by then he had been able to attack 13 more women, killing two of them.
Rowley told the BBC’s Today programme: “That’s one of the things we’ve apologised for but of course there are two mistakes in that: you’ve got he was released on licence by the prison service, having sexually assaulted in prison one of its people, I don’t understand that decision either.
“I’m prepared to come here and be accountable, we’ve got two officers … we’ve referred to be investigated by the independent office of police complaints, we take our accountability seriously.
“The rest of the system is not doing that. The prison service should not have released somebody who’s indecently assaulting its staff.”
Mina Smallman, whose daughters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman were killed in a north London park in 2020 by teenager Danyal Hussein, said Britain’s biggest police force was incapable of change. Two police officers were jailed in 2021 after taking photographs of the dead bodies of her daughters and sharing the images in WhatsApp groups, referring to them as “dead birds”.
Commenting on the police investigation into Levy, she said: “One of the women that were murdered, because she was a sex worker, she wasn’t taken seriously. They didn’t look into her murder until he murdered a mother of four, and then they joined the two cases together.
“How ridiculous is that. Once again, the Met is deciding who matters. Both those women’s lives were important to their families, how dare they decide that they weren’t going to look into that case.”
Levy, who this week was given a whole-life sentence for his crimes, was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the underground in London between 2023 and 2025.
Smallman said she had been in contact with Rowley, after reading about the case. She told the Today programme: “After reading this case I sent a text message to Sir Mark and said: ‘How many times are you going to stand up publicly and apologise for failures in the Met?’
“It becomes a joke. The truth is, the Metropolitan police is too big for any senior team to be able to have a hands-on understanding of the day-to-day activities of that organisation.”
She said the Met was incapable of change because it was “too big”. “I believe that Sir Mark Rowley wants to change the Met and wants to do things differently, but they haven’t got a clue.”
She added: “We are asking them to do too much, they haven’t got the finances, it has become riddled with inactivity, corruption, misogyny, racism and they just can’t do it.”
The crime and policing minister, Sarah Jones, previously described Levy as a monster and said the failings that had allowed him to remain free were “deeply concerning”.
Jones signalled the government would allow the relevant institutions and police watchdog to establish what had gone wrong. “The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning,” she said. “It raises serious questions that require urgent answers.”
Rowley denied that the Met had not done enough, saying: “The inference that the Met didn’t try on this death is not true, the Met tried.”
The Prison Service has been approached for a comment.

Taboos to avoid during Taiwan's Ghost Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:40:33 UTC
16:40:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Ghost Month officially began Thursday with the start of the seventh lunar month, when Taiwanese folklore holds that the gates of the underworld open and spirits enter the mortal realm.
During the month, many people observe traditional taboos intended to avoid attracting ghosts, often referred to respectfully as "good brothers" (好兄弟). Numerology expert Tang Chen-wei (湯鎮瑋) and folk custom expert Yang Teng-kei (楊登嵙) shared several customs they said could help people avoid negative energy, per UDN.
1. Avoid extreme sadness or anger
Tang said strong emotions such as grief and anger are believed to increase yin energy. Because Ghost Month marks a seasonal shift from yang to yin, people are thought to be more vulnerable to negative influences if they cannot regulate their emotions.
Maintaining emotional balance, Tang said, is believed to promote steadier fortune throughout the month.
2. Avoid nighttime adventures
Tang advised staying away from isolated or sparsely populated places after dark, particularly locations considered to have heavy yin energy. Exploring abandoned buildings or other eerie sites at night is traditionally believed to disturb spirits and attract unwanted supernatural attention.
3. Avoid moving or renovating at night
Moving house or beginning construction is not strictly prohibited during Ghost Month, Tang said, but such activities should be scheduled during daylight hours and on an auspicious date selected from the traditional farmer's almanac. He recommended completing renovations before 5 p.m. and avoiding last-minute nighttime moves.
Yang offered additional advice on clothing during Ghost Month. He said people born in the Year of the Rat, Ox, Rabbit, and Horse should be particularly cautious this year, per UDN.
4. Do not wear solid black, white, or red
According to Yang, all-black clothing is believed to attract spirits, while all-white attire may signal mourning and draw wandering ghosts. Solid red clothing is said to remind spirits of bloodshed and provoke unrest.
He suggested adding colorful accessories or choosing natural colors instead.
5. Avoid revealing your shoulders
Traditional belief holds that people possess three protective spiritual flames: one on the head and one on each shoulder. Yang said revealing the shoulders, particularly in places associated with yin energy such as cemeteries, hospitals, columbariums, slaughterhouses, and abandoned buildings, is thought to weaken this protection.
6. Avoid ghost-like clothing
Distressed or ripped clothing, wedding dresses, messy hair, and ghost costumes are also discouraged during Ghost Month, Yang said. Ripped clothing may cause spirits to mistake someone for a wandering ghost, while bridal attire and ghost-themed costumes are believed to attract unwanted supernatural attention.
UDN noted that the advice reflects folk belief and cautioned readers against excessive superstition. For many families, Ghost Month remains a time to show respect for ancestors and wandering spirits through offerings, temple ceremonies, and everyday acts of caution.

16:40:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection and Taiwan Intellectual Property Office held a joint press conference Wednesday warning that uninspected or pirated toys can pose safety and intellectual property risks, according to a Standards Bureau press release.
The agencies said toys are products designed for children under 14, with 31 categories subject to mandatory inspection before import or release from factories. Products must bear the Commodity Inspection Mark before they can be sold domestically.
Tests cover chemicals such as plasticizers and heavy metals, mechanical hazards such as small parts and sharp edges, electrical faults, microbial counts, and warning labels.
The bureau said it conducts annual market inspections and sampling tests, focusing in particular on new and trending toys. Vendors selling products that have not completed required inspections can be fined NT$200,000 to NT$2 million (US$6,200 to US$62,000).
If the total value of non-compliant goods is under NT$100,000, fines range from NT$10,000 to NT$100,000. Businesses must also recall or correct the products within a specified period, with failure to comply carrying an additional fine of NT$100,000 to NT$1 million.
The bureau said it posts overseas toy safety alerts, including notices from the US Consumer Product Safety Commission and the EU’s Safety Gate, on its Product Safety Information Network. It also notifies the Ministry of Health and Welfare, warns the public and childcare facilities to stop using affected products, and asks domestic e-commerce platforms to remove them as a precaution.
The Taiwan Intellectual Property Office warned that toys or packaging printed with unauthorized artwork may violate copyright law, while use of identical or similar registered trademarks without permission may infringe trademark rights. The office added that pirated toys may also be of questionable quality.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs urged consumers to buy licensed, age-appropriate toys bearing the inspection mark and complete Chinese labels. It also advised adults not to let children chew toys, to watch for small parts that could be swallowed, and to have children wash their hands after playing.
The bureau said it will continue monitoring emerging toy risks and changes to international standards to update inspection rules as needed. The office added that suspected infringements can be reported with evidence to the Criminal Investigation Bureau’s Intellectual Property Rights Investigation Corps or local police.

Russian Ships Use First and Second World War Camo and Cages Against Ukrainian Drones

Russian Ships Use First and Second World War Camo and Cages Against Ukrainian Drones
Russian commercial vessels navigating the Black Sea during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine have begun adopting physical and optical protective measures to guard against Ukrainian aerial and naval uncrewed systems.
Shipping monitors and maritime observers recently identified several vessels carrying crude oil and general cargo, including a 28-year-old Suezmax tanker laden with approximately 1 million barrels of crude, as reported by The Insider on August 12.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among these ships is a 119-meter cargo vessel built in 1987, which was spotted outfitted with protective netting, metal cage structures, and geometric camouflage patterns similar to dazzle designs utilized during the First and Second World Wars.
Shipping monitors and maritime observers recently identified several vessels, including a 28-year-old Suezmax tanker carrying approximately 1 million barrels of crude oil and a 119-meter general cargo ship built in 1987, outfitted with protective netting, metal cage structures, and geometric camouflage patterns similar to dazzle designs utilized during the First and Second World Wars.
Monitoring service TankerTrackers.com spotted the Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax crude oil tanker CARUZO passing through Istanbul with around 1 million barrels of Russian crude oil.
The 28-year-old vessel is subject to sanctions imposed by the United Kingdom, the European Union, New Zealand, Canada, Switzerland, and Australia, though it is not listed on US sanction registers.
Environmental group Greenpeace identifies the vessel as part of the Russian shadow fleet, while Ukrainian military intelligence states that CARUZO has been involved in exporting Russian oil products outside G7 embargo guidelines and price caps since at least October 2023, including ship-to-ship transfers near the Kerch Strait in January 2024.
Crew members on board CARUZO completely enclosed the vessel's superstructure with protective netting, essentially enclosing the crew spaces.
The ship also features metal frame structures hanging from both sides of the stern section, which analysts indicate are designed to protect the engine room from attacks by explosive sea drones.
According to tracking data from Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the ship has regularly turned off its Automatic Identification System upon entering the Black Sea since July 2025 while recording static positions in the Bosphorus for months. Beyond the Black Sea, records list CARUZO visiting ports and terminals across Turkey, China, India, Malaysia, Morocco, Egypt, and Vietnam.
In a separate observation, Turkish merchant captain Murat Fırtına documented a distinct defensive modification on the Russian-flagged cargo ship MECHTA S in the port of Haydarpaşa on August 10.
The 119-meter vessel, built in 1987 as Sormovskiy-3059 and designed for Black Sea and river-sea transport, was photographed displaying bold geometric shapes in shades of blue, dark blue, white, and gray across its hull, bow, stern, and superstructure.
The design mirrors the dazzle camouflage historically used during World War I and World War II to visually disrupt a ship's outline, obscuring its size, orientation, speed, and vulnerable impact points from optical targeting systems. Commenting on the vessel's appearance, Fırtına noted that older photographs of MECHTA S showed standard painting without geometric shapes.
"If considering that today even merchant ships in the Black Sea face threats from unmanned aerial vehicles and naval drones, it cannot be ruled out that such painting has not only an aesthetic purpose, but also represents military camouflage designed to complicate optical detection of the vessel and targeting," he stated, adding, "But it must be admitted: seeing a merchant ship in 2026 in the middle of Istanbul, in Haydarpaşa, looking as if it came off the pages of wartime history, is quite unusual."
The vessel MECHTA S is not currently included in official sanction lists or shadow fleet registries. Tracking records from Starboard Maritime Intelligence spanning 3,294 days—roughly nine years—indicate that Novorossiysk is the ship's most frequently visited port, with 83 recorded port calls totaling over 72 days.
The vessel recently underwent a 26-day maintenance period from July 15 to August 10 in Yalova, Turkey, before appearing in Istanbul.
Starboard data shows that the ship lacked active AIS tracking for approximately 930 days and 6 hours, representing about 28% of the monitored timeframe, while also lacking verifiable insurance coverage through recognized P&I clubs.
Earlier, Russia was seen fitting anti-drone netting to an FSB Coast Guard Project 22460 Okhotnik-class patrol ship based in temporarily occupied Crimea. The improvised protection reflected a broader trend of adding physical drone defenses to Russian naval vessels as Ukraine expanded its use of aerial and maritime drones.

By the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine's account, Mykhailo, one of its soldiers, deployed to the forest in October 2024 with the rapid-response border commandant unit Shkval and held off Russian assaults while fortifying the ground under constant drone attack.
Holding a position like that on a static, drone-saturated front takes endurance as much as firepower. A unit has to supply itself, down to digging its own water under fire. The Serebryanskyi forest, on the border of Luhansk and Donetsk oblasts, has been contested since 2022. Euromaidan Press has previously reported on Ukrainian storming operations in the forest and on Azov's account of driving Russian forces from some positions there in 2024.
Mykhailo worked abroad in construction after his studies, then signed a contract with the State Border Guard Service in 2020. He served first at the Nismychi unit, then at Belz, where he worked as a district inspector, before the October 2024 rotation with Shkval put him on the positions for 115 days.
"Logistics were not easy. Drones delivered the food, and we also had to supply the positions with water. So we even dug our own well, to have our own water and to be able to bring in more food," Mykhailo recalled.
He returns repeatedly to the men around him. When his own endurance ran out, he said, it was his brothers-in-arms who kept him in place.
"Your brothers-in-arms motivate you. When I said I couldn't take it anymore, they said: 'Sit tight. Together to the end.' And so we all sat there together to the end," he said.
Mykhailo is motivated by his family, which he considers his greatest incentive to defend Ukraine.

Gaza cancer patients face rising death rate amid Israeli curbs, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:35:16 UTC
16:35:16 KST

Gaza cancer patients face rising death rate amid Israeli curbs, doctors say
CAIRO/GAZA – Gaza cancer patients are dying at two to three times the pace they did before the start of the war in the territory, as Israel blocks many from travelling for treatment after destroying the only local specialised facility, Gaza doctors said.
Israel blew up Gaza’s specialised cancer hospital in 2025 after saying troops found a tunnel used by Hamas militants running beneath it. That means that an estimated 17,000 Gazans with cancer have no local option for chemotherapy or other advanced therapy.
Few Palestinians can afford to travel for treatment, and those who can face Israeli restrictions. The military imposes strict caps on daily crossings to Egypt, despite a 2025 Israel-Hamas ceasefire deal that requires free movement in and out.
Asked for comment, COGAT, the Israeli military agency that controls access to Gaza, said it coordinates medical evacuations with the World Health Organization (WHO). To depart, Gazans must have a valid request from a receiving country and pass “required security screening”, COGAT said.
The WHO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Race against time
For Khuloud Abu Sahmoud, a Palestinian mother of two with advanced ovarian cancer, the wait for treatment abroad has become a race against time as her cancer spreads.
“Every day my disease progresses, and my condition is tragic. My fingernails have all fallen out – I have none left. I am just waiting to die.”
Abu Sahmoud, 33, said she has been waiting to exit Gaza for treatment in Egypt or further afield since the ceasefire was struck in October. In that time, the cancer has spread to her lungs and bones, she says.
COGAT said around 5,800 Gazans needing medical treatment have exited to Egypt since Israel agreed in February to a limited reopening of the Rafah border crossing, largely shut during the war, which began in 2023.
“Medical evacuations are in no sense restricted by the State of Israel but are wholly dependent on the receiving country’s request; without the official request, COGAT cannot coordinate a patient’s leave,” COGAT said.
Palestinian health officials said 11,000 people, including patients, had gone through Rafah since it reopened, fewer than half the number that had been expected under the ceasefire deal.
A further 20,000 patients, including 5,000 with cancer, are registered for treatment abroad but not yet permitted to leave, the officials said.
Toxic chemical exposure
The ceasefire ended major fighting but left Israeli forces in control of more than half of Gaza, since expanded to around two-thirds. Nearly all of Gaza’s more than two million people live in a Hamas-controlled strip along the coast, mostly in makeshift tents or shelters in damaged buildings.
Before the war, local health services had made advances thanks to investment from abroad and persistence from local doctors, a Reuters investigation found.
But most Gaza hospitals were destroyed or damaged in the war, and those that remain operational have been stripped of up to 70 per cent of essential medical supplies, including those needed for cancer treatment and diagnostic services, doctors said.
Among those killed by Israel during the war were dozens of highly qualified specialists, including cancer experts operating in the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, demolished in an Israeli controlled demolition in March 2025.
“We have been recording a significant number of deaths, ranging from three to five daily, because patients are not receiving the chemotherapy needed to save their lives,” said Mohamed Abu Selmia, head of Gaza’s biggest hospital, Al Shifa.
Sobhi Skaik, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital, said the death rate before the war was about one or two a day. Some pre-war statistics put the figure at around 1.7 a day, he said.
He said the rising deaths were due mostly to an absence of local treatment and to border restrictions. But he also said that cancer itself may be spreading at a faster rate due to the presence of toxic materials from Israeli explosives dropped on Gaza.
There were some 11,000 registered cancer patients in Gaza before the war started following the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on southern Israel, after which registrations largely stopped, Skaik said.
He estimated that another 6,000 Gazans had likely developed cancer since.
“Some people can be treated if diagnosed in early stages, but they are wandering around the tents sick, unaware, and with no help,” Skaik said. REUTERS

The four contested islands, seized by Russia during World War II, have gained importance since the end of the conflict, providing strategic military bases to the Kremlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the far-eastern Kuril islands for the first time on Thursday, prompting a "strong" protest by Japan which also claims the territory.
Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by tensions over the contested islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.
The Kremlin posted a video of Putin in the Kuril Islands, with Russian media saying he visited a fish-processing plant where he was given caviar. Putin travelled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.
In Sakhalin, Putin held a meeting "on ensuring the security of Russia's eastern borders," state-run media outlet RIA Novosti said.
Japan, whose ties with Russia have worsened further since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – just as Moscow's relations with China and North Korea have warmed – objected strongly.
"The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," said Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi in a statement.
The Soviet Union took the strategically located volcanic archipelago north of Hokkaido in the final days of World War II, and has maintained a military presence there ever since.
In 2010 then-president Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian leader to visit the disputed territory. Medvedev also went there several times subsequently as prime minister under Putin’s presidency.
The four contested isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, which runs in a broad arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island Hokkaido. The Soviet Union only declared war on Japan on August 8, 1945, after the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima and six days before the end of the conflict.
The islands' names are similar in both countries -- Kunashir, Habomai, Shikotan and Iturup in Russian, while in Japanese they are known as Kunashiri, Habomai, Shikotan and Etorofu.
Their population of about 20,000 Russian citizens live in harsh climates, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds. After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.
Thereafter the islands acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the United States and its closest ally in the Pacific, Japan.
On several occasions it appeared that off-and-on talks between Tokyo and Moscow were making progress and in 1956, when diplomatic relations were established, where Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested two of the disputed islands might be returned under a peace treaty.
Although the talks resumed after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, no progress has been made and they remain in Russian control.

Germany's dry rivers spark battle on engineering vs restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:28:00 UTC
16:28:00 KST

An empty cargo ship navigates at the Duisburg harbor during low water levels of Rhine River caused by a heat wave and a prolonged drought in Duisburg, Germany. Tuesday. Aug. 11, 2026.
As a heat wave dries Germany’s rivers, government ministers are at odds over what to do about it: Re-engineer the waterways or restore them to their natural state.
The debate has flared as precariously falling water levels have revealed vast sandbanks on the Rhine, Danube, Elbe and other rivers, severely impacting cargo shipping crucial for many industries.
With climate change driving new heat records and longer dry spells in Europe and beyond, scientists warn that the problem will intensify in coming years.
Germany’s new transport minister, Steffen Bilger, convened a recent crisis summit with shipping, port and logistics operators on the problem impacting the European Union’s biggest economy.
The key short-term counter measure he announced was to temporarily lift a ban on truck transports on Sundays and public holidays to help ease cargo bottlenecks.
In the longer term, Germany needs to dredge deeper navigation channels and develop a new class of low-draft ships, argued Bilger, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU bloc.
“We must make our waterways more efficient while simultaneously making ships suitable for times of low water,” Bilger said on Aug. 12 after talks with state transport ministers.
“That is why we are pushing ahead with important expansion projects,” he added, vowing that environmental protection would be “kept firmly in mind.” Speaking in Berlin on the same day, Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of junior coalition partner the center-left SPD offered a radically different vision, centered on restoring rivers.
After a campaign over hundreds of years saw rivers tamed for commercial use, he urged a shift back “toward natural rivers featuring meandering branches and floodplains that retain water across the landscape.”
“In past centuries, Germany was a land rich in water,” he said.
“Great effort went into straightening rivers to harness them for our use, but also into enabling agriculture by draining the wetlands.”
Now, however, climate change has turned water into a scarce resource, requiring a shift in thinking, Schneider argued.
His views echoed those of environmental groups that oppose deepening shipping channels. 
“They do more harm than good,” said Beatrice Claus of the WWF.
“Expansion and straightening cause water to drain away into the North Sea and Baltic Sea even faster, rather than being retained in the surrounding area.”
Dredging is not a permanent solution, critics argue, because rivers constantly fill the channels with new sediment.
Environmentalists also say river bank fortifications destroy shallow-water zones where aquatic life and insects breed, and the adjoining natural floodplains that act like sponges at times of excess water.
“Dredging rivers creates the illusion of taking action,” said Olaf Bandt, head of environmental group BUND.
For now, most German states have lifted the Sunday trucking ban, banking on a mode of transport with a far heavier carbon footprint than river boats.
Thomas Puls of the German Economic Institute said he did not expect the move to make much difference, telling news weekly Der Spiegel that it takes at least 150 trucks to replace a single inland waterway vessel.

Rail Baltica’s first phase in Latvia planned with major cost-cutting measures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
07:24:50 UTC
16:24:50 KST

The first phase of the Rail Baltica main line in Latvia is planned within its existing scope, including the creation of a cross-border Rail Baltica connection from Lithuania to the Estonian border, as well as the completion of construction works at Riga Airport and the southern section of Riga Central Station. This would allow Rail Baltica to be connected to Latvia’s existing railway network, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (New Unity) told reporters on Wednesday following a meeting of the thematic committee overseeing the project.
The minister stressed that this solution applies specifically to the project’s first phase and that the idea of the so-called “Riga loop” has not been abandoned. “We would like to look at it differently, but we are in 2026 and we have to think rationally,” Kozlovskis said.
The committee on Wednesday heard a report on the results of an in-depth review of the Rail Baltica project, which outlined three possible scenarios. “One scenario was to continue what had been started and proceed as before, which is neither acceptable nor possible. The second scenario is to review and reduce the requirements, while the third is to immediately terminate any further activities,” Kozlovskis explained. He stressed that the project must move towards optimisation – building and financing only what is technically essential rather than “funding various visions and, to some extent, dreams”.
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said Latvia must establish a “minimum programme”, or a basic scenario for the project. According to him, consultants found that, for example, the approximately 600-kilometre Madrid–Barcelona high-speed railway technically has two stations, with one serving as the main stop, whereas Latvia’s roughly 200-kilometre section has been designed with 17 stations.
Station platforms have also been planned at 400 metres in length,
although technically they could be reduced to 200 metres.
The prime minister said the Transport Ministry must prepare proposals by the 15th of September for reducing technical and construction-material requirements for the first phase of Rail Baltica to the minimum level necessary to create a functional and permanently operational railway line. “So we go down to the minimum to understand what we can build and what we cannot,” Kulbergs said.
Taking into account the consultants’ assessment of project costs, the Finance Ministry and State Treasury, together with the Transport Ministry and Economics Ministry, have also been tasked with assessing by the 15th of September how much state budget funding could be allocated to Rail Baltica in the coming years, as well as identifying other sources of financing and opportunities to attract investment.
Kulbergs noted that the law now also recognises Rail Baltica’s role in military mobility, potentially opening the door to military funding that had not previously been explicitly envisaged. “We have to think outside the box about what other opportunities exist, because Europe will not provide enough money in the next funding envelope to implement this project,” he stressed.
A third task involves the State Chancellery and Transport Ministry
assessing proposed changes to the project’s governance. Kulbergs said the project has so far been poorly managed, arguing that Latvia’s interests have not been sufficiently protected in negotiations with contractors.
He also criticised the contract for construction of the main line signed in December 2023, saying it had “put us in a stranglehold” because it was concluded without specialist verification and complete project documentation.
According to Kulbergs, the contract does not set an effective maximum cost ceiling or define the maximum requirements Latvia can afford. “This is a good contractor capable of building the project, but the question is whether we can afford it. This contractor costs a very significant amount every month. If we continue building as we have until now, nobody will know when it will be completed or how it will be financed.
Nor will anyone be able to afford a train ticket,”
Kulbergs said.
The Transport Ministry said the results of the in-depth Rail Baltica review were presented on Wednesday by consultants from Alvarez & Marsal Infrastructure & Capital Projects, who analysed the causes of the project’s previous problems and proposed further steps. The assessment is classified as a restricted-access document.
The review concluded that if Latvia continues implementing Rail Baltica in the same way as before, the full cost of the Latvian section could increase significantly and the project could not be completed solely with available EU funding. Consultants also concluded that successful implementation would be unlikely without clearly assigning overall responsibility and establishing a project management team experienced in projects of a similar scale.
According to the ministry, Alvarez & Marsal recommends first deciding how much annual state budget funding Latvia can realistically allocate to Rail Baltica in the coming years. Latvia should then consult Estonia, Lithuania and the European Commission to agree on minimum technical requirements for the project, particularly regarding maximum train speeds.
The Transport Ministry also presented potential cost-saving solutions
prepared together with Eiropas Dzelzceļa līnijas (EDzL) and contractors for the 33-kilometre Rail Baltica section between Misa and the Latvian-Lithuanian border.
By rationalising the design and introducing standardised solutions for engineering structures, construction elements and environmental measures, construction costs could reportedly be reduced by 24.8%, generating around 108 million euros in savings on future construction works.
Among the proposed measures, the average height of the railway line could be lowered by approximately three metres and the thickness of the frost-protection layer reduced by 37%. This would cut embankment construction volumes by 46% and excavation and soil replacement works by 25%. It could also potentially eliminate the need to construct 13.2 kilometres of noise barriers.
The government launched the in-depth Rail Baltica review on the 3rd of November last year, appointing international consultancy Alvarez & Marsal to carry it out. The value of the consultancy contract is confidential.
The purpose of the assessment is to provide an objective and comprehensive analysis
of Rail Baltica’s implementation, examine risks and the project’s financial and contractual position, and develop recommendations and a practical action plan for more efficient, transparent and sustainable implementation.
At the end of July, the government also established a thematic committee on Rail Baltica implementation comprising ten members of the government. Chaired by Prime Minister Kulbergs, it is intended to coordinate cross-sectoral government decisions on the technically functional and financially sustainable continuation of the project.
In addition to Kulbergs, the committee includes Foreign Minister Baiba Braže, Climate and Energy Minister Jānis Vitenbergs, Education and Science Minister Ilze Indriksone, Finance Minister Māris Kučinskis, Transport Minister Rihards Kozlovskis, Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, Justice Minister Edvards Smiltēns, Smart Administration and Regional Development Minister Edgars Tavars, and Economics Minister Viktors Valainis.
The estimated cost of Rail Baltica’s first phase across the Baltic states could reach 14.3 billion euros,
including around 5.5 billion euros in Latvia, although indexation could push Latvia’s share to approximately 6 billion euros.
According to the latest cost-benefit analysis, the entire Rail Baltica project across the Baltic states could cost as much as 23.8 billion euros. By comparison, the previous cost-benefit analysis conducted in 2017 estimated the total cost at 5.8 billion euros.
Rail Baltica is intended to create a European standard-gauge railway connecting Tallinn with the Lithuanian-Polish border and, from there, linking the Baltic states with the wider European rail network. The project envisages approximately 870 kilometres of new 1,435 mm standard-gauge railway across the Baltic states, designed for maximum train speeds of up to 240 kilometres per hour.

Israel holding nearly 370 Palestinian children behind bars – rights groups
Nearly 370 Palestinian children are being held in Israeli prisons, many without having been convicted of a crime, RT’s Charlotte Dubenskij has reported, citing Palestinian and Israeli rights organizations.
The number of minors held under administrative detention – which allows imprisonment without charge or trial – has almost doubled in just over a year, according to the latest figures from Israel’s prison service.
Israel says around 90% of the detained minors are being held for security-related reasons but have not been convicted, according to an RT report. Prison terms generally range from two to three years, although some minors have received sentences of between ten and 20 years.
Israeli police also report that around 100 minors are detained each month for entering Israel without a permit.
The detentions have come amid mounting allegations of mistreatment inside Israeli prisons. Former detainees and rights organizations have reported abuse, torture, starvation, physical and psychological harm, sexual violence and denial of medical treatment.
Israel is also holding the bodies of more than 100 Palestinians who died in its custody, according to a recent report cited by RT.
The situation in the West Bank has received comparatively little international attention amid the war in Gaza, where Israeli military operations have caused widespread destruction and displacement.
Gaza’s Health Ministry has put the Palestinian death toll since October 2023 at 73,386, with another 174,250 people wounded. Israel launched its military campaign following the Hamas-led October 7 attack on southern Israel, in which around 1,200 people were killed and more than 250 taken hostage.
Meanwhile, arrests and raids have continued across the West Bank, leaving a growing number of Palestinian minors in Israeli custody.

The Trump administration plans to spend at least $900 million on construction projects across the White House grounds, with most of the funding expected to come from taxpayers, media reports said on Wednesday.
The Washington Post reported that the administration has assembled funding through transfers from federal agencies and private donations rather than seeking direct congressional appropriations.
The money has reportedly been directed into the Executive Residence's White House Repair and Restoration account for what the administration describes as "modernization projects."
According to the report, the projects include a planned East Wing ballroom, upgrades to Lafayette Square, construction of a helipad, a new visitor screening center and other improvements, bringing the estimated total cost to at least $927 million.
The developments come after a federal appeals court ruled Friday that congressional approval is required for the East Wing ballroom project.
"Congress has exclusive authority to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures," Judges Patricia A. Millett and Bradley N. Garcia wrote in their opinion.
President Donald Trump has said he will appeal the decision.
The White House has not disclosed the overall cost of the planned construction or detailed the sources of most of the funding.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said the projects are being carried out in a "manner consistent with" Congress's intent.
"President Trump continues to implement long-overdue and necessary renovations to beautify the People's House," Ingle said, adding that the White House "will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come."
According to the report, Congress has traditionally approved funding for major White House construction projects.
Budget records cited by the newspaper show the administration has directed $875 million into the Executive Residence maintenance account since Trump took office, compared with annual appropriations of $2.5 million in recent years.
The report also said the administration has routed contracts through the Executive Residence, an office that is not subject to the same public disclosure requirements as most federal agencies.
