Half a million visitors flock to Spain’s path of total solar eclipse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:28:57 UTC
15:28:57 KST

In Medinaceli, a hilltop town in north-eastern Spain, spectators arrived hours early with chairs, hats and eclipse glasses to secure a clear view before the event reached totality shortly before sunset.
Getxo, a coastal town just north-west of Bilbao in the Basque Country, also lay within the narrow path of totality. There, the Moon completely covered the Sun for only a few seconds at around 20:27 CEST, with the Sun just 8 degrees above the western horizon.
Totality lasted for about one minute in Spain before the eclipse moved towards the Mediterranean. The longest total phase, lasting less than 2.5 minutes, was recorded farther north off Iceland's west coast.
Spanish authorities had expected at least 500,000 additional visitors along the eclipse path, putting pressure on hotels and local services. The event also came as Spain faced scorching summer temperatures and wildfires, prompting authorities to launch a major public safety campaign.

UK economy expands 0.4% in Q2 as services offset stagnant production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:26:51 UTC
15:26:51 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
13 August 2026•Update: 13 August 2026
- Economy grows 0.3% in June, beating expectations for contraction
The UK economy expanded 0.4% in the second quarter of 2026 as growth in services and construction offset stagnant production, official data showed Thursday.
The April-June increase followed growth of 0.6% in the first quarter and matched market expectations, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
The economy grew 1.2% compared with the same quarter last year, exceeding expectations of a 1.1% expansion.
Services output increased 0.5%, led by gains in information and communication as well as professional, scientific and technical activities. Construction grew 0.3%, while production showed no growth.
Manufacturing output rose 1%, but this was offset by declines in electricity and gas supply and water and waste-management activities.
Household consumption increased 0.3%, while gross fixed capital formation rose 1.2% and business investment climbed 1.7%. Government consumption fell 0.3%.
GDP per capita grew 0.4% from the previous quarter and 1% year-on-year.
The ONS also reported that the economy expanded 0.3% in June, beating market expectations for a 0.1% contraction.
June’s growth followed no change in May, revised down from an earlier estimate of 0.1% growth, and a 0.1% contraction in April.
Although the data pointed to resilience in the first half of the year, the economic impact of the Iran war is expected to become more visible in the coming months as disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz feed into household and business costs.
British households are also facing a 13% increase in the energy price cap that took effect in July, adding to inflationary pressures and potentially complicating the Bank of England’s interest-rate outlook.

Baltics' first AI factory to open in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:25:00 UTC
15:25:00 KST

Baltics' first AI factory to open in Estonia
Dutch cloud company Nebius' Tallinn AI factory will begin operating at Greenergy Data Centers' data center this year. With a capacity of 22 megawatts, it will be the largest in the Baltics.
Nasdaq-listed Nebius announced Wednesday that it signed agreements in the second quarter to expand the company's AI infrastructure network in Europe. The first phase of its Tallinn AI factory, with a capacity of 22 megawatts, is expected to begin operating later this year.
Nebius Head of Communications Tom Blackwell said Estonia was a natural choice for the company thanks to its world-class engineers, vibrant digital economy and startup culture, as well as its ambitious plans for both artificial intelligence and the transition to clean energy.
"Nebius' Tallinn AI factory, which is being developed in partnership with Greenergy Data Centers, will provide state-of-the-art infrastructure to support Estonia's growing innovation ecosystem and help accelerate the development and adoption of artificial intelligence," he said.
Nebius' global capacity network has expanded rapidly. In Europe, the company is developing large-scale AI factories in Lappeenranta, Finland, and Béthune, France. It also has an operating center in Mäntsälä, Finland, as well as AI infrastructure projects in the United Kingdom, Spain and Iceland. Nebius' major customers include Microsoft and Meta.
Greenergy Data Centers CEO Kert Evert said Nebius' decision to choose Greenergy shows that Estonia is emerging as a competitive destination for large-scale AI infrastructure projects.
Blackwell said Nebius wants to work closely with the Estonian government, businesses and universities to develop AI skills, broaden access to artificial intelligence capabilities and strengthen Estonia's position as a leading hub for AI innovation.
Martin Salo, co-founder of Tensor Estate, a group of Estonian entrepreneurs that became a shareholder in Greenergy Data Centers last month, said the newly announced project is the first phase of a larger development that will make Estonia one of the international hubs for AI infrastructure in the coming years.
"Until now, Northern Europe's major AI factories have been concentrated primarily in Finland, Sweden and Norway, thanks to favorable electricity prices, renewable energy and a suitable climate. Having the Baltics' first AI factory come here means Estonia is joining the club of countries where the world's leading AI companies are building their infrastructure," Salo said.
In late July, Greenergy Data Centers' Head of Hyperscale Martin Rungi told ERR that attracting one major international customer to Estonia would make it significantly easier for data centers to secure additional customers, as the market develops after the first breakthrough.
In Nebius' case, however, the question of its ties to Russian technology company Yandex cannot be overlooked, as Nebius emerged after Yandex came under sanctions following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In 2024, the company sold its Russian business units and changed its name to Nebius Group, which is headquartered in the Netherlands. Nebius CEO Arkady Volozh is also a co-founder of Yandex, but has since renounced his Russian citizenship.
A Greenergy representative said last month that such labeling was inappropriate, arguing that Nebius is probably one of the most thoroughly vetted organizations, given that despite its former ties to Russia, it has earned the trust of Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, the U.S. government and the New York Stock Exchange.
Economy minister: We have consulted security agencies
As government agencies have had concerns about Nebius and the workforce at the AI factory set to operate in Hüüru, Estonian security agencies have been consulted, Minister of Economic Affairs and Industry Erkki Keldo said.
"On the one hand, cutting-edge investments like these /.../ are certainly very welcome in Estonia, but on the other hand, the government has an obligation to look at the broader security picture. So yes, we are aware of the background, we are also in contact with Estonian authorities and will certainly minimize the risks," he said, adding that it is very important to understand that the factory is purely a private investment.
If questions arise about a company's background or workforce, there are rules and security agencies in place, and those agencies have also informed the public about potential risks and threats, the minister noted.
"We certainly have to ensure that any sensitive data, sensitive sectors and sensitive technologies do not, for example, fall into the hands of high-risk countries. And when using different types of data, we have to pay attention to whose technology we are using and where we use and store data, to ensure that it is protected. That is certainly what we are doing," Keldo said.
According to Keldo, Nebius was also discussed at a Cabinet meeting on Thursday and discussions on the matter will continue in the coming weeks.
"Estonian businesses need to understand these potential risks, including the company itself and that people with Russian backgrounds and Russian contacts are not welcomed here with overly open arms. We are certainly somewhat more vigilant about this than perhaps other European countries are, and that will remain the case in the future," Keldo said.
The article was updated to add comments from Minister Erkki Keldo.

Colombia’s earthquake is déjà vu for Venezuelans. The government response is anything but
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:23:01 UTC
15:23:01 KST

Colombia’s earthquake is déjà vu for Venezuelans. The government response is anything but
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — For the second time in two months, the ground was shaking in South America. Once again, families flooded social media with pleas for help finding missing loved ones under flattened buildings. Once again, governments across political divides and continents pledged aid.
But in many ways, the contrast between Colombia’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake on Monday and Venezuela’s back-to-back temblors on June 24 could not have been more stark.
In Venezuela, acting President Delcy Rodríguez waited nearly four hours before addressing the nation. In Colombia, newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an emergency command post to oversee rescue efforts barely an hour after the earthquake struck. For weeks, Venezuelan civilians were clawing through rubble by hand. Hours after the earthquake in Colombia, rescue teams were searching for survivors with cranes and excavators.
In Venezuela, Rodríguez relied on rescuers from around the world to fill critical gaps in the state’s response. Colombia has so far declined foreign crews except for those from the United States, saying it has enough personnel and has requested humanitarian supplies instead.
The contrast is a reminder of the differences between the neighboring nations — their political systems, resources and the strength of their institutions — and a demonstration of how those can take on life-or-death importance in catastrophes.
“The differences between an authoritarian regime and a democratic system can be seen clearly in the institutions and in their capacity to respond to an emergency,” said Ronal Rodríguez, a Venezuela specialist at Colombia’s Rosario University. “Crises are also political opportunities.”
In Colombia, a political newcomer takes charge
De la Espriella, a conservative former criminal defense lawyer with no previous political experience, was sworn in as president in Colombia’s third-largest city, Cali, less than 72 hours before the earthquake toppled buildings there and across the country’s far-flung provinces — the very regions he’d pledged to prioritize on the campaign trail.
Even before the earthquake, the political novice was navigating a fraught transition from predecessor Gustavo Petro, Colombia’s first leftist president, who at first refused to recognize de la Espriella’s narrow victory and alleged electoral fraud.
Their feud derailed Colombia’s formal handover process, leaving key agencies — including the national disaster management agency — in the hands of officials de la Espriella attacked as a candidate.
But humanitarian workers say the government’s earthquake response has transcended those tensions, reflecting the resilience of Colombia’s democracy.
“All the institutions have worked,” said María José Torres Macho, the United Nations’ top official in Colombia. “Our ability to be working with them has not been affected by the change of government.”
Just an hour after the quake, de la Espriella posted a video saying he would “personally assume leadership” of the disaster response. “You’re not alone,” he told Colombians in the country’s hard-hit coffee-growing region.
Hours later, he was in Bogota, coordinating with government officials and relief agencies. Within 36 hours, he had toured disaster zones in the western cities of Quibdo, Cali and Pereira and dispatched ministers further afield.
“There is an entire system that means that even when you change the person at the top, the institution keeps functioning,” said Ana Karina García, director of Fundación Juntos Se Puede, a Venezuelan migrant aid group based in Colombia.
Still, Colombia’s response has not been without controversy. De la Espriella’s rejection of rescue teams from around the world has raised questions about his handling of foreign aid, with China’s ambassador complaining on social media that he did not even know which Colombian official was responsible for coordinating international assistance.
Rugged terrain, poor infrastructure and communication disruptions have slowed casualty reports from the hardest-hit areas. The government’s national toll of at least 265 dead and 500 missing lags far behind counts from local authorities, while an independent database lists over 4,100 as unaccounted for.
In Venezuela, a political veteran comes under fire
Despite Rodríguez’s nearly two decades at the highest levels of Venezuela’s government, she struggled to project authority over the disaster response.
Hours before Rodríguez took to the airwaves to declare a national emergency, her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, called state television with damage reports — a sign of their competing claims to power within the ruling party.
Later, when Rodríguez gave the government’s initial casualty toll, she reported just 32 dead, a count that didn’t include the epicenter of La Guaira, site of the worst destruction. Many of La Guaira’s victims lived in government-built housing complexes thrown up cheaply during the oil boom of the early 2000s, part of the self-declared socialist party’s vast subsidized housing program that became a pillar of its political patronage system.
Rodríguez remained ensconced in Caracas for a full day before visiting La Guaira and assessing the damage. The government updated the death toll daily in the week that followed without offering a figure for missing people, fueling concerns of a vast undercount as civilians struggled to recover the dead without heavy machinery.
Now, more than six weeks after the quakes, a widely cited opposition-run database lists 29,000 people as unaccounted for. Government officials update the death toll once a week; as of Monday it stood at 6,301.
Years of political repression deepened Venezuelans’ distrust of the official earthquake response.
“It was very difficult for citizens to access important information about the emergency, get themselves to safety and know where to seek help,” said Gabriel Bastidas, a Venezuelan journalist based in Argentina who runs Monitoreamos.com, an independent news website critical of Venezuela’s governing political movement that’s among dozens of media outlets blocked in the country.
A stronger state swings into action
But even if Venezuela’s response had been perfect, the aftermath might still have looked very different from Colombia’s: The twin quakes struck densely populated La Guaira around nightfall, complicating reconnaissance, while Colombia’s hit largely rural areas in daylight.
Experts caution that it often takes weeks for a full picture to emerge after a disaster of this magnitude. Colombia is only days into its response, with thousands still missing.
Still, many Venezuelans marvel at how the Colombian government has drawn on resources that years of economic crisis and mass migration under former President Nicolás Maduro have hollowed out in their country.
“From the very beginning, we saw the news media broadcasting live from the sites of the catastrophe; mayors, governors, health secretaries, emergency officials providing details about the dead and missing,” Bastidas said.
Juan Mogollon, a 28-year-old Venezuelan living in Orlando, Florida, learned from a TV broadcast Monday morning that his 16-year-old cousin, José Juan Vivas, and the boy’s grandparents were trapped in the ruins of their apartment building in Cali. Vivas, a U.S. permanent resident, was living there with his grandparents, who settled in Colombia after leaving Venezuela.
Having watched people back home plead for rescuers and equipment after Venezuela’s June earthquakes, Mogollon feared the worst.
Yet within a few hours, he said, footage from the collapse site showed excavators, cranes and other heavy machinery, along with firefighters flown in from Bogota. Security forces deployed dogs and drones equipped with thermal cameras to identify victims across stricken towns.
“They are prepared, they have the equipment, they have the protocols, they know what to do,” Mogollon said, still anxiously waiting to hear if his relatives survived. “That’s the least we should expect as citizens in every country, you know? That’s the difference between my country and Colombia right now.
___
Associated Press writer Astrid Suárez in Bogota, Colombia, contributed to this report.

A punishing European drought shrivels crops from Dutch potatoes to Bosnian corn
WOLPHAARTSDIJK, Netherlands (AP) — A cloud of dust billows behind Maarten Janse’s tractor as he spreads a mixture of compost, straw and manure over a field to nourish the parched soil.
Janse’s farm on the fertile land of the Netherlands’ southwestern Zeeland Province is drying out despite his efforts to make it more drought resistant as accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Nino batter fields across Europe.
The drought that is roasting much of Europe this summer is taking a heavy toll on crops across the continent, from potatoes in the Netherlands to corn in Bosnia and grapes in Italy. Even when farmers try to adapt, the extreme weather is hitting their crops and water supplies.
Triodos, a Dutch bank that has a focus on sustainability, published an analysis this week that estimated the heatwaves and drought could reduce gross domestic product across the European Union by 1% for 2026 or around 180 billion euros ($208 billion). Farmers are among the hardest hit, with their crops set to be badly affected by soaring temperatures and lack of water. In large parts of the Netherlands, farmers are no longer allowed to use water from streams and drainage channels to irrigate fields and orchards.
Just add water? Dutch crops suffer from the drought
Another farmer in Zeeland, Hendrik Jan ten Cate, looks at a field full of withered potato plants that are almost all ready for harvest — a month early and with a significantly reduced crop. His potatoes are used to make French fries for companies including McDonald’s, but they’re likely going to be too small this year.
“People want long fries,” he says as he holds one of the potatoes. “That’s going to be tough this year.”
Ten Cate is one of the lucky farmers because he is allowed to irrigate his crops. But, even so, he estimates his harvest this year will be down by about one-third compared to average years.
“It’s not just the drought that is the problem,” he says. “It is also the sun, the dry air and especially the hot days we have had this year. The potatoes just can’t handle that combination very well.”
Bosnian agriculture, a key driver of the economy, is suffering
In Bosnia, where agriculture contributes roughly 5% of annual GDP and 10% of all employment, grain farmer Slavisa Lukic stood in one of his corn fields as stalks blew limply in the breeze. His crops have been hit by repeated heat waves and drought conditions. He said this year’s corn yield would be very poor, if he manages to harvest one at all.
Lukic remembers when he grew 6 to 7 tons per hectare on his farm. He expects this year’s corn yield will be around 1.5 to 2 tons per hectare.
Pointing to the drought-stricken land in northeastern Bosnia, Lukic said clover fields that once grew abundantly have all but disappeared. “Now they literally do not exist,” he said. “Nothing.”
Czech brewers fear bad hop harvest
The drought is even hitting one of the Czech Republic’s most famous products: beer.
Plzeňský Prazdroj, the country’s largest beer producer, expects to incur losses this year due to a stunted hops yield.
Jakub Zaoral, the brewer’s sustainability manager, said that changes in rainfall patterns — characterized by long periods of dryness with occasional heavy storms — mean that when rain does fall, it runs off the dry soil. That results in inconsistent yields and increasingly low groundwater levels.
“There’s no choice but to simply accept the fact that one year will be great and the next won’t be,” he said. “If it were to happen three times in a row, that could very well become an existential problem for hop growers.”
Drought takes a toll across the Danube region
In Romania, some heat and drought-resistant crops like sunflowers have been less affected by the extreme conditions and yields have been plentiful. But the drought is still hitting home with record-low water levels on the Danube River disrupting grain transport, causing chronically congested terminals and an increasing pileup of crops with nowhere to go.
“In a short time, maximum 10 days, we will enter full blast in sunflower harvest, to be followed by corn,” Cezar Gheorghe, founder of grain consultancy firm Agricolumn, told The Associated Press. “Already farmers are in panic mode. They can’t find a place to store the corn and sunflower seeds.”
Cattle grazing plains in Hungary are turning to dust. No rain has fallen on Sándor Molnár’s dairy farm since late May and he is having to buy expensive feed for his 130 cows.
“We’re trying to hang in there and hope for the best, hoping next year will be better,” he added. “To be honest, we’ve been saying that for a few years now, but maybe this time it will be.”
Huge UK farm that invested in irrigation is feeling the heat
Elveden Estate, with more than 10,000 acres of farmland on the Suffolk-Norfolk border in eastern England, has built a reservoir that can hold enough water to fill about 200 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Less than a year after opening, it’s almost dry. Another reservoir is at about 20% capacity.
But the farm’s water policy is paying off.
“The fact that we’ve invested significantly in reservoir storage and the infrastructure associated with pumping water has meant that we’ve been in a very strong position to continue to irrigate our crops through this growing season,” the farm’s managing director, Andrew Blenkiron, said.
But every drop counts.
“We’re very concerned that we haven’t got enough water to see us through this season,” Blenkiron said. “We’ve got probably, if this weather stays as it is, six weeks of watering left to do.”
Diversify and feed the soil
Janse uses no-till farming on his fields — not plowing the soil, planting crops to cover the ground year-round and adding organic matter — to help cope with the whims of the weather as climate change triggers more extremes.
He has also diversified by running a popular campsite on his farm near the picturesque town of Veere. As he tends to his fields, guests walk by toward a lake where yachts and a river cruise ship sail past.
And as dry weather causes an increase in soil salinity in fields, Janse grows samphire, also known as sea asparagus, on a small patch of land. It’s a crop that can thrive in salty conditions. But with no rainfall, even that is struggling this year.
“Samphire needs fresh water, and if there is only saltwater it doesn’t grow either,” he said.
___
Nadja Lovadinov in London, Mustakim Hasnath in Suffolk, Stanislav Hodina in Prague, Czech Republic, Justin Spike in Budapest, Hungary, and Stephen McGrath in Leamington Spa, England, contributed to this report.

Platforms failed to stop death threats against activists, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

Threats of rape, murder and deepfake porn used against women who challenged abusive video games
In short:
A women's rights group has released a report detailing death threats it received after campaigning to remove video games depicting violence against women from online platforms.
Collective Shout is calling for tech platforms to do more to identify and remove hateful and violent content.
What's next?
The women from Collective Shout want the federal government to prioritise reforms about tech-facilitated violence against women.
WARNING: This story contains graphic depictions of gender-based violence.
A year ago, Coralie Alison woke to find her personal phone number, date of birth and passwords had been posted online.
In the hours that followed, she received horrific deepfake images of herself.
"Images of my throat slit, my body burned alive, decapitated, stripped of my clothing and minced alive,"
Ms Alison was one of five members of the women's rights group Collective Shout who found themselves the target of violent abuse after the group successfully campaigned to remove video games depicting rape, incest and violence towards women and girls from online platforms.
The United Nations' special rapporteur on violence against women, Reem Alsalem, described the backlash that followed as "the most serious form of online violence against women human rights defenders" she had seen "in a long time".
The women detailed the abuse they received in a report released on Wednesday, while the Online Hate Prevention Institute (OHPI) was also commissioned to write a report on their experience.
The report found the targeted abuse was fuelled by misogyny and disinformation that tech platforms were unwilling or unable to stop.
Online terror begins
The furore started when payment processors including PayPal, Visa and Mastercard introduced new rules that compelled video game content to adhere to payment policies.
"Thousands of perpetrators across multiple platforms and countries mobilised to punish us for our 'crime' of successfully persuading gaming platforms, through their payment providers, to halt the sale of games featuring rape, sexual torture and child sexual abuse and incest," said Collective Shout director Melinda Tankard Reist.
Elon Musk, the owner of X, weighed in on the Collective Shout debate, endorsing a petition calling on the payment platforms to reverse their decision by reposting it on X along with the statement, "bravo".
X has no discernible Australian or global press office for the ABC to contact for comment.
Ms Tankard Reist said the coordinated abuse was intended to "humiliate, threaten and endanger our safety."
"The system [that was] supposed to protect us did not."
The women said their families were also targeted and their home addresses published on the internet.
Toxic masculinity
Patrick Scolyer-Gray, author of the OHPI report, told supporters gathered at Australia's Parliament House on Wednesday that the case of Collective Shout was internationally significant.
He said the abuse was dressed up to appear as a defence of free speech and anti-censorship concerns.
"It was never about video games, and it was never about free speech, and the backlash can't be understood without recognising the central role of misogyny," he said.
"Nearly every institution that should or could have interrupted this campaign failed to do so.
"Platform moderation systems proved inadequate, disinformation spread faster than corrections, abusive material remained online long enough to create the appearance of public consensus."
The OHPI report made 47 recommendations, the first being that harmful and sexist content specific to women should be identified immediately.
The report suggested the content should be"classified as misogynistic and a form of gender-based hate speech" before being removed by online platforms.
The authors also called on media organisations to act quickly to debunk misinformation.
Hopeful future
E-Safety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant has been calling for more safeguards ot protect women online.
She said the technology industry needed to step up to stop these platforms from being weaponised.
Collective Shout member Caitlin Roper said she was surprised by the profiles of the abusers.
"Some might [think] that the abuse was perpetrated by a very specific subset of misogynistic men in the dark corners of the internet," she said.
"The reality is that many of our abusers are 'regular men', who threatened to rape us, hunt us down and kill us from their actual social media accounts, showing them smiling alongside their wives and sometimes daughters."
Ms Roper said Collective Shout aimed to bring positive change that would "create a different world for our daughters".
"My greatest hope for this report is that the next woman who speaks out against male violence is protected, not punished for refusing to be silenced," said group member Renee Chopping.

Zelensky Says 5% of US Patriot Missiles Could Save Ukraine This Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:22:00 UTC
15:22:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky has asked the US for more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying 5% of the current US stockpile could help Ukraine survive the winter, while 10% could allow Kyiv to destroy all Russian ballistic missiles, CNN reported Thursday, Aug. 13.
Zelensky said Ukraine currently has only 1% of the Patriot interceptors it needs, while Russia has sharply increased the number of ballistic missiles it launches each month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“If they can sell us 5%, we will go through the winter and save people’s lives. If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%,” Zelensky said.
Russia is launching more ballistic missiles
Zelensky said Ukraine’s interceptor stocks have fallen sharply compared with last year, while Russia has increased the intensity of its ballistic missile attacks.
“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025. Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before,” he said.
The shortage is particularly dangerous ahead of winter, when Russia is expected to intensify attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to the United Nations.
Zelensky said Russian attacks now include several particularly heavy bombardments each month, leaving Ukrainian air defenses under increasing pressure.
“There are terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they are tired,” he said.
Putin Visits Disputed Kuril Islands for First Time as Russia-Japan Tensions Deepen
The global shortage of Patriot interceptors has also been worsened by the US war with Iran, where the systems have been used against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
Zelensky says he is fighting for every missile
Zelensky described securing additional Patriot interceptors as one of his main daily priorities, involving negotiations with the US and other international partners.
“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls,” he said.
Zelensky said he was pursuing various arrangements to obtain additional missiles but declined to disclose details of some of them.
“I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it,” he said.
Ukraine has also been negotiating with European countries for additional interceptors as US stocks remain constrained.
Ukraine’s Patriot production plans remain uncertain
Zelensky also said he remains uncertain whether Washington will ultimately allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptors under license.
US President Donald Trump initially said during the NATO summit in Ankara that Ukraine would receive a license to produce the missiles domestically. He later appeared to back away from the proposal, citing concerns over transferring sensitive technology.
US Patriot manufacturers have sent representatives to Kyiv to discuss possible production, but no final agreement has been reached.
“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”
Zelensky confirms call with Vance
Zelensky also confirmed that he recently spoke with US Vice President JD Vance but declined to discuss the details.
The Financial Times previously reported that Vance had raised concerns about Ukrainian attacks on a Russian oil port in the Black Sea, which could affect US companies and global energy prices.
Zelensky did not say whether the issue was discussed during his conversation with Vance.
Kyiv wants more US involvement in peace talks
Zelensky said Ukraine has also presented new proposals for the US-led peace process, which has stalled in recent months.
“We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan,” he said, arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin does not currently appear ready to end the war and that Moscow is not facing enough pressure.
Zelensky rejected the possibility of Ukraine surrendering the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of Donbas sought by Russia.
He said security guarantees are essential because a ceasefire could give Russia time to rebuild its military and launch another invasion.
“Why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president also said he agreed with Western assessments that Putin could eventually seek to expand the war against NATO, potentially targeting the Baltic states.
“He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control,” Zelensky said.

A-level results: students across England, Wales and Northern Ireland await grades – latest news
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:21:58 UTC
15:21:58 KST

The gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades and the equivalent figure in both north-east England and the East Midlands has reached a new record size.
32.7% of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1% in 2025 and the highest for any region in England, the exam results show.
The north-east and the East Midlands had the joint lowest rate, at 23.1%.
The gap between London and each of these two regions now stands at 9.6 percentage points, the largest since the present system of grading began in 2010, according to Press Association analysis.
In north-east England, the gap has widened from 9.2 points in 2025, though the proportion of entries getting A or A* rose slightly this year, from 22.9% to 23.1%.
By contrast, the East Midlands saw a drop in entries awarded the top grades, from 23.8% to 23.1%, the biggest fall of any region. This pushed the gap with London up from 8.3 points in 2025 to 9.6 points this year.
At a national level, 10.7% of A-level entries this year in Wales received A*, higher than the equivalent figure for England (9.6%) and Northern Ireland (8.8%).
For entries awarded A or above, Northern Ireland was ahead at 30.7%, above Wales (29.6%) and England (28.3%).
Whatever the grades, well done to everyone who received their results today. Best of luck to those hoping to secure a university place through clearing.
For those considering university next year, we will be publishing the Guardian’s University Guide 2027 in early September with our rankings of the top universities and lots of useful advice on choosing the right course and institution for you. You can read last year’s guide here.
Here is a summary of today’s events:
Sixth-formers have basked in a summer of record-breaking exam results in academic and vocational subjects, allowing more than a quarter of a million 18-year-olds to go on to higher education. The proportion of students in England gaining the highest grade of A* in A-level subjects rose to 9.7%, up from 9.4% last year, setting a new record outside the pandemic era, when exams were scrapped.
Northern Ireland was the best-performing country, with 30.7% of grades being As and A*s, followed by 29.6% in Wales and 28.7% in England. The A-level results followed last week’s improved results in Scotland, where the proportion of students awarded Highers and Advanced Highers qualifications rose above 2019 pre-pandemic levels, and a record 18,000 Scottish school-leavers gained higher education places.
Boys have outperformed girls in terms of top grades again, after doing so for the first time in seven years last year. Overall, 28.9% of boys’ A-level entries scored an A* or A this summer, compared to 28.0% of their female classmates’ entries – a gap of 0.9 percentage points.
The gap between the proportion of A-level entries in London getting the top grades and the equivalent figure in both north-east England and the East Midlands has reached a new record size. 32.7% of entries in the capital were awarded A or A* this year, up from 32.1% in 2025 and the highest for any region in England, the exam results show.
Councils in the south of England have topped the league tables this year. In Guildford, half of all A-levels recieved an A grade or above, while Richmond in London saw 49% of grades achieve at least an A. Not all Southern areas did as well. Harlow in Essex saw just 7% of grades achieve at least an A, while Test Valley in Hampshire saw 10% (the average for England was 28%).
Results for students taking vocational and technical qualifications (VTQs) have taken a more prominent role during results day this year, after prime minister Andy Burnham declared his ambition to build parity between academic and vocational paths. More than 300,000 VTQ results across 420 qualifications were awarded, according to the Joint Council for Qualifications, with business, administration and law the most popular subject areas.
Students at private schools in England saw their top grades remain relatively flat this year – with 48.6% receiving an A* or A grade, up just 0.5 percentage points on last year. Meanwhile, students at sixth form colleges saw grades rise 0.5 points, academies saw grades rise 0.4 points, and local authority controlled comprehensives saw a 0.3 point rise. Grammar schools saw a slight fall in A and A* grades.
While the improvement in national A-level results in England is taking the headlines, social mobility experts say they are alarmed by the widening gap in performance between students in London and the south of England and their peers in other parts of the country. Nick Harrison, head of the Sutton Trust that campaigns on improving social mobility through education, said the results “reveal an increasingly stark regional divide, as London continues to pull further ahead of the rest of England”.
Shakespeare is out, while Isaac Newton is in, the figures show. This year’s results have continued the squeezing of arts and humanities subjects – which made up just over a quarter of exam entries. Ten years ago, they made up 40% of A-level exams. As we’ve written earlier, the squeeze is mainly driven by maths, other STEM subjects, and increasingly social science subjects like economics.
Exam boards pushed back on any suggestion of grade inflation after A-level students recorded record levels at A and A*. Presenting the results at a briefing by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), Richard Henry, director of qualifications and assessment at the Welsh exam board, WJEC, insisted grades could be trusted.
Results day is always governed by strict embargo, but some anxious students got their news early after the University of Surrey accidentally sent out text messages to successful applicants last night. Instead of sending the information at 8.10am Thursday morning, text messages went out to 2,400 successful applicants (about half the total) at 8.10pm last night when the nation was enjoying the eclipse.
The number of UK school leavers accepted on to degree courses has risen to a record high this year, Ucas figures show. A total of 262,820 UK 18-year-olds have gained a place at university or college – up 3% on the same point last year, according to data published by the university admissions service.
For international students, 53,740 applicants have been accepted on to undergraduate courses – up by 2% on the 52,640 who were successful last year. Accepted applicants from China rose to 13,870 from 12,380 last year.
Councils in the south of England have topped the league tables this year. In Guildford, half of all A Levels recieved an A grade or above, while Richmond in London saw 49% of grades achieve at least an A.
Not all Southern areas did as well. Harlow in Essex saw just 7% of grades achieve at least an A, while Test Valley in Hampshire saw 10% (the average for England was 28%).

James, 18, will study for a rural land and property management degree at the university in Cirencester after joining thousands of teenagers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland who received their A-level results.
James’s grades and the subjects he studied at the private Radley College in Oxfordshire have not been disclosed, PA report.
In light of Andy Burnham’s stated ambition to bridge England’s deep-rooted north-south regional divide, today’s A-level results only confirm the scale of the challenge he faces.
London continues to extend its lead with 32.7% of pupils receiving grade A or above, up from 31.9% last year. This is the largest increase of any region, and extends the gap between the capital and the north-east to 9.6 percentage points. Before Covid it was 3.9pp.
The gap in A* grades has also widened substantially, from 2 percentage points in 2019 before the pandemic – to 5.1 points in 2026.
Chris Zarraga, director of Schools North East which represents over 1,150 schools in the region, said:
There is not a north-south divide in the quality of schools or in the potential and ambition of young people. There is a structural divide in the circumstances and opportunities surrounding them.
Schools in different parts of England are not operating on a level playing field. In the north-east, schools are working within communities facing entrenched disadvantage, intense pressure on public services, growing SEND [special educational needs and disabilities] needs and very different access to opportunities and infrastructure.
Increasingly, schools are being asked to compensate for all of those things.
That does not mean accepting lower outcomes. These divides are not inevitable. But we will not close them simply by demanding more from schools while leaving the conditions around them unchanged.
Government needs to treat this as a system challenge. We need a long-term approach that connects education with early years, health, SEND, transport, skills and economic development, alongside high-quality academic and vocational pathways.
Results day should reflect young people’s potential and hard work, not the structural advantages or disadvantages of where they happen to grow up.
Commenting on today’s figures, which show record demand for higher education and a record number of UK 18-year-olds applying to university, University Alliance chief executive Vanessa Wilson said:
Firstly, congratulations to everyone receiving their results today. Whether you’ve secured your first-choice place, are exploring options through clearing, or are still deciding what’s right for you, this is an important milestone and you should be proud of what you’ve achieved.
The continued growth in demand for higher education shows that students recognise the value of developing the knowledge, skills and experience they need to succeed in the rapidly changing world of work. Professional and technical universities play a crucial role in this, combining academic learning with practical, work-related experience and foundational partnerships with employers.
For students who got different results than expected, it’s not too late to find a course that’s right for you. There are excellent opportunities available through clearing. Our universities are on hand to support and advise you to find the right opportunity.
As London continued to stretch its lead ahead of the rest of the country, one of the capital’s highest-scoring schools celebrated a stellar set of A-level results which will enable one in 10 students to realise their dream and go on to study medicine at university.
At Michaela Community School in Brent, students achieved an average of AAA across all subjects, while one in three exams were graded A* and 90% were B or above.
Head teacher Katharine Birbalsingh, star of a TV documentary called Britain’s Strictest Headteacher, celebrated her pupils’ success with a string of touching result reveal clips on X.
“We are delighted with these fantastic results,” she said, adding, “11% of students are going to study medicine, 85% will be going off to Russell Group Universities.”
Shakespeare is out, while Isaac Newton is in, the figures show. This year’s results have continued the squeezing of arts and humanities subjects – which made up just over a quarter of exam entries.
Ten years ago, they made up 40% of A-level exams. As we’ve written earlier, the squeeze is mainly driven by maths, other STEM subjects, and increasingly social science subjects like economics.
For English, the writing may not quite yet be on the wall, but its not looking great.
Students at private schools in England saw their top grades remain relatively flat this year – with 48.6% receiving an A* or A grade, up just 0.5 percentage points on last year.
Meanwhile students at sixth form colleges saw grades rise 0.5 points, academies saw grades rise 0.4 points, and local authority controlled comprehensives saw a 0.3 point rise. Meanwhile grammar school saw a slight fall in A and A* grades.
During the pandemic – when grades were teacher assessed – private schools saw a larger jump in top grades compared to other centres. Since then the gap between private and state funded schools has narrowed, and in recent years has remained steady.
Results for students taking vocational and technical qualifications (VTQs) have taken a more prominent role during results day this year, after prime minister Andy Burnham declared his ambition to build parity between academic and vocational paths.
More than 300,000 VTQ results across 420 qualifications were awarded, according to the Joint Council for Qualifications, with business, administration and law the most popular subject areas.
The number of students receiving results for T-levels – which are two-year technical education courses available in England and equivalent in size to three A-levels – jumped 65% on last year as the qualification continues to establish itself. Almost 20,000 students received results, up from 12,000 last year, with a pass rate of over 90%.
The prime minister congratulated students, saying: “It’s brilliant to see more students succeeding in T-levels, more taking maths and STEM subjects, and more young people progressing to the next stage of their education or training.
“The talent is there in every town and city in this country. Our task is to match that talent with opportunity, whether that’s through university, an apprenticeship or a technical pathway that leads to a great career. That’s how we’ll build a stronger Britain, restore hope and ensure every young person can look to the future with confidence.”
Dani Payne, head of education and social mobility at the Social Market Foundation thinktank, said today’s results showed the scale of the challenge facing the government. “T-level growth offers real encouragement for Andy Burnham’s push to put technical education on a more equal footing with academic routes.
“The number of students receiving a T-level technical qualification result has risen by around two-thirds in just one year, while outcomes remain strong, suggesting that expanding these qualifications does not have to come at the expense of standards.”
But higher education remains by far the more established and visible route for young people, she said. “More than 320,000 students received A-level results today, compared with fewer than 20,000 receiving T level results, while a record 262,820 UK 18-year-olds have already been placed at university.
“If [Burnham] wants technical education to command genuine parity of esteem, creating new pathways will only be the beginning. It will require sustained investment in further education, to ensure these new pathways lead somewhere meaningful: into good jobs, training and further study.”
While the improvement in national A-level results in England is taking the headlines, social mobility experts say they are alarmed by the widening gap in performance between students in London and the south of England and their peers in other parts of the country.
Nick Harrison, head of the Sutton Trust that campaigns on improving social mobility through education, said the results “reveal an increasingly stark regional divide, as London continues to pull further ahead of the rest of England”.
Harrison said:
A young person’s chances shouldn’t depend so heavily on where they go to school, and these results underline the need for concerted action to tackle the attainment gap and regional differences across England.
Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, noted that even within London there were stark inequality geps between the capital’s boroughs:
London’s success at a regional level is masking some severe inequalities within the capital itself. It’s a reminder that we can improve opportunities throughout the country, even in the regions that seem to be the most successful.
The proportion of top grades can more than double just by crossing the river. Almost half of every A-level result in Richmond-upon-Thames was an A or A*. In neighbouring Hounslow that figure is closer to one in five.
Prime minister Andy Burnham offered his congratulations to A-level students this morning.
He said:
I want to congratulate everyone receiving their results today. I know there will have been a mix of excitement, nerves and relief this morning, but you should all be proud of the hard work that got you here.
It’s brilliant to see more students succeeding in T-levels, more taking maths and Stem subjects, and more young people progressing to the next stage of their education or training.
The talent is there in every town and city in this country. Our task is to match that talent with opportunity, whether that’s through university, an apprenticeship or a technical pathway that leads to a great career. That’s how we’ll build a stronger Britain, restore hope and ensure every young person can look to the future with confidence.
This year’s top 10 most chosen subjects is once again the same as last year– but there has been some movement.
Once again, maths has dominated - with more than 107,000 students taking the subject in England (and that’s not including almost 20,000 further maths entries).
Economics has shot up the rankings to become the fifth most popular subject, overtaking sociology, physics and business. History was also a big winner, rising three places to become the 6th most popular subject.
Sociology fell four places – but the drop was more than made up by rises in students taking other social sciences. Politics, law and psychology – like economics – all saw significant rises in entries.
Results day is always governed by strict embargo, but some anxious students got their news early after the University of Surrey accidentally sent out text messages to successful applicants last night.
Instead of sending the information at 8.10am Thursday morning, text messages went out to 2,400 successful applicants (about half the total) at 8.10pm last night when the nation was enjoying the eclipse.
A spokesperson for the University of Surrey said:
A scheduled results day text message was sent at the wrong time to some University of Surrey offer holders.
The information and recipients were correct, but the message was sent at 8.10pm on Wednesday rather than 8.10am on Thursday.
We are extremely sorry for this error. We self-reported to Ucas and worked closely with their team through the evening.
We immediately put in place a dedicated line for people who received the messages in error and were available to provide support through the night.
Among the most striking trends in A-levels this year is the surge in popularity of economics at A-level which jumped to the fifth most popular course, up from 10th position last year, with more than 47,000 entries.
Myles McGinley, managing director of the Cambridge OCR exam board, speaking at a briefing by the Joint Council for Qualifications (JCQ), said: “The students getting their A-level results today were born around 2008.
“So they’re the children of the financial crisis [and they] will have experienced the implications and impacts of that through Covid and beyond, and those forces that really shape the world.
So I think it feels natural that they should be interested in that. And of course we know that economics provides excellent career options.”

FSSAI proposes nutritional tables instead of warning labels on food packs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:21:33 UTC
15:21:33 KST

FSSAI has suggested a tabular declaration of the recommended daily requirement of added sugar, saturated fats and salt.
Citing industry’s opposition to warning labels on food packets, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has suggested a tabular declaration of the recommended daily requirement of added sugar, saturated fats and salt.The FSSAI’s affidavit filed in the Supreme Court only mentions the food industry’s opposition but has ignored the evidence in favour of warning label to help discourage consumption of foods high in added saturated fats, sugar and salt submitted by civil society representatives.FSSAI’s ‘compliance’ affidavit in response to the Supreme Court order directing it to frame Front of Pack labelling regulation states that a “majority of industry organizations were against the inclusion of ‘warning labels’ on the product,” and goes on to suggest a nutrition table giving “the daily allowance for added sugar, added saturated fat and salt vis a vis their presence in per serve of packed food product” on the front of the pack.“The proposed numerical table format being suggested by FSSAI would force consumers to do math at the supermarket shelf. The FSSAI has called it a ‘compliance’ affidavit but in reality, it is defiance. The Supreme Court had explicitly said that the exercise so far had not yielded any positive or good result and it had given FSSAI four weeks to revert. And six months later, FSSAI has filed an affidavit that abandons warning labels altogether and avoids defining HFSS (high fat, salt and sugar) foods.
Clearly, FSSAI has bowed to food industry’s interests,” said Dr Arun Gupta of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPi).FSSAI stated in the affidavit that it had held a stakeholder consultation on March 19, 2026 involving consumer groups, food industry representatives and farmer organisations. It stated that industry bodies argued that “consumers should be able to make an informed decision without creating fear amongst the consumers”. The affidavit was silent on the input given by consumer organisations, which had sought warning labels that have been shown to be the most effective in reducing consumption of junk food high in salt, sugar and saturated fats in several countries. NAPi had also given FSSAI evidence generated from studies conducted in India and other countries showing how effective warning labels are.

Polls open in Zambia presidential election as economic reforms tested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:20:46 UTC
15:20:46 KST

Zambians vote in presidential election as economic reforms tested
The vote will test if incumbent Hakainde Hichilema’s reforms are enough to overcome widespread frustration with living costs.
Zambians are casting their ballots in a presidential election pitting incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema against former minister Brian Mundubile.
Polls opened at 6am (04:00 GMT) on Thursday in a race dominated by economic concerns, and are expected to close at 16:00 GMT. Some 8.7 million people are registered to cast their ballots.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Zambia to vote as economic hardship tests government reforms
- list 2 of 4Zambia delaying US deals over minerals and data demands
- list 3 of 4Minerals for aid: Are new US health deals ‘exploiting’ African countries?
- list 4 of 4All the big elections to look out for in 2026
The vote will test whether economic reforms introduced by Hichilema’s government are enough to overcome widespread concerns over a rising cost of living.
More than 70 percent of Zambia’s 22 million people live on less than $3 a day, according to World Bank data.
While inflation fell to 6.8 percent in April and the kwacha currency has strengthened, many still face high food and energy costs. The unemployment rate is about 10 percent.
Long regarded as one of Africa’s more stable democracies, Zambia has come under scrutiny over concerns that Hichilema’s government has narrowed the space for dissent even as it promises stronger economic recovery.
Hichilema, 64, won a 2021 election on his sixth attempt and is betting on job creation and an ambitious infrastructure drive to secure a second five-year term.
Before casting his ballot on Thursday, Hichilema urged Zambians to vote peacefully. “Today, the future of our nation is in your hands,” he wrote on X. “Please vote peacefully, respect one another and remember that we are One Zambia, One Nation.”
His main challenger Mundubile, a former minister in the Patriotic Front (PF) government that ruled from 2011 to 2021, is backed by an alliance of opposition parties and has campaigned on promises to tackle the rising cost of living, improve agriculture and restore freedoms.
He entered the race in May, injecting uncertainty into a contest that had long appeared to be Hichilema’s to lose.
“I have just come from firing someone,” said Samuel Chitendwe, a 47-year-old welder and father of four who said he voted for Mundubile. “We are tired of stories about economic progress.”
‘Looking forward to greater things’
European Union election observers are watching Thursday’s election at a polling station in the capital.
A local observer cited by the Associated Press news agency said confusion over voter rolls, inadequate directions and poor crowd management at some polling stations caused delays and frustration that could discourage some people from voting.
Beene Siloka, a first-time voter, said casting her ballot was a proud moment despite some initial confusion about where to wait in line.
“I’ve cast my vote, and I’m proud,” she said. “It’s my first time voting, and we’re looking forward to greater things for Zambia.”
Speaking to the AFP news agency on Wednesday, Mundubile said the government had tightened restrictions on his party’s campaign and he did not see the election as being free and fair.
He said an opposition victory would begin with “a national reset” and reconciliation in a country he described as deeply divided. “There’s very little development you can do with a divided country,” he said.
Voters are also electing candidates for 226 parliament seats, up from the previous 156.
Voting has traditionally followed regional lines, with Hichilema’s party strongest in the south and west, and the PF retaining pockets of support in the north and Copperbelt.
Results of the presidential vote are expected by August 17. The winner needs more than 50 percent of votes to avoid a run-off.

Tamil Nadu mandates Tamil Thaai Vazhthu as first song at official events
The Tamil Nadu government has issued an order making ‘Tamil Thaai Vazhthu’, the state song, the first song to be rendered at all official events.The order applies to public, educational and government functions and mandates that attendees stand while the song is being played, with an exemption for persons with disabilities.The government order, issued by chief secretary M Sai Kumar on Wednesday, follows a unanimous resolution passed by the Tamil Nadu Assembly on August 10. It applies to all educational institutions, universities, government offices and public sector undertakings.The order also referred to the resolution piloted by chief minister C Joseph Vijay, stating that the “Assembly proudly records that Tamil is the ancient classical language of the world and Tamil civilisation is one of the oldest cultural traditions in the world.”Tamil Thaai Vazhthu was officially accorded the status of Tamil Nadu’s State Song on December 12, 2021, with its rendition made mandatory before programmes at educational institutions, universities, government offices, public sector undertakings and other public institutions in the state.
The song is taken from Manonmaniam, a play written by Manonmaniam Sundaranar in 1891. It has been sung at the beginning of government functions since November 23, 1970, and was formally recognised as the state song in December 2021.
The latest mandate comes amid observations by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs in a July 9 letter on the rendition of the State Song, including guidance on the sequence of songs and a reference to Vande Mataram.President Droupadi Murmu has given her assent to the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, granting Vande Mataram, India’s national song, the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana.The legislation amends the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. Parliament passed the Bill last month, and with the President’s assent, the amendments have now come into force as law.

Veteran journalist Oren Nahari dies at 70 after battle with ALS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:20:18 UTC
15:20:18 KST

Veteran Israeli journalist and broadcaster Oren Nahari died Thursday at age 70 after battling ALS.  
Nahari revealed in March that he had been diagnosed with the incurable disease and that his condition was deteriorating rapidly. In an interview on Kan 11’s “Pgisha” with Roni Kuban, he said the disease had begun affecting his limbs and that he was already using a walker. “I am a very clear-eyed person. There is no denial in me,” he said at the time, adding: “The greatest sorrow is that I will not have time with Vered and the grandchildren, because they are young, so they will not remember.”
Oren Nahari’s final broadcast:
Just five days ago, Nahari was forced to say goodbye to his radio work. In his final program, broadcast on Kan Reshet Bet, he announced that he had to stop hosting “Shabbat with Oren Nahari” and working on the podcast “A Year in an Hour” because of the progression of the disease.
“First, a difficult announcement,” Nahari, 70, said on his program. “This is the final program. As many of you know, I have ALS. The disease is progressing quickly. It is already affecting my breathing, walking and speech, and I will not be able to continue broadcasting. I am not saying goodbye to the world for now. I am only saying goodbye to the studio and the microphone, to this frequency that accompanied me for so many years.”
Nahari addressed his listeners, saying: “The stories will continue to be written without me. Remember, the world is wide, complex, and one must look at it with open eyes. That was my mission, and this is my final request of you: Continue to look, to listen, to ask questions, not to take things for granted and to keep being interested. Thank you for being with me all the way.”
After Nahari’s death was announced, President Isaac Herzog paid tribute to him: “With deep sorrow, I received the news of the passing of Oren Nahari, one of Israel’s senior journalists and media figures. Only a few days ago, I greeted him on air during his final program. For decades, Oren opened a window for all of us to the wider world, and he did so with rare talent, curiosity, professionalism and an open heart. Oren leaves behind a rich journalistic and cultural legacy and a unique voice that will be greatly missed. My heartfelt condolences to his family and all who loved him. May his memory be a blessing.”
Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid also eulogized Nahari: “In a world of fast media and instant gratification, Oren Nahari was a voice of culture, sanity, broad knowledge and genuine intellectual curiosity. May his memory be a blessing.” Knesset member Gilad Kariv also paid tribute to Nahari, calling him “a wise and brave journalist. A broad-minded intellectual with vast knowledge. A man of the wider world who loved this country with all his heart and grieved over what was happening in it. A man of public broadcasting. May his memory be a blessing. May he and those like him be a source of inspiration for Israeli media.”
The stories will continue to be written without me. Remember, the world is wide, complex, and one must look at it with open eyes. That was my mission
Nahari was born in Haifa and began his television career in the late 1970s in the sports department. In 1985, he moved to the Channel 1 news department, where he served as a foreign news correspondent and later became foreign news editor. Over the years, he was among the founders of the foreign news programs “Roim Olam” and “Globus,” which became a significant part of Channel 1’s programming for many years, and he covered many of the defining events of the late 20th century and the first decades of the 21st.
Alongside his television work, Nahari worked throughout his career in radio, wrote columns, including for ynet, and edited and wrote books. In recent years, he was especially identified with his current affairs and history program on Kan Reshet Bet, “Shabbat with Oren Nahari,” and with the podcast “A Year in an Hour.” Nahari continued broadcasting in recent months, even after revealing his illness, until the disease forced him to retire.
In parallel with his journalistic work, Nahari wrote nonfiction books and lectured on history, international relations and current affairs. His broad knowledge and ability to connect current events to wider historical contexts made him over the years one of Israel’s most recognizable and respected media figures in those fields.
In a joint interview with his wife, poet and poetry scholar Vered Ariel-Nahari, published in La’Isha in April, Nahari said that after the diagnosis, he began preparing for the future and even opened a folder on his computer that he called “Oren’s death.”
Nahari is survived by his wife, Vered, his two children and his grandchildren.

Reform UK's Farage faces off against Count Binface in election
LONDON, Aug 13 - Voters cast their ballots on Thursday in a local English election pitting Nigel Farage against his main challenger, a comedian dressed as a trash can, in a test of opposition to the Reform UK leader's brand of populist politics.
After weeks of facing accusations that he failed to properly declare millions of pounds received from a wealthy backer, Farage abruptly resigned from parliament last month to seek a new mandate in a "people against the establishment" election in the seaside resort of Clacton.
While Farage aims to demonstrate his strong local support to bolster his position against the charges, the decision by major parties not to put up candidates has left him facing more than 30 rivals, including comedians and independents, in what will be the longest ballot paper in British political history.
His main rival is likely to be Count Binface, a silver cape-clad character created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has run against three prime ministers over the last decade to poke fun at them.
DONATIONS BEING INVESTIGATED
Joke candidates are a normal feature of British elections, where it only costs £500 ($676) to enter a contest, but they are usually not the main competition.
Farage said last month the vote would allow his constituents to judge the allegations that he failed to properly declare a £5 million($6.8 million) donation from a billionaire.
Lawmakers must normally declare donations received in the year before an election within a month of taking office and parliament's standards commissioner has opened an investigation into whether any rules were broken.
If Farage is found to have breached the rules, he could face sanctions that trigger another election in the area.
Farage has repeatedly denied having an obligation to disclose the donation, which he said was a personal gift.
The area of Clacton in eastern England was once a popular holiday destination for Londoners but is now a fading seaside town that includes the village of Jaywick, rated as the nation's most deprived neighbourhood.
In 2024, Farage won 46% of the vote on a turnout of 58%. REUTERS

Rescuers search for five missing after Indonesia ferry fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
06:18:54 UTC
15:18:54 KST

Rescuers searched the Lombok Strait off Indonesia's Bali island on Thursday for five people missing after a ferry caught fire, killing one passenger and forcing dozens of others to jump overboard, officials said.
A total of 211 people were rescued and brought ashore by vessels that rushed to the scene on Wednesday, including a navy ship and another ferry nearby.
A 19-year-old Indonesian woman was found dead.
By Thursday, rescue efforts had shifted to searching for the five passengers still unaccounted for, the search and rescue office in Mataram on Lombok island said in a statement.
The ferry was travelling from Bali to Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of Wednesday.
"In addition to direct searches, we have also instructed ships passing through the Lombok Strait to provide initial assistance or immediately inform the command post if they find any victims," the statement quoted search and rescue official Muhamad Hariyadi as saying.
Survivors recall chaotic evacuation
Survivor Kiky Okta Pradika, 25, told reporters in Lembar on Lombok on Wednesday that he grabbed a life jacket before jumping overboard with several other passengers.
"There were a few hours before there was any help," he said.
Another survivor, 45-year-old Sutrisna, recalled passengers panicking and scrambling for life jackets as lifeboats were lowered from the stricken ferry.
"The evacuation was difficult because the waves were big, and when the rescue ship came, the waves were even bigger than the ferry we were on," Sutrisna said.
Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that relies heavily on boat connections for daily transport and tourism.
Lax safety standards and unpredictable weather are among the main factors behind such disasters.
Five people died last week after another ferry caught fire off Java island.
Last month, a ferry carrying more than 70 people sank near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi. Four bodies were recovered before the search operation ended, with 14 people still officially missing.

Large crowds gathered across Switzerland to watch solar eclipse
Applause rang out across Switzerland as the solar eclipse reached its peak at around 8:20pm. Armed with solar eclipse glasses, camping chairs and high spirits, many people turned out to watch the sky on Wednesday.
The spectacle began in the north-east of the country at around 7:25 pm and ended at around 8:45 pm in Geneva. At the Signal de Bernex, the second-highest point in the canton of Geneva, around a thousand people gathered, according to a Keystone-ATS journalist.
In Bern, large numbers of people gathered at the Rosengarten to watch the eclipse, according to a Keystone-ATS journalist on the scene. Dozens of onlookers had taken their places on the low walls and paths overlooking the bear pit. While waiting for the event to begin, people enjoyed picnics and drinks.
More
Rare solar eclipse to be observable from Switzerland
On a bluff in Murten in canton Fribourg overlooking the lake, around twenty people, including families, picnicked while watching the eclipse. The eclipse glasses were passed from hand to hand and lent to those who didn’t have their own, which encouraged conversations between strangers, according to a Keystone-ATS journalist at the scene.
Peaks taken by storm
The peaks of the Jura Arc, such as Chasseral and Tête-de-Ran, were swamped with visitors, as was the case in Moléson in canton Fribourg.
On the road leading to Chasseral in the Bernese Jura, traffic jams formed and the road was closed. Many hikers walked the remaining four or five kilometres on foot. “The Neuchâtel police intervened at the request of our Bernese colleagues, as the situation is complicated,” the cantonal police headquarters told ArcInfo.
In Valais, nearly 200 people watched the eclipse from the St-Luc observatory in the Val d’Anniviers. “In St-Luc, we were able to observe a partial eclipse of 91%, slightly less than in Geneva, while it was total in Spain,” said Guillaume Buro, chairman of the board of the François-Xavier Bagnoud Observatory Foundation, speaking on Swiss public television RTS.
In Ticino, nobody wanted to miss the astronomical event. Around 150 people gathered to watch the eclipse at Cardada, above Locarno, according to a Keystone-ATS photographer.
See you in 2081
The last partial eclipse of such significance in Switzerland took place in 1999, with the Sun being obscured by up to 99.5% in some places. To experience a similar event in Switzerland again, we will have to wait until 2075.
And for the next total eclipse, we will have to wait until 2081. The last total eclipse of the Sun took place in the Mendrisiotto and Val Poschiavo in 1842. In the Mittelland region, such an event was last witnessed in 1724.

Russian Shahed drone attacks passenger train in Odesa Oblast, killing driver and assistant
A Russian jet-powered Shahed drone has attacked a passenger train in Odesa Oblast, killing the train driver and assistant driver.
Source: Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, Chairman of the Board of the state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways); Ukrzaliznytsia press service
Quote from Pertsovskyi: "A jet-powered Shahed hit the locomotive of a passenger train in Odesa Oblast. Sadly, I have to report the worst news first-hand: early reports indicate that this strike left our locomotive crew – the driver and assistant driver – with no chance of survival."
Details: Pertsovskyi said a UAV threat had been detected shortly beforehand and the monitoring team issued an order to stop the train. The train was pulling into a station to allow passengers to be evacuated safely.
"The sudden manoeuvre of a jet-powered Shahed happened in a matter of minutes, giving the locomotive crew too little time to bring the train to a complete stop and evacuate the passengers and crew," he said.
The 340 passengers and train crew members, none of whom were injured, were evacuated to a safe location. Buses are currently being arranged to transport the passengers to Odesa.
Ukrzaliznytsia added that the circumstances of the incident are still being investigated.
Update: Kiper has said the train was carrying 340 passengers, including 67 children, along with the train crew.
Quote from Kiper: "Thanks to coordination by Odesa Oblast Military Administration and the joint work of all the appropriate services, people were promptly evacuated from the site of the strike. They were subsequently taken by 12 buses to a safe location in the city of Odesa. Ambulances were on standby along the evacuation route for passengers' safety."

Drapaty suspends head of Zakarpattia Territorial TRC – ombudsman
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
09:15:37 EEST
15:15:37 KST

The head of the Zakarpattia Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center (TRC) has been suspended from his post following allegations of human rights violations and corruption risks in the center’s operations, reported Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets.
"There are no untouchables. By decision of the Commander-in-Chief, the head of the Zakarpattia TRC has been suspended from office! Today we have a concrete result: an order to suspend the head of the Zakarpattia TRC. This is precisely the case where a signal about a problem did not remain without a response, a concrete decision was made on it," Lubinets wrote on Telegram.
The Ombudsman noted that human rights violations and corruption risks had already been recorded repeatedly, particularly in the activities of the head of the Zakarpattia TRC, which were spoken of publicly, addressed through official responses, and met with demands to cease violations.
"But instead of correcting the problem, they decided to fight those who pointed it out. First, attempts to hush up the revealed facts. When that didn’t work, informational pressure and even intentions to fabricate criminal proceedings against my employees who uncovered these violations. But that didn’t work," he said.
Lubinets considers this issue much broader than a single personnel change and questioned why the situation became possible in the first place.
"This is the result of more than one day and not the actions of one person. When there is no proper control for years, and systemic problems are not reacted to, a sense of impunity forms. This is precisely what, in my conviction, happened in Zakarpattia. And here one cannot overlook the inaction of the former leadership of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, which should have reacted to problems in the TRC system much earlier," he emphasized.
The Ombudsman separately thanked Commander-in-Chief of the AFU Mykhailo Drapatyi for his clear stance and response.
"This is exactly how the system works: we identify a problem, the responsible authorities eliminate it. Without hushing up, dragging out, or attempts to shift responsibility onto those who speak about the problem. Only such interaction yields real results and guarantees that human rights will be respected!" Lubinets stated.
As reported, Operational Command "West" declared its readiness to verify all circumstances regarding the activities of certain territorial recruitment and social support centers of Zakarpattia region and provide the competent authorities with necessary materials.
