TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Entie Bank said financial markets in the second half of the year will present risks and opportunities, advising investors to focus on geopolitical developments, US Federal Reserve policy, and corporate earnings while maintaining diversified asset allocations.
The bank said the Middle East conflict was the biggest factor affecting financial markets in the first half of the year, pushing oil prices as high as US$120 (NT$3,860) per barrel. Higher energy prices fueled inflation concerns and led to expectations of interest rate cuts, while semiconductor stocks led global markets amid strong corporate earnings and continued expansion in AI capital expenditures, per UDN.
Facing potentially high market volatility in the second half of the year, the bank recommended that investors adopt a strategy based on three principles: focusing on risks, grasping turning points, and diversifying allocations.
First, investors should monitor the secondary effects of geopolitical developments and policy changes on inflation and interest rates, the bank said. With the US midterm elections approaching in November, differences in fiscal and regulatory policies between the two major parties could further increase market uncertainty.
Second, the bank said investors should closely monitor the US Federal Reserve’s monetary policy. Stabilizing oil prices and base effects could gradually reduce inflation expectations, but the probability that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged during the second half of the year remains high. As a result, the expected rate-cut cycle could be delayed, with the timing of actual cuts potentially pushed back to 2027, Entie Bank said.
Third, the AI industry is shifting from a focus on capital expenditures toward verifying profitability and return on investment. Markets will closely examine whether spending by cloud computing giants can translate into actual profits, which will determine whether highly valued technology stocks face further valuation adjustments.
The bank said asset allocation in the second half of the year should return to fundamentals and risk management, with investors strengthening portfolio resilience. In equities, Entie Bank expects the third quarter to be a period of consolidation, followed by a shift toward earnings-driven growth in the fourth quarter, per UDN.
The traditional peak season for electronics in the fourth quarter, combined with stronger confirmation of fundamentals in the AI and semiconductor industries, could shift market attention back toward profit growth and trigger a new upward trend, the bank said.
For investors with medium- to long-term investment horizons and fixed-income needs, the current high-yield environment remains an attractive opportunity to lock in returns and allocate assets, the bank said.
In the foreign exchange market, easing geopolitical risks could lead safe-haven funds to flow out of the US dollar, causing the US dollar index to weaken with fluctuations in the second half of the year. The Taiwan dollar is expected to remain range-bound due to factors including foreign dividend outflows, export demand, and the central bank’s exchange-rate stabilization policy, Entie Bank said.
Thus, the bank advised investors to diversify across currencies and asset classes to reduce the impact of volatility in any single market or currency. Cross-asset allocation across stocks, bonds, and currencies can help reduce the impact of market fluctuations, strengthen portfolio resilience, and allow investors to pursue medium- to long-term opportunities when market conditions reach key turning points, said the bank.

Italy's Meloni has a youth problem as election approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:05:07 UTC
14:05:07 KST

Italy's Meloni has a youth problem as election approaches
ROME, Aug 13 - Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government is increasingly unpopular among young voters, opinion polls show, a trend that could prove costly ahead of a national election due next year.
Since taking office in 2022, Meloni has done little on the economic front to increase opportunities for the young, analysts say, while passing a raft of law-and-order measures that often disproportionately affect them.
The result is a disaffection among 18- to 34-year-olds that may be crucial at a 2027 election shaping up as a neck-and-neck race between her rightist coalition and the centre-left opposition.
"Younger voters are clearly leaning towards the centre-left," Lorenzo Pregliasco, head of the Youtrend polling agency, told Reuters.
Meloni's coalition, comprising her Brothers of Italy Party (FDI), Matteo Salvini's League and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani's more moderate Forza Italia, now commands less than 30% of voting support among under-35s, Pregliasco said.
That compares with almost 50% in the same age group for the opposition bloc dominated by the Democratic Party (PD), the 5-Star Movement and the Left-Green Alliance (AVS).
At the peak of Meloni's popularity in 2023, Youtrend polling showed her party alone attracted roughly the same support among young people as the whole ruling coalition does now.
Young Italians also present the same gender gap seen in other European countries, with men tending to vote more for the right and women favouring the left, according to a study last year by Milan's Bocconi University based on data from polling firm SWG.
The sharpest party divides showed support for Meloni's FDI at 15% among 18- to 29-year-old men and just 4.2% among women, while 5-Star was backed by 18% of women under 30, and just 5.1% of men.
LACK OF REFORMS TO BOOST YOUTH OPPORTUNITIES
Lorenzo De Sio, political science professor at Rome's Luiss University, said the main reason for young people's hostility towards the government was its inertia on economic policy.
"Meloni has made no significant economic reforms," he said.
"That is fine if you benefit from the status quo, but very bad for those least protected by it, which often means young people."
Meloni's office declined to answer questions from Reuters for this article.
Italy's employment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds is the lowest in the 21-nation euro zone, Eurostat data shows, and it invests less in education than almost all its partners in the bloc.
A young graduate in Germany earns on average 80% more than an Italian peer, according to the Bank of Italy, and tens of thousands of young Italians leave the country every year in search of better prospects abroad.
The government's approval rating among under-35 voters is just 25% compared with 35% among the overall population, Youtrend data shows.
Meloni also faces competition for what remains of the youth vote in her own ideological camp. National Future, a far-right opposition party formed in February by former army general Roberto Vannacci is already polling at about 7%.
Surveys show its strongest support comes from middle-aged men, but Vannacci also has a significant following among anti-immigrant urban youths who like his pledge to return thousands of migrants to their countries of origin.
"Vannacci is certainly holding up better with young voters than the ruling parties are," Pregliasco said.
LAW-AND-ORDER CRACKDOWNS
The government's security measures have affected a range of groups from prisoners to migrants, but young people have often found themselves in the eye of the storm.
After cracking down on rave parties in Meloni's first law decree four years ago, subsequent government steps have targeted production of so-called "light" cannabis, disruptive street protests, squatters, and juvenile crime.
A nationwide student protest dubbed 'No Meloni Day' in November last year saw thousands march against the security decrees, education spending cuts and Meloni's support for Israel in Gaza.
In one of its latest moves the government last month presented a bill to change the rules on the criminal responsibility of minors.
Those aged between 14 and 17 who commit crimes will be considered fully responsible unless proven otherwise, reversing current rules by which a judge must show they understood the implications of their actions.
A 2023 decree toughening sanctions for offending minors has already triggered a 50% rise in the juvenile prison population, according to prisoners' rights group Antigone.
Yet while teenagers are to be fully responsible for their crimes, they cannot receive sex education in school without their parents' written consent, under another government step.
YOUNG VOTERS HELPED SINK MELONI-BACKED REFERENDUM
Meloni's failure to attract the young has often been masked by voter apathy. Turnout in Italy is normally low among under-35s, who rather than express their dissatisfaction by voting against the government have simply opted not to vote.
However, this trend reversed abruptly at a referendum in March on a reform of the justice system championed by Meloni.
Some 67% of under-35s cast a ballot, with 60% of them rejecting the reform, compared with an overall turnout of 59% of whom 54% voted 'no'.
Sensing trouble, days before the crucial referendum Meloni had joined an irreverent podcast hosted by a popular rapper in a bid to reach younger voters.
"The referendum showed what impact the young can have if they vote en masse," De Sio said. "At the next election they could be decisive." REUTERS

Taking the stairs could be better for your heart than you think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:04:27 UTC
14:04:27 KST

Taking the stairs can significantly reduce the risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, according to a major new study.
With more than a quarter of adults worldwide failing to meet recommended levels of physical activity, taking the stairs instead of the lift could be more beneficial than many might think.
Researchers from the University of East Anglia, and Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital found that people who regularly climbed stairs were 39% less likely to die from cardiovascular disease and 24% less likely to die from any cause than those who climbed stairs less often.
They were also less likely to develop major cardiovascular conditions, including heart attacks, strokes and heart failure.
“Taking the stairs is a practical and often overlooked way to build physical activity into daily life,” Vassilios Vassiliou of Norwich Medical School at the University of East Anglia said.
The researchers analysed data from more than 480,000 participants aged between 35 and 84, drawing on nine high-quality studies with a median follow-up period of 14 years.
“Unlike going to the gym or doing a workout, climbing the stairs is something you can easily fit into your day at home, at work or when you're out,” said Sophie Paddock, from Norwich Medical School at the University of East Anglia.
“It’s a good option for people who don’t have much time or easy access to exercise. So if you have the choice of taking the stairs or the lift, go for the stairs as it will help your heart.”
Just a few minutes of stair climbing several times a week can improve cardiorespiratory fitness and lower cholesterol, according to the research.
“Some of the studies we looked at showed that the more stairs climbed, the greater the health benefits. But even small changes had a measurable impact,” Paddock said.
The findings highlight the importance of promoting everyday physical activity, including in workplaces and homes, to encourage healthier lifestyles and reduce the risks associated with cardiovascular disease, the researchers said.
The findings were initially presented at a scientific congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC).

Taiwan says it was hit by ‘abnormal’ AI-assisted cyber-attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:02:28 UTC
14:02:28 KST

Taiwan says it detected AI-assisted cyber-attacks on government agencies that came from overseas last month, a new kind of threat that has been reported as “first-of-a-kind breach”.
The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MDA) said its cybersecurity monitoring units detected the “abnormal attack” targeting government agencies, which began on 20 July. The National Institute of Cyber Security issued a series of warning alerts while it investigated.
The Financial Times quoted Dream – an Israeli AI company that detected the intrusion – as saying the attackers used open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool that behaved like a coordinated cyber team, describing it as a first-of-a-kind breach.
Dream was reported as saying that the tool compromised “at least 85 government user accounts, extracting more than 2,500 personnel records before expanding the attack to Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and at least seven energy companies”.
Taiwan has in recent years complained about what it sees as China’s “hybrid warfare” – from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and cyber-attacks – as Beijing ramps up military and political pressure on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty.
Though Taiwanese officials did not direct accusations at China, the FT on Wednesday reported that China-linked hackers were suspected. Dream did not attribute the attack to a specific group, but said the use of Simplified Chinese in internal communications linked to the hack meant there was a high probability the operator was connected to China, the FT reported.
Chinese cyber-attacks on Taiwan’s key infrastructure, from hospitals to banks, rose 6% in 2025 from the previous year to an average of 2.63m attacks a day, the island’s National Security Bureau said in January, adding some hacks were synchronised with military drills in “hybrid threats” to paralyse the island.
The investigation into the AI-assisted attack said it showed clear characteristics of an “overseas source”, with hackers employing a hybrid approach that combined manual operations with AI agent-assisted attacks, such as Open Claw, the MDA said.
“The relevant attack sources, methods, and scope of impact have all been fully investigated, and the affected units have successively completed their handling,” the ministry added.
In response to this new type of threat, the government has established protective guidelines and strengthened system monitoring to block attacks early, it said.
The statement did not mention China, and China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the attack.
Taiwan’s MDA and Chinese authorities did not comment on the earlier FT report.
The threat of AI-assisted hacking campaigns has been growing for years but ramped up dramatically over the past few months after top AI labs released models, such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which can rapidly conduct reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities, and take advantage of them.
Cris Thomas, a researcher who works as a security advocate at the code security company Semgrep, said the spy campaign was an illustration of just how quickly AI-assisted hackers could hit their mark.
Thomas cautioned against exaggerating the power of AI agents, however.
“There’s still a human in there somewhere. Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive,” he said. “It’s not totally 100% autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that.”
Reuters contributed to this report

Category C and women’s prisons could be upgraded to ease overcrowding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

Ministers are examining a possible upgrade of security at men’s category C and women’s prisons to deal with an overcrowding crisis across the England and Wales estate, the Guardian understands.
Officials have explored diverting prisoners on remand or serving short sentences away from category B “reception” prisons such as HMPs Liverpool, Manchester and Pentonville in north London.
Instead, they are assessing the feasibility of holding male prisoners in alternative sites, such as men’s training prisons or repurposed and emptied women’s jails, once security has been improved.
Andy Burnham asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, this week to deliver a plan to free up more space in overcrowded jails. It follows intense pressure on the new government over how to block the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers.
Ministers have been advised that they can only move prisoners from category B to category C or women’s prisons if security is improved.
There are 30 men’s reception prisons across England and Wales. Also known as local prisons, they tend to be Victorian and severely overcrowded, holding remand and short-term prisoners.
They tend to have high walls and fences, often topped with razor wire, bars on windows, CCTV and controlled access and internal partitions.
Remand prisoners comprise approximately one-fifth of the total prison population in England and Wales, a proportion that has risen steeply in recent years because of court backlogs.
X-ray body scanners are deployed across category B local prisons and are used on many prisoners entering the estate to detect internal concealment of contraband including drugs, phones and weapons.
About half of England and Wales’s 86,000 prisoners are held in category C prisons, which specialise in preparing offenders for work and resettlement.
Prisoners in category C jails are assessed as a low to moderate security risk and are held in “closed” conditions but do not face high security such as razor wire and internal partitions. They tend to face fewer body scans and searches.
For more than a year, Ministry of Justice officials have been seriously examining schemes to divert female offenders out of jail.
But experts have pointed out that converting a women’s prison so that it could hold more men should also include a major security upgrade.
Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the prison officers union, the POA, said converting the security of category C or women’s prisons will take too long to ease the crisis currently facing the Prison Service.
“The category C estate is currently tight for space due to delays in transferring suitable prisoners from closed to open conditions,” he said.
“We need to consider reducing the remand population so we are not consistently struggling for cell space.
“Upgrading security in any prison is a long drawn-out process and will take time that we do not have.”
Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, said: “Many of the problems now facing category C prisons are also facing category B prisons – they are also overcrowded and are not rehabilitating those held there.
“I would be concerned that this plan, if implemented, could just further erode the difference between the categories. Is the government just accepting that there is no room for rehabilitation in prisons that were designed to offer it to people held there? If so, this is a counsel of despair.”
Burnham ordered Norris to draw up plans to free up prison space for serious offenders, and said he is “increasingly confident” that PC Harper’s killers will not be released early from their sentences as a result.
The prime minister was asked on Tuesday if he had a message for Aimee Harper, the sister of the police officer who died in the line of duty in 2019, and who had shared with the broadcaster LBC her experience of sitting in the courtroom with his killers.
Asked what he would say to Harper, Burnham replied: “That I hear you, I feel for you. I wouldn’t forgive myself if I didn’t do everything I possibly could to try and lessen your anguish, and I am doing that.
“I am turning over every stone. I am looking at everything. I am pushing the system to go further.”
He added: “That’s the way I go about my job. I listen to people. I continually push myself and the system to do more. In this instance, I think there is more that can be done.”
In a further development, the Estonian government has rejected a plan supported by the Conservatives and Reform UK of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis.
Justice minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC that Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a bilateral deal.
The Tories and Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.
Keir Starmer’s government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:49 UTC
14:00:49 KST

In his exquisite The French Menu Cookbook, Richard Olney has clear ideas and strong opinions about everything, including dessert. He believed that rich desserts should follow only the simplest of meals, whereas with most menus (meaning all the sophisticated menus in his book), something light, airy and playful is best. His suggestions read like a summer fruit poem: peach melba, apple mousse with peaches, apricot fritters dusted with icing sugar, strawberries in sweetened orange juice, strawberries in beaujolais, strawberry mousse with raspberry puree, iced cherries and fresh almonds. One of his late summer/early autumn menus also suggests fresh figs with raspberry cream (figues à la crème framboise), which is both fun to make (the red puree streaking through the cream for a raspberry ripple) and to eat.
An airy and playful pudding calls for an airy and playful biscuit. What better than lingue di gatto, or cat tongues, so called because of their flat, elongated shape. Made from butter, sugar, flour, and egg whites, lingue di gatto are not complicated to make, but do require a piping bag, which can be mimicked by a zip-lock bag – just remember to scrape the mixture into the bag first, and only snip the end off when you are ready to pipe.
This recipe is from Italian pastry chef Iginio Massari’s Non solo zucchero [Not Only Sugar] Volume 1, an invaluable step-by-step guide to short pastry, sponge cakes, butter masses, creams, cream puffs and meringues aimed at professional pastry chefs, but just as suitable (and revelatory) for enthusiastic but chaotic pastry cooks like me.
There are various ways to serve this pudding. Olney suggests a large serving dish, which, considering his warning never to put tomato dishes on a red plate or those including spinach on a green one, should not be pink. Olney arranges the chilled fig slices first, then pours the raspberry cream over the top, which baffles me slightly, because the cream is so thick. An alternative is serving in individual bowls, saucers or glasses: a spoonful of the raspberry cream first, then topping it with a small pile of fruit (figs, the whole raspberries you’ve set aside, plus redcurrants and mint leaves). The cat tongue biscuits can be stuck in the cream like fairy wings, put on the side of the plate, or passed around the table on a separate plate so everyone can help themselves.
Figs with raspberry cream and cat tongue biscuits
Serves 8
4-6 ripe figs (pale green or dark purple)
  250g raspberries, washed
  250ml whipping cream
  1-2 tbsp icing sugar
  A few redcurrants
  A few mint leaves
For the biscuits
50g soft butter
  60g icing sugar
  3 egg whites (50g)
60g plain flour, sifted
30g flaked almonds
Put the softened butter and icing sugar in a bowl, and use a spatula to mix them together. Fold in the egg whites, before adding the sifted flour and mixing again.
Scrape the mixture into a pastry bag with a smooth 10mm nozzle (or a zip-lock bag you can snip the corner from). On a baking tray lined with baking paper, squeeze out lines that are 10cm long, ensuring you leave 4cm between each one. Top each one with three or four almonds, then bake at 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 for about eight minutes, until golden. Leave to cool a little before lifting on to a cooling rack.
It is up to you whether you peel the figs before you slice each one into four; chill. Set aside half of the raspberries, then press the rest through a fine sieve for a smooth, bright-red puree. Whip the cream until stiff, then stir in the icing sugar to taste and the raspberry puree for a mottled effect.
Divide the cream between four individual bowls or glasses, top with wedges of fig and a few raspberries, plus some redcurrants and mint leaves. Serve with the biscuits.

Jason Arday is now the stick the right will use to beat back racial equality. Don’t let that happen | Afua Hirsch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

In 1987, a college at the University of Cambridge considered offering a prestigious position to a black man in what would be the first appointment of its kind. Not only did the man not have a degree, but he had left school at the age of 13, struggling with dyslexia and – at the time – unable to read or write. That he would later to go on to accumulate 20 honorary doctorates and become a professor of creative writing is only one way, and in my view not the best one, of measuring his talent.
The man was the late, great poet Benjamin Zephaniah. And he had been nothing but transparent about his lack of credentials. In fact it was his background that made him eligible for this fellowship, which was designed to reach out to somebody in the community who didn’t have a degree, to give them the opportunity to have a connection with the university.
Zephaniah had been privately offered the role but a formal offer had not yet been made when it was leaked to the rightwing press. The Sun and the Daily Mail newspapers enjoyed a feeding frenzy at the prospect of a black man – one with locs, no less – becoming a fellow at Cambridge.
“Would you let this man near your daughter?” asked the Sun. “Just what are his qualities which have appealed to Trinity College?” the paper asked. Then, not bothering to hide its starkly racist views, it answered that there were none. No qualities, only problems, listed in order of severity: “He is black. He is a Rastafarian. He has tasted approved schools and Borstals.”
The Sun offered no evidence whatsoever for the implication that Zephaniah was a rapist, as the headline suggested. Apparently none was needed – the audience already understood that a black man from Handsworth, Birmingham, who had “tasted Borstals” could not possibly be an appropriate or safe person to be associated with Cambridge University.
In the years since Zephaniah did not receive the fellowship that should have been his due, Cambridge – like many elite universities – has been mired in actual scandals of rape, nepotism, plagiarism and more. Remember them? You probably don’t, because they barely made the news.
For a period beginning in 2019, Trinity Hall, Cambridge, was embroiled in controversy after it emerged that not one but three people who worked at the college had been accused of sexual misconduct by students. The ensuing outcry led the master to resign.
In 2023, a professor from the same college was allowed to keep his job after having been found to have plagiarised material from a student essay.
In 2015, a row broke out in which the renowned University of Leeds sociologist Zygmunt Bauman was accused of multiple instances of “self-plagiarism”. Colleagues claimed those allegations were motivated by another scholar’s “personal agenda” and said they were “tantamount to a form of intellectual violence wrapped in objective scholarship that plagues the academy”.
Maybe it’s just my algorithm, but social media seems flooded with hot takes on Jason Arday. I have worked with him – we were developing a project together at one point – and I have thought a lot about him in the years since.
The fact is that many of Arday’s black peers in academic sociology have been voicing concerns about him for a while. He seemed, to them, to have come out of nowhere. His performance at high-profile academic events did not match the credentials that were being touted. I have had various conversations with sociology professors in which this has been the main topic of conversation, and their questions began to mount into a list. They did not voice them publicly because we all know that whatever the truth or the outcome, he would be unlikely to be treated fairly and we would all be damaged in the process. As for me, I was an interested observer to allegations the veracity of which I couldn’t personally verify. But hearing them from fellow black academics I respect was enough to put me on alert and raise a red flag for anyone who asked me whether publicly supporting him was a good idea.
Some of the people who did sign those letters are now feeling very angry that Arday did not protect them from what he must have known to be lies before they used their own reputations to defend his. Others are angry that he appears to be using his neurodivergence as an excuse for dishonesty, which of course it’s not.
The media cannot conceal its excitement about his transgressions. Arday doesn’t need to be a fantasist to be the kind of man commentators would rather not see at a university like Cambridge – being black is enough. For them, the fact that he made stuff up is simply a massive bonus. Which explains why they have moved so quickly from identifying mistakes he has made to indulging in an orgy of delight at the prospect of smearing all black academics.
Indeed, I seriously question whether Donald Trump received as much scrutiny for starting a war with Iran as Arday did for exaggerating his athletic and academic credentials.
Nor does the media care about protecting students, by the way. That is not an issue that sells newspapers, drives clicks or feeds the agendas of the rightwing billionaires who own most of our media.
I have lost count of the number of emails, text messages, DMs and WhatsApps I received asking me to condemn the allegations against Arday. Not one of these messages asked me first if I know him, what my opinion about the allegations is or whether I actually agree with their assertion that they are baseless.
It probably looks as if I support a lot of open letters and petitions, and I do. In recent months these have addressed unlawful deportations, the intimidation tactics of the far right, Labour’s imitation of the far right, the crackdown on free speech rights and protests for Gaza.
The due diligence involved in joining these causes includes checking the facts and legal basis of the petitions, and researching the backgrounds of individuals and organisations involved. I love that we show up for each other. I love that we take a stand. But knowing exactly what it is that we are supporting is essential.
I have no idea what made Arday say things that are obviously fabricated. I hope he is OK, and I am unequivocal about condemning the media pile-on, which ranges from overt to dog-whistle racism, and which is completely disproportionate.
What I do have to say about Jason Arday is really very simple. The overwhelmingly white dons and administrators at Cambridge chose one academic – unrecognised by many of his black peers in the field – and felt his was an appointment with which they could feel comfortable. This resembles a pattern we see elsewhere in public life, where the disproportionately few black people who are selected by white gatekeepers are sometimes chosen for reasons that seem to have little legitimacy among black peers.
Black academics, and black people in general, have never and – it’s my confident prediction – will never demand the right to plagiarise, lie or fabricate our credentials. What we have been demanding is to be treated equally. To be appointed to the levels commensurate with our actual credentials, to have our work taken seriously by intellectual peers, and to be paid fairly and on equal terms for our labour. To not have opportunities taken away because of our race. To have our work, performance and legacy held to the same standards as everyone else’s.
We are very far from anything resembling this. You don’t need a Cambridge degree to see how conveniently the Arday story is serving as a distraction while the media drags us even further in the wrong direction.
I said people signed the petitions for Arday because we are overwhelmed by very legitimate, abundant instances of racism and the sometimes onerous task of doing the due diligence. The last takeaway from this sorry saga relates to this last point, and it’s important. I have heard people say that they assumed the allegations against Arday were baseless because Cambridge said so.
We are too quick to look up to the institutions of the British establishment, and this makes us vulnerable. This is the same reason we accept OBEs, even as they insult our ancestry, and celebrate black “power” even when what that means is high status positions in companies, political parties or organisations that are harmful to our community.
I’m not saying we can avoid these institutions – we are all navigating the same society. But we can be much smarter about how we interact with them, and whether we do so from a place of awe, or whether we do so from a place of strategy, with our eyes wide open.
- 
  Afua Hirsch is a writer, broadcaster and academic. This is a version of an article first published on her Substack

Ranked: The world's best stargazing destinations – and the No.1 is in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:36 UTC
14:00:36 KST

In a new ‘clean sky index’ of the world’s best stargazing destinations, Pic du Midi in France came out on top for its combination of sky quality and accessibility.
Stargazing has become a trending topic for travellers, with more trips now built around finding skies dark enough to reveal the Milky Way and passing meteor showers.
To rank the best destinations, eSIM provider Holafly has created its first “Clean Sky Index”. Rather than just highlighting the darkest places on Earth, the index identifies destinations that offer the “best overall balance between exceptional night skies and practical travel”.
Researchers analysed various stargazing locations using four weighted criteria: light pollution (35%), based on Sky Quality Meter readings and the Bortle scale; clear-night frequency (30%), measuring the percentage of cloud-free nights annually; accessibility (20%), based on travel time from a major international hub; and Dark Sky certification (15%), recognising destinations designated by DarkSky International.
"To ensure geographical diversity, no more than three destinations from the same country were included in the final shortlist, while both certified and non-certified locations were assessed to prioritise real sky quality over certification alone," Holafly said.
Ranked at No.1 in the index, Pic du Midi in France was highlighted thanks to its balance of strong sky conditions and easy reach, with the French observatory accessible in under four hours from London, unlike other destinations which lost out for their remote locations.
Top 10 clean sky destinations for summer 2026
- 1. Pic du Midi, France
- 2. Warrumbungle National Park, Australia
- 3. Grasslands National Park, Canada
- 4. NamibRand Nature Reserve, Namibia
- 5. AlUla, Saudi Arabia
- 6. Atacama Desert, Chile
- 7. La Palma, Spain
- 8. Aoraki Mackenzie, New Zealand
- 9. Mauna Kea, Hawaii, USA
- 10. Cherry Springs State Park, USA
Other top destinations for stargazing
Warrumbungle National Park in New South Wales placed second. Recognised as Australia's first Dark Sky Park, it is home to the Siding Spring Observatory.
Grasslands National Park came in third. It was designated in 2009 as the Canada's darkest Dark Sky Preserve with a top rating on the Bortle scale.
Placed fourth, NamibRand Nature Reserve in Namibia recorded the darkest skies in the study, but lost points for its remote location. It came ahead of AlUla in Saudi Arabia in fifth, which holds the world's third-largest Dark Sky Park designation, spanning more than 6,000 square kilometres of protected desert.
Chile's Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth, rounded out the top six.
The index shows that remoteness isn't always required for great stargazing. La Palma in Spain, Aoraki Mackenzie in New Zealand and Cherry Springs State Park in the US all made the top 10, proving that world-class dark skies can be found within easier reach than many travellers might expect.

Wildfires in Europe: Is 2026 already the worst year on record?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:12 UTC
14:00:12 KST

As of early August, 2026 is the worst year for several European countries over the last 15 years in terms of cumulative area burnt by wildfires. Euronews Business takes a closer look at the countries hit the hardest.
Wildfires have been hitting Europe this summer. In France and Spain alone, more than 320,000 people had been evacuated as of late July. Wildfires continue as heatwaves spread with mid-August approaching.
Measuring the cost of wildfires is complicated. Burnt area is easy to measure, but the economic impact, and other effects, need more effort.
"Europe's wildfires this year confirm that their economic cost reaches far beyond restoring burnt land,” Professor Simone Varotto, from Henley Business School at University of Reading, said.
“The eventual bill will include destroyed homes, businesses and crops, disrupted tourism and industry, smoke-related health effects, added strain on public finances and potentially higher insurance premiums.”
Still, the burnt area shows the scale of wildfires and their possible impacts.
So, how many hectares of land have burnt in Europe so far in 2026? Which countries lost the largest burnt area? Were wildfires in 2026 more costly than in previous years in Europe?
2026: Fourth-largest area burnt as of early August
As of early August, 2026 ranks fourth in the EU for cumulative area burnt by wildfires according to Our World in Data, which relies on the Global Wildfire Information System.
As of the 31st week, 489,826 hectares had burnt in the EU. This is the highest figure after 2012 (863,122 ha), 2022 (799,040 ha), and 2017 (743,906 ha).
The average of the fourteen years from 2012 to 2025 in this period was 434,711 ha in the EU. 2026 is 55,115 ha, or 13%, higher than this average.
All figures compare the same point in the year, which is the end of week 31.
Varotto noted that Europe's fires have mainly struck forests, scrubland, pastures and farmland, with several also reaching towns and peri-urban areas.
38% of the EU’s wildfire-burnt area is in Spain
Spain has been the hardest-hit EU country by wildfires in terms of area burnt. As of early August in 2026, 185,948 hectares had burnt this year. This accounts for 38% of the EU total.
Between 2012 and 2025, an average of 85,626 hectares had burnt in Spain by week 31 each year. In 2026, the figure is more than double that average.
As of week 31, 2026 is the third-worst year for Spain's cumulative area burnt by wildfires since 2012 where the data starts in this comparison.
Spain lost 258,340 ha in 2022, and 211,350 ha in 2012.
2026 is the worst year for France
France is second, with 99,092 ha over this period, corresponding to 20% of the EU total.
The 14-year average for France is 31,648 hectares. The 2026 figure is more than three times this average.
2026 is the worst year for France since 2012. France lost 86,888 ha to wildfires in 2019, the second-highest figure.
As of early August in 2026, Italy (79,084 ha), Portugal (47,776 ha) and Greece (23,839 ha) have also been heavily affected by wildfires.
For Italy, 2026 is the fifth-worst year in the last 15 years for area burnt by wildfires. The same is true for Portugal.
By comparison, 2026 has been a less severe year for Greece. The country recorded larger areas burnt by wildfires in several previous years.
Several countries saw a significant rise in 2026
While the cumulative area burnt by wildfires is comparatively lower, several countries recorded a significant rise in 2026 compared with their 14-year average.
For example, Austria lost 1,687 ha this year as of early August, compared with 513 ha on average. Denmark lost 1,177 ha compared with 404 ha. Germany lost 6,045 ha compared with 3,098 ha. The Netherlands lost 1,677 ha compared with 352 ha.
This is the case for the UK too, losing 22,206 ha compared with 12,311 ha. 2026 has been the worst-hit year not only for the UK but also several European countries over the last 15 years. This is, of course, only as of early August.
Turkey saw significantly fewer wildfires this year. Turkey lost 39,556 ha this year so far, compared with 134,707 ha on average.
“Fire risk is no longer confined to the Mediterranean”
Simone Varotto warned British authorities, suggesting the UK should treat southern Europe as an early warning.
“This summer's heatwaves and wildfires in southern England, which have already burnt more than 20,000 hectares, show that fire risk is no longer confined to the Mediterranean,” he said.

Millions of solar eclipse glasses could end up in landfill: Here’s what to do instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

Be a responsible consumer by following expert advice on what to do with your glasses now the eclipse is over.
On Wednesday evening, millions of Europeans gazed at the sky as a solar eclipse plunged them into early darkness.
The display was the most dramatic since 1999, with large parts of Spain and smaller areas of Portugal, Greenland and Iceland witnessing the full effect of a total eclipse.
But looking directly at the phenomenon – even for a split second – carried the risk of permanent retinal damage called ‘solar burn’.
In the lead up to the event, a rush to buy protective eyewear left shop shelves empty of eclipse glasses and last-minute viewers scrambling for homemade alternatives.
But what happens to the mountains of cardboard and plastic framed spectacles when the eclipse is over?
Here’s what to do with your solar eclipse glasses.
Can I recycle my eclipse glasses?
Eclipse glasses can generally be recycled – but only partially.
The lenses feature specialised solar filters made from black polymer – a resin mixed with carbon particles that absorb light – or a thin polyester film coated with a microscopic layer of metal to reflect intense sunlight.
These generally can’t be processed by municipal recycling facilities, meaning you must remove the lenses from the frames beforehand.
Clean cardboard and paper frames can then be placed in your standard cardboard recycling collection. Most plastic frames, however, cannot be recycled.
Can I reuse my eclipse glasses?
For the 2026 solar eclipse, viewers who held onto their 1999 eyewear were advised not to reuse the vintage specs. This is because glasses manufactured before 2015 were made of materials that degrade more quickly than modern alternatives, meaning the 27-year-old glasses may no longer be safe.
Modern eclipse glasses that meet the ISO 12312-2 safety standard do not expire and can last indefinitely. However, they should not be used if there is any sign of wear such as scratches, punctures or loose filters, and experts generally advise that they can be reused for up to 10 years.
You can check for pinholes by looking at a big light through your glasses. If you see total darkness, they remain safe to use. So pack them away somewhere safe where they won’t get damaged.
The next two years have been dubbed the ‘Golden Age of Eclipses’ for a reason: a further two total solar eclipses are in the pipeline – albeit only partially visible on the continent.
On 2 August 2027, a spectacular ‘eclipse of the century’ is expected to last more than six minutes over Luxor, Egypt. On 22 July 2028, Australia and New Zealand will be treated to the phenomenon, which will be the first seen in Sydney since 1857.
Where to donate your eclipse glasses
If you’re unlikely to travel for these upcoming astrological events, don’t deconstruct your eyewear just yet.
Some organisations partner with libraries, museums and schools to collect lightly used eyewear and distribute them to communities in-need around the world. So check on local social media for collection points.
Check out which countries will have eclipses in the coming years. If you have a friend or family member in one of those places, post your glasses off to them so they can be reused.

Tourist guides raise the alarm as Europe braces for another heatwave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:09 UTC
14:00:09 KST

Last summer, a 56-year-old guide died after collapsing while leading a visit of the Colosseum in Rome in scorching heat.
Standing eight hours per day in an archaeological site with no shade or leading a city tour in temperatures of at least 30C : in the midst of the touristic season and while Europe is facing record-breaking temperatures, several tourist guides warn they are on the frontline during heatwaves.
Last summer, Giovanna Maria Giammarino, a 56-year-old Italian guide died after collapsing while leading a visit of the Colosseum in Rome in scorching heat.
Following her death, the Italian tour guides' associations Federagit and AGTA called for reforms such as updated summer protocols in the cultural tourism sector. But the issue still prevails, including beyond Italian borders.
Difficult cancellations
"This afternoon, we went to Pérouges, which is a small medieval town northeast of Lyon and it’s more than 40C in the sun, it’s quite complicated," says Gabriel Quentin-Gerbault.
The French guide says, while self-employed tourist guides may ask their customers to cancel or postpone a visit because of the heat, it is often not an option for guides working for intermediaries since the visits are sometimes booked well in advance.
"Most of the time, we work for an agency, a tour operator, or a cruise-line. It can be very varied. And they are the ones who choose, very clearly. And most of the time it’s not canceled, but it happens," Gabriel says.
Instead of cancelling a visit, some of his colleagues have for instance asked their employers to turn a bike tour into a bus tour, or to replace a walking tour of the city by a visit of an air-conditioned museum.
Gabriel says these changes are also in the interest of the visitors, as most of his customers are above 60 years old and some do not support the heat.
Extended opening hours
Meanwhile, while the UK is set to face its hottest summer on record, Themis Halvantzi-Stringer, head of training for the European Federation of Tourist Guide Associations, which represents around 60,000 professional tourist guides, says sites should extend their opening hours to allow early and late visits during the coolest part of the day.
"In Greece a lot of museums and open-air sites open very early in the morning and they remain open until 8, 9 o'clock in the evening. So people can visit at times which are more comfortable rather than in the midday sun," the tourist guide, who is based in London says.
Themis also encourages museums and sites to build covers for groups to wait in the shade while queuing to enter or when stopping for explanations.
Other solutions include distributing water bottles, increasing the number of public water fountains and installing misters to cool visitors down.
While heatwaves are set to become more intense and more frequent due to climate change, visitors could also favor a trip in May or September rather than at the height of summer.
"We will have to rethink our consumption patterns, Gabriel says, and this also applies to tourism."

China’s YMTC breaks into global top 3 flash-memory suppliers with 14% market share
The chipmaker captured a larger proportion of bit shipments, but still ranks fifth by revenue due to heavier exposure to lower-value products
Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC) has broken into the world’s top three NAND flash memory suppliers by volume for the first time, marking a milestone for China’s semiconductor ambitions as it strives to narrow the revenue gap with global rivals in high-value data-centre storage.
The Wuhan-based chipmaker captured 14 per cent of global NAND bit shipments – a measure of total storage capacity shipped rather than total chip units – in the second quarter, narrowly overtaking Japan’s Kioxia, according to data from Counterpoint Research published on Wednesday.
Samsung Electronics retained the global lead with a 25 per cent market share, while SK Hynix – including its Solidigm subsidiary – was second at 22 per cent.
YMTC’s shipments climbed 22 per cent year on year and 5 per cent quarter on quarter, driven by expanding supplies to domestic electronics manufacturers and the increased production of its latest-generation 3D NAND architecture, Counterpoint said.
Despite its surge in shipment volume, YMTC’s market position lags in dollar terms. The company ranked fifth globally in NAND revenue for the quarter, placing it behind both US-based Micron Technology and Kioxia.
The gap stems from YMTC’s heavy exposure to lower-margin consumer products and a relatively small footprint in enterprise solid-state drives (eSSDs), which command higher pricing.
The product mix imbalance is increasingly squeezing revenue as artificial intelligence reshapes global storage demand.

Sexual assault survivors in Lithuania face long waits for help – and lost evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

People who have survived drug-facilitated sexual assault in Lithuania say they are being let down by a system with too few specialist services, no reliable way to preserve evidence, and long waits for care. The country's social security ministry says changes are coming, but for now, campaigners say, survivors are often left to navigate the process largely on their own.
"A black screen, then nothing"
Ten years ago, comedian and human rights advocate Vita Žiba was sexually assaulted after being drugged. She says it took her a while afterwards to understand what had happened to her.
"First of all, you barely remember anything, because those drugs are usually designed specifically to suppress memory. I just remember having one drink, then another, and then – a black screen. The next thing I remember is being in some room, I don't even know where, with some man's hands all over me," she said.
When Žiba shared her story on social media, she received an outpouring of support – within a week, roughly 800 women had come forward with their own experiences of sexual violence. But she also faced abuse online.
"A lot of older men wrote things like 'you had it coming', 'it's your own fault', or 'you should be grateful someone wanted you'," she said.
Campaigners note that the substances used in these assaults aren't limited to spiked drinks – they can also be administered by injection.
Cases are likely a fraction of the true total
Lithuanian prosecutors opened 13 pre-trial investigations two years ago into suspected sexual assaults involving psychoactive substances; seven were later dropped.
"That's the tip of the iceberg. It's very hard to say how many cases there really are, because very often people don't recognise what happened to them, don't come forward, are afraid to seek help, or simply don't remember," said Reda Jureliavičiūtė, co-founder of the organisation Ribologija, which works on the issue.
Getting help isn't straightforward, either. Specialist care is currently available at only five hospitals, all in Lithuania's largest cities.
"If you live somewhere more rural, you have to get to a hospital, wait an hour to be seen – because sexual offences aren't treated as a priority – then wait again for transport to be arranged to the nearest of those five hospitals. And once you're there, you're back in a general queue," Jureliavičiūtė said.
Advocates are calling for a clearer referral pathway that would route survivors directly to the right service, rather than leaving them to find it themselves.
"Right now everything is scattered – institutions don't even know where to send you. You go to the police, they say go to a doctor, the doctor sends you somewhere else, and you get lost in the process. Meanwhile, if drugs were used, they clear the body within a limited window," Žiba said.
Evidence not being preserved
Unlike in some other European countries, forensic samples collected from survivors in Lithuania are not currently retained for any length of time, meaning evidence can be lost even when a case is reported.
"We need to be able to collect that evidence first, and hold onto it while the person decides whether to pursue a case. Right now we don't have that, there's no window built in for someone to make that decision," said Dalia Puidokienė, head of the support centre Prabilk (Speak Out).
What the government is proposing
The social security and labour ministry says changes are on the way, including a new helpline and investment in dedicated support centres.
"Our starting position is that healthcare providers should be required to notify the relevant support centre within 24 hours, so that someone is assigned to accompany the person through the entire process, from first contact onward," said Deputy Social Security and Labour Minister Rita Grigalienė.
In the autumn, the ministry plans to bring amendments to parliament on Lithuania's law on protection against domestic violence, which would introduce a longer-term protection order for perpetrators alongside the existing 15-day emergency order.
"The survivor would go to court, supported through that process, with all the necessary documentation prepared by specialist centres. We're still discussing whether the longer-term order should run for two, four or six months," Grigalienė said.
If approved by parliament, the changes would take effect from June next year.

TOKYO, August 13. /TASS/. Japan expresses a "strong protest" over Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to the Kuril Island of Iturup, according to a statemen by the Japanese foreign ministry.
The ministry claims that all the "northern territories," as Tokyo refers to the southern part of the Kuril Islands, including Iturup, are an "ancestral [Japanese] territory from both the historical and legal standpoints."
On Thursday, Putin for the first time visited the Kuril Islands. Russian heads of state and government visited the Kuril Islands five times. Dmitry Medvedev made trips there four times: in 2010, when he was Russian president, and in 2012, 2015, and 2019, when he was prime minister. In 2021, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited Iturup.
Russia and Japan have been negotiating a post-World War II peace treaty since the mid-20th century. The main stumbling block is the issue of who owns the South Kuril Islands. After the end of World War II, all Kuril Islands were incorporated into the Soviet Union. However, Japan claimed the Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan islands and a number of uninhabited islands of the Lesser Kuril Ridge called the Habomai Islands in Japan as its own.
In 1956, the Soviet Union and Japan signed a joint declaration on ceasing the state of war. The two countries resumed diplomatic and other relations, but have still not signed a peace treaty.
The Russian foreign ministry has repeatedly said that Russia’s sovereignty over the Kuril Islands is not up for debate, as international agreements stipulate that they belong to Russia.

Putin can no longer claim victory in Ukraine, Nobel Peace Prize winner tells BBC
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
05:55:58 BST
13:55:58 KST

Putin can no longer claim victory in Ukraine, Nobel Peace Prize winner tells BBC
- Published
At the Moscow offices of newspaper Novaya Gazeta, the corridors are silent.
There is an overwhelming sense of emptiness.
"There is no newspaper anymore," former chief editor Dmitry Muratov tells me in an exclusive interview, published on the BBC News YouTube channel, external.
Muratov, 64, co-founded Novaya Gazeta more than 30 years ago. It became the flagship for hard-hitting independent journalism in Russia, shining a light on human rights abuses and high-level corruption.
In 2021 Muratov was joint winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression." The Nobel Committee noted that "six of [Novaya Gazeta's] journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya who wrote revealing articles on the war in Chechnya."
It was recognition for courageous reporting.
But it didn't protect the paper.
"Putin issued a decree and the newspaper's printing presses were nationalised," Muratov explains. "Its registration was revoked."
Novaya Gazeta does retain a presence online. But only just: the authorities have blocked access to its website. It can only be accessed from abroad, or with the help of VPNs – virtual private networks used to circumvent restrictions.
The newspaper's difficulties reflect the broader crackdown on free speech in Russia which has accelerated since the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Most opinion leaders have been declared 'foreign agents', 'extremists' or 'terrorists'. Several hundred," says Muratov.
"Figures vary, but at a conservative estimate, since the start of Russia's 'special military operation' [in Ukraine] at least 1,500 people are now in prison having spoken out against current state policy. That's three times more than during the savage days of the KGB in the USSR."
In his 1975 Nobel Peace Prize lecture dissident Andrei Sakharov listed the names of more than 120 political prisoners he was aware of in the Soviet Union. A decade later Amnesty International estimated more than 600 prisoners of conscience in the USSR.
What the Kremlin had assumed in 2022 would be a short, successful "military operation" has become the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two.
Yet a confident President Vladimir Putin continues to predict victory for Russia.
"There will never be 'victory'," counters Muratov. "Because what has been going on for nearly five years – no matter how it ends – can no longer be considered a victory.
"It cannot be a victory when two Slavic nations have ripped a million people to shreds. Or more than a million."
"It seems to me that the situation with Ukraine now is this: you can destroy it, but you cannot conquer it. What do I mean by destroy? Continued escalation all the way to the use of a nuclear weapon."
Does he really believe the Kremlin leader would use nuclear weapons in this war?
"All those political experts who say 'Putin thinks this' or 'Putin is scared of that'…they're all charlatans," claims Muratov. "It's in the same league as astrology. Nobody knows what's going on in Vladimir Putin's head. And I don't know.
"I see things only as a journalist. I study big data. And since the beginning of the year the need to use nuclear weapons has been mentioned more than 500 times. When wackos say this, I pay no attention. But I've heard it discussed on state TV. And at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a state-run event, one of the speakers talked up the use of nuclear weapons as something favourable, something good."
When he announced the mass invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Putin spoke of "ensuring the security of Russia."
"Tell me, has security increased?" Muratov asks. "With Ukrainian drones now attacking warehouses of [Russia's largest online retailer] Wildberries; with the petrol crisis, the disruption to mobile internet, the political prisoners? Has security increased, or not?"
Despite opinion polls registering a fall in Putin's domestic approval ratings, Russia's president – Muratov believes - retains a tight grip on power.
"Sorry, I don't believe all this talk about a split among members of the elite, about secret conspiracies. The country is run by Vladimir Putin. They're frightened of him.
"And this fear is reinforced in every way by his main support base: the Federal Security Service (FSB)."
As critical as he is of his own government, he has few illusions about the West.
"[Putin] knows very well the true value of European leaders. On the one hand they talk to him about human rights. He laughs out loud because, with the other hand, they sign agreements – or used to sign agreements – with Russia on trading oil, gas, diamonds…all that stuff. When they talk to Putin about European values, he truly laughs out loud. He knows the true value of people who preached to him those values."
In Russia Muratov has been designated a "foreign agent", a label often used to punish critics of the Kremlin. "Foreign agents" have limited rights: they're banned from teaching, from taking part in elections; if they sell their flat, they can't access the assets. The label is also designed to stigmatise, to create the sense in society of an enemy within.
Yet the journalist appears reluctant to focus on the pressures he's under, preferring instead to highlight the plight of compatriots in prison.
"What worries me most right now is that no one in the world is interested in the political prisoners who were first to speak out against the land grab in our neighbouring country," Muratov explains.
He opens a folder and takes out a stack of large photographs: portraits of prisoners.
One shows four journalists - Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger – convicted and jailed on extremism charges. They'd been accused of links to the anti-corruption organisation of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny.
There's a photo of Alexei Gorinov: a city councillor jailed for "knowingly spreading false information" about the Russian military after he spoke out against the war in Ukraine.
"And here's a wonderful pianist, Pavel Kushnir," says Miratov. "An outstanding performer of Rachmaninoff and Schubert."
The musician was arrested after posting anti-war videos. Muratov holds up a second video.
"And this is him in his coffin."
Pavel Kushnir died in a pre-trial detention centre during a hunger strike. He was 39.
The stream of photos and prison stories highlights the dangers for individuals framed as opponents of those in power. It's a reminder of the risks that public criticism of the authorities and the war carry.
"Does being a Nobel Prize laureate give you at least some protection to say what you want?" I ask.
"This is not a question for me," replies Muratov. "Whenever you have the opportunity, ask the authorities that."
There is one more photo. From April.
"This is the newspaper's lawyer when she was waiting to get into the building. The police were searching our office. Thirteen hours it took. And they wouldn't let the lawyers in. Our managing editor Oleg Roldugin is now under house arrest."
Muratov paints a bleak picture of life in Russia for critics of the authorities.
Yet there are moments of hope.
"We live in a time when you stay quiet. But so many people support what we do. On the streets of Moscow, my colleagues and I hear only words of gratitude. They are spoken in a whisper. But what people think is very important."

According to eyewitnesses, the first explosions were heard at around 09:10 local time. They also reported that air defence systems were responding and sirens were sounding.
Update: Exilenova+ has also reported a fire at a large warehouse and distribution complex belonging to Wildberries in the Chishminsky district in Bashkortostan. Wildberries is Russia's largest online retailer.
According to the Telegram channel, the facility is used for the storage, sorting and subsequent distribution of dual-use goods. A fire has broken out at the hub following the attack.
For reference: Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat is one of Russia's largest oil refining complexes. The facility processes around 10 million tonnes of oil per year.
According to Astra, the refinery processed around 7.2 million tonnes of crude oil in 2024, accounting for approximately 2.7% of Russia's total crude oil refining volume.
The refinery has previously been subjected to drone attacks. Following a strike on 14 July, the refinery temporarily suspended operations.
In September 2025, Ukrainian drones attacked the plant twice, on 18 and 24 September. Following the 24 September attack, the ELOU-AVT-6 primary oil refining unit was damaged, according to Astra.

Japan summons Russian ambassador after Putin visits disputed Kuril islands
Japan’s foreign minister summoned the Russian ambassador in Tokyo to lodge a “strong protest” against President Vladimir Putin’s surprise visit to the Kuril islands on Thursday. Tokyo maintains its claim to the disputed islands near Japan's northernmost Hokkaido island since they were seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
President Vladimir Putin visited Russia's far-eastern Kuril islands for the first time on Thursday, prompting protests by Japan, which also claims the territory.
Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the contested islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.
The Kremlin posted a video of Putin on one of the Kurils' four main islands, with Russian media saying he visited a fish-processing plant and was given caviar.
It was the first visit by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.
"The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law," Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters.
Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable", she said, adding that it "made it more difficult to restore relations in the medium to long term".
Putin travelled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin on Wednesday, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.
In Sakhalin, Putin, 73, held a meeting "on ensuring the security of Russia's eastern borders", RIA Novosti said.
Also on Thursday, Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned Russian ambassador to Japan Nikolai Nozdrev to lodge a "strong protest" against Putin's surprise move.
Motegi told the ambassador in the meeting that Putin's visit would "have an extremely negative impact on Japan-Russia relations" already complicated by Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the ministry's statement.
Ukraine sanctions
Ties between Japan and Russia – which fought a war in 1904-5 – have worsened since the full-scale conflict in Ukraine began in 2022.
Japan has joined other G7 countries in sanctioning Russia and giving money and non-lethal defence aid to Kyiv.
Putin on Wednesday called Japan's sanctions "unprovoked".
"Japan has identified Russia as a main source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan... On the contrary it has territorial claims against our country," Putin said.
Russia and China have also moved closer, with their navies and air forces conducting joint exercises in areas around Japan, promoting frequent scrambles by Japanese jets.
North Korea, which this month termed Japan's military build-up a "transformation into a war state", has also sent troops and artillery shells to help Russia's war against Ukraine.
Read moreZelensky accuses Russia of using North Korean missiles in deadly attack
Japan's latest defence white paper issued this month again highlighted growing risks from all three countries.
The New York Times reported in July that Russia had turned Japan into a "den of spies" and a key source of dual-use technology needed for its war in Ukraine.
Harsh climate, few people
The Soviet Union took the strategically located volcanic archipelago north of Hokkaido in the final days of World War II, and has maintained a military presence there ever since.
The contested isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, which runs in a broad arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island Hokkaido.
Their population of about 20,000 Russian citizens lives in a harsh climate, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds.
After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.
The islands then acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the United States and Japan.
"The Kurils have been fortified with Bastion coastal defence missile systems and SU-35 fighter aircraft. These provide Russia with instruments of control over sea lanes in the region, as well as leverage against Japan's claim to the islands," said Yee Kuang Heng, a professor at the Graduate School of Public Policy at the University of Tokyo.
"Putin's visit may be a reminder of the cards he holds and also his displeasure with Japan's continuing sanctions on Russia imposed after the invasion of Ukraine," Heng told AFP.
