Low-income Australians should accept substandard homes, Liberal frontbencher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:43:15 UTC
10:43:15 KST

in brief
- Liberals are this week pushing for a reduced housing code, which could streamline construction at the cost of quality.
- Opposition housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg conceded that the proposal would come with "trade-offs".
The Coalition's plan to boost housing stock will involve "trade-offs", a Liberal frontbencher has said, after suggesting low-income households should accept living in substandard homes.
Opposition housing and homelessness spokesperson Andrew Bragg announced on Wednesday that the Opposition would reduce the national housing code from 2,000 pages to 80 if elected.
When asked by ABC Radio National on Thursday morning whether his policy means low-income earners should just accept living in substandard housing, he replied: "Yes, definitely."
He went on to say that building more homes under a streamlined code would come with "trade-offs".
"It's more important to have a house than to not have a house. And so, given the affordability crisis we have in the housing system, we need to just build more houses," he told the ABC.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Bragg's comments follow remarks made by his Liberal colleague and treasury spokesman Tim Wilson, who suggested in some cases people could put "a jumper on in winter rather than spending huge amounts of money" on improving housing quality.
He told ABC RN on Wednesday there should not be a one-size-fits-all policy — such as mandated energy efficiency — for construction.
"There are some places in the country where you will get cold spells or hot spells for a very small amount of the year, whereas for the rest of the year, it's not necessary," he said.
"We have a risk that Australians can't afford to rent or to buy their own home by the government's own budget design. We need housing stock that meets different needs in different environmental conditions. Queensland is not the same as Tasmania or Victoria. Western Australia is different again."
Proposal does 'nothing to fix' housing crisis, advocate says
Affordable housing advocates told SBS News that stripping back construction regulations is a way for developers to profit from "unliveable" homes.
"Too many renters are already living in homes that are freezing in winter, stifling in summer, riddled with mould and damp, and expensive to heat and cool," Everybody's Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said in a statement.
"Older people and people with disability already struggle to find homes they can safely and comfortably live in."
Azize added that the government should focus on social housing that is "built to last".
"We have a housing crisis because people cannot afford a home. Building more poor-quality homes does nothing to fix that crisis. It simply gives developers another way to profit from it," Azize said.
Australian Council of Social Services CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie agreed, adding that construction of social housing should "drastically scale up".
She described Bragg's comments as shocking.
"The changes to the building code proposed by Senator Bragg would simply remove costs from the builder and move them onto the household - locking them into higher power bills for decades, deepening inequality, risking lives, leaving future generations with homes that are expensive to run," she told SBS News.
The Housing Industry Association on Wednesday welcomed Senator Bragg's announcement, but argued it was more important to disentangle layers of complexity than target a specific size of the code.
Cutting red tape
The national housing codes set minimum requirements for the safety, health, amenity, accessibility, and sustainability of certain buildings, as detailed in over 2,000 pages.
The Coalition's new standards will focus on cost-effective structural, fire safety and health-related building standards.
Bragg said reducing the code has been a shifting policy for the Coalition.
"This was in Angus Taylor's budget reply back in May, and we have committed to getting it to 200 pages, but we actually found a way to get it to less than 100 pages. It tends to be by picking up the New Zealand building code, which is about 80," he explained.
While New Zealand's building code appears to be about 80 pages long, the country has other compulsory building requirements on durability and energy efficiency, outlined in separate documents that builders must comply with.
Labor announced it would freeze the National Construction Code following its productivity roundtable in mid-2026.
Housing Minister Clare O'Neil brushed off calls from the Coalition to cut the construction standards to 200 pages earlier in 2026.
"I've talked to builders about that, they laugh their heads off. That is absolutely ridiculous," O'Neil told the National Press Club in May.
The government is not far off presenting a final plan to the building minister later this year to streamline the code, Treasurer Jim Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Wednesday.
Bragg has also called for the creation of a federal pattern book of model homes that could receive automatic approval from the states and territories.
— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

IN-SPACe approved country’s first fully commercial earth observation sat constellation: Jitendra Singh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:41:36 UTC
10:41:36 KST

The consortium named Allied Orbits Private Limited is led by Pixxel Space India and includes Dhruva Space, PierSight Space and Satsure Analytics India
NEW DELHI: Space regulator IN-SPACe has approved and signed under the PPP model an agreement with a private consortium for the country’s first indigenous, fully commercial earth observation constellation, with a view to enhancing the country’s space-based observation capabilities and building a self-reliant earth observation (EO) ecosystem in the country, minister for department of space Jitendra Singh informed Lok Sabha on Wednesday in response to a Parliament question.The consortium named Allied Orbits Private Limited is led by Pixxel Space India and includes Dhruva Space, PierSight Space and Satsure Analytics India. It will invest more than Rs 1,200 crore for setting up the constellation, which is to be developed and operationalised by 2029.
The consortium will design, build, own and operate the 12-satellite constellation, which will have panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) capabilities, supported by indigenous ground infrastructure. All satellites are to be manufactured domestically and launched on Indian launch vehicles, with mission control based in the country.The programme includes designing, fabrication, integration and the testing of EO satellites, including five ultra-high resolution optical satellites with 4 bands, 3 multispectral satellites with 8 bands, 2 hyperspectral optical satellites with 250 bands and 2 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in X-band, by the Indian industry. The EO programme will use Indian launch vehicles (either private or Isro facilities) for placing the satellites into orbit. The programme also allows collaboration with academic and research institutions for capacity building and application development, the minister said.

- 
  Ukrainian forces have recaptured 745 sq km (288 sq miles) of Russian-occupied land in a key sector this year, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said. “This offensive operation of ours was carried out with precision – exactly as planned.” Ukraine’s president outlined gains broadly in line with assessments from the well-regarded Ukrainian open-source group DeepState. Russia’s battlefield advances have slowed this year across much of the front, analysts say, though Russian forces still threaten cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. The Russian military still regularly announces the “capture” of villages, though observers say these are often shortlived flag-raising incursions involving a handful of troops.
- 
  “From January to August of this year, our warriors of the airborne assault forces and other units carried out an effective offensive operation in the Oleksandrivskyi sector … Russian losses amounted to at least 9,550 people killed and more than 6,600 people wounded.” Ukraine’s “exchange fund” was also replenished, Zelenskyy said, referring to Russian prisoners of war who can be swapped for Ukrainians held by Russia.
- 
  The Oleksandrivskyi sector is a 60km (37-mile) stretch of the front taking in parts of Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk oblasts where they meet. Zelenskyy said 26 settlements there had been brought back under Kyiv’s control. DeepState, which tracks both sides’ positions on the front, said in its latest assessment that Ukrainian forces had restored control over 19 settlements along the frontline, and pushed back Russian troops in six more settlements. The US-based Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment that Russian online sources were likely using AI-enhanced video footage to support Moscow’s claims of advances.
- 
  A major Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk hit warships at a naval base and forced two major grain terminals to halt operations on Wednesday, according to Russian and Ukrainian officials as well as grain industry sources. Zelenskyy said two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels were hit. Describing the attack as having “strategic significance”, Ukraine’s SBU security service said Kyiv’s forces hit the Novorossiysk naval base with drones and missiles. The Russian regional governor, Veniamin Kondratyev, said the attacks killed at least two people including an eight-year-old child.
- 
  Novorossiysk also hosts oil export infrastructure, including for the Caspian Pipeline Consortium owned partly by US oil companies Chevron and Exxon Mobil, and carries Kazakh oil exports to market. The Financial Times (paywall) reported on Wednesday that after a request from JD Vance, the US vice-president, Ukraine agreed not to target CPC infrastructure and non-Russian vessels, as long as they were not under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or other cargo.
- 
  Ukraine needs 5% of US Patriot interceptors to get through the winter and 10% to destroy all the ballistic missiles fired by Russia, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has told CNN. Ukraine this year “had two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025 … Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before. This year, I’m asking American partners to sell me 5% of missiles [that] they have in their stocks.”
- 
  As of today he had “1%”, Zelenskyy said. “From 1% to 5%, I have some months and millions [of] phone calls and anything else. I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s out of the law. But I can’t speak about it.” Ukraine’s air force said on Wednesday it would stop publishing detailed figures on Russian ballistic missile strikes. Real-time warnings would continue unchanged, and the air force would keep providing generalised figures on Russian missile launches.
- 
  Russia’s Orenburg region has introduced fuel rationing after a Ukrainian drone strike on the Orsk refinery this week in the Urals mountain province. “Dear residents of our region, I will be frank: a difficult fuel situation is developing in the region,” said Yevgeny Solntsev, the regional governor. He announced restrictions on gasoline sales, including a ban on filling up containers, limits on sale volume, and sales on odd or even days based on licence plate numbers. Other Russian regions were already under similar restrictions.
- 
  A group of Ukrainian soldiers appealed to their military leadership for help in a video where they told of spending four months on the frontline without rotation and drinking urine during a 12-day stint when drone-dropped water supplies did not arrive. Ukraine’s 121st Brigade command confirmed the social media video’s authenticity and said the brigade “continues to take all necessary measures to properly supply the servicemen” in what it described as “extremely difficult” battlefield conditions.
- 
  Platoon commander Anatoliy Saichuk accused senior officers of lying to soldiers’ families by assuring them the men were fully supplied. “Some of my servicemen were semi-conscious for several days due to lack of water and food,” he added, saying he had eventually decided to abandon the positions when circumstances allowed. The South joint forces group, which commands the area, said the platoon was fighting in a “difficult and dynamic sector of the front”, adding the video showed “an isolated fragment of a complex operational environment”.
- 
  Moldova has agreed to give Ukraine a 50% discount on rail cargo shipments until the end of the year, according to both governments. Ukraine, a major grain exporter by sea, has sought the alternative route because of Russian attacks on its ports and shipping. Russia struck Ukraine’s Izmail port area in the southern Odesa region over Wednesday night, causing damage and fire, local authorities said. Izmail, close to the Romanian border, is home to Ukraine’s largest Danube port, handling grain and other commodities. Russia’s agriculture ministry has also said it is working to redirect its export flows to alternative routes because of Ukrainian attacks in the Black Sea.

In the city of Pereira, crews focused on a collapsed bakery where they believe a street vendor trapped since Monday's earthquake may still be alive beneath the rubble.
Using equipment that detects vibrations, rescuers said they had picked up possible signs of life from Pablo Loaiza, prompting anxious relatives to gather outside the wreckage.
"They tell us it could be him," said 16-year-old Sara Loaiza, his niece. "My heart is about to burst out of my chest," she cried.
Relatives said the trapped man appeared to respond when rescuers asked him to knock twice, then three times from beneath the rubble, drawing applause from those gathered at the scene.
Crews are approaching 72 hours since the quake, a period when survivors are considered most likely to be found alive beneath collapsed buildings.
"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said Wednesday. "That doesn't mean there won't be survivors afterwards, but it is more difficult."
In Cali and Pereira, emergency crews prepared to work through a third night with their bare hands, cranes and sniffer dogs, stopping not to rest, but to listen for signs of life.
"Every half hour we make everyone be quiet to see if we can find people alive," volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez told AFP.
"So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead."
Colombia's newly installed president has declared the disaster an "economic emergency" and announced three days of national mourning.
"We will do what is necessary," President Abelardo de la Espriella said in a statement, vowing to "emerge again as a country and as a society".

Overseeing jury trials – the demanding job of a High Court judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:10 UTC
10:30:10 KST

Overseeing jury trials – the demanding job of a High Court judge
A complex and lengthy criminal trial, often conducted under the glare of public scrutiny, is perhaps the greatest test of a judge’s mettle
Jury trials are a rarity among the world’s legal traditions, but a fundamental bedrock of the common law system.
The jury’s role as the decider of a defendant’s guilt makes them the natural centrepiece of a criminal trial, but an often overlooked part of the process is the role of the trial judge.
The judge does not sit in the back seat while waiting for the jury to deliver its verdict; rather, the judge acts as a conductor of an orchestra, ensuring that each party plays their proper role and that the case can be tried smoothly.
This is no easy task, especially when complex criminal cases can easily last for many weeks, and involve difficult points of fact and law.
That burden is made heavier by the chronic understaffing of the judiciary in Hong Kong. With too few judges for the volume and complexity of work, cases press harder and harder upon sitting judges.
Multiple long trials are often fixed together in close succession, with any free days in the court’s calendar quickly filled up with several shorter hearings, such as sentencing and bail applications, that need to be handled quickly to ensure swift access to justice for defendants.

Stop mourning Hong Kong. It’s evolving, not dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:07 UTC
10:30:07 KST

Hong Kong has changed since the turmoil of 2019-20. Few people would dispute this. The more important question is what kind of city it is becoming.
It is evolving into a more nationally integrated yet still distinctive city. The emerging model seeks to combine market dynamism and international connectivity with clearer alignment to national development. This is not decline. It is a search for a viable identity and role.
Critics such as Stephen Roach 
have argued
 that the Hong Kong of old is finished and that the city has become little more than another large Chinese city. The conclusion rests on a particular assumption: that sharp political and institutional change, especially when it compresses earlier expectations of autonomy, amounts to the end of the place itself. This assumption is selective.
Political systems everywhere have experienced sharp institutional shifts. Brexit permanently altered Britain’s relationship with Europe. In the United States, the Trump administration has 
moved to dissolve
 the United States Agency for International Development, sharply downsize the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and remove or attempt to remove leaders of other independent bodies.
The US Supreme Court has expanded presidential authority to dismiss heads of such agencies without cause. Few observers would conclude from these changes that America is therefore “over”. The same restraint should apply when assessing Hong Kong.
The claim that Beijing 
cut in half
 its promised 50-year high degree of autonomy also needs precision. Article 5 of the Basic Law protects the capitalist system and way of life for 50 years. This high degree of autonomy is an authorisation under China’s Constitution and the Basic Law.

Former US sheriff deputies arrested for using licence plate reader cameras to stalk people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Former US sheriff deputies arrested for using licence plate reader cameras to stalk people
Michael Levenson
ATLANTA, Georgia – Three former Georgia sheriff’s deputies have been arrested on charges that they used Flock cameras to stalk people, the latest cases to raise concerns about potential abuse involving the widely used network of licence-plate readers.
The Bibb County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement that an internal audit conducted with help from Flock revealed that the deputies had used the camera system’s licence plate data for “personal, non-law-enforcement purposes”.
All three were involved in separate incidents tracking people with whom they had a “personal relationship at the time”, the sheriff’s office said.
The deputies were arrested on Aug 10 on charges that included stalking, prohibited use of licence plate data and violating their oaths as public officers. They have since been released on bond.
Two of those charged, Toni Lewis and Coznavian Stubbs, resigned from their positions as patrol deputies during the investigation, and the third, Joseph Callaway, resigned as a K-9 deputy shortly after his arrest, the office said.
The Bibb County sheriff, David Davis, said that a tool that Flock introduced in April, called Audit Assistance, had uncovered the deputies’ misuse of the system. Flock says the tool continuously monitors system activity and flags search patterns that “fall outside an agency’s typical usage”, allowing police departments to identify instances of potential abuse.
“I was saddened by it,” Davis said in an interview on Aug 12.
“Each one of these deputies were good deputies who had been here for several years and were doing a good job. However, they made some poor decisions and crossed the line.”
Stubbs said on Aug 12 that he had been accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his girlfriend but that he had only used the system to look up the licence plate on his own car. The case, he said, had been “blown way out” of proportion.
Callaway declined to comment on the charges. Lewis could not be reached at phone numbers listed under her name, and it was not immediately clear if she had a lawyer.
A national debate has been brewing over Flock cameras, which can be found on roads in every state but Alaska. About 7,000 law enforcement agencies, or 40 per cent of all departments in the United States, have contracts with the company, which is based in Atlanta.
Flock’s cameras, which use artificial intelligence to automatically identify and track vehicles, are connected, creating a vast, searchable network. Investigators have praised the system as a valuable tool that helps them track down stolen cars, find missing or wanted people, and solve crimes
Critics, including local watchdog groups and civil liberties organisations, have said the cameras create an umbrella of surveillance that can be easily misused.
In Milwaukee, an officer was charged with using camera data to track someone he was dating and the person’s ex. In Texas, an officer used the cameras to track a woman across state lines who was suspected of self-administering an abortion. In Georgia, a former Polk County officer was charged with using the camera system “for non-law-enforcement purposes”. Other officers across the country have been disciplined or fired for tracking romantic partners.
In Bibb County, Georgia, which is home to about 158,000 people and includes Macon, Davis announced in June 2023 that his office had been awarded a US$1.6 million (S$2.05 million) state grant to deploy Flock cameras and to set up a Strategic Information Centre to monitor the licence-plate data they collect.
Davis said that at one point more than 220 deputies had access to the cameras, but that number had since been cut to around 160. He said he planned to work with community members to ensure the system is only used for legitimate investigations.
“We will continue to monitor and audit the use of this technology and take appropriate action whenever those standards are violated,” Davis said in a statement. “Protecting the public also means protecting the public’s trust.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Trump signed memo to allow use of cyber tools to target transnational criminal organisations, White House says

Trump signed memo to allow use of cyber tools to target transnational criminal organisations, White House says
- US President Trump signed a memo to allow federal law enforcement and private companies to use cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations targeting Americans.
- The memo creates a framework for private firms to collaborate with government agencies to gather threat information and conduct cyber operations under government control.
- The Department of Homeland Security will oversee a programme for cyber operations that disrupt foreign criminal groups, with companies required to maintain a US$1 million bond.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump signed a memo on Aug 12 that the White House said was aimed at empowering federal law enforcement to use cyber tools against transnational criminal organisations that operate in foreign jurisdictions to attack Americans.
Trump signed the national security presidential memorandum directing his administration to “leverage the capability and innovation of the private sector to help conduct these cyber operations under the direction, control, and authority of the US Government,” the White House said.
The White House, in a fact sheet about the memo, cited ransomware attacks, financial frauds and other crimes run by foreign-based criminal organisations, referred to in the memo as “transnational criminal organizations.”
The memo creates a framework that encourages private sector companies to enter into agreements with other private entities, as well as federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies to gather threat information on transnational criminal organisations and propose cyber operations to address those threats, the White House added.
The memo directs the Department of Homeland Security, through the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Centre, to create a programme “to conduct specific cyber operations that disrupt foreign TCOs” that will be overseen by DHS and the Department of Justice.
Under the supervision of the federal government, participating companies, once vetted, will conduct “cyber surveillance operations” and “cyber effects operations” against specified targets, according to the memo.
“Cyber effects includes the potential manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems, networks, physical or virtual infrastructure controlled by information systems, or information resident thereon,” according to the memo.
Participating companies will have to maintain a bond or escrow of at least US$1 million (S$1.28 million), according to the memo.
The idea of private sector firms participating in cyber operations against criminal and other targets is not new, and has been controversial in the past, for fears of escalation, inadvertent consequences, and inter-agency coordination issues.
DHS and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for additional details about the programme. REUTERS

Large-scale operation shuts down 94 scam call centers across Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said this in a Facebook post.
"Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the National Police are carrying out a large-scale operation to expose such centers across the country. Since the beginning of last week alone, 411 searches have been conducted, 94 fraudulent call centers have been shut down, and 1,794 operator workstations have been dismantled," the statement said.
Investigative actions were carried out in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Zakarpattia, Zaporizhzhia and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, as well as in other parts of the country.
During the searches, law enforcement officers seized more than 3,336 pieces of computer equipment, 1,346 phones, 5,238 SIM cards, 20 crypto wallets and 90 bank cards.
They also seized 22 vehicles, including Porsche Cayenne, Cadillac Escalade, Bentley Bentayga, Dodge Charger, Audi, Lexus, BMW and Mercedes-Benz GLS 450 cars, as well as BMW motorcycles.
More than $2 million, EUR 64,000, cash in Ukrainian hryvnias, a kilogram of investment gold bars, luxury watches by Rolex, Cartier, Rado and Certina, and other jewelry were also found.
"The schemes varied, but the goal was always the same – to steal other people's money. The organizers recruited staff who spoke foreign languages, trained operators using specially prepared scripts and, in many cases, subjected employees to polygraph tests in an attempt to protect their criminal activities from exposure," Kravchenko said.
According to him, some operators posed as consultants offering lucrative investment opportunities. Others lured people onto fake trading platforms. Still others targeted people who had already lost money to scammers and defrauded them again, allegedly offering assistance in "recovering their investments."
"To make [their schemes] more convincing, they used forged documents, posed as lawyers, bank employees and government officials, and employed deepfake technology. In some cases, after people lost their savings, they were persuaded to take out loans, borrow money and sell their property," Kravchenko said.
The proceeds were converted into cryptocurrency, split among electronic wallets and withdrawn through third-party accounts. The profits were invested in luxury real estate, land, premium vehicles and other luxury goods.
The victims included citizens of Ukraine, Israel, Kazakhstan, Lithuania, Latvia and other European Union and Central Asian countries. Preliminary estimates put the total losses at more than $100 million.
"To dismantle these transnational fraud networks, we are cooperating with foreign partners through joint international investigative teams. So far, 26 people have been formally notified that they are under suspicion. Further work will involve analyzing the seized data, identifying all victims, organizers and everyone else involved," Kravchenko said.
Law enforcement officers previously shut down a network of pseudo-investment fraud centers operating in various regions of Ukraine. Their members are suspected of using the guise of cryptocurrency investments to defraud Ukrainian citizens and citizens of other countries of more than UAH 40 million.

Ex-officer accused of plotting New Orleans attack is released after grand jury declines to indict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ex-officer accused of plotting New Orleans attack is released after grand jury declines to indict
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — A former law enforcement officer accused of planning to kill Black people in a mass shooting at a New Orleans festival was quietly released from custody over the summer after a grand jury found there was not enough evidence to charge him with a crime.
A Louisiana grand jury in June declined to indict Christopher Gillum on a state terrorism charge that could have carried up to a 15-year sentence, court records show.
Gillum, who had been held without bond, was released shortly after the grand jury’s decision and is not facing charges in any other jurisdictions, according to his attorney, Dylan Utley. He declined to comment further.
Gillum’s release has not previously been reported.
The 45-year-old ex-police officer, who is from Chapel Hill, North Carolina, had been arrested in Florida in April with hundreds of rounds of ammunition and a handgun while on his way to Louisiana to commit a mass shooting, according to the Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office. The investigation had involved the FBI and authorities across Louisiana, North Carolina and Florida.
Authorities did not name the event Gillum was allegedly targeting, but his arrest came on the eve of the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, which attracts hundreds of thousands of festivalgoers annually.
Gillum, who is white, had “expressed recent threats to harm ‘Black people’ ”, according to authorities. His family had reported him missing in North Carolina and said he had a history of self-harm.
Lester Duhe, a spokesperson for Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, said in a statement that Gillum’s family had taken him “to a treatment facility out of the state” and that he is not facing additional criminal charges.
Duhe said there were “several jurisdictional issues” that complicated the case after Gillum was extradited to Louisiana following his arrest.
“The threat relayed to a family member actually occurred in North Carolina,” Duhe said. “The defendant never entered the State of Louisiana until after his arrest.”
Gillum had been planning to travel to the Florida Keys “during the same period he would have been suspected to travel to Louisiana,” Duhe added.
Gillum was charged under a Louisiana statute for the crime of “terrorizing,” which requires that “a crime of violence is imminent or in progress or that a circumstance dangerous to human life exists or is about to exist.”
Jonathan Guidry, the foreperson for the grand jury, declined to comment on the decision to not indict Gillum.
Katherine Schweit, a former Chicago prosecutor and FBI executive who ran the agency’s active shooter program, said that thwarted acts of mass violence do not always lead to indictments, but prosecutors often seek an array of criminal charges when possible.
“It’s very difficult to convince a jury, or to convince a grand jury, that something might have happened,” Schweit told The Associated Press.
Law enforcement authorities in North Carolina, where Louisiana court records list Gillum as residing, told the AP that they were not aware he had been released from custody.
“If we’ve got an individual that was accused of such an action, we would want to know if in fact he did return to Alamance County,” said Byron Tucker, a spokesperson for the Alamance County Sheriff’s Office in North Carolina.
Nazneen Ahmed, a spokesperson for North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, said there are no plans for the state to pursue charges against Gillum.
The office of the Florida Attorney General did not respond to a request for comment about whether Gillum may face additional criminal charges in its jurisdiction. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in the Eastern District of Louisiana also did not return messages seeking comment.
In a statement, the FBI New Orleans office said the decision whether to charge Gillum rested with prosecutors.
The New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival declined to comment.

The lawmakers focused particular attention on the administration’s stated justification for slowing new sanctions.
Their letter cited Bessent telling Congress in February that the administration wanted to “see where the peace talks go” before resuming some counter-evasion measures against Russia.
Warren and Coons noted that Washington continued imposing sanctions on Iran and Cuba even while conducting talks with those governments.
They also pointed to Rubio’s acknowledgment in May that negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had failed to produce meaningful progress and that no active peace talks were taking place at the time.
The senators therefore asked why Washington had not restored routine sanctions pressure once the diplomatic track stalled.
“If the administration paused regular Russia sanctions because of peace talks, and those talks stalled months ago, why hasn’t the Administration resumed routine and frequent US sanctions to rebuild leverage for a just peace in Ukraine?” the senators asked.
They gave Rubio and Bessent until Aug. 28 to respond.
The dispute comes as Congress considers broader measures intended to raise the economic cost of Russia’s war.
The Senate passed new Russia sanctions legislation earlier this month.

Britain plans safeguards to stop terrorists using AI for bioweapons

- The government seeks coordination with global centres to tackle the worldwide risk, while also monitoring AI firms' partnerships with genome research institutions.
- Warnings from scientists and AI firms highlight AI's potential misuse for dangerous pathogens, prompting Britain to lead in AI safety with new guidance and the AI Security Institute.
AI generated
LONDON – The British government is planning to regulate the use of artificial intelligence in gene synthesis as officials become increasingly concerned that a lack of global guardrails could make it easier to use the technology to create biological weapons.
Ministers are looking at ways to prevent terrorists and other bad actors or careless researchers from using the process to make synthetic DNA, including by introducing new biological weapons legislation, according to people familiar with the matter.
One option is to amend existing laws to introduce gene synthesis screening, one said.
That would require laboratories to establish the legitimacy of their customers and inform authorities of any red flags, like sequences requested which cause concern.
The government is also considering whether and to what extent it should intervene in how closely AI firms partner with academic institutions that specialise in and have large datasets on genome sequencing, they said.
To be sure, there are limits to what British regulation can achieve unless it is implemented in coordination with other major centres of gene synthesis, given the global nature of the threat.
The British proposal comes amid growing warnings in recent months from the technology and science industries, as well as concern among government officials, about the potential for malign groups or individuals to create dangerous pathogens using sequences they’ve instructed AI models to write for them.
“We are monitoring the risks posed by emerging technologies closely, actively weighing at all times what more may be needed,” a government spokesperson said. “We will always take whatever action is necessary to keep the public safe.”
Bloomberg reported in 2024 on the early concerns in the industry that AI could help create weapons of mass destruction, fears that prompted the Biden administration to call on nearly every federal agency to help prevent AI threats.
But US President Donald Trump revoked that executive order when he entered office in 2025.
In June, Trump passed an order calling for tech firms to give the US government voluntary access to its models, but stopped short of requiring developers to seek explicit approval.
Similarly, Britain’s approach is so far limited to providing guidance to firms on how to mitigate risks of accidental or deliberate misuse, which was published in 2024.
The two work closely together on AI, though the fractured nature of international regulation complicates nations’ abilities to control AI’s global risks.
Scientists and AI firms like Anthropic have ramped up warnings recently.
Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei in June said AI models should undergo mandatory testing by third parties to assess the risk they pose, including enabling biological weapons.
The New York Times in April reported that unnamed AI bots themselves told scientists how to make biological weapons, including by instructing how to buy raw genetic material, turn it into deadly weapons and deploy them in public spaces, some even brainstorming ways to evade detection.
Last week, the newspaper reported scientists used AI to create new kinds of viruses.
That could unlock huge potential for medical advancements but also raises biosecurity risks due to accidental or deliberate misuse.
Britain has taken a more lax approach to AI regulation than the European Union, but it is leading the way on tech safety, having established its AI Security Institute in 2023 to evaluate the safety of cutting-edge models.
Last week, it published findings that revealed AI models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic carried out “unsanctioned” actions, including hacking a website and attempting to inject harmful code into software during safety testing.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has taken a more hawkish approach to AI in his first weeks in office, particularly in his warnings about the impact on jobs and young people.
He chose to disband the government’s technology department, which was met with criticism from the industry, though he did choose to promote his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, to the Cabinet.
“Gene synthesis is unlocking enormous benefits across medicine, food and clean energy, but ensuring the safety and security of our country will always be of paramount importance,” the British government spokesperson said.
“The UK was the second country in the world to publish guidance on screening who should be able to buy synthetic DNA, and the DNA sequence they are ordering - but we are not standing still.” BLOOMBERG

Colombia has declared three days of mourning to honour the victims of Monday's devastating 7.4-magnitude earthquake, as the death toll rose to 265, with at least 3,494 people injured and 496 remaining missing.
President Abelardo De La Espriella announced that national flags will fly at half-mast on all public buildings and diplomatic missions.
The quake, which occurred at 07:34 local time (12:34 GMT) Monday near San Jose del Palmar, Choco, at a depth of 107 kilometres, is the deadliest to strike Colombia this century.
Emergency crews worked around the clock in major cities such as Pereira and Cali, using heavy machinery, search dogs, and human chains.
"Our efforts are focused on the disappeared," De La Espriella said.
Damage scale and aid controversy

UNGRD director David Santiago Tamayo announced that the government would prioritise technical rescue deployments from four partner nations: the US, Israel, Ecuador, and El Salvador, citing strict operational criteria.
The policy drew criticism from former President Gustavo Petro, who posted on X: "It is a mistake to apply an ideological filter to international aid.
Officials clarified that Colombia has not formally excluded aid from any nation.
Despite the debate, Mexico's civilian volunteer group Brigada Internacional de Rescate Topos Azteca arrived in Cali on Wednesday to join search efforts.
Impact was severe in rural areas near the epicentre.
In El Cairo, Valle del Cauca, local emergency posts reported that 80 percent of urban infrastructure sustained damage, with roughly 10 percent of local buildings collapsing completely.

HUNTSVILLE, Alabama – The Pentagon is moving to speed up the deployment of high-powered lasers and other counter-drone systems around key US facilities, amid increased threats from unmanned aircraft.
The Defence Department will sign an agreement within days with the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Aviation Administration to use new technologies to bring down unmanned aircraft systems at airports and other installations in the US, David Bagnati, who leads a Pentagon taskforce on the issue, said on Aug 12.

California couple’s surrogate gives birth in Texas after judge orders life-saving care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:53:02 UTC
09:53:02 KST

California couple’s surrogate gives birth in Texas after judge orders life-saving care
DALLAS (AP) — A California couple’s surrogate who went to Texas in an escalating dispute over treating a congenital heart condition gave birth Wednesday, a day after a judge in Dallas ordered life-sustaining care for the newborn.
The child was receiving stabilizing care and scheduled to undergo surgery at a Texas hospital, according to an attorney for McKenna West, the surrogate mother whose case has drawn widening national support from right-to-life groups and Republican officials.
West was carrying the child for a California couple she has accused of wanting to end the pregnancy after the fetus was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a life-threatening heart condition.
A judge on Tuesday ordered the child to receive life-sustaining treatment after Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in support of the surrogate.
“She has taken on great personal risk to herself,” said Lincoln Davis Wilson, an attorney for West.
The couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, have denied in court filings that they intended to refuse surgery once the child was born. Lee Budner, an attorney for the couple, did not immediately return emails and phone messages seeking comment Wednesday.
In a statement to The Texas Tribune, Budner said the baby was receiving medical care and accused West and Paxton of turning a family tragedy into “political theater.”
“Our clients’ only focus at this time is ensuring that their baby receives the medical care that he vitally needs and that they, as his parents, are able to spend every precious moment they can with him,” Budner said.
Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is a condition where the left side of the heart prevents normal blood flow. If untreated, the condition causes severe symptoms such as breathing problems, weak pulse and ashen or bluish skin.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the condition must be treated with multiple surgeries that are complex and challenging. About 925 babies in the U.S. are born with HLHS each year, according to the CDC.
Without treatment, children affected by the heart defect can die within days or weeks. Surgical repairs are not necessarily cures, and additional surgeries or heart transplants may be needed, according to the CDC.
West’s lawyers have alleged the couple spent weeks pressuring West to seek an abortion after learning of the diagnosis at 20 weeks.
In court documents, the couple argues that West broke a surrogacy contract and that a California court determined she has no rights to legal or physical custody of the child.
They also dispute they intended to refuse surgery, saying that medical professionals had told them it was not possible to determine whether the baby would be a candidate for open-heart surgery.
“That is not and has never been our position,” Ahmed wrote in court documents filed in Texas. “Since Ms. West moved to Texas, we have consistently sought the opportunity to consult with physicians caring for our child to make informed medical decisions for him as his parents.”
West was not able to see or hold the child because of a temporary restraining order that was entered by the couple, according to Wilson.
University of Texas School of Law professor Rachel Rebouché, who specializes in reproductive law, said disputes like this one are rare.
Contracts usually include language where parents and surrogates agree on issues of medical care and when or how to end a pregnancy, but she said “those are aspirational, not enforceable in court.”
Texas law gives parents the rights to make decisions about medical care, but they don’t have the right to deny care in a manner that amounts to medical abuse or neglect, Rebouché said. She said Texas courts have extensive powers to issues orders in the best interest of the child, Rebouché said.
“There is case law in Texas that supports intervention if there is the possibility of denying life-saving care, once born, for a child in medical need,” she said. ___
Wilder and Vertuno reported from Austin, Texas.

Trading platforms offer cash vouchers for 'high-risk' investments, watchdog says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:44:10 UTC
09:44:10 KST

A review by corporate watchdog ASIC finds retail investors are being offered incentives to engage in "high-risk" investments on online platforms.
Clients have been offered fee-free or discounted trading, or allowed to attempt sign-up questionnaires an "unlimited" amount of times.
What's next?
ASIC is considering taking further action against some entities in relation to matters raised by the review.
Retail investors are allegedly being offered cash vouchers and airline reward points as encouragement to use online platforms for their financial trade, a corporate watchdog has found.
Nine online trading platforms were reviewed by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), including Moomoo, Sharesies and Webull.
Their review found some providers were offering fee-free or discounted trading and other incentives to engage in "high-risk" investments.
ASIC did not attribute individual findings to any one company and said not every company had committed every infraction.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said trading platforms were increasingly offering complex financial instruments to users who did not fully understand them.
"These are products where it can be hard to understand, but unfortunately easy to lose money, and easy to lose [it] quickly," she said.
"Take a short-dated exchange trading option. You can put a little bit of money in there, a small amount of money in a small window of time.
"Yes, you can potentially make a lot, but you can really lose a lot."
"These are not just high complexity, but of course high-risk products."
Practices improved since review
In some entities, the review found:
Deficiencies in target market determinations, including insufficient details on how products met the likely objectives, situations and needs of clients.
Onboarding shortcomings, including limited tailoring of questions and repeated/unlimited attempts to pass onboarding questionnaires.
Unclear client disclosure which failed to explain the risks and costs associated with fractional trading.
Since the review, two of the companies have stopped onboarding new clients while remediation is underway, and five more have improved compliance practices.
One has exited the Australian market entirely.
ASIC said it was considering further regulatory and enforcement action in relation to matters identified in the review.
Monash University's Tamara Wilkinson, who specialises in corporate law and regulation, said the watchdog could crack down on companies by tightening rules.
And it could also look to retail investors to prove their competency before investing, which is done in the United Kingdom.
"What it seems like is happening here with these risky financial products is that there is a bit of a gap in the regulation and the protection of retail investors," Dr Wilkinson said.
"Increasing the regulatory protections in this area would bring it more in line with the rest of Australia's regulatory regime."
Ms Constant urged investors to be hypercritical of the agreements they entered into.
"Don't invest simply because it's easy to invest and access, or because there's an inducement to invest in airline points," she said
"Invest because it's a good investment that you understand, and you know it to be a good investment because you understand it."

What the Cockroach movement revealed about Modi's India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:38:03 UTC
09:38:03 KST

Breadcrumb
What the Cockroach movement revealed about Modi's India
The Chief Justice of India likely never imagined that a fleeting, derogatory remark comparing frustrated young people to "cockroaches" would give birth to one of the country's largest youth-led protest movements in recent years.
In May 2026, activists reclaimed the slur by launching the satirical Cockroach Janata Party (CJP). Founded by Abhijeet Dipke, who serves as its president, the movement emerged amid widespread anger over the cancellation of India's national medical entrance examination, known as the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET). Medical student aspirants studied for long periods, took the notoriously tough exam, only to be forced to resit it following news that the questions had been leaked.
Multiple students committed suicide following all the distress that they had endured.
Relying extensively on generative AI to produce its public-facing campaign material, the movement rapidly gained traction online. By the time of writing, CJP's Instagram page amassed over 26 million followers, surpassing even the BJP's official Instagram account, which has over 9 million followers.
Following the mass mobilisations that provided the movement with leverage, the CJP leadership put forward a list of principal demands: the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, and the equivalent of around $105,000 (One crore Indian Rupees) in compensation for the families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.
But the anger that brought people to the streets was wider than these demands. It reflected growing unemployment, an increasingly commercialised education system serving the interests of the ruling class, and a broader frustration with the shrinking space for dissent under Modi's government. For many, the CJP became a vehicle through which these anxieties could converge.
Indeed, in many ways the CJP became a telling story less about the protests themselves than about the political homelessness of sections of India's liberal middle class. After 12 years of BJP rule, institutional collapse and a weakened opposition, many were desperately looking for something that felt like politics again.
The movement became a container for that hope. But hope can also become a political blind spot, making us less willing to ask whether a movement's demands can transform the structures it seeks to challenge.
However, the question was never simply whether the CJP succeeded. It was what success should look like under the Modi regime’s authoritarianism. And the CJP made its biggest mistake the moment it believed a fascist state could be trusted.
On 20 July, while students in the heart of India's capital were being met with tear gas, electric batons, pellet guns, lathi charges and mass detentions, the CJP leadership was negotiating on their behalf inside the residence of J.P. Nadda, the Union Minister for Health and Family Welfare, alongside Jitendra Singh, the Minister of State in the Prime Minister's Office.
Five days later, the same leaders appeared beside those ministers at a joint press conference to announce that the protests would be called off with immediate effect.
Almost overnight, the protest site at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, which had drawn thousands of students and supporters for over a month, was dismantled.
Meanwhile, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, only to be replaced by Pralhad Joshi, a five-time Member of Parliament and one of Modi's longest-serving cabinet ministers. Joshi had previously defended the release of the men convicted of the gang rape of Bilkis Bano during the 2002 anti-Muslim violence in Gujarat. The change therefore offered a symbolic concession without altering the political architecture surrounding the crisis.
Additionally, the very institution that was responsible for the NEET exam issues remained structurally intact, as did the broader architecture that produced it.
For whom was democracy restored?
The most revealing aspect of the CJP movement was also the language that surrounded it. On the day of the 20 July negotiations, arguably the movement's defining moment, the CJP leadership declared that "democracy had died" after the brutal police crackdown on students. Then just five days later, following negotiations with the government, Chief Spokesperson Saurav Das declared that "democracy has been restored."
But what do such declarations mean when the institutions that keep producing the crisis remain intact?
Even the resignation was quickly reframed by the BJP, with Dharmendra Pradhan presenting himself as a martyr who had stepped down to prevent the exploitation of "anti-national elements". This allowed the government to absorb the least possible accountability while conceding the greatest symbolic victory.
Ultimately, the problem that developed within the protest movement was not simply the result of poor negotiation; it was also the result of a single-issue-based political strategy.
The CJP's greatest missed opportunity came from the scale of the moment itself. For perhaps the first time in years, a large and politically diverse group of young people had mobilised against the government's handling of education and were confronting the coercive power of the state.
That created an opportunity to connect their demands to struggles that had long existed outside their immediate political world: farmers fighting for their livelihoods, workers confronting precarity, communities resisting displacement, people fighting against the suppression of dissent, and movements confronting rising unemployment, poverty and the climate crisis.
The question was not whether the CJP could take up every struggle at once, but whether it could recognise that these struggles were connected and use its unprecedented visibility to build something larger.
In contrast to some within the protest movement, politics has never been optional for large sections of Indian society. Adivasi communities resisting land acquisition, Muslim communities confronting the violence of the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), Kashmiris living under militarisation, workers fighting precarity, and political prisoners incarcerated for dissent have long experienced the violence of the state as a daily reality.
The CJP resonated most deeply with an urban liberal constituency for whom that inevitability arrived much later. As India's education system entered crisis, many encountered the coercive power of the state in ways they had not before, including through violence. But recognising this as a beginning risks obscuring the much longer histories of resistance that made this moment legible in the first place.
The contrast was visible throughout the weeks of protest. While the CJP occupied the national imagination, activist Amit Bhatnagar and Adivasi communities were also on an indefinite hunger strike against the Ken-Betwa river-linking project, which threatens widespread displacement and ecological destruction.
Their protest site was dismantled by police before dawn with little national attention or public outcry.
This is not an argument against the protesters, nor is it a competition over suffering. Clearly, some struggles become nationally legible only when they enter the social and emotional universe of those with greater cultural visibility, while others continue for years at the margins of public attention.
For many, the CJP was the beginning of political awakening. For others, it was another chapter in a struggle that had never paused.
How the CJP will be remembered
The CJP had reached a rare moment of political power. Thousands of young people had mobilised, the protests had captured national attention, and the state had been forced to negotiate. This should have led to a refusal to allow the government to define the limits of what the movement could demand.
Instead, the protests were called off at the government's behest, and an unusual opening for broader political challenge came to an end.
The CJP may eventually be remembered not only for what it achieved, but for what it revealed. It reminded us that people are still willing to organise, still willing to occupy the streets, still willing to risk police violence for a different future. But it also revealed how desperately India's opposition has come to mistake moments for movements, symbolism for strategy and hope for organisation.
The RSS did not spend a century building Hindutva through isolated protests or reactionary demands; it patiently established institutions, ideology and cadre. The opposition cannot afford to respond only when another crisis erupts, or another movement captures public imagination. It must do the slower, less glamorous work of building an alternative political imagination, one rooted in ideology, organisation and solidarity.
Hope may bring people to the streets. But organisation determines what it leaves behind.
Shrishti Khanna is a political activist, writer and former mental health worker based in Mumbai, India. Having worked in government psychiatric wards and as a teacher, her work focuses on India-Israel relations, authoritarianism, digital surveillance, Palestine and Chronic Illness/disability. Her activism and writing have been featured in publications including Middle East Eye, Maktoob Media, Article 14 and Free Speech Collective, among others.

Zambia heads to polls with President Hichilema expected to win second term
Zambians vote Thursday in a general election widely expected to give President Hakainde Hichilema a second term, as his economic record faces a test from voters frustrated by the cost of living and opposition parties seek to capitalise on discontent despite deep divisions.
Zambia goes to the polls on Thursday in a general election widely expected to give President Hakainde Hichilema a second term, although frustration over the cost of living may dent his support.
Hichilema has led the southern African copper producer since 2021 and is running on his economic record, having steered Zambia through a debt restructuring and economic rebound since it defaulted on its sovereign debt in 2020.
His main challenger is Brian Mundubile, an experienced parliamentarian but first-time presidential candidate who is leading an opposition alliance backed by supporters of Hichilema's predecessor, the late former president Edgar Lungu.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Opposition weakened by divisions
The presidential, parliamentary and local government elections will be held simultaneously. A presidential candidate must receive more than 50 percent of votes cast in order to win in the first round, or faces a run-off between the top two contenders.
"I am tempted to think the ruling party will carry the day despite the huge crowds we are seeing at the rallies for (Mundubile)," said historian and analyst Euston Chiputa.
"One of the serious weaknesses in the opposition camp is that it is splintered," he said, with parliamentary and local government candidates from Mundubile's party and those from his running-mate's party competing against each other in some places.
Investors said they widely expect Hichilema to win, with the bigger question being whether he can turn the post-default macroeconomic turnaround into job-creating growth if given a second term.
Many Zambians say that although economic indicators have improved and inflation has fallen to its lowest level in years, they have yet to feel the benefits in their daily lives.
Read moreFive things to know about Zambia as it goes to the polls
Some concerns over fairness of vote
The lead-up to the vote has been marred by some allegations of political repression in the country of 22 million people, although the government denies this.
Zambia is rated as "partly free" by US non-profit group Freedom House, which says that although there are regular multi-party elections, opposition parties face "onerous legal and practical obstacles to fair competition".
"The competition is still there because the opposition has support in Lusaka and Copperbelt Province, which have large numbers of registered voters," said Lee Habasonda, a political science lecturer at the University of Zambia.
"If the opposition had rallied behind one candidate earlier, this would have been one of the toughest elections for the ruling party," he said.
Polls are open from 6am (0400 GMT) to 6pm and results are scheduled for Monday, according to the Electoral Commission. If the presidential vote goes to a second round, the run-off must be held within 37 days of the first poll.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Watchdog Presses DOD to Fix Decaying Infrastructure at Pacific Air Bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:32:39 UTC
09:32:39 KST

The Pentagon’s watchdog has identified serious concerns over corrosion, mold, and the structural decline of “critical infrastructure” at Air Force bases and other military installations in the Pacific, according to a recent report.
The Department of Defense Inspector General was working on a project evaluating bases under U.S. Pacific Command for how shielding against electromagnetic pulses when it came across deeper infrastructure concerns, according to the Aug. 6 report.
Inspectors said the issues affected both “mission‑critical systems” and “other critical infrastructure … and housing infrastructure” that support troops to complete their missions. They were looking at 11 bases across the region, but most of the report focused on installations in Japan—for the Air Force, that included Kadena Air Base and Yokota Air Base.
So far, the IG is characterizing the issues as “unresolved” until it receives documentation from the Pentagon, U.S. Pacific Command, and U.S. Forces Japan that they identified the “root causes” for the deficiencies and identified the funding to correct the problems, the report states.
Some of the issues identified in the report are redacted, as are many responses from the various military services, commands, and organizations that run these installations. But the public report does detail signs of decay and poor maintenance such as “visible corrosion, visible mold, … visible cracks on the building exterior and interior, visible concrete spalling, and exposed rebar,” lead‑based paint, and asbestos in infrastructure used for operational and communications as well as maintenance and storage.
There were also problems with the water infrastructure at both air bases, including “reduced water capacity, increased waterline breaks and water disruption and pipeline infrastructure beyond service life,” the report states
Military housing is also in ill-repair at Kadena. A ceiling collapse affected 139 homes in one development, and hundreds of homes showed signs of mold growth and concrete spalling, the report states, adding that maintenance issues have forced dozens of residents to relocate.
In 2024, Dr. Ravi Chaudhary, the assistant secretary of the Air Force for energy, installations, and environment at the time, launched an Installation Infrastructure Action Plan aimed at reversing years of disrepair across Air Force and Space Force bases.
At the time, the action plan stated that “70 percent of utility systems at Pacific Air Forces locations are severely degraded due to the highly corrosive environment.”
Defense Department officials stationed at the 1970s-era bases the IG visited in Japan reiterated that point, saying their locations are “subject to recurring environmental conditions such as typhoons, earthquakes, and tsunamis that further degrade the infrastructure,” according to the report. DOD officials added that “in some cases, falling debris—ranging from small fragments to large slabs—poses an ongoing risk to personnel safety.”
Personnel shortages and the cost of repairs and upkeep are also issues, the officials said.
The IG recommended that the responsible commanders submit a “prioritized list of infrastructure repair or replacement projects based on risk to critical missions.”
Lt. Gen. Laura Lenderman, deputy commander of Pacific Air Forces, submitted a response, but it was redacted in the public version of the report. A PACAF spokesperson could not provide a comment by press time.
The IG’s response to Lenderman’s comments does say that she “provided examples of prioritized projects related to infrastructure,” but the watchdog says its recommendation will remain open until “we receive documentation verifying Pacific Air Forces’ internal prioritization of ongoing efforts” list of the installations in the region.
According to Master Sgt. Kristopher Dunn, superintendent for wing plans at the 374th Civil Engineering Squadron at Yokota Air Base, “with more money and people we could get after the issues,” according to the report.
A second recommendation in the report called on the Air Force and other services to work with the Pentagon, PACOM, and U.S Forces Japan to “conduct a root cause analysis including identifying funding sources and correct infrastructure deficiencies identified” in the report.
In response, Mark Sinder, deputy assistant secretary for the Defense Department’s office of infrastructure, modernization and resilience, said the Air Force and other services will “take the lead” to address all infrastructure deficiencies and “develop and execute a comprehensive plan to program, budget for, and execute the necessary repairs and replacements” and establish a detailed timeline for correcting all deficiencies listed in the report.
Pacific Command also agreed with the IG’s recommendation, stating it will “support U.S. military services in correcting the issues identified in this report, to include the service’s efforts to develop and implement a corrective action plan based on the provided recommendations,” according to the report.
But Sinder’s and PACOM’s responses did not satisfy the IG. After discussions with the Pentagon’s office of energy, installations, and environment, “we redirected the recommendation to the military services” to work in coordination with Pacific Command and U.S. Forces Japan, the report states.
“Therefore, we consider Recommendation 2 unresolved,” the IG states in the report. “We request that within 30 days the appropriate office provide official management comments on the final report.”

SSU foils spy ring coordinating enemy attacks on Defense Forces in three regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:32:00 UTC
09:32:00 KST

SSU foils spy ring coordinating enemy attacks on Defense Forces in three regions
According to Ukrinform, the SSU reported this.
Following a multi-stage special operation, SSU officers simultaneously detained four enemy informants in the eastern and central regions of Ukraine.
The investigation revealed that the suspects operated independently of one another but had a common handler based in Russia.
The enemy’s priority targets were logistics depots containing weapons and ammunition for the Defense Forces, as well as air defense combat positions.
In addition, the agents collected data on locations with the highest concentrations of personnel and military equipment of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
It was established that the perpetrators came to the attention of Russian intelligence when they posted anti-Ukrainian comments in Telegram channel chat rooms.
One of the network’s members turned out to be a former employee of a machine-building plant in Kramatorsk, who was gathering geolocation data on operational airfields and fortifications in the region.
Two other agents passed on the coordinates of military facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region to the Russians. Among them were an employee of a municipal utility company from Kamianske and a deserter from Pavlohrad.
Also, in the Kirovohrad region, an unemployed man from Znamianka was detained; acting on orders from the FSB, he had been patrolling the city and recording geolocations that he believed were being used by the Defense Forces.
To maintain secrecy, the suspects transmitted intelligence data to a Russian intelligence officer via an anonymous chat in a messaging app and deleted the chat history after each communication session.
SSU officers uncovered the subversive activities of the enemy agents in advance, documented their crimes, and detained all four participants.
During searches, mobile phones containing evidence of their work for the FSB were seized from the detainees.
SSU investigators notified the suspects that they are suspected of violating Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (treason committed under martial law).
The suspects are currently in custody. They face life imprisonment with confiscation of property.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Security Service of Ukraine detained a Russian agent in Kropyvnytskyi who was preparing new missile and drone attacks on facilities of Ukraine’s fuel and energy complex.

In FocusWhat comes next for Hong Kong as a global financial hub?
Hong Kong needs more yuan products, commodity trading infrastructure and fintech innovation, market participants say
With a symbolic press of a button, top officials and securities regulators from Hong Kong and mainland China earlier this month marked a historic moment for the city’s financial markets.
The August 3 launch of the first offshore Chinese government yuan-denominated bond futures contract, along with related cross-border policies, underscored what Beijing called a critical upgrade of Hong Kong’s status as the country’s largest offshore yuan trade-settlement market.
A key theme is on reimagining the economy, finance and trade and in this, analysts say, Hong Kong will have to do much more to raise its status as an international financial centre.
Market participants and policy experts, meanwhile, have called for expanded yuan products, commodity trading infrastructure, a diversified talent pool and fintech innovation to reinforce Hong Kong’s capacity to channel global capital into the country while mitigating geopolitical and currency risks.

US Pacific bases severely degraded, Pentagon inspector warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
00:28:00 UTC
09:28:00 KST

US Pacific bases severely degraded, Pentagon inspector-general warns
- US military bases in the Pacific are severely degraded, with corrosion, mold, asbestos, and structural damage affecting key facilities and housing for troops and families.
- The problems stem from aging buildings dating back to the 1970s, environmental challenges, and shortages in personnel and funding, impacting mission readiness.
- Pentagon officials acknowledge the issues and plan to address infrastructure deficiencies with detailed timelines, involving multiple military departments and stakeholders.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US military facilities across the Pacific are in a worrying state of decay, the Pentagon inspector-general warned, raising concerns about bases that are critical to deterring China.
Corrosion and holes in buildings, falling ceilings and the presence of mould and asbestos were among the problems identified through inspections of 11 US facilities across the region and relayed to a dozen senior Defence Department officials in an emergency management advisory in August.
The issues have affected infrastructure essential to US forces’ preparedness as well as troop and family facilities, according to an Aug 6 notice by Randolph Stone, assistant inspector-general for evaluations.
Such “management advisories” are issued during an ongoing audit to flag issues to senior management that need immediate attention.
Much of the advisory is heavily redacted as “Controlled Unclassified Information”.
The Pentagon declined on Aug 12 to provide any additional comments on issues raised in the advisory beyond those already offered to the inspector-general.
The advisory factored in comments received from various Pentagon offices, including the deputy assistant secretary for infrastructure modernisation, the commander of the US Pacific Command, the assistant Army secretary for installations, the deputy assistant Navy secretary for installations and Pacific Air Forces deputy commander.
“We considered management’s comments on the draft advisory,” it said.
Mark Sinder, the deputy assistant for infrastructure modernisation, said in the report that “military departments, in coordination with the identified stakeholders, will take the lead in addressing the infrastructure deficiencies identified” and that a “detailed timeline for correcting all deficiencies will be established”.
In the advisory, the inspector-general “identified concerns related to other critical infrastructure, such as water and housing infrastructure, supporting missions” across the US Pacific Command.
Although the water and housing infrastructure is not directly related to “mission critical” combat capabilities, “it is critical to support” service members in the region, the inspector-general said.
Unnamed Pentagon officials explained the “severe degradation” by noting that “many of the buildings date back to the 1970s” and citing environmental conditions such as earthquakes and tsunamis, as well as personnel and funding shortages, according to the report.
Kadena Air Base, for example, is a key hub for US air power in the Pacific, housing US$836 million (S$1.07 billion) worth of munitions.
A photo of one of its hangars, attached to the report, shows a wall with several holes in it, exposing stored items to the outdoors.
Photos of another base facility – an aircraft hangar – show a dilapidated building, rusted and corroded through.
At Kadena, which hosts about 20,000 Americans, at least 243 homes on the base had to be vacated because of spalling – when the surface of a structure becomes chipped or peels – according to the document.
Separately, 139 houses were “affected by ceiling collapse.”
These problems are not unique to Kadena. Yokota Air Base and Marine Base Camp Courtney are facing similar challenges.
For all three US bases in Japan, the report also cited concerns about operations and communications infrastructure, including mould, fire damage, building cracks, water intrusion, the presence of lead and asbestos in construction materials.
The inspection also identified problems with maintenance and storage infrastructure at the Kadena and Yokota airbases to the extent that some facilities did not meet facility requirements.
Pentagon watchdogs have identified issues with US military facilities before, warning of substandard conditions and neglect that could impact operations.
In late 2025, an inspector-general report pointed to health and safety concerns with housing for US Army troops posted along the southern border as part of the Trump administration’s ramped-up immigration enforcement.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in 2025 created a task force to identify and improve substandard housing. BLOOMBERG

Jewish businessmen Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner are purchasing the NBA’s storied Los Angeles Lakers, ESPN reported Wednesday, in a stunning, record-setting $12.5 billion deal.
The sale comes barely a year after the team’s controlling stake was sold for $10 billion to Mark Walter, the billionaire CEO of Guggenheim Partners who also owns MLB’s Los Angeles Dodgers, the WNBA’s LA Sparks, Premier League club Chelsea, the Professional Women’s Hockey League, and Cadillac’s Formula 1 team.
Walter, who is not Jewish, is reportedly seeking cash to pay down loans in response to a Department of Justice investigation.
